# Spike: EF Core Tenant Isolation (Finbuckle.MultiTenant Compared With a Custom Implementation)

## Question

How should eShop enforce per-tenant data isolation in a shared database per service, given
the decision to use EF Core global query filters only (no PostgreSQL row-level security)?

## Why

Query filters are the only line of defence, so the mechanism must be hard to get wrong. It
must:

- apply the filter to every `ITenantOwned` entity automatically;
- set `TenantId` on save;
- block changes to `TenantId`;
- make skipping the filter explicit and easy to audit.

## Investigate

- **Finbuckle.MultiTenant** (`MultiTenantDbContext`, `IsMultiTenant()`, tenant stores and
  resolution strategies) compared with a small custom implementation (an `ITenantOwned`
  convention, a `SaveChangesInterceptor`, and a model-building convention that adds
  `HasQueryFilter`). Compare:
  - fit with Aspire and `AddNpgsqlDbContext`;
  - DbContext pooling;
  - the compiled model;
  - migrations;
  - testability.
- **Query filters in EF Core 10:** named filters, whether several filters on one entity
  combine, and how `IgnoreQueryFilters` behaves.
- **DbContext pooling:** how the tenant reaches a pooled context safely (`ITenantContext`
  captured per request, not per context instance).
- **Raw SQL and Dapper paths** in the existing services (for example Ordering queries) that
  skip the filters, and how to cover them.
- **Architecture tests** (NetArchTest or Roslyn analyzers) that fail when:
  - an entity with a `TenantId` property doesn't implement `ITenantOwned`;
  - `IgnoreQueryFilters()` is used outside the allow-listed namespace.
- **Backfill migration pattern** for existing tables (AdventureWorks GUID default, then
  non-null, then indexes).

## Deliverable

A recommendation with a small proof of concept on one DbContext, the chosen library or custom
design, and the architecture-test approach. Feeds TENANT-1 and TENANT-5.
<!-- board-ticket:source:end -->

items.title: LiteLLM multi-tenant: shared proxy with per-tenant virtual keys
items.body:
## Status: Likely Obsolete

With the move to Spawn as a custom OpenCode provider (#39), LiteLLM may no longer be needed.

### Why LiteLLM existed
- Proxy all AI calls through a central gateway
- Per-tenant virtual keys and rate limits
- Usage tracking for billing
- Centralized API key management

### Why it's probably unnecessary now
- **OpenCode handles model routing natively** — providers are a first-class concept
- **Spawn IS the provider** — we meter at our API endpoint, not via a proxy
- **Free models (Copilot) don't need metering** — no API cost to track
- **BYOK users manage their own keys** — not our concern

### If we still need metering
The Spawn provider endpoint (#39) can track usage directly without a separate LiteLLM layer. Much simpler.

## Decision
Close this issue if we confirm LiteLLM is removed. Keep open only if there's a specific use case that requires a proxy layer.

## Related
- #39 (Spawn as provider — replaces LiteLLM's role)
- #31 (billing rethink)

items.title: Feature 004: Cloud Training Pipeline
items.body:
## Summary

Add a cloud-oriented training entrypoint to sigil-ml that runs as a K8s CronJob. Reads synced event data from Postgres, trains per-user models, optionally trains aggregate models from pooled opted-in data, and saves weights to S3. Replaces the local background training scheduler in cloud deployments.

## Motivation

Cloud-deployed sigil-ml needs a way to retrain models periodically without the local training scheduler. A CronJob-based training pipeline enables per-tenant model updates, aggregate model training for team tiers, and operational observability.

## Work Packages

- [ ] WP01: Cloud Training Entrypoint & CLI (P0)
- [ ] WP02: Per-Tenant Training Logic (P0)
- [ ] WP03: Batch Training & Tenant Discovery (P1)
- [ ] WP04: Concurrent Training Lock (P1)
- [ ] WP05: Aggregate Model Training (P2)
- [ ] WP06: Training Observability & Structured Output (P2)

## Spec & Plan

- Spec: `kitty-specs/004-cloud-training-pipeline/spec.md`
- Plan: `kitty-specs/004-cloud-training-pipeline/plan.md`
- Tasks: `kitty-specs/004-cloud-training-pipeline/tasks.md`

## Dependencies

Depends on Feature 002 (Storage Abstraction) and Feature 003 (Model Storage Abstraction).

items.title: Phase 60.5: InferenceOrchestrator — End-to-End Model Serving Pipeline
items.body:
# Phase 60.5 — InferenceOrchestrator

## Overview

The InferenceOrchestrator unifies all Phase 60 components into a production-ready model serving system. It manages the complete inference lifecycle from request reception to response delivery, with auto-scaling, model parallelism routing, and multi-model serving capabilities.

## Key Features

### End-to-End Serving Pipeline
- Request preprocessing (tokenization, prompt formatting)
- Inference execution with optimized attention and caching
- Response postprocessing (detokenization, streaming)
- Observability: metrics, tracing, logging at each stage

### Auto-Scaling
- Horizontal scaling based on queue depth and latency
- Vertical scaling: dynamic batch size adjustment
- Scale-to-zero for cost optimization
- Predictive scaling based on traffic patterns (time-of-day, events)

### Model Parallelism Routing
- Tensor parallelism across GPUs for large models
- Pipeline parallelism with micro-batch scheduling
- Expert parallelism for MoE models
- Automatic parallelism strategy selection based on model and hardware

### Latency/Throughput Optimization
- Adaptive configuration tuning (batch size, draft length, cache size)
- A/B testing framework for serving configurations
- Profiling-guided optimization recommendations
- Cost-per-token tracking and optimization

### Multi-Model Serving
- Shared GPU memory pool across models (LoRA multi-tenant)
- Model routing based on request characteristics
- Warm model pool with LRU eviction
- Zero-downtime model updates and rollbacks

## Technical Specification

```typescript
interface ServingConfig {
  models: ModelDeployment[];
  scaling: ScalingPolicy;
  routing: RoutingPolicy;
  monitoring: MonitoringConfig;
  kvCache: KVCacheConfig;
  attention: AttentionConfig;
  speculative: SpeculativeConfig;
  scheduler: SchedulerConfig;
}

interface InferenceOrchestrator {
  deploy(model: ModelConfig, resources: ResourceSpec): DeploymentHandle;
  infer(request: InferenceRequest): AsyncIterator<Token>;
  scale(deployment: string, policy: ScalingPolicy): void;
  getMetrics(): ServingMetrics;
  updateModel(deployment: string, newModel: ModelConfig): void;
  optimize(deployment: string): OptimizationReport;
}
```

## Component Integration

```
Client Request
    │
    ▼
InferenceOrchestrator
    ├── Request Router (model selection, priority assignment)
    ├── BatchScheduler (60.4) — continuous batching, SLA-aware
    │   ├── Prefill Stage
    │   │   ├── AttentionOptimizer (60.3) — FlashAttention
    │   │   └── KVCacheManager (60.1) — block allocation
    │   └── Decode Stage
    │       ├── SpeculativeDecoder (60.2) — draft + verify
    │       ├── AttentionOptimizer (60.3) — FlashDecoding
    │       └── KVCacheManager (60.1) — incremental append
    ├── Auto-Scaler (horizontal + vertical)
    └── Metrics Collector (Prometheus/OpenTelemetry)
```

## Dependencies
- Phase 60.1 (KVCacheManager) — memory management
- Phase 60.2 (SpeculativeDecoder) — generation acceleration
- Phase 60.3 (AttentionOptimizer) — compute optimization
- Phase 60.4 (BatchScheduler) — request scheduling
- Phase 42 (Distributed Systems) — multi-node coordination
- Phase 59 (PEFT) — adapter serving for multi-tenant

## References
- vLLM — Open-source LLM serving engine
- TensorRT-LLM — NVIDIA's production inference stack
- SGLang — Structured generation language
- Lorax — Multi-LoRA serving
- Ray Serve — Scalable model serving framework

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] End-to-end serving pipeline with streaming support
- [ ] Auto-scaling with < 30s reaction time
- [ ] Multi-model serving with shared GPU memory
- [ ] Model parallelism with automatic strategy selection
- [ ] Comprehensive metrics dashboard (TTFT, TBT, throughput, cache hit rate)
- [ ] Zero-downtime model updates
- [ ] Integration tests with all Phase 60 components
- [ ] Unit tests with > 95% coverage

Depends on: #1130, #1131, #1132, #1133
Planning: #1129

items.body:
## Situation

There is no capacity model. Cluster node pools, CloudNativePG instance classes, Redis memory, JetStream stream limits and KEDA scaling bounds are currently set to whatever number was plausible when the manifest was first written, and nobody can answer the two questions that decide whether the platform survives its next twelve months: *how much load can we take before something breaks*, and *what does onboarding the next hospital cost in infrastructure*.

The consequences are already visible in the shape of the business. Sales commits to onboarding a 600-bed tertiary hospital with a go-live date, and engineering has no basis to say whether that tenant fits inside the current India-region footprint or requires a new node pool and a larger Postgres primary with a six-week lead time on quota. The reverse failure is equally real: over-provisioning to feel safe, in a market where per-bed pricing leaves little room for idle infrastructure. And because data residency is a hard boundary, capacity cannot be borrowed across regions — the India deployment must be sized on its own, and Nepal and Afghanistan will each need their own model rather than a share of a global pool.

Three platform-specific factors make generic cloud autoscaling insufficient here.

**Growth is stepwise, not smooth.** SaaS capacity models assume gradual user growth. Hospital onboarding is discrete and large: a single tenant going live adds its entire daily census, OPD footfall, prescription volume and lab throughput on one morning. A forecast built on a trend line through historical usage will miss it entirely. The model must be driven by the onboarding pipeline — beds, expected OPD footfall, module mix — not just by observed traffic.

**Demand is sharply peaked and calendar-bound.** OPD load concentrates into 08:00–11:00 IST; pharmacy follows; month-end brings a billing and TPA claim spike that is uncorrelated with clinical volume. Sizing on daily averages under-provisions the only hours that matter. Autoscaling absorbs part of this but not the parts with cold-start or state cost — Postgres connections, JetStream storage, Redis working set.

**Some capacity cannot be autoscaled into existence.** Persistent volume size, Postgres `max_connections`, JetStream stream limits, regional GPU and CPU quota, and IP address ranges are all decisions with a lead time. These are precisely the constraints that cause an outage nobody could scale out of.

Affected: the SRE team, who own the sizing decisions with no evidence; the hospital administrator whose go-live date depends on infrastructure being ready; finance, who cannot forecast cloud spend per tenant; and — through EmergencyConnect, which the brief requires to hold reserved headroom — ambulance crews, whose dispatch path must not be the thing that runs out of room when a large tenant goes live.

#603 delivers the measurement capability. This issue turns those measurements into a forward-looking model, headroom policy and procurement trigger.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE and the engineering leadership sizing the India regional deployment
**I want** a capacity model that converts observed resource consumption and the tenant onboarding pipeline into a forward demand forecast against known ceilings, with explicit headroom policy and lead-time alerts
**So that** we can onboard a committed hospital knowing the infrastructure will hold, raise long-lead quota before it becomes an outage, and protect EmergencyConnect's reserved headroom under any forecast.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A capacity inventory of every ceiling that cannot be crossed by autoscaling alone: node pool maxima and regional CPU/memory quota, PostgreSQL 16 primary vCPU/memory/`max_connections` and volume size, replica count, Redis memory and eviction policy, JetStream per-stream storage and consumer limits, object-storage growth, and Cloudflare and Istio ingress throughput — each with its current value, current utilisation and lead time to change.
* A per-tenant demand unit model: normalised resource cost per bed, per daily OPD visit, per prescription, per lab order and per active mobile user, derived by regression from production telemetry and calibrated against #603's synthetic-corpus runs.
* A forecast engine combining three inputs — observed trend on existing tenants, the committed onboarding pipeline with go-live dates and tenant profile, and seasonal/calendar factors (month-end billing, seasonal outpatient peaks) — producing a 90-day and 12-month projection per resource.
* An explicit headroom policy per resource class, differentiated by criticality: EmergencyConnect's reserved capacity carries the highest floor and is excluded from general-pool reallocation.
* Lead-time-aware alerting: an alert fires when the forecast crosses a ceiling *inside the lead time to change it*, not when utilisation crosses a fixed percentage.
* A capacity view in the AdminConnect platform-operations console showing per-resource utilisation, forecast, ceiling and time-to-ceiling, restricted to the SRE and platform-operations groups.
* A tenant-onboarding capacity check: a pre-go-live assessment that sizes a prospective tenant against remaining headroom and returns a fit/no-fit result with the additional provisioning required.
* Cost attribution per tenant per month, sufficient for unit-economics review.

**Out of scope**

* Building the load-generation harness, synthetic corpus and performance baselines — owned by #603. This issue consumes them.
* Per-endpoint latency budgets and optimisation — owned by #595.
* Read-replica routing, partitioning and connection-pool implementation — owned by #596; this issue tells #596 when the current shape runs out.
* Cache sizing implementation and eviction tuning — owned by #597.
* Worker autoscaling and queue backpressure implementation — owned by #599 and #600; this issue sets the ceilings their KEDA bounds respect.
* Multi-zone topology and failover behaviour — owned by #601; the model reserves capacity for zone loss but does not implement failover.
* Backup storage sizing and restore capacity — owned by #602.
* Subscription pricing, billing and invoicing. Cost attribution here is an internal engineering output, not a billing source of truth.

---

## Recommended Solution

A `capacity` Go module in the platform-operations service, deliberately built as a model over telemetry rather than a second monitoring system.

**Ingest.** OpenTelemetry metrics are already collected; capacity reads from the metrics backend on a schedule rather than instrumenting anything new. A daily Temporal workflow, `CapacityRollupWorkflow`, materialises per-tenant daily resource consumption and per-resource cluster utilisation at p50, p95 and peak — peak, not mean, because the OPD morning window is the sizing case.

```sql
CREATE TABLE capacity.resource (
  resource_key    text PRIMARY KEY,        -- 'pg.primary.connections'
  class           text NOT NULL,           -- compute|storage|connections|throughput|quota
  scaling_mode    text NOT NULL CHECK (scaling_mode IN ('auto','manual','procurement')),
  ceiling_value   numeric NOT NULL,
  unit            text NOT NULL,
  lead_time_days  int NOT NULL,            -- 0 for auto, 42 for regional quota
  headroom_floor  numeric NOT NULL,        -- fraction of ceiling that must stay free
  reserved_for    text                     -- 'emergencyconnect' where applicable
);

CREATE TABLE capacity.observation (
  resource_key text NOT NULL REFERENCES capacity.resource,
  observed_on  date NOT NULL,
  p50          numeric NOT NULL,
  p95          numeric NOT NULL,
  peak         numeric NOT NULL,
  peak_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (resource_key, observed_on)
);

CREATE TABLE capacity.demand_unit (
  driver        text NOT NULL,             -- 'bed','opd_visit','prescription','lab_order'
  resource_key  text NOT NULL REFERENCES capacity.resource,
  coefficient   numeric NOT NULL,          -- resource units per driver unit at peak
  r_squared     numeric NOT NULL,
  sample_days   int NOT NULL,
  calibrated_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (driver, resource_key)
);

CREATE TABLE capacity.pipeline_tenant (
  tenant_ref     text PRIMARY KEY,
  go_live_on     date NOT NULL,
  confidence     text NOT NULL CHECK (confidence IN ('committed','probable','speculative')),
  beds           int NOT NULL,
  opd_daily      int NOT NULL,
  modules        text[] NOT NULL,
  ramp_weeks     int NOT NULL DEFAULT 6
);

CREATE TABLE capacity.forecast (
  resource_key text NOT NULL REFERENCES capacity.resource,
  horizon_on   date NOT NULL,
  projected    numeric NOT NULL,
  p90_upper    numeric NOT NULL,
  generated_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (resource_key, horizon_on, generated_at)
);
```

`scaling_mode` and `lead_time_days` are the load-bearing columns. A resource with `scaling_mode = 'auto'` and `lead_time_days = 0` needs only a headroom check; regional CPU quota with `lead_time_days = 42` needs an alert six weeks before the crossing, which is a fundamentally different alert and cannot be expressed as "utilisation above 80%".

**Demand units.** Coefficients are fitted by ordinary least squares over `capacity.observation` joined to per-tenant driver counts, refreshed monthly. `r_squared` is stored and surfaced: a coefficient fitted at R² 0.31 is displayed as low-confidence and widens the forecast band rather than silently producing a confident wrong number. Where production history is thin — a new module, a new region — the coefficient is seeded from a #603 synthetic run at a known scale point and flagged as `synthetic` until enough production days accumulate to refit.

**Forecast.** `projected(t) = existing_trend(t) + Σ pipeline_tenant demand(t) × ramp(t) + seasonal(t)`, where pipeline tenants contribute on a linear ramp over `ramp_weeks` from `go_live_on` (a hospital does not reach full digital throughput on day one), weighted by confidence — committed at 1.0, probable at 0.6, speculative excluded from the alerting forecast but shown as a separate band. Seasonal factors are month-end billing multipliers and observed outpatient seasonality. The upper band is the p90 of a bootstrap over residuals; alerting uses the upper band, not the central estimate, because being wrong upward costs money and being wrong downward costs an outage during OPD peak.

**Headroom and reservation.** EmergencyConnect's reserved capacity is modelled as a first-class resource with its own `headroom_floor` and `reserved_for = 'emergencyconnect'`, and the forecast engine subtracts it from the general pool before assessing fit. A tenant onboarding that fits only by consuming the emergency reserve returns `no_fit`. Node-level enforcement is by dedicated node pool with taints and Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` and `PriorityClass`; the model's job is to ensure the reserve is never planned away, and #601's zone-loss scenario is included by requiring the forecast to fit within `n-1` zones.

**API.**

```
GET  /internal/v1/capacity/resources
GET  /internal/v1/capacity/forecast?horizon=90d
POST /internal/v1/capacity/onboarding-assessment   -- {beds, opd_daily, modules, go_live_on}
GET  /internal/v1/capacity/attribution?month=2026-07
POST /internal/v1/capacity/pipeline                -- register or update a pipeline tenant
```

The onboarding assessment returns per-resource fit, the binding constraint, and the provisioning actions with their lead times:

```json
{
  "verdict": "no_fit",
  "binding_constraint": "pg.primary.connections",
  "shortfall": { "required": 412, "available": 190, "unit": "connections" },
  "actions": [
    { "resource_key": "pg.primary.connections", "change": "resize primary to 32 vCPU / raise pool",
      "lead_time_days": 14, "latest_start_on": "2026-08-04" },
    { "resource_key": "gcp.quota.cpu.asia-south1", "change": "raise regional CPU quota by 400",
      "lead_time_days": 42, "latest_start_on": "2026-07-07" }
  ]
}
```

`latest_start_on` in the past is itself the alert condition.

**Events and access.** The workflow publishes `CapacityForecastGenerated` daily and `CapacityThresholdBreached` when a projection crosses a ceiling within lead time; the latter routes to the SRE on-call channel and creates a tracked action. Consumes `PerfRunCompleted` from #603 to refresh synthetic-seeded coefficients, and `TenantProvisioned` from AdminConnect to move a pipeline tenant into the observed set.

Capacity data is infrastructure telemetry and contains no PHI, but per-tenant consumption and cost are commercially sensitive across tenants. OpenFGA:

```
type capacity_view
  relations
    define platform_operator: [user, group#member]
    define finance_analyst:   [group#member]
    define viewer: platform_operator or finance_analyst
    define cost_viewer: platform_operator or finance_analyst
```

No tenant-scoped role has any relation to `capacity_view`; there is no customer-facing capacity surface, and per-tenant attribution is never exposed to another tenant.

**Sequencing.** #603 must land first — coefficients for unmeasured modules and any pre-production sizing depend on its runs. #596's replica and pooling model determines what `pg.primary.connections` actually means, so its shape must be settled before that resource's ceiling is meaningful. #601 must define the zone topology before `n-1` fit can be asserted. #599 and #600's KEDA bounds should be derived from this model's ceilings rather than set independently.

**Risks.** A model that nobody trusts is a model that gets ignored: mitigated by storing `r_squared` and sample size on every coefficient, showing forecast bands rather than point estimates, and backtesting each monthly refit against the previous 90 days with the error published. Pipeline data going stale and producing forecasts against tenants that were never signed: mitigated by expiring `pipeline_tenant` rows whose `go_live_on` has passed without a `TenantProvisioned` event and flagging them for review. Cost attribution being mistaken for a billing figure: mitigated by labelling it internal engineering cost and keeping it out of any tenant-visible surface. Over-fitting to India: the demand-unit model is keyed by country profile from the outset so the Nepal deployment refits rather than inherits.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** 90 days of observation data, calibrated demand-unit coefficients, and a committed 600-bed tertiary tenant registered in the pipeline with a go-live 10 weeks out
**When** the daily `CapacityRollupWorkflow` runs and an SRE requests the 90-day forecast
**Then** the forecast includes the new tenant's ramped demand from its go-live date, each resource shows projected utilisation with a p90 upper band against its ceiling and its remaining headroom net of the EmergencyConnect reserve, resources projected to cross their ceiling inside their lead time are listed with a `latest_start_on` date, `CapacityForecastGenerated` is published, and the platform-operations console renders the same view to an authorised operator.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the metrics backend is unavailable when the rollup workflow runs, so today's observations cannot be materialised
**When** the workflow executes
**Then** it retries on its Temporal policy, fails the activity explicitly rather than writing zero or interpolated observations into `capacity.observation`, leaves the previous forecast in place clearly labelled with its `generated_at` age, raises a data-freshness alert to the SRE channel, and the onboarding-assessment endpoint returns `stale_data` with the forecast age instead of returning a fit verdict from an incomplete model.

### Edge Cases

* An onboarding assessment fits only by consuming EmergencyConnect's reserved headroom — the verdict is `no_fit` with the reserve named as the binding constraint, and no configuration permits an operator to satisfy the assessment by lowering that reserve without an explicit, audited policy change.
* A forecast fits within total regional capacity but not within `n-1` zones — the verdict is `no_fit`, because capacity that only exists while every zone is healthy is not capacity.
* A demand-unit coefficient is fitted at R² below 0.5 — the forecast widens its band, the console marks the resource low-confidence, and the coefficient is excluded from automated procurement alerting until refitted.
* A pipeline tenant's go-live slips by four months — the forecast recomputes on the updated date and the previously issued procurement action is withdrawn rather than left open, so lead-time alerts do not accumulate as noise.
* A single tenant's OPD footfall triples after a merger with no new tenant record — trend-based growth on the existing tenant is captured independently of the pipeline, and does not require a pipeline entry to appear in the forecast.
* A resource with `scaling_mode = 'auto'` reaches 95% utilisation during the month-end billing spike and returns to 40% — this does not raise a procurement alert, since the autoscaler absorbed it; only sustained breach of the headroom floor at peak does.
* A finance analyst requests per-tenant attribution — cost figures are returned without any clinical or volume detail beyond the billing drivers, and no PHI-derived counts are exposed.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** an SRE can state, for any resource, current utilisation, the 90-day and 12-month forecast, the ceiling, and the date by which action must start — and can size a prospective hospital against remaining headroom in under a minute.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** hospital go-live dates are committed against verified infrastructure fit rather than optimism; long-lead quota and instance changes are raised before they become incidents; EmergencyConnect's reserved headroom survives every onboarding decision; and cloud spend per tenant becomes a reviewable unit-economics figure.
* **Success metric or validation method:** 90-day forecast mean absolute percentage error below 15% for compute and connection resources and below 25% for storage, measured by monthly backtest against actuals; 100% of long-lead resources carrying a lead-time-aware alert rather than a fixed-threshold one; zero capacity-related production incidents where the binding constraint was already visible in the model and no alert fired; every onboarding in the monitoring period preceded by a recorded assessment, with the actual post-go-live consumption within 20% of the assessed figure; cross-tenant attribution access denied across the full role matrix in adversarial tests.
* **Monitoring period, where applicable:** two quarters, with a monthly forecast-accuracy backtest published to engineering leadership, coefficient refits reviewed each month, and the headroom policy reviewed at the end of each quarter against observed peak behaviour.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

None — all guardrails apply. Accessibility applies in full to the platform-operations capacity view even though its audience is internal: forecast bands and headroom status must be conveyed by label and shape as well as colour, since a red/amber utilisation chart is the single most common place a colour-only status indicator is shipped, and the charts must expose an accessible tabular equivalent of the underlying figures.

items.title: Implement Tenant Isolation and Secure Deserialization for RAG Module
items.body:
### Describe the bug

The RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) module currently lacks tenant isolation, which results in a significant data leak between users. Specifically:

1. **Global Feedback Pool**: The `RAGFeedback` model does not have an `owner_id`. Any question asked or feedback given is stored in a global table.
2. **Information Disclosure**: The `GET /api/v1/rag/low-quality-chunks` endpoint returns feedback and source chunks for *all* users to any authenticated user on the Scale tier. This exposes the specific regulatory questions and source document snippets of one company to another.
3. **Insecure Deserialization**: The vector store loader in `backend/app/modules/rag/vector_store.py` uses `allow_dangerous_deserialization=True` with FAISS, which is a known security risk (RCE) if the index files are tampered with.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create two different users (User A and User B).
2. Have User A query the RAG module with a sensitive question.
3. Login as User B (Scale tier).
4. Call `GET /api/v1/rag/low-quality-chunks`.
5. User B can now see the chunks and questions associated with User A's session.

### Expected behaviour

- The `RAGFeedback` model should include an `owner_id` to isolate data between tenants.
- Endpoints should filter queries based on the `current_user.id`.
- Vector store loading should use safe deserialization methods or enforce strict path validation.

### Actual behaviour

- Data is stored and retrieved globally, violating multi-tenancy principles required for a GRC/Compliance tool.

### AegisAI version / commit
0.1.x (current)

items.title: [Refactor/Chore] Pooled DB connections are held across model, vector-store and thread waits in many request paths: name the holders and stop new ones
items.body:
### Self Checks

- [x] I have read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Language Policy](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/issues/1542).
- [x] This is only for refactors or chores; if you would like to ask a question, please head to [Discussions](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/discussions/categories/general).
- [x] I have searched for existing issues [search for existing issues](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/issues), including closed ones.
- [x] I confirm that I am using English to submit this report, otherwise it will be closed.
- [x] 【中文用户 & Non English User】请使用英语提交，否则会被关闭 ：）
- [x] Please do not modify this template :) and fill in all the required fields.

### Description

Several request paths keep a pooled database connection checked out while they wait on something that is not the database: a model, a vector store, another thread, a whole workflow run. Each one works at low concurrency. Once the number of such requests reaches the pool capacity (40 with the defaults), every request in the process waits for `SQLALCHEMY_POOL_TIMEOUT` and then fails, and the error names the request that could not get a connection, not the ones holding them.

Four instances were found one at a time by load-testing one path after another: #46241, #46253, #46278, #46354. That does not scale, and nothing stops the next one from being added. Two things make the pattern easy to write and hard to see:

- **`db.session` outside request handlers.** It keeps its connection until something ends the transaction, and in worker threads, generators and Celery tasks nothing does. `models/engine.py` already carries a notice asking new code not to use `db` outside `controllers`, but nothing enforces it. On `main` at 29f044b57 there are 236 uses outside `controllers`, `commands`, `migrations` and tests (core 103, tasks 50, services 48, schedule 15, events 11, extensions 6, others 3).
- **No signal until the pool is empty.** A held connection produces no log line, no metric and no failing test. The first symptom is the pool timeout under load.

This issue proposes two small pieces that make the class visible and stop it from growing, and tracks the holders that are still open.

### Motivation

**1. A monitor that names the holders** (opt-in, pull request to follow). It listens to the pool's checkout and check-in events, records the application frame that checked each connection out, and logs two things: a connection that was held longer than a limit, and the holders of every connection at the moment the pool is fully checked out.

Mounted into stock 1.19.0 with a 0.3 s limit and run over thirteen scenarios at 10 concurrent requests (30 requests each, model stand-in answering in 2 s, embedding stand-in in 200 ms), it reported these checkout sites:

| Scenario | Process | Connections held, median | Checked out at | Known as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workflow, blocking (three variants) | API | 30 of 30, 2.3–2.6 s | `WorkflowService.get_published_workflow` ← `AppGenerateService._get_workflow` | #46253 |
| Chat app, streaming and blocking | API | 30 of 30, 2.1 s | `Message.app` ← `TokenBufferMemory.get_history_prompt_messages` | #46278 |
| Chatflow, streaming | worker | 30 of 30, 2.1 s | same site | #46278 |
| Chat app, blocking | API | 30 of 30, 2.3 s | `AppService.get_app_by_id` ← `service_api/wraps.py` `decorated_view` | #46241 |
| Chat app with two knowledge bases | API | 56, 0.4 s | `DatasetRetrieval._retriever` ← `_run_retriever_thread` | #46354 |
| Workflow with two knowledge bases | worker | 60, 0.8 s | same site | #46354 |
| `POST /v1/datasets/{id}/retrieve` | API | 29 of 30, 0.4 s | `DatasetService.get_dataset` ← `hit_testing_base.get_and_validate_dataset`; `get_active_key_scope` ← `service_api/wraps.py` `decorated` | new, see below |
| Indexing one document | worker | 10, 1.2 s | `CacheEmbedding.embed_documents` | 1.19.0 only; already fixed on `main` |
| Workflow, streaming, 20 nodes | worker | 7 reports in 30 runs, 1.1–1.2 s | node and run persistence writes | not waits: the worker was CPU-bound |
| Workflow with an HTTP or LLM node, streaming | — | none | — | — |

So one run of a few minutes re-found the four known instances and one that was not known. The retrieval API one is confirmed: with every open fix mounted, 100 concurrent `POST /v1/datasets/{id}/retrieve` complete 28 of 200 in 62 s, and the monitor's own report at that moment reads:

```
Database connection pool is fully checked out (40 of 40), 0 earlier reports left out. Holders: 15 x services/knowledge/dataset_service.py:468 in get_dataset, called from controllers/console/datasets/hit_testing_base.py:94 in get_and_validate_dataset (oldest 61.5 s); 13 x repositories/knowledge/dataset_api_key_bindings.py:103 in get_active_key_scope, called from controllers/service_api/wraps.py:407 in decorated (oldest 0.1 s); ...
```

The request session loads the dataset and stays in its transaction while `HitTestingService.retrieve` runs, and the retrieval threads need connections of their own. I will open a separate issue and fix for that path.

**2. A guard against net-new `db.session` outside controllers** (pull request to follow). Same mechanism as `no-new-controller-sqlalchemy`: an ast-grep rule over changed lines, existing uses untouched, `# guard-ignore: no-new-global-db-session -- <reason>` for the cases that need it. It enforces what the notice in `models/engine.py` asks for and lets the 236 existing uses go down without new ones being added.

Not in these two pull requests, listed so the scope is clear:

- Removing the existing holders. Open pull requests cover four (#46244, #46254, #46279, #46355). Still open: the retrieval API path above, `DatasetRetrieval.single_retrieve`, and whatever the monitor reports for paths I have no scenario for (agent apps, external knowledge, plugins and tools).
- Turning the monitor on by default, and shortening the pool timeout so a missed holder fails one request quickly instead of stalling the process for 30 s. Both are worth doing once the known holders are gone; before that they would only add noise and errors.

### Additional Context

- The monitor costs about 2.4 µs per checkout and check-in pair in a micro-benchmark on a real `QueuePool` with a shallow stack; it walks the stack to find the application frame, so the cost grows with stack depth. It installs nothing when the setting is 0.
- A larger pool or a connection pooler in front of PostgreSQL does not remove the problem: a connection that is idle in a transaction is pinned either way. With the pool at 250 per process, 150 concurrent requests exhausted a 200-connection PostgreSQL in an earlier test.
- Scripts and raw numbers are available if useful.

items.title: Make row-level security on by default (second isolation layer)
items.body:
Make Postgres row-level security a second layer of tenant isolation that is **on by default** in every copy, so that a query missing its `tenantId` predicate returns nothing instead of another organisation's rows.

Follows #141, where the `neon` spike passed: correct under 200 concurrent mixed-tenant requests, fail-closed outside a transaction, `42501` on cross-tenant writes, and no extra latency when the scope is sent as one batch. Numbers are in `docs/RLS.md` on `docs/rls-neon-spike`.

## Where things stand

- Every tenant table has a `tenantIsolation()` policy (`apps/web/src/db/schema/rls.ts`), and `rls-coverage.test.ts` enforces that. `documents` and `chunks` add `platformReadable()`.
- `scripts/db-roles.ts` creates `rocketflare_app` as `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS`, and gives it LOGIN when `APP_DATABASE_URL` is set.
- `withTenantScope(db, tenantId, mode, fn)` exists (`apps/web/src/db/tenant-scope.ts`) but **nothing in `apps/web/src` calls it**.
- `databaseMiddleware` opens a single owner handle per request (`openDatabase(env)`). The owner bypasses RLS, so `TENANT_SCOPE_MODE = "enforce"` changes nothing today.
- `TENANT_SCOPE_MODE` defaults to `off` (`config.ts`), and both tomls say `off`.

## Design

### 1. Two handles, chosen by name

The owner handle and the tenant handle get different names, so a cross-tenant query is visible in the code and the type system.

- **`c.get('db')`** becomes the tenant handle, on the app-role connection. It is bound to `tenant.id` once auth has resolved the tenant, so every existing `c.get('db')` call site gets RLS without changing.
- **`c.get('ownerDb')`** (name to settle) is the owner handle. It is for code that is cross-tenant on purpose:
  - `/api/admin/*` behind `globalAdminMiddleware`;
  - the pre-tenant sign-in path (`services/auth.ts`: invitation lookup by email, membership count);
  - the crons (`pruneInvitations`, `runPruneAiSpans`, `pruneExpired`);
  - the ownership ceiling (`assertMayOwnAnother`);
  - migrations and `db-roles`.
- Before a tenant is resolved (public routes, `/auth/*`), `c.get('db')` is either the owner handle or unset. Unset is safer, because it fails loudly; decide which.
- `CORE_UNSCOPED_ALLOWLIST` in `tests/config/unscoped-allowlist.test.ts` becomes the list of call sites allowed to take `ownerDb`. The test should fail when `ownerDb` is used outside it.

### 2. How a statement is scoped: per statement, not per request

**Do not wrap the whole request in one transaction.** Chat and agent routes stream for minutes (SSE, model calls), and holding a pooled connection in an open transaction for that long exhausts the pool. `docs/RLS.md` step 5 warns about this.

Instead, every statement on the tenant handle carries the scope:

- **`neon` (default):**
  - A single statement goes as a non-interactive HTTP transaction, `[set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true), <statement>]`. That is one round trip with bound parameters; the spike's `httpTransactionCount` check passed.
  - An interactive `db.transaction(fn)` on the WebSocket pool runs `set_config(…, true)` first. The batched simple-protocol form measured 21.6 ms p95 26 ms, the same as a bare select; four separate awaits cost 4×.
- **`postgres` (postgres.js / Hyperdrive):**
  - Same shape: `set_config` + statement in one transaction, pipelined and not awaited one by one.
  - The tenant UUID must be regex-checked if it is ever interpolated into a simple-protocol batch.
  - Blocked on the Hyperdrive spike: the query-cache leak check, with caching on and off. `HYPERDRIVE_APP` must be created `--caching-disabled` if the cache leaks.

The implementation should probably be a drizzle session/driver wrapper in `apps/web/src/db/client.ts`, which is the only place the drivers differ (Non-Negotiable: driver seam). That keeps services unchanged and `tests/driver/` proving both drivers. `withTenantScope` becomes the explicit form for multi-statement work; it is re-entrant for the same tenant and throws `TenantScopeConflictError` for a different one, as it does today.

### 3. Every entry point gets the right handle

| Entry | Tenant from | Handle |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP routes after auth | session / API key | tenant |
| `/api/admin/*` | URL, behind global admin | owner (named) |
| Queue jobs (`queues/jobs.ts`) | the payload a server-side producer wrote | tenant, per job |
| Workflows (`workflows/agent-run.ts`, `plugins/api/workflow.ts`) | run row / payload, re-read on resume | tenant |
| Crons (`scheduled.ts`) | none, or per-tenant loops | owner for sweeps; tenant inside a per-tenant loop |
| Durable Objects (`NotificationsHub`) | the socket's authenticated tenant | tenant |
| Span store (`observability/span-store.ts`) | the trace's tenant | tenant (insert-only) or owner, with a reason |
| Email (`api/email.ts`), route helpers | caller | inherit |

### 4. Plugins

- The context a plugin receives (`@/plugins/api`) hands it the tenant handle by default. A plugin that needs cross-tenant access asks for the owner handle explicitly, and its own `UNSCOPED_ALLOWLIST` entry carries the reason.
- This is a plugin API change: regenerate `docs/plugin-api.md` and add a porting note.
- The `analytics` plugin's cubes and the `global-search` index are query surfaces of their own. Check that they run on the tenant handle, or document why not.
- Re-run `pnpm plugin check` and each plugin repo's gate with enforcement on.

### 5. Configuration and provisioning

- **`neon`:** an `APP_DATABASE_URL` Worker secret, the app role's **pooled** URI.
  - `pnpm provision` creates the role credential and sets the secret per environment.
  - `db-roles.ts` already reconciles the password to the URL.
- **`postgres`:** a second Hyperdrive, `HYPERDRIVE_APP`, with caching disabled, in **both** tomls (the parity test), plus a `localConnectionString` for the local app role.
- **Local dev and tests:** `.dev.vars.example` and `.env.test` get an app-role URL for the Docker Postgres and the Neon proxy. `pnpm dev:db:up` and `pnpm bootstrap` set it.
- **Default:** `TENANT_SCOPE_MODE` defaults to **`enforce`** in `config.ts` and both tomls. Rollback is `off`, as documented.
- **Single tenancy:** recommend `enforce` in `single` mode too, for one code path and no mode-specific bugs. The batching means it costs nothing. Revisit only if measurements say otherwise.

### 6. Tests

- **Run the whole `api` suite under `enforce`** on the app role, under both drivers. Every existing test then proves the routes still work with RLS on. A 404 for a row the user should see is the signature regression (`docs/RLS.md` → Watch).
- **New enforcement test** (`tests/api/rls-enforcement.test.ts`, the one `docs/RLS.md` says is not written yet):
  - a predicate-less read on the tenant handle returns only the tenant's rows;
  - the tenant handle with no tenant set returns zero rows;
  - a cross-tenant insert, or moving a row to another tenant, gives `42501`;
  - a cross-tenant update or delete affects 0 rows;
  - `platformReadable` rows are readable and not writable;
  - the GUC does not survive into the next pooled use.
- **A mutation proof:** delete a `tenantId` predicate from one service in a test fixture, and show the enforcement layer still returns no foreign rows.
- **Driver conformance:** `tests/driver/` covers the scoped single-statement path and the scoped interactive transaction on both drivers.
- **Guard:** a config test fails if `ownerDb` is used outside the allow-list.

### 7. Docs and release

- `docs/RLS.md`:
  - rewrite from "inert scaffolding" to "on by default";
  - keep the threat-model note (RLS defends a forgotten predicate, not SQL injection, because the app role can call `set_config` itself);
  - keep the rollback section.
- `docs/CONCEPTS.md` (Database + Known gaps), `docs/THREAT-MODEL.md`: "Row-level security is inert by default" becomes a second layer that is on.
- `docs/DEPLOY.md`, `SETUP.md` (the `APP_DATABASE_URL` secret), `.claude/rules/database.md`, `apps/web/src/db/CLAUDE.md`, `apps/web/src/db/schema/CLAUDE.md`.
- `docs/upgrades/unreleased.md`: a porting note for copies. Adopting it means setting `APP_DATABASE_URL`, running `pnpm db:migrate`, and running the gate with `enforce`. Copies that are not ready set `TENANT_SCOPE_MODE = "off"`.
- The www `/security/` posture list gains the second layer.

## Order of work

1. Hyperdrive spike (`postgres` path), with results in `docs/RLS.md`. If it is a no-go, `enforce` ships for `neon` only and `postgres` keeps `off`, with the reason documented.
2. Same spike from a Worker on `neon` (`wrangler dev --remote` or a preview deploy), for real latency numbers.
3. Two-handle split plus the per-statement scoping wrapper in `client.ts`; route every entry point (table above).
4. Run the suite under `enforce`; fix every legitimate cross-tenant read by moving it to `ownerDb` with an allow-list reason.
5. Plugins: context change, `plugin-api.md`, a gate in every plugin repo.
6. Provisioning, local dev and test env.
7. Flip the default, write the docs and porting note, and release (run `/rf-security standard` over the diff first: this touches the tenancy boundary).

## Done when

- `TENANT_SCOPE_MODE` defaults to `enforce`, and a fresh `pnpm bootstrap` copy runs with RLS on, with no manual steps.
- The full gate passes with `enforce` under both drivers, the enforcement test exists, and the mutation proof shows a missing predicate is caught.
- Every cross-tenant query uses the named owner handle and is on the allow-list with a reason.
- p95 request latency with `enforce` is within ~10 ms of `off`, measured from a Worker.
- Docs, porting note and plugin API are updated; plugin repos pass.

items.title: [Enterprise] Multi-tenancy / Mandantenfähigkeit
items.body:
## Future — Multi-Tenancy

The single biggest remaining enterprise gap. Separate data isolation, configuration, branding, and user management per tenant.

### What It Means
- Tenant-scoped data isolation (chats, configs, users, apps)
- Per-tenant branding and configuration
- Tenant-scoped admin users
- Cross-tenant analytics for platform operator
- Tenant provisioning API

### Current State
ihub-apps is single-tenant. Group-based RBAC exists but is not tenant isolation. Each deployment is a separate instance.

### Complexity
HIGH — touches auth, storage, config, admin, and all Phase 1-3 features. Every database query and config access needs tenant context.

### Interim Workaround
Deploy separate instances per tenant. This works for <10 tenants but doesn't scale operationally.

### Recommendation
Scope as a dedicated initiative after Phase 3. Can be implemented incrementally:
1. Tenant model + database schema changes
2. Tenant-scoped middleware (inject tenant context from subdomain/header)
3. Migrate all queries to include tenant filter
4. Tenant admin UI

**Priority:** High — demanded by the largest enterprise tenders (municipal platforms, cantonal PaaS deployments). Schedule after Phase 3 based on deal pipeline.

items.title: [Feature] Ingest externally-measured usage into virtual-key spend tracking (async batch traffic bypassing the proxy)

labels.name: Cost & Budgeting
labels.description: Wrong or missing spend/cost, pricing and cost-map rows, budgets and spend limits

items.body:
**Context**
We rely on LiteLLM virtual keys for auth, budgets, and spend attribution across our platform. Some inference traffic goes through the LiteLLM proxy as usual, but we also run an asynchronous batch path (OpenAI Batch API style, built on `llm-d-batch-gateway`): users upload JSONL files with thousands of requests, and a batch processor dispatches each line directly to model gateway / inference-pool endpoints.

This direct path bypasses the LiteLLM proxy **on purpose**: sustained batch throughput would make the proxy a bottleneck, and batch calls don't need proxy-time features (retry/fallback routing, per-request guardrail decisions).

**The gap**
- Usage data exists: batch output rows carry per-request `usage` (prompt/completion tokens), and key/tenant identity is propagated from job submission through the batch pipeline.
- Spend for this traffic never lands in LiteLLM's spend tables, because spend is only written by the proxy logging pipeline for requests that pass through it.
- We checked current master (`spend_management_endpoints.py`): spend endpoints are read/report-only (`/spend/calculate`, `/global/spend/reset|refresh`) — there is no supported way for an external system to record usage against a virtual key/team.

**Questions / proposal**
1. Is there a recommended pattern today for attributing usage of non-proxied traffic to virtual keys (short of writing `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` rows directly, which we'd rather not depend on)?
2. If not, would you accept a contribution adding an ingestion entry point (endpoint or documented internal API) that accepts externally-measured usage — key, model, tokens, timestamp, metadata — and feeds it through the same spend-update pipeline (key/team/user spend logs, budget accounting)? Happy to implement and upstream it in whatever shape maintainers prefer.

The broader goal: keep budgets/spend coherent in LiteLLM as the single metering system, even in deployments where part of the traffic legitimately bypasses the proxy.

items.title: Multi-tenant dashboard isolation: design proposal for per-profile scoping

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

items.body:
## Context

We run one host with 8 gateway profiles, each owned by a different person or function, and we want to give each owner a browser dashboard for their own profile and nothing else. `dashboard/serve --isolated` looks like it should be that boundary, but today it is a UI convenience, not an access-control boundary. We have built and are running a patch series (7 patches against the dashboard backend) that turns it into one, and I would like to propose upstreaming the concept as a first-class feature rather than carrying it forever. Filing as a design issue first since it is too big for a drive-by PR; if maintainers want it, I can contribute the series in reviewable pieces against current main.

## What we found when we treated --isolated as a security boundary

Two separate doors bypass the profile scope, plus a set of smaller leaks:

1. **The `?profile=` door.** Endpoints resolve a client-supplied `?profile=<name>` query. An isolated dashboard for profile A would happily operate on profile B: `_resolve_profile_dir`, the cron profile home, and the enumeration endpoints all honored the parameter.

2. **The absolute-path door.** The file-browser and git rails (`/api/fs/*`, `/api/git/*`) take a client-supplied absolute path and no profile parameter at all. An isolated backend would read or write any file the service user can reach, including sibling profiles' homes, shared credential state, and the user's own `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config/gh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.kube`, `~/.netrc` and similar credential stores. That is lateral movement from a single leaked dashboard session.

3. **Smaller leaks that break the boundary in practice:** `/api/files/*`, backup and import endpoints operating cross-profile; `GET /api/profiles/active` reporting the machine-global sticky active profile (so the SPA banners and queries target the wrong profile and then 403); and the model/provider surface (`/api/model/*`, `/api/credentials/pool`, `/api/config`, analytics `by_model`) exposing platform-level configuration and credentials to a per-profile owner.

## Proposed design

- **Deny-by-default containment at the path chokepoint.** One guard on the fs/git path resolver: the resolved real path must be inside the isolated profile's own home, or in an explicitly allowed workspace root; sibling profile homes, shared machine state, and a hard denylist of the service user's credential stores are 403 for read and write. Deny-by-default matters: we first shipped an allowlist-of-known-bad and kept finding new routes; inverting it is what made the boundary hold.
- **Profile pinning.** When `--isolated`, the profile is fixed at serve time: `?profile=` for any other profile is 403 everywhere, enumeration endpoints return only the pinned profile, and `GET /api/profiles/active` reports the pinned profile so the SPA is coherent without client changes.
- **A headless token auth provider.** A per-backend session token (env-provided, sent as a header, constant-time compared, entropy-checked, fail-closed) that authenticates the full gated surface as a cookie-session stand-in. This makes it practical to bind each isolated dashboard on a private network interface with auth on. Deliberately narrower in shape than the existing per-route token seam so a service credential can never unlock a broader surface than intended.
- **Capability scoping for platform-level surfaces.** On an isolated dashboard, model selection, provider credentials, and raw config are platform decisions, not profile-owner decisions: writes are refused and reads are scrubbed, with a neutral notice. Non-isolated dashboards are completely unaffected.

Everything is a no-op unless `--isolated` is set, so single-user setups see zero change.

## Why upstream

Any multi-profile deployment that wants to hand a dashboard to more than one human needs this, and it is the kind of boundary that is dangerous to half-have: the flag reads like isolation, so people will deploy it as isolation. We have been running the full series in production across 8 profiles; the deny-by-default containment has been exercised by real traffic, and the pinning fixes are what made the stock SPA usable per owner without forking it.

I am happy to break this into a reviewable series (containment guard, profile pinning, token auth provider, capability scoping) if there is interest, or to adjust the design to fit how you would rather shape it. Earlier reports from this deployment: #30896, #30897, #31618, #32730.

items.body:
## Destination

A **document intelligence platform** that runs as:
- **CLI** (`hacienda-backend`) for owners
- **MCP server** (`hacienda-mcp`) for agents (Claude Code Desktop, Codex, AI clients)
- **Plugin** for folder/mail connectors (future)

With **PII-safe** guarantees (gaze + xberg core unchanged), **configurable** embeddings/reranking/NER, **cross-OS/memory** operation, and **agent-facing** search/rehydrate/sync surfaces.

## Notes

- **Core invariant**: gaze + xberg redaction pipeline stays exactly as implemented (epics 1-4). New work is *around* it.
- **Trust boundary**: Agent sees only class-stable `<Class_…>` tokens + search results. Raw PII never leaves owner machine.
- **Configurability**: Embedding model, reranker, NER (GLiNER), batch sizes, thread pools, device (CPU/MPS/CUDA) — all via `hacienda.toml` + env.
- **Connectors**: Folder (done), Mail (IMAP/Gmail/Graph), future: SharePoint, Confluence, etc. Each connector feeds xberg extraction → same pipeline.
- **Deployment**: Single binary per platform (CLI + MCP in one). Owner runs MCP locally; agents connect via stdio/HTTP.

## Decisions so far

- ✅ Epics 1-4: PII-safe extraction core (gaze + xberg dual-store, rehydration CLI, class-stable projection, folder sync)
- ✅ Intel macOS workaround (`ort-sys` rc.12 load-dynamic)
- ✅ xberg plugin seam (same-name `redaction` replacement) — zero basemind fork changes

## Not yet specified (fog → tickets)

### Platform & Delivery
- [ ] **MCP server** (`hacienda-mcp`): stdio + HTTP transport, tool registry, PrincipalResolver for per-agent auth
- [ ] **Single binary build**: CLI + MCP merged, cross-platform (macOS ARM/Intel, Linux x86_64/ARM, Windows)
- [ ] **Install/packaging**: Homebrew, cargo-binstall, GitHub Releases, maybe `pipx`/`uvx` for Python agents

### Configurability (Embeddings / Reranking / NER)
- [ ] **Embedding pipeline**: ONNX Runtime (ort) + model zoo (bge-small, e5-small, mxbai, custom). Device selector (CPU/MPS/CUDA). Batch size, max seq len.
- [ ] **Reranker pipeline**: Cross-encoder (bge-reranker, jina-reranker). Optional, gated by `SensitivityTier`.
- [ ] **NER/GLiNER**: Opt-in GLiNER model (ner-gliner, span-marker). Device, threshold, label map. Falls back to gaze core floor.
- [ ] **Config schema**: `hacienda.toml` `[embeddings]`, `[reranker]`, `[ner]` sections with device, batch, model path/URL, cache dir.
- [ ] **Model cache**: `~/.cache/hacienda/models/` with integrity checks, offline mode.

### Agent-Facing Search (MCP Tools)
- [ ] **`search` tool**: Hybrid BM25 (class-stable `<Class_…>`) + vector (embedding) + optional cross-encoder rerank. Returns tokenized snippets + doc IDs.
- [ ] **`rehydrate` tool**: Owner-gated, per-export review, audit log (same as CLI). **Never returns raw PII to agent** — only to owner via file/TTY.
- [ ] **`sync` tool**: Trigger incremental/full rebuild, returns status.
- [ ] **`status` tool**: Index stats, fingerprint, last sync, model versions.

### Connectors (Folder + Mail)
- [ ] **Folder connector** (done): watcher + manual refresh, engine-era fingerprint rebuild
- [ ] **Mail connector**: IMAP/Gmail/Graph API → extract attachments + bodies → same xberg pipeline → same index
- [ ] **Connector SDK**: Trait `DocumentConnector { fn list() -> Vec<DocRef>; fn fetch(DocRef) -> ExtractedDocument; }`
- [ ] **Per-connector config**: Sync interval, filters, label mapping, fingerprint namespace

### Cross-Platform / Memory
- [ ] **Device abstraction**: `Device::Cpu / Mps / Cuda(idx)` with auto-detect, fallback chain
- [ ] **Thread pool sizing**: `rayon` global pool tuned to logical cores / memory
- [ ] **Model memory budget**: LRU cache with `max_mem_mb`, offload to disk
- [ ] **Windows support**: notify watcher (ReadDirectoryChangesW), path handling, binary signing

### Observability / Ops
- [ ] **Structured logging**: `tracing` + `tracing-subscriber`, JSON for MCP, human for CLI
- [ ] **Metrics**: Prometheus exporter (index size, sync latency, search QPS, rehydration count)
- [ ] **Health endpoint**: `/healthz` for MCP HTTP mode

## Out of scope
- Changing gaze/xberg core (epics 1-4 are frozen)
- Multi-tenant SaaS (owner-local only)
- Training/fine-tuning models (inference only)

items.title: design review: Rust-native evidence-first OCR engine
items.body:
Parent: #1. Related reviews: #3, #4, #6 and #7.

## Direction

Build a Tesserix-owned OCR engine and production runtime in Rust. Established external OCR systems are benchmark competitors only; we do not adopt or copy another project’s runtime, pipeline, source or public contract.

“Our OCR” means Tesserix owns preprocessing, inference pipeline, model contract, deployed artefacts, normalization, evidence, calibration, evaluation and release gates. Training experiments may use Python; production inference remains Rust with signed exported model artefacts.

## Product niche

Agent-grade, evidence-first document OCR:

- immutable original-page evidence for every recognized value;
- calibrated uncertainty and explicit unusable, unknown and partial outcomes;
- forms, receipts, invoices, statements, IDs, contracts and mobile scans;
- deterministic validation and human-review routing;
- untrusted-content and prompt-injection signals for agents;
- streaming pages, bounded resources and private/self-hosted execution.

## Proposed runtime

- Rust stable, Tokio, Axum/Tower, SQLx, thiserror, serde and tracing/OTel.
- ONNX Runtime through a pinned Rust integration as the initial CPU/CUDA/TensorRT execution layer.
- Separate crates for domain, image transforms, detection, recognition, layout, runtime, evaluation and service.
- Sandboxed decode/inference workers because codecs, GPU drivers and ONNX Runtime remain native/unsafe dependencies.
- Models are warmed and pooled per device/version, batched by bounded shape/pixel budgets and promoted independently.

## Required design and benchmark gate

- [ ] Approve the first narrow cohort: printed English scans/mobile images plus source geometry and reading order.
- [ ] Select legally usable bootstrap detector/recognizer weights after model-license review.
- [ ] Define signed model manifest, tensor contracts, calibration and rollback predecessor.
- [ ] Build identical-hardware baselines against established open-source and approved cloud OCR.
- [ ] Measure CER/WER, evidence IoU, reading order, layout/table cohorts, p50/p95/p99, pages/s, CPU/GPU/memory and cost.
- [ ] Prove warmed sessions, bounded batching, page streaming and memory ceilings.
- [ ] Prove transforms map all evidence back to immutable original-page coordinates.
- [ ] Fuzz decoders, tensor validation, geometry and post-processing.
- [ ] Prove raw text and field values never enter logs/traces.
- [ ] Keep VLM use limited to bounded low-confidence regions with separate provenance.

## Temporal risk gate

Temporal Rust SDK v0.8.0 is Public Preview/pre-release as of 2026-09-02. Before production selection, prove replay, worker versioning, cancellation, signals, child workflows, heartbeats, 300-page history bounds, crash recovery and a 24-hour upgrade soak. If it fails, use a narrow stable Go Temporal runner calling the Rust service; do not build a custom durable state machine merely for language purity.

## Approval

- [ ] Rust/service owner
- [ ] OCR/ML owner
- [ ] Model licensing/data-governance owner
- [ ] Temporal/platform owner
- [ ] Security/native supply-chain owner
- [ ] SRE approves measured benefit, cost and failure isolation

Implementation #8 remains blocked until this review records the selected first profile, model artefacts, benchmark thresholds and workflow runtime.

items.title: spike(voice): ElevenAgents as governed voice and WhatsApp frontend for MCTL

labels.name: spike:scout
labels.description: Spike draft proposed by the daily scout digest (mctl-agents#797)

items.body:
Source / discovery:
- Campaign landing page: https://join.elevenlabs.io/agents/v6
- Primary product docs: https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/overview
- WhatsApp behavior and limitations: https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/whatsapp
- WhatsApp billing/provider constraints: https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/whatsapp/troubleshooting
- Tools/MCP: https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/customization/tools/mcp/
- Agent pricing: https://elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents

**Question:** Can MCTL use ElevenLabs ElevenAgents as a governed voice/WhatsApp frontend (or only a replaceable speech provider) while preserving MCTL-owned tenant identity, consent, context isolation, exact-action approval, policy, budget/ledger and audit — *without building a competing conversational-agent control plane or blocking existing managed-runtime delivery*?

**Lifecycle:** PROPOSED / discovery only; no paid pilot or production changes authorized.
**Priority:** P2 discovery, non-blocking.
**Timebox:** up to 2 working days for inventory + decision report; optionally a separately approved, capped synthetic POC.
**Decision:** ADAPTER_ONLY | HYBRID | FULL_CHANNEL_GATED | DEFER | REJECT (owner verdict required).

## Why / current product facts to verify
ElevenAgents has voice, WhatsApp Business messages/voice notes/calls, hosted workflows, knowledge bases, webhooks, MCP tools and BYO-model options. This is **more than STT/TTS** and creates actual overlap with MCTL Assistant + managed runtime.

As of investigation intake, ElevenLabs documentation explicitly says:
- The WhatsApp Business number cannot currently be imported if owned by another provider or active in WhatsApp Business app; coexistence must be proven, not presumed.
- WhatsApp Flows, inbound video, message batching and human handoff are not currently supported in the documented channel.
- Voice notes incur extra STT/TTS costs, LLM and Meta charges are separate; $0.08/additional call minute and $0.003/text message are *pricing inputs to revalidate*, not a quote for a completed order.
- ElevenAgents ↔ external MCP integrates tools but enabling MCP has workspace-wide terms/setting; MCP is not available in Zero Retention Mode/HIPAA configurations according to current docs.
Capture the documentation date/plan/region and flag changes at the time of the report; treat marketing capabilities as UNVERIFIED until reproduced.

## Existing work / boundaries (inventory live status first)
- mctlhq/mctl-telegram#1002 — Telegram product epic; #1088 — **Telegram** managed runtime and hard preview/production gates. This spike must not change these gates, pooled worker, model selection, claim authority, pricing or flags.
- mctlhq/mctl-telegram#1046 — external runtime contract/threat model gate (if relevant to a vendor-hosted runner).
- mctlhq/mctl-telegram#1097 — **personal WhatsApp ↔ Telegram forum** isolated spike; not the same as WhatsApp Business onboarding/Meta API. No duplicate WhatsApp relay implementation.
- mctlhq/.github#181 — canonical identity, decision assurance and exact-action approval; reuse, do not emulate authorization inside vendor prompt.
- mctlhq/.github#173 — Agent Commerce foundations, cost attribution and budgets; historical epic may be closed, but no real money / billing enablement is authorized by this spike.
- mctlhq/.github#309 — shared team assistants/skills/memory/tenancy economics; reuse current-state matrix as applicable. Check for any existing ElevenLabs/speech/WhatsApp integration in repos before proposing work.

## Investigate — options with explicit ownership
**A. ADAPTER_ONLY (default hypothesis):** MCTL owns WhatsApp Business channel (where applicable), lifecycle, dialogue context and governed actions; ElevenLabs used only for STT/TTS or real-time voice transport. Check actual supported streaming interfaces; do not assume a native relay API exists.

**B. HYBRID:** ElevenAgents hosts voice/conversation UX (web/phone/WhatsApp); all reads/actions use tightly scoped MCTL gateway/API/MCP, no direct CRM/order mutation. Need authenticated caller→MCTL tenant/principal mapping, short-lived per-session authorization and end-to-end event correlation.

**C. FULL_CHANNEL_GATED:** ElevenLabs owns WhatsApp Business number and active conversation; MCTL remains action authority and audit/ledger source. Test handoff, data export, number portability, failure/recovery and channel ownership before any GO. If provider coexistence or required handoff is absent, this option cannot be called production-ready.

**D. BASELINE:** Existing MCTL-owned assistant/managed runtime + independently selected STT/TTS. Compare on same synthetic cases; do not double-count costs or assume current pipeline supports WhatsApp calls.

## Research / POC questions
1. **API and channel reality:** WhatsApp Business onboarding, one-number exclusivity, third-party BSP conflict, voice notes versus *live calls*, inbound/outbound rules, available webhooks and delivery receipts, latency, multilingual support and actual human escalation. Separate provider-documented vs verified.
2. **Voice quality:** on synthetic consented scripts test English, Russian, and an optional Algerian Arabic dialect example. Measure end-to-end speech response p50/p95, transcription WER/intent/slot accuracy where labeled, interruptions/barge-in, fallback, timeout and real-world message splitting. No customer data.
3. **Authority and tenant identity:** map caller ID/WhatsApp BSUID/agent ID → authenticated tenant/principal and explicit consent. Prevent forged dynamic variables or conversation-initiation payloads from granting authority. All mutations go through existing MCTL policy → exact approval → execution → immutable result; no vendor tool executes an order/payment directly.
4. **Security and data:** MCP/webhook credential scope, signed callbacks, replay/idempotency, provider revocation, SSRF/prompt injection/tool-output injection, cross-tenant contamination, opt-in audio recording, storage/retention/region, data deletion/export and vendor service failure. Test what Zero Retention Mode blocks.
5. **Operational fit:** agent-as-code export/config drift, observability/trace and conversation IDs, usage/event webhooks, human handoff and provider-change rollback. Show vendor-outage behavior without silent order loss or duplicate sends.
6. **Cost/economics:** reproducible model per successful 1-minute call, 3-minute call, 1 voice-note exchange, 1 text order and an interrupted/failed order. Include ElevenAgents minutes/messages, STT, TTS, LLM, WhatsApp/Meta fees, concurrency/burst, retries, data egress, and MCTL runtime infra. Distinguish vendor COGS vs tenant charge; calculate best/base/worst and cap per tenant/job, clearly label assumptions.
7. **Competitive/product decision:** where ElevenAgents genuinely replaces an MCTL surface vs where a narrow adapter adds value. Scope the minimal product use case: synthetic restaurant order by WhatsApp voice note → basket draft → explicit customer confirmation → governed mock submit (NO actual order, payment or customer contact).

## Bounded stages and gates
- **Stage 0: evidence-only inventory.** Read source repos/ADRs/contracts and current vendor docs, available account tiers, Meta limits/terms, and security/retention. Produce option matrix and questions that cannot be answered without credentials or a phone number.
- **Stage 1: reproducible offline tests.** Synthetic audio/text, recorded/mock HTTP interactions, negative cases for forgery/replay/cross-tenant and exact-action approval. No live channel import, real WhatsApp number, production API key, real call or spend.
- **Stage 2: optional live POC — STOP for owner decision.** Before a real ElevenLabs workspace/account, any paid inference, number onboarding, vendor MCP opt-in, Meta assets, test calls or externally reachable endpoints, obtain explicit owner approval of test identities, budget, credentials, scope and rollback. Do not run automatically from this issue.
- **Stage 3: architecture + economics report and human verdict.** No implementation issue automatically triggered, no rollout flags changed.

## Evidence / deliverables
- Reviewed `docs/spikes/elevenagents-voice-whatsapp-frontend.md` (or existing canonical spike-doc location) with dated provider links, live MCTL current-state/duplicate map, candidate integration/dataflow diagrams and authority ownership table.
- A/B/C/D capability + cost + lock-in comparison; status VERIFIED / PROVIDER-DOCUMENTED / UNTESTED / UNSUPPORTED per claim.
- Synthetic E2E and negative test plan/results, reproducible fixture or explicit blocker, transcripts redacted and zero personal data.
- Decision record with exactly one recommendation: **ADAPTER_ONLY / HYBRID / FULL_CHANNEL_GATED / DEFER / REJECT**, open prerequisites, smallest possible follow-up issue(s) and owner approval requirements.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Current repos, duplicate efforts, and authority seams mapped with precise refs; never treat Telegram managed runtime as an existing WhatsApp Business deployment.
- [ ] WhatsApp Business channel ownership, number portability, call/voice-note differences and human handoff limitations confirmed from primary sources.
- [ ] An externally hosted ElevenLabs agent cannot bypass MCTL authorization, digest-bound approval, tenant boundary, idempotency, ledger and audit (negative test design + evidence).
- [ ] Quantitative per-successful-interaction cost and latency baseline includes failures, concurrency/burst and Meta/LLM/STT/TTS fees, without unverified price claims.
- [ ] Data retention/region/consent, MCP setup restrictions, provider outage and rollback assessed; UNKNOWN is not PASS.
- [ ] At least one feasible minimal architecture and clear no-go triggers identified, or explicit DEFER/REJECT with evidence.
- [ ] Owner accepts verdict before any pilot/production action; existing #1088 / #889 / #334 gates remain intact.

## Explicit non-goals
No new conversational-agent orchestrator; no direct ElevenLabs→business write bypass; no real customer/phone/WhatsApp account onboarding, production worker or release flag changes; no unapproved subscription/spend; no claim that ElevenLabs human handoff or coexistence works until independently proven.

items.title: EPIC: hosted multi-tenant AuroraBoot
items.body:
### Goal Run a hosted, multi-tenant AuroraBoot on the decommissioned OVH bare metal, where approved users sign in, build Kairos artifacts and download them. AuroraBoot must stay a first-class local tool: nothing in this epic may change the behaviour of a local deployment. ### How this epic is worked Items below are **not** separate tickets yet. A sub-ticket is opened only when someone picks an item up, and it is linked here at that point. Do not start implementing an item from this list without its ticket: order matters (see the dependencies on each item), and work that jumps ahead will have to be redone. ### Decisions so far - **Local deployments are the single-tenant case of the same code, not a separate code path.** Every resource belongs to a workspace and every query is scoped, in both modes. Locally, the admin password maps to one built-in workspace with one admin. Deployment differences live behind a few interfaces selected at startup (`Authenticator`, `BuildPolicy`, `QuotaPolicy`, `ArtifactStore`, `Builder`) and a `--profile=local|hosted` preset. No per-feature flags in handlers. - **Features the hosted service cannot offer are route modules that are not mounted**, not code paths that check a mode. Netboot/PXE, Redfish/BMC and node fleet management stay in the binary and are unmounted in the hosted profile. The UI reads `GET /api/v1/capabilities` and hides what is absent. - **Ownership unit is the workspace.** Users are members of workspaces with roles. Every user gets a personal workspace. Quotas, secure boot keys and (later) fleets attach to a workspace. - **Identity:** AuroraBoot speaks generic OIDC. A Dex instance (or any OIDC provider) supplies GitHub/Google login. - **Access at launch is gated:** anyone can sign in, an admin approves accounts before they can build. Open signup is a later step and the quota and abuse controls are designed with it in mind. - **Builds at launch are curated only:** base image from an allowlist, cloud-config, extensions from the catalog. No user Dockerfiles, `ExtraSteps` or arbitrary base images, because those run user code on our hardware. The curated restriction is a `BuildPolicy` admission rule, and the builder receives an execution class, so custom builds can be enabled later by adding a policy tier and a sandboxed runtime class, without reworking the builder. - **Anti-abuse model:** a miner needs sustained CPU, a pool connection and an account that lives long enough. Controls: per-build timeouts and CPU limits, a per-workspace CPU-minute budget from cgroup accounting, concurrency caps, egress restricted to an allowlist for any step that runs user code, detection of the miner CPU profile, and account gating. - **Caching:** shared and content-addressed for everything derived only from public inputs (kairosified image, rootfs, base ISO), per workspace for anything that touches cloud-config, keys or overlays. A zot pull-through cache for image pulls. - **Infrastructure:** a k3s cluster across the OVH boxes, using the `operator` builder. Object storage is S3-compatible behind an interface; the backend (AWS S3, Garage, SeaweedFS, Rook/Ceph RGW, ...) is chosen in its own ticket. ### Phases Each item is a placeholder for a future ticket; its details are in the collapsible sections at the bottom.
