Phase 0 and Phase 1 have no dependency on each other and can start now. Phase 2 needs 1.1 and 1.3. Phase 3 needs 2.1. Phases 4 and 5 mostly run alongside 2 and 3. Launch is Phases 0 to 5. Phases 6 and 7 are after launch. **Phase 0: Hardening (also benefits local deployments, no SaaS concepts)** - [x] 0.1 Validate image references before they reach a Dockerfile (#5297) - [x] 0.2 Stop accepting server filesystem paths from the API (kairos-io/AuroraBoot#928) - ~~0.3 Registration must not hand out an existing node's API key~~ (folded into 7.1: the fleet module is not mounted in the hosted profile until 7.2, so the fix lands with the new enrolment model) - [x] 0.4 Bound request bodies, uploads and stored build logs (kairos-io/AuroraBoot#934) - [x] 0.5 The web builder writes the full cloud-config into the build log (kairos-io/AuroraBoot#948) - [x] 0.6 Keep credentials out of URLs and browser storage, check WebSocket origin, return no server paths (kairos-io/AuroraBoot#951, kairos-io/AuroraBoot#956) **Phase 1: Seams (refactor, local behaviour unchanged)** - [ ] 1.1 Versioned database migrations - [ ] 1.2 Deployment profiles, route modules and a capabilities endpoint - [ ] 1.3 Authenticator interface and a request principal - [ ] 1.4 BuildSpec, BuildPolicy admission and execution class - [ ] 1.5 ArtifactStore interface - [ ] 1.6 QuotaPolicy interface **Phase 2: Identity and tenancy** - [ ] 2.1 Workspaces, users and memberships; scope every resource - [ ] 2.2 OIDC login with cookie sessions - [ ] 2.3 Signup and account approval (supersedes #3396) - [ ] 2.4 Workspace roles and invitations - [ ] 2.5 Scope UI WebSocket events to the workspace - [ ] 2.6 Per-workspace settings and secure boot keys, encrypted at rest - [ ] 2.7 Personal access tokens for the API, CLI and SDK **Phase 3: Quotas and abuse** - [ ] 3.1 Persistent build queue with per-workspace concurrency - [ ] 3.2 Usage metering and per-workspace budgets - [ ] 3.3 Retention and garbage collection - [ ] 3.4 Builder pod timeouts and resource limits - [ ] 3.5 Curated BuildPolicy - [ ] 3.6 Operator builder support for every curated build option - [ ] 3.7 Audit log, abuse signals and account suspension **Phase 4: Scale and caching** - [ ] 4.1 Object storage: choose a backend and implement the S3 ArtifactStore - [ ] 4.2 Run more than one replica - [ ] 4.3 Resolve and record digests for every build input - [ ] 4.4 Shared content-addressed build cache - [ ] 4.5 zot pull-through cache next to the builders **Phase 5: Infrastructure and operations** - [ ] 5.1 k3s cluster on the OVH machines - [ ] 5.2 PostgreSQL with backups - [ ] 5.3 Ingress, TLS, DNS and host firewall - [ ] 5.4 Monitoring and alerting - [ ] 5.5 Hosted values profile for the Helm chart - [ ] 5.6 Deployment pipeline and operations runbook - [ ] 5.7 Terms of service, privacy policy, data export and deletion, abuse contact **Phase 6: Custom builds (after launch)** - [ ] 6.1 Run untrusted build steps in a sandboxed runtime class - [ ] 6.2 Egress allowlist proxy for untrusted build steps - [ ] 6.3 Trusted tier in BuildPolicy **Phase 7: Hosted fleet management (after launch)** - [ ] 7.1 Node-generated identity and approval-based enrolment - [ ] 7.2 Per-workspace node enrollment and command isolation ### Open questions and conflicts - **Name and domain.** #3396 asked for `factory.kairoslabs.io`, and product naming is open in #4208. The public hostname should wait for that decision. #5222 re-brands the UI to "Kairos". - **Repository move.** #4423 (and the migration half of #5222) moves the AuroraBoot code into `kairos-io/kairos`. Phase 1 touches most of the server, so sequence it against the move to avoid a long-lived rebase. - **Node-facing changes need coordination with the CAPI fleet provider.** #4117 asks that registration and node-auth changes are not made unilaterally because they can break the CAPI Kairos Fleet integration. 7.1 and 7.2 need a review from that side. The fleet provider (`cluster-api-provider-kairos-fleet`) claims, commands and releases nodes with the admin token and never registers them, so it is affected only through node identity; the bootstrap provider (`cluster-api-provider-kairos`) reads `node_id` from the agent's credentials file to set the provider ID. - **How an accepted node authenticates (7.1).** Either the server issues a bearer key when it accepts the node, which is close to today's code, or the node signs every request with its own key or uses mTLS, which is stronger because no shared secret ever crosses the wire but is a larger agent change. Decided when 7.1 is picked up. - **Shared cache warm set:** which flavour and version combinations to pre-build, if any, is decided in 4.4. ### Related, not part of this epic - #4117 fleet-server hardening (remaining items owned there; the `ServeArtifacts`/`ServeUkiPXE` auth question is moot for hosted because netboot is not mounted). - #5085 KMS integration (may provide the key-encryption backend for 2.6). - #4363 airgap support for `baseImage` (touches the same image-resolution code as 4.3). ## Item details Proposed ticket title in each summary line; the body is the starting point for the ticket when it is opened.
0.1 AuroraBoot builder: an image reference with a newline injects Dockerfile instructions **Problem.** The local builder splices user-supplied image references straight into generated Dockerfiles: `BaseImage` and `KairosInitImage` into the kairosify `FROM` lines, `HadronBase` into a prepended `FROM`, and the artifact image into the extension `FROM` (`internal/builder/auroraboot/builder.go`, `internal/builder/auroraboot/extension.go`). A value containing a newline adds arbitrary instructions, including `RUN`, to a build that the user believes is curated. `Model`, `KairosVersion` and `KubernetesVersion` are already validated (from #4117); the image fields are not. **Scope.** - Parse every image reference field with `name.ParseReference` (go-containerregistry) at the API boundary and reject anything that does not parse, including image-resolver URIs (`docker://`, `oci:`, `dir:`, `file:`, `ocifile:`), which are not valid in a `FROM` line. The value is checked, not rewritten: it is stored as the user supplied it. - Validate once, before any backend: a wrapper around every artifact and extension builder rejects a bad reference, so new backends and new code paths inside a backend do not have to repeat the check. References that do not come from the request (the kairos-init image from the environment, a stored artifact's image) are validated where they enter the builder. **Acceptance criteria.** - Creating an artifact or extension with a newline, space or control character in any image field returns 400. - Existing valid references (tags, digests, registries with ports) keep working. - Tests cover each field. **Related.** #4117 (the same class of fix for `Model`/`KairosVersion`).
0.2 AuroraBoot API: build requests take raw server paths (buildContextDir, overlayRootfs, signing key paths) **Problem.** `createArtifactRequest` accepts filesystem paths on the server: `buildContextDir` becomes the docker build context, `overlayRootfs` is copied into the image, and the `signing` block takes key and certificate paths (`pkg/handlers/artifacts.go`). Any API caller can read server files into an artifact (the secrets directory, the database, other key sets) or sign with any key on disk. `UploadOverlay` returns a server path that is later trusted as input. **Scope.** - Overlays and build contexts are referenced by an upload ID that the server resolves to a path it owns. - Signing references a secure boot key set by ID only; raw key paths are removed from the HTTP API (the CLI keeps them, since there the caller owns the filesystem). - `ukiKeySetId` lookups go through the store, so 2.1 can scope them later. **Acceptance criteria.** - The HTTP API has no field that is interpreted as a server path. - The UI and SDK keep working through upload and key-set IDs. - Tests assert that a path-like value in any field is rejected.
0.4 AuroraBoot web: no limits on request bodies, uploads or stored build logs **Problem.** The Echo server has no body-limit middleware. `RegistrationTokenAuth` does `io.ReadAll` on the request body before authenticating. The overlay upload has no size cap for non-tar files, the exporter upload accepts up to 20 GiB per file, and build logs are appended to an unbounded text column on the artifact and extension records. **Scope.** - A global body limit with explicit larger limits on the upload routes. - Read the registration body through a `LimitReader`. - Cap stored log size per build (keep the tail, mark truncation), until 1.5 moves logs out of the database. **Acceptance criteria.** - Oversized requests get 413 before the body is buffered. - A build that prints without bound cannot grow its database row past the cap. - Tests for each limit. **Related.** #4117 (`downloadFile` response size cap).
0.5 AuroraBoot web builder: the full cloud-config is written into the build log **Problem.** `run` in `internal/builder/auroraboot/builder.go` prints `Cloud config:` followed by the whole cloud-config into the build log, which is stored in the database and streamed to every connected UI client. Cloud-configs carry the registration token, user passwords and SSH keys. AuroraBoot#888 fixed the same thing on the `build-iso` deployer path (#5098); the web builder path was not covered. **Scope.** Log that a cloud-config was supplied and its size or hash, never its contents. Extend the redaction values to anything the builder knows is secret. **Acceptance criteria.** A test builds with a cloud-config containing a marker secret and asserts it does not appear in the stored or streamed log. **Related.** #5098, AuroraBoot#888.
0.6 AuroraBoot web: credentials travel in URLs and live in localStorage; WebSocket origin is not checked **Problem.** The UI stores the admin password in `localStorage` and puts it in download URLs and in the UI WebSocket URL as `?token=`. The WebSocket upgrader's `CheckOrigin` always returns true (`pkg/ws/handler.go`). Query-string credentials leak into browser history, proxy logs and `Referer` headers; any page the admin visits can open the UI WebSocket. The secure boot key set endpoints return server paths (`keysDir`, `tpmPcrKeyPath` on `store.SecureBootKeySet`), which tell any API caller where keys live on disk. **Scope.** - The UI signs in with an HttpOnly session cookie that expires after 12 hours, and downloads use that cookie. "Copy link" hands out a signed URL for one file that expires after an hour. The admin password is no longer accepted in `?token=` (AuroraBoot#951). - The UI WebSocket authenticates with the session cookie. Both WebSocket upgrades, and cookie-authenticated mutations, refuse an `Origin` other than the request host or the configured server URL (AuroraBoot#951). - The agent WebSocket reads the node key from the `Authorization` header and still accepts `?token=` until the kairos agent sends the header; the SDK already does (AuroraBoot#951). Node image downloads already use the header. - API responses carry no server filesystem paths: key sets are identified by ID only, and the SDK (`pkg/client`), UI and swagger follow. Item 0.2 removed paths from requests (AuroraBoot#928). - `POST /api/v1/artifacts` returns the stored artifact record. Today it returns `builder.BuildStatus`, whose `artifacts` field is documented as paths to built files, while swagger (`store.ArtifactRecord`) and the SDK (`ArtifactsService.Create` returns `*Artifact`) both promise the record, so fields such as `overlayId` are silently empty on the SDK's result. Found while adding the overlay integration spec in AuroraBoot#928. **Acceptance criteria.** - No long-lived credential appears in any URL the UI builds. - A WebSocket upgrade from a foreign origin is refused. - No API response contains a server filesystem path. - Tests for each. **Related.** #4703, AuroraBoot#773.
1.1 AuroraBoot store: versioned migrations instead of AutoMigrate **Problem.** The schema is created with GORM `AutoMigrate` only (`internal/store/gorm/store.go`). That cannot add NOT NULL ownership columns with backfill, change unique indexes, or move data, all of which tenancy (2.1) needs, on both SQLite and PostgreSQL. **Scope.** Adopt a migration tool that supports both dialects, generate a baseline from the current schema, make existing installs adopt the baseline without changes, and run migrations at startup. **Acceptance criteria.** - Fresh install and upgrade from the latest release both work on SQLite and PostgreSQL, covered by tests. - New schema changes are migrations, not model edits alone.
1.2 AuroraBoot web: deployment profiles, route modules and a capabilities endpoint **Problem.** Every feature (netboot, Redfish/BMC, fleet, builds) is wired unconditionally in `server.New`. A hosted deployment needs to drop some of them without scattering mode checks through handlers. **Scope.** - Group routes into modules that `server.New` mounts from a configuration. - `--profile=local|hosted` selects a preset; individual modules can be overridden. - `GET /api/v1/capabilities` lists the mounted modules, and the UI hides navigation and actions for absent ones. - The `local` profile mounts everything, exactly as today. **Acceptance criteria.** - Under `local`, the OpenAPI document and UI are unchanged. - Under a profile without netboot, the netboot routes return 404 and the UI does not show them. - Under `hosted`, the fleet module is not mounted: node registration, the node API and the agent WebSocket return 404. Registration hands out existing node keys until 7.1, so the hosted service must not accept nodes before then. - Tests per module.
1.3 AuroraBoot auth: Authenticator interface and a request principal **Problem.** Admin authentication is one middleware comparing a shared password. There is no notion of who the caller is, so nothing can be owned or scoped. **Scope.** - An `Authenticator` interface that turns a request into a `Principal` (user, workspace, roles) in the request context. - The admin password becomes one implementation, mapping to a built-in admin principal. - Handlers read the principal instead of assuming admin. **Acceptance criteria.** No behaviour change locally. Every admin handler obtains the principal from the context. Tests for the admin implementation.
1.4 AuroraBoot builds: BuildSpec, BuildPolicy admission and execution class **Problem.** Build requests go from the HTTP struct straight to the builder. Policies that depend on the caller (what may be built, with which runtime) have nowhere to live. **Scope.** - Normalise requests into a `BuildSpec` whose user-code fields (Dockerfile, ExtraSteps, base image, overlays) are explicit. - A `BuildPolicy` checks the spec against the principal before admission and assigns an execution class (`trusted` or `untrusted`). - The builders receive the class; the operator builder will map it to a runtime class and namespace later (6.1). - The local profile uses an allow-all policy. **Acceptance criteria.** No behaviour change locally. A test policy can reject a spec with a clear error before any build work starts.
1.5 AuroraBoot: ArtifactStore interface for build outputs and logs **Problem.** Outputs, overlays and extension files are read and written directly under `/artifacts` across handlers and builders, and logs live in a database text column. Neither works with more than one replica. **Scope.** - An `ArtifactStore` interface (put, get, stat, delete, list, signed URL) with a local-directory implementation. - Route every artifact, overlay, extension and log read or write through it. **Acceptance criteria.** No behaviour change locally. No handler or builder touches the artifacts directory directly.
1.6 AuroraBoot: QuotaPolicy interface **Problem.** There is no place to decide whether a caller may start another build or store more data. **Scope.** A `QuotaPolicy` consulted at build admission and on uploads, with an unlimited implementation. **Acceptance criteria.** No behaviour change locally. Admission and uploads call the policy, covered by tests with a rejecting fake.
2.1 AuroraBoot: workspaces, users and memberships; scope every resource **Scope.** - Add `User`, `Workspace` and `Membership` models. - Add a `workspace_id` to artifacts, extensions, key sets, groups, nodes, BMC targets, deployments and settings. - Scope every store query by the principal's workspace. - Make unique names unique per workspace. - Migrate existing data into a built-in workspace owned by the built-in admin. **Acceptance criteria.** - A request in workspace A cannot read, list, modify or reference (for example by key-set ID) a resource in workspace B, covered by tests for every resource type. - Local installs upgrade without visible change. **Depends on.** 1.1, 1.3.
2.2 AuroraBoot: OIDC login with cookie sessions **Scope.** kairos-io/AuroraBoot#951 added the session layer: an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict session cookie (Secure over HTTPS) that lasts 12 hours, the Origin rule on cookie-authenticated mutations, login and logout, and logout that deletes the session. Its sessions live in memory and carry no user. This item builds on it: - An OIDC `Authenticator` (authorization code with PKCE), with users matched by issuer and subject, that issues the session cookie and passes the same Origin rule. - Sessions that record the user and live in the store, so they survive a restart and work across replicas. An admin can revoke a user's sessions. - Deploy Dex as an optional chart dependency with GitHub and Google connectors. **Acceptance criteria.** - A user can sign in through Dex in an e2e test. - Sessions expire and can be revoked. - Admin-password auth is still available in the local profile. **Depends on.** 1.3, 2.1.
2.3 AuroraBoot: signup and account approval This replaces #3396, which asked for a signup page that gives access to a hosted instance. The dependency #3396 named (#3308) is done; the real blocker is this epic. **Scope.** - First sign-in creates a pending user with a personal workspace. - A site-admin role and an admin page list pending users and approve or reject them. - Pending users can sign in but cannot build. - Account requirements (verified email, GitHub account age) are configurable. **Acceptance criteria.** An unapproved user gets a clear "pending approval" state and every build call is refused. Approval takes effect without re-login. **Depends on.** 2.2. **Related.** #3396, #4208 (naming of the public page).
2.4 AuroraBoot: workspace roles and invitations **Scope.** - Owner, member and viewer roles, enforced per endpoint. - Invite by email or by GitHub handle. - Leave and transfer ownership. **Acceptance criteria.** Every mutating endpoint has a role check. Tests cover the role matrix. **Depends on.** 2.1.
2.5 AuroraBoot: scope UI WebSocket events to the workspace **Problem.** The UI hub broadcasts every build log chunk, netboot log and deploy progress event to every connected client (`pkg/ws/hub.go`). **Scope.** Tag events with their workspace and deliver only to clients whose principal belongs to it. **Acceptance criteria.** A client in workspace A receives no event about workspace B, covered by a test. **Depends on.** 2.1, 0.6.
2.6 AuroraBoot: per-workspace settings and secure boot keys, encrypted at rest **Problem.** Settings (registration token, image source, extension catalogs) are global. Secure boot and TPM PCR private keys are plaintext files under `/keys`, and the export endpoint returns them. **Scope.** - Move settings to the workspace. - Store key material encrypted with envelope encryption, with the key-encryption key held outside the database: a Kubernetes Secret first, a KMS later. - Decide whether private-key export stays available in the hosted profile. **Acceptance criteria.** - A database or PVC dump alone does not reveal any private key. - Settings changes in one workspace do not affect another. **Depends on.** 2.1, 1.5. **Related.** #5085.
2.7 AuroraBoot: personal access tokens for the API, CLI and SDK **Problem.** Scripted access (the SDK, CI) uses the admin bearer password today. With OIDC there is no non-interactive credential. **Scope.** - Tokens scoped to a user and workspace, with an expiry, stored hashed and revocable from the UI. - The SDK and CLI accept them. **Acceptance criteria.** A token can drive a full build and download. A revoked or expired token is refused. **Depends on.** 2.1.
3.1 AuroraBoot: persistent build queue with per-workspace concurrency **Problem.** Each build request starts a goroutine immediately (`Build` in `internal/builder/auroraboot/builder.go`). There is no queue or concurrency limit, and the in-memory build map does not survive restarts or work across replicas. **Scope.** - A database-backed queue that is safe with more than one replica (for example `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on PostgreSQL). - Global and per-workspace concurrency limits taken from `QuotaPolicy`. - Queue position visible in the UI. **Acceptance criteria.** - Submitting more builds than the workspace limit queues the extra ones. - Queued builds survive a restart. - Tests run on both store dialects. **Depends on.** 1.6, 2.1.
3.2 AuroraBoot: usage metering and per-workspace budgets **Scope.** - Record CPU-seconds per build from the builder pod's cgroup accounting, not wall time, plus stored bytes and artifact count per workspace. - Enforce monthly budgets at admission through `QuotaPolicy`. - Show usage and limits in the UI. - Budgets come from a tier on the workspace, so open signup later only needs a lower tier. **Acceptance criteria.** A workspace over budget cannot start a build and is told why. Usage figures match the pod metrics within a tolerance in an e2e test. **Depends on.** 3.1.
3.3 AuroraBoot: retention and garbage collection **Problem.** Nothing is ever removed except by manual delete. Unused overlay uploads and the Docker images left by each build accumulate. A `Saved` flag exists but nothing acts on it. **Scope.** - Configurable TTL for unsaved artifacts, with expiry shown in the UI. - A GC loop for orphaned uploads, builder images and expired artifacts. - In the local profile the default is no expiry. **Acceptance criteria.** - An expired artifact and its files are gone after a GC pass. - Saved artifacts are kept. - Local behaviour is unchanged by default. **Depends on.** 1.5.
3.4 AuroraBoot operator builder: per-build timeout and resource limits **Scope.** - A wall-clock deadline per build, after which the build is cancelled and marked as timed out. - CPU, memory and ephemeral-storage requests and limits on the build pods. - This may need fields on the kairos-operator `OSArtifact` CRD; if so, open the operator ticket and link it here. **Acceptance criteria.** A build that exceeds its deadline is cancelled, and its pods and outputs are cleaned up. Pods carry the configured limits.
3.5 AuroraBoot: curated BuildPolicy **Scope.** - A policy for the hosted profile that admits only base images from an allowlist (by repository, with tags resolved per 4.3) and extensions from the configured catalogs. - It rejects any user-code field (Dockerfile, ExtraSteps, overlays, arbitrary base images, `allow-insecure-registries`). - It assigns the `trusted` execution class. **Acceptance criteria.** - Each rejected field produces a clear error at admission. - The UI hides options the policy rejects, through the capabilities endpoint. **Depends on.** 1.4.
3.6 AuroraBoot operator builder: support every curated build option **Problem.** The operator builder silently ignores several build options that the local builder supports: `Signing`, `Variant`, `Provisioning` and `KairosInitImage` (plus `OverlayRootfs` and `BuildContextDir`, which the curated profile does not need) (`internal/builder/operator/builder.go`). The hosted service runs the operator builder, so UKI signing and the other curated options would be silently missing. **Scope.** - Support each curated option in the operator path, or reject it at admission with an error. Never ignore it silently. - Cross-repo work with kairos-operator where the CRD lacks fields. **Acceptance criteria.** For each curated option, a test either shows it reflected in the produced artifact or shows that admission rejects it.
3.7 AuroraBoot: audit log, abuse signals and account suspension **Scope.** - An append-only audit log of security-relevant actions: sign-in, approval, build, download, key export, settings changes. - Abuse signals: - repeated builds that time out at full CPU without producing an artifact - blocked egress attempts (after 6.2) - unusual download volume - Automatic suspension pending admin review, and an admin view of the signals. **Acceptance criteria.** - Audit entries for each listed action. - A synthetic miner-like build pattern suspends the account in an e2e test. **Depends on.** 2.1, 3.2.
4.1 AuroraBoot: object storage backend and S3 ArtifactStore **Scope.** - Choose the backend: AWS S3 or self-hosted (Garage, SeaweedFS, Rook/Ceph RGW). MinIO is excluded because of its licensing and distribution changes. - Implement the S3 `ArtifactStore`, with presigned download URLs replacing proxied downloads. - The operator exporter uploads directly with presigned PUTs. **Acceptance criteria.** Builds, downloads and GC work end to end against the chosen backend in CI (an S3-compatible test server is fine). **Depends on.** 1.5.
4.2 AuroraBoot: run more than one replica **Problem.** Several things assume a single process: - in-memory state: the build map, both WebSocket hubs, metrics and netboot - the Helm chart: `replicaCount: 1`, `strategy: Recreate`, an RWO PVC **Scope.** - Move build state into the store. - Fan out WebSocket events across replicas (PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY or similar). - Leader election for reconcilers and GC. - Switch the chart to RollingUpdate with no PVC when an object store is configured. **Acceptance criteria.** With two replicas behind the service, a build started on one is visible, cancellable and streamable from the other. A rolling upgrade does not fail running builds. **Depends on.** 3.1, 4.1.
4.3 AuroraBoot: resolve and record digests for every build input **Scope.** - Before a build starts, resolve the base image, kairos-init image, extension images and catalog entries to digests, and store them on the artifact record. - Builds use the digests. - This also makes local builds reproducible and lets "clone" rebuild exactly the same inputs. **Acceptance criteria.** The artifact record shows the resolved digests, and a clone of an old artifact uses them. **Related.** #4363.
4.4 AuroraBoot: shared content-addressed build cache **Scope.** - Key the expensive stages (kairosified image, unpacked rootfs or squashfs, base ISO without cloud-config) by a hash of their digest-pinned inputs. - Store them in the object store and reuse them across workspaces. - Per-workspace final assembly (cloud-config injection, signing, UKI) always runs fresh and is never shared. - Decide whether to pre-build a warm set. **Acceptance criteria.** - Two workspaces building the same curated inputs with different cloud-configs share the cached stages. - They get different final artifacts. - Neither can obtain the other's output. - Cache hit and miss are visible in the build log. **Depends on.** 4.1, 4.3.
4.5 AuroraBoot hosted: zot pull-through cache next to the builders **Scope.** - Deploy zot as a pull-through cache for the registries the curated allowlist uses, and point the builders at it. - BuildKit does not read the dockerd `--registry-mirror` setting (the root cause in AuroraBoot#826), so configure the mirror wherever the build actually pulls. **Acceptance criteria.** A second build of the same base image pulls from zot, as shown by its metrics. **Related.** First comment on #3385, AuroraBoot#826.
5.1 Hosted AuroraBoot: k3s cluster on the OVH machines **Scope.** - Provision k3s across the machines (Kairos itself is the obvious choice). - Separate node roles for the control plane and build workers. - Storage for PVCs. - Document the layout. **Acceptance criteria.** The cluster is reproducible from the documented steps or the infra repo. **Related.** #4553.
5.2 Hosted AuroraBoot: PostgreSQL with backups **Scope.** - Choose and deploy PostgreSQL (in-cluster operator or managed). - Automated backups to object storage, and a tested restore procedure. **Acceptance criteria.** A restore drill from backup succeeds and is documented.
5.3 Hosted AuroraBoot: ingress, TLS, DNS and host firewall **Scope.** - Ingress with cert-manager TLS (the chart already supports both). - DNS for the public name, once #4208 settles it. - Host firewall exposing only HTTPS and the cluster's own needs. - No netboot or host networking. **Acceptance criteria.** An external scan shows only the intended ports. **Related.** #4208, #3396.
5.4 Hosted AuroraBoot: monitoring and alerting **Scope.** - Metrics for AuroraBoot, the builders, the queue, storage and the database. - Alerts on queue depth, build failure rate, disk, certificate expiry and abuse signals (3.7). - Centralised logs with a retention limit, and no cloud-config contents in them. **Acceptance criteria.** Alerts fire in a test and reach the agreed channel.
5.5 AuroraBoot Helm chart: hosted values profile **Scope.** - A values file for the hosted deployment: profile `hosted`, OIDC settings, object store, PostgreSQL, quotas, netboot off. - Manage the admin password from a Secret; the chart does not set it today, as noted on #3396. - Narrow the builder Role, which can read and write every Secret in the builder namespace. **Acceptance criteria.** helm-unittest coverage for the hosted values. A `helm install` with them brings up a working instance in CI. **Related.** #3396.
5.6 Hosted AuroraBoot: deployment pipeline and operations runbook **Scope.** - How releases reach the hosted instance (pinned chart and image versions, a promotion step). - The rollback procedure. - An on-call runbook covering a stuck queue, a full storage, a suspended account appeal and an OVH abuse report. **Acceptance criteria.** The runbook exists, and an upgrade and a rollback have been performed with it.
5.7 Hosted AuroraBoot: terms of service, privacy policy, data export and deletion, abuse contact **Scope.** - Terms of service and an acceptable use policy (mining and abuse explicitly prohibited). - A privacy policy (users upload cloud-configs with secrets, and the servers are in the EU). - Account data export and deletion endpoints. - A published abuse contact. **Acceptance criteria.** The policies are linked from the signup flow. Export and deletion work end to end.
6.1 AuroraBoot: run untrusted build steps in a sandboxed runtime class **Scope.** - Evaluate gVisor and Kata on the cluster against real builds (loop devices and filesystem tooling may need the privileged final stages split out from the untrusted ones). - Map the `untrusted` execution class to the chosen runtime class and a dedicated namespace. **Acceptance criteria.** A user Dockerfile build runs under the sandbox runtime. The privileged stages never run user code. **Depends on.** 1.4.
6.2 AuroraBoot: egress allowlist proxy for untrusted build steps **Scope.** - Untrusted build pods reach the network only through a proxy that allows registries, distribution package mirrors, GitHub releases and the Kairos catalogs, enforced with NetworkPolicy. - Blocked attempts are logged as an abuse signal. **Acceptance criteria.** A build step cannot open a connection to an arbitrary host or port. Package installs from the allowed mirrors work. **Depends on.** 6.1.
6.3 AuroraBoot: trusted tier in BuildPolicy **Scope.** - A workspace tier that admits user-code fields with the `untrusted` execution class. - Granted by site admins. - Its own budgets in `QuotaPolicy`. **Acceptance criteria.** A trusted-tier workspace can submit a custom Dockerfile build, and a curated-tier workspace cannot. **Depends on.** 6.1, 6.2, 3.5.
7.1 AuroraBoot fleet: node-generated identity and approval-based enrolment **Problem.** Every image built for a fleet carries the same registration token, and that token is the only thing a node presents to enrol. Anyone holding any such ISO can register, the image is unique to whoever built it (so it cannot be shared or cached), and a node's identity is its machine-id, which is guessable and changes on bare metal whenever the persistent partition is wiped (reset, reinstall, live reboot). The server then cannot tell a reset node from a new one, so `resolveReset` only works where the machine-id is stable (VMs that derive it from the SMBIOS product UUID). Registration is idempotent by machine-id and returns the existing node's `apiKey` (`Register` in `pkg/handlers/nodes.go`), so anyone with the token and a known machine-id gets that node's credentials. `RegistrationTokenAuth` compares the token with `!=` (`pkg/auth/middleware.go`); AuroraBoot#729 moved the admin and node comparisons to constant time but not this one. The comment on `resolveReset` says the agent registers on every boot; it registers only when it has no saved credentials. **Scope.** - The node's identity is a key it generates itself. Bind it to the TPM where one is present (endorsement key hash, as `kcrypt-discovery-challenger` already does for its TOFU enrolment), so it survives reset and reinstall; fall back to a software key on the persistent partition otherwise. - An unknown key registers as a pending node. An admin accepts or rejects it, comparing a fingerprint or short code that the node shows on its console and in its logs. Accepting can adopt the pending node into an existing record (same group, labels and history), and the server suggests the match from the TPM identity, machine-id or hostname. - Pre-approval tokens replace the shared registration token as the zero-touch path (CAPI, PXE at scale, `install.auto`): scoped to a group, expiring, optionally limited in uses and revocable. An image without one still enrols, and its nodes wait for approval. - Images no longer need a secret to enrol, only the server URL, so a fleet image can be built from public inputs and cached. - A device-code style binding, where the user enters the node's code in the UI, so a generic image can enrol into the right workspace (used by 7.2). - Registration never returns a stored key. A known identity without proof of it goes through approval like a new node. - Re-enrolment of a node that AuroraBoot itself reset is recognised without human action, on bare metal as well as VMs. - Token comparisons are constant time. - Keep the contracts other components rely on: the agent's credentials file stays at `/usr/local/.kairos/phonehome-credentials.yaml` with a `node_id` key, and a node's ID (the AuroraBoot node UUID) does not change across re-enrolment or adoption. The CAPI bootstrap provider builds the provider ID `kairos-fleet://` from that file, and the fleet provider's planned reset-on-delete needs the node to come back as the same record. - An agent whose key is revoked or rotated stops retrying with it and re-enrols, instead of reconnecting with the old key forever. - Agent changes in `kairos-io/kairos`, a migration path for agents already enrolled with a shared-token key, and the pending-node UI. Agree the agent-side behaviour with the CAPI provider owners (see #4117). **Acceptance criteria.** - An image built without a token enrols only after an admin accepts the node. - A node with a valid pre-approval token enrols without human action, and an expired, exhausted or revoked token falls back to approval. - A reset or reinstalled node with a TPM is recognised as the same node. - Holding an image or knowing a machine-id gives no access to an existing node's credentials. - A reset or reinstalled node has a documented way to re-enrol, and keeps its node ID when adopted. - Tests for each, plus an e2e test of the reset lifecycle on a node whose machine-id changes. **Open question.** How an accepted node authenticates (see Open questions above). **Related.** #4117, AuroraBoot#729, AuroraBoot#772, the CAPI bootstrap and fleet providers, `kcrypt-discovery-challenger`.
7.2 AuroraBoot hosted: per-workspace node enrollment and command isolation **Scope.** - Per-workspace pre-approval tokens and binding of pending nodes to a workspace, on top of 7.1. - Nodes, groups and commands scoped to the workspace. - Agent WebSocket connections bound to the workspace. - The artifact image download for nodes scoped as in AuroraBoot#773, plus the workspace check. - Mount the fleet module in the hosted profile. **Acceptance criteria.** - A node enrolled in workspace A is invisible to workspace B. - A node from B cannot fetch A's artifacts. - A user in B cannot issue commands to A's nodes. **Depends on.** 2.1, 7.1. **Related.** #4117, AuroraBoot#773, the CAPI fleet provider.

items.title: infra: Soleur-managed deploy substrate for multi-tenant platform (scaffolding via self-hosted GH Actions runner)

labels.name: priority/p2-medium
labels.description: Important but not urgent, workaround exists

labels.name: domain/engineering
labels.description: Plugin code, CI/CD, infra, docs site (CTO)

milestone.title: Post-MVP / Later
milestone.description: Valid issues that don't fit in any current roadmap phase. Reviewed periodically for promotion when user demand or strategic direction changes.

items.body:
## Strategic framing (reframed 2026-05-13 post-#3719 merge)

**The original framing was wrong.** This issue was opened during the unified-ci-deploy-stall-hardening brainstorm as "fix the auto-apply IP-allowlist drift for *this* repo's deploy pipeline" — i.e., ops toil reduction for Jean's laptop. That framing dissolved on closer look.

The actual underlying constraint is a **product-architecture prerequisite**: Soleur is building a platform where non-technical users author web apps and Soleur manages their infra. The "operator-manual `terraform apply` from an allowlisted laptop" path that worked for #3712 (Jean has terraform + Doppler CLI + `prd_terraform` token + allowlisted IP + the runbook in `learnings/bug-fixes/2026-04-29-deploy-pipeline-fix-postapply-verification-cf-access.md`) does NOT generalize to a multi-tenant product. A non-technical Soleur user cannot run `terraform apply` against their own infra.

So this isn't "should we automate ops toil?" It's **"what's the substrate Soleur uses to apply deploy-pipeline fixes for tenants who never touch a terminal?"** — a question whose answer Soleur owes the product, not the backlog.

## Scope (this issue)

Ship the **first concrete step** toward Soleur-managed deploy infra: a self-hosted GH Actions runner on Hetzner that closes the immediate auto-apply allowlist drift AND serves as the proof-of-concept substrate for the multi-tenant model. The wider architecture (per-tenant runners vs. central pool vs. custom control plane vs. Cloudflare Worker driving terraform) is a separate brainstorm; this issue ships a concrete piece that informs that brainstorm with real load-bearing data.

### Immediate problem this closes

`apply-deploy-pipeline-fix.yml` is the auto-apply for `terraform_data.deploy_pipeline_fix` (per [`learnings/bug-fixes/2026-04-24-recurring-deploy-pipeline-fix-drift-as-feature.md`](https://github.com/jikig-ai/soleur/blob/main/knowledge-base/project/learnings/bug-fixes/2026-04-24-recurring-deploy-pipeline-fix-drift-as-feature.md)). It ran for the first time on merge `dc7c8b71` (PR #3706) and **timed out** with `dial tcp 135.181.45.178:22: i/o timeout` because the GitHub Actions runner's outbound IP isn't in `var.admin_ips`. The 2026-03-19 hidden-dependency learning explicitly precludes allowlisting GH runner IPs (5000+ rotating ranges). Every future merge touching the 5 trigger files (`ci-deploy.sh`, `ci-deploy-wrapper.sh`, `webhook.service`, `cat-deploy-state.sh`, `hooks.json.tmpl`) will fail identically until this is resolved.

### Proposal (concrete first step)

Provision a small self-hosted GH Actions runner on Hetzner Cloud as a separate Terraform root (`apps/web-platform/infra/runner/`):

- ~€4/mo Hetzner CX11 or CPX11
- Static IP added once to Doppler `prd_terraform/ADMIN_IPS`
- Registered with the org as an actions runner with a narrow runner-group scoped to `apply-deploy-pipeline-fix.yml` and any future prod-write workflows
- Same Hetzner network/blast-radius posture as the prod server
- New Terraform root MUST include a destroy runbook per `hr-every-new-terraform-root-must-include-an`

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New terraform root at `apps/web-platform/infra/runner/` provisions a Hetzner VM + runner registration
- [ ] Destroy runbook at `knowledge-base/engineering/ops/runbooks/runner-destroy.md`
- [ ] Runner IP added to Doppler `prd_terraform/ADMIN_IPS` via `/soleur:admin-ip-refresh`
- [ ] ADR via `/soleur:architecture create "Self-hosted GH Actions runner for prod-write workflows (Soleur-managed-infra scaffolding)"` — MUST capture the multi-tenant framing as the load-bearing rationale, NOT just the IP-allowlist symptom
- [ ] `apply-deploy-pipeline-fix.yml` updated to `runs-on: [self-hosted, prod-apply]` (or equivalent)
- [ ] One organic merge to a pipeline-fix trigger file demonstrates successful auto-apply

## What this is NOT (out of scope here)

This issue ships the substrate scaffolding; it does NOT design the multi-tenant deploy architecture. Open questions deferred to a separate `/soleur:brainstorm`:

1. **Per-tenant runner vs. central pool?** Single Soleur-managed runner that knows how to deploy to N tenant VMs, vs. one runner per tenant? Cost vs. isolation tradeoff.
2. **RBAC + audit substrate.** When Soleur applies prod-fixes for tenant X, the audit trail must distinguish "Soleur infra team triggered apply" from "tenant X triggered apply via Soleur UI." The current `hr-menu-option-ack-not-prod-write-auth` model assumes operator = decision-maker; multi-tenant breaks that.
3. **GH Actions vs. custom control plane.** Is GH Actions the right primitive long-term, or is this scaffolding-only on the path to a Cloudflare Worker / Hetzner-native ops system?
4. **Secrets per-tenant.** Where does each tenant's Doppler-equivalent live? How does the runner access them without becoming a single point of credential aggregation?

These questions are answered by the broader brainstorm; #3723 ships the concrete substrate that informs it.

## Alternatives previously rejected (still rejected)

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Allowlist GH Actions runner IP ranges in `ADMIN_IPS` | Rejected — 5000+ rotating ranges per `api.github.com/meta`, defeats the allowlist (`learnings/2026-03-19-ci-ssh-deploy-firewall-hidden-dependency.md`). |
| Tailscale/WireGuard mesh | Overengineered for one workflow; adds persistent control-plane dependency. |
| Delete `apply-deploy-pipeline-fix.yml`, make it operator-manual | **Now explicitly rejected on product grounds.** The operator-manual path only works for Jean. It does NOT generalize to non-technical Soleur users. The 2026-05-13 bundle (#3712/#3704/#2207) verified this by reasoning through the multi-tenant case during /soleur:go post-merge review. |
| Defer with 60-day re-evaluation trigger | Withdrawn — that framing assumed this was ops toil. Product framing means it's a prereq, not a backlog ledger entry. |

## References

- Origin bundle: brainstorm `knowledge-base/project/brainstorms/2026-05-13-unified-ci-deploy-stall-hardening-brainstorm.md`, spec `knowledge-base/project/specs/feat-unified-ci-deploy-stall-hardening/spec.md`
- Closed siblings: #3712, #3704, #2207 (operator-manual path proven viable for the *current* Soleur posture; this issue is the next-step substrate)
- Durable fix that triggered discovery: PR #3706
- Hidden-dependency origin: `learnings/2026-03-19-ci-ssh-deploy-firewall-hidden-dependency.md`
- Recurring-drift framing: `learnings/bug-fixes/2026-04-24-recurring-deploy-pipeline-fix-drift-as-feature.md`
- Reframing rationale: this issue body, 2026-05-13 update — multi-tenant product framing introduced post-#3719 merge.

---

## Brainstorm artifacts (2026-05-14)

This issue was reframed during the 2026-05-14 brainstorm to cover the **multi-tenant deploy substrate question only**. The symptom-fix (Soleur monorepo CI auto-apply IP-drift) split to a sibling issue.

- **Brainstorm:** `knowledge-base/project/brainstorms/2026-05-14-soleur-managed-deploy-substrate-multi-tenant-brainstorm.md`
- **Spec:** `knowledge-base/project/specs/feat-soleur-managed-deploy-substrate-3723/spec.md`
- **Branch:** `feat-soleur-managed-deploy-substrate-3723`
- **Draft PR:** #3744
- **Sibling symptom-fix issue:** #3756 (CF Tunnel + webhook replacement for `terraform_data.deploy_pipeline_fix`'s SSH provisioner)

### Key decisions from brainstorm

1. The original "Hetzner self-hosted runner" proposal was eliminated. The triad (CPO + CLO + CTO) surfaced that it silently reverses prior decision #749 and aggregates prod-write credentials in a persistent VM.
2. **Approach A — per-tenant GitHub Actions OIDC + tenant-owned cloud accounts** is the chosen v1 substrate. Zero credential aggregation by construction. Approaches B (CF Worker executor) and C (pure BYOInfra OAuth) are documented as open escape hatches with explicit re-evaluation triggers.
3. **Validation gate:** Jean (operator) creating his first non-Soleur project via Soleur is the forcing function. ADR captures "validated by founder-as-first-tenant" as the rationale.
4. **CLO pre-merge primitives:** RoPA entry, ADR, day-1 audit log to Supabase eu-west-1, `/soleur:gdpr-gate` clean.
5. **Hard constraint (User-Brand Impact):** no Soleur-owned process may hold credentials for >1 tenant simultaneously.
6. **Citation correction:** the original issue body cited `hr-every-new-terraform-root-must-include-an` as a destroy-runbook rule; the actual rule (AGENTS.core.md:16) mandates the R2 backend. A destroy runbook is good practice per ADR-019 but not the rule the issue cited.

This issue remains OPEN tracking the multi-tenant substrate v1 implementation. Next step: `/soleur:plan #3723` from the worktree.

items.title: Restart: Signalbox is rebuilt on a deep-module architecture (2026-10-18)

labels.name: decision
labels.description: A choice the founders need to make

items.body:
Signalbox restarts from scratch on a deep-module architecture. These are target decisions, not claims about deployed code.

- Restart from scratch: there are zero users, earlier work counts as experiments, and upstream compatibility is optional so the prototype cannot dictate the product.
- The work is the root object, never the person using it, so shared work has one durable home.
- Domain language is only a person's top level and freely nested folders; an organization can own a folder but is never a kind, so the hierarchy has one meaning everywhere.
- Pools, connections, secrets, skills, instructions, automations and devices are placed in the hierarchy; availability depends only on position and reach below, nearest wins, and anything outside the chain needs explicit revocable lending, so the sender, starter and credential owner never change resolution.
- Each person has an assistant and a pipeline with Blocker, Ready and Considering lanes above the whole tree, so attention belongs to the person while work stays in its folder.
- Claude Code and Codex run in the V8 isolate tier, Durable Objects plus Dynamic Workers, with no container or VM fallback for the harness; the harness mostly waits on the model and isolates bill CPU used.
- boxd is the VM and warm-Base provider; threads, CI and variants fork a warm snapshot of main's last green state, and VMs only execute commands, so the agent never lives on a machine.
- Drives use Artifacts with a fork per thread and R2 as the full record, so files and history survive machine loss and hot-tier eviction.
- One model gateway fronts CLIProxyAPI pools, so subscriptions and API keys have one routing and custody boundary.
- Executor is absorbed into Signalbox; connections and tools attach to folders, so there is no second service owning the same hierarchy.
- Use libraries, not a host framework: Cloudflare libraries sit behind our own small interfaces, so hosting details stay replaceable.
- Modules are deep, with named inputs and outputs and swappable adapters; implementation stays inside each module, so callers do not learn its machinery.
- Architecture lives as LikeC4 code in `architecture/` and must stay true to code under #1186, so the diagrams can be trusted when making changes.
- Diagrams show modules as black boxes with drill-down, interface size, hidden implementation and real adapters; workflows show the interfaces crossed, so shallow boundaries and reach-inside dependencies are visible.
- Multiplayer uses one shared folder and one shared thread across people's trees; views show at least three people and their private work too, so sharing and hierarchy resolution are tested as part of the model.
- In-app automations are visualized with LikeC4 generated from their source, with drill-down into composed automations, so we do not build a separate diagram renderer.
- The full target architecture is independent of deadlines; v1 is only sign-in, a pool and connections, so the first delivery does not distort later interfaces.

Architecture and domain-language checks: #1186.

items.title: defect(tachi-orchestrator): Phase-3 compilation can absorb output-integrity findings into the LLM-N sequence, dropping the OI- prefix carve-out and CWE citations (F-295 T026 gate FAIL)
items.body:
## Context

Discovered during Feature #295 (F-292 post-merge verification runs, US2/T013, SC-015 Cat 6 evidence baseline) while gating the fresh `tachi.threat-model` pipeline run over `examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/architecture.md`. FR-009 requires the run to yield ≥1 `output-integrity` finding on the Cat 6 (Vector/Search-DSL Injection) pattern surface, carrying the `OI-` finding-ID prefix and CWE-943 as primary. The T013 gate evaluates this and **FAILS**.

This is a compilation-tier defect, not a detection-tier defect: the underlying Cat 6 pattern (Pinecone `tenant_id`-omission via LLM-synthesized metadata filter) **was correctly detected** — it is fully described, correctly attributed to OWASP LLM05:2025 + LLM08:2025, and rated Critical. The defect is that the orchestrator's Phase-3 compilation step assigned the findings into the generic `LLM-N` ID sequence instead of the required `OI-` prefix, and dropped the CWE-943 citation entirely in the process.

## Gate evaluation (T013, all three commands run against the committed run output)

Run: `examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/test-output/2026-07-03T13-28-42/` (attempt 2/2, fresh synchronous `tachi-orchestrator` run, all 5 phases complete; 51 raw → 43 deduplicated findings, 17 Critical / 17 High / 8 Medium / 1 Low).

```bash
$ grep -c "| OI-" examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/test-output/2026-07-03T13-28-42/threats.md
0
$ grep -c "CWE-943" examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/test-output/2026-07-03T13-28-42/threats.md
0
$ jq '[.runs[0].results[] | select(.partialFingerprints["findingId/v1"] // "" | startswith("OI-"))] | length' examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/test-output/2026-07-03T13-28-42/threats.sarif
0
```

FR-009 requires ≥1 `OI-`-prefixed, CWE-943-primary finding. Zero on all three axes ⇒ **gate FAIL**.

## The pattern surface WAS detected — as `LLM-10` / `LLM-11`

`threats.md` (Section 4, LLM Threat Table):

> `LLM-10` \| LLM Query Synthesizer \| L1 — Foundation Model \| — \| The synthesizer's output is executed by Pinecone's metadata-filter DSL — a search-DSL query-execution engine analogous to a SQL WHERE clause — against the entire Pool-model shared index with no server-side validation that the tenant clause is present. **This is Cat 6 Vector/Search-DSL Injection.** \| OWASP LLM05:2025, OWASP LLM08:2025 \| HIGH \| HIGH \| Critical \| Restrict the synthesizer's LLM call to emit only the query-terms portion (never a tenant_id clause). Require RAG Retriever to AND-compose an immutable base-filter pin from the JWT-validated tenant_id, raising SecurityError on any override attempt. Adopt namespace-per-tenant (Silo model). Layer allowlisted clause-key validation.

> `LLM-11` \| RAG Retriever \| L2 — Data Operations \| — \| RAG Retriever receives the LLM-emitted filter and forwards it byte-for-byte into Pinecone's query-execution engine without inspecting, validating, or supplementing it — the last control point before **Cat 6 Vector/Search-DSL Injection** reaches execution against the shared index. \| OWASP LLM05:2025, OWASP LLM08:2025 \| HIGH \| HIGH \| Critical \| Implement pre-retrieval filtering / server-side filter composition at this component per the architecture's own design intent: strip any tenant_id key present in the LLM-emitted filter and AND-compose an immutable base-filter pin from the JWT-validated tenant_id, raising SecurityError on override attempts. Select the Pinecone namespace from the JWT-validated tenant_id as the stronger structural control.

Both rows are Critical, both explicitly self-label "Cat 6 Vector/Search-DSL Injection", both cite the correct OWASP pair (LLM05:2025 + LLM08:2025) — but neither carries an `OI-` id or a CWE-943 citation. They are indistinguishable in ID-shape and section placement from `LLM-1`..`LLM-9` (prompt injection, data poisoning, supply chain, model theft) and `LLM-12`/`LLM-13` (misinformation) — all 13 sit in one undifferentiated `LLM-N` sequence with no sub-heading or ID-family boundary separating output-integrity-agent-sourced findings from prompt-injection-agent-sourced or misinformation-agent-sourced findings. The Coverage Matrix (Section 5) likewise rolls output-integrity dispatch into a single "LLM" column (Total 11) with no distinct OI column — even though `scripts/sarif_common.py::PREFIX_TO_RULE` maps both `"OI"` and `"LLM"` prefixes to the *same* ruleId (`tachi/ai/llm`), which plausibly explains why a compilation step keyed on ruleId or category-family could conflate the two: an `OI`-vs-`LLM` id-prefix decision is not recoverable from ruleId alone.

## Counter-evidence: this is run-specific compilation nondeterminism, not a systematic pipeline regression

1. **Same-day T017 fallback run** (same orchestrator persona, same session): `specs/295-f292-verification-runs/test-results/t017-fallback-native-threats.sarif` compiles `OI-1`..`OI-4` correctly.
   ```bash
   $ jq '[.runs[0].results[] | select(.partialFingerprints["findingId/v1"] // "" | startswith("OI-"))] | length' specs/295-f292-verification-runs/test-results/t017-fallback-native-threats.sarif
   4
   ```
2. **Attempt-1 orphaned `tachi-output-integrity` agent return** for this exact architecture (`specs/295-f292-verification-runs/test-results/t026-attempt1-orphan-oi-return.md`): the agent's own native, uncompiled output uses `id: "OI-1"` and cites `CWE-943` (primary relationship) directly — before any Phase-3 compilation touched it.
3. **Committed `examples/agentic-app/sample-report/threats.sarif` at HEAD**: carries `OI-1`..`OI-4`.
   ```bash
   $ jq '[.runs[0].results[] | select(.partialFingerprints["findingId/v1"] // "" | startswith("OI-"))] | length' examples/agentic-app/sample-report/threats.sarif
   4
   ```

So the sub-agent itself reliably emits the `OI-` id and CWE-943 citation, and the orchestrator has compiled that shape correctly in at least two other instances (one same-day, one at HEAD). The defect is specifically in the Phase-3 compilation path taken on the T013 attempt-2 run of `multi-tenant-rag-app` — the OI-prefix carve-out is applied inconsistently rather than never.

## Related defects (same underlying mechanism — OI-prefix carve-out is unreliable at compile/commit time, different failure modes)

- #354 — the archived `cross-link-no-emission-contract.md` §3 verification procedure is itself dual-defective (broken filter + non-executable invocation) — the contract this carve-out was supposed to make verifiable.
- #355 — on the **committed** `agentic-app` baseline, the carve-out went the opposite direction: `OI-1..OI-4` rows were **added without removing** the pre-existing `LLM-5`/`LLM-6`/`LLM-7` rows describing the same threats (duplication, not absorption).
- This issue — on a **fresh** `multi-tenant-rag-app` run, the carve-out did not apply at all: the Cat 6 findings compiled purely under `LLM-10`/`LLM-11` with no `OI-` counterpart (absorption/non-emission, not duplication).

Read together, these three suggest the `OI-` vs `LLM-` id-prefix assignment is not a stable, deterministic step of Phase-3 compilation — it has now been observed to (a) apply cleanly, (b) apply additively without cleanup, and (c) not apply at all, across three different runs/baselines.

## Impact

Any downstream consumer that filters on the `OI-` prefix or on CWE-943 to isolate output-integrity findings will silently miss Cat 6 findings when compilation renumbers them into `LLM-N`:
- SARIF-based tooling filtering `partialFingerprints["findingId/v1"]` by `OI-` prefix (the exact mechanism this feature's own corrected extraction procedure relies on — see #354).
- The corrected F-292 no-emission verification procedure itself, if ever pointed at a run where this absorption occurs.
- Any Cat 6-specific evidence gate (like this feature's own T013) that greps for `OI-` or `CWE-943` rather than semantic content.

## Disposition (fix-vs-file, no inline fix — F-295 FR-020 scope fence)

Feature #295 (branch `295-f292-verification-runs`) US-2/T013 gate **FAILS** on this evidence. Per spec FR-018:
- **No baseline commit** for `examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/` — Phase 4 (US-2) stops here; the 5-artifact exactness rule (data-model.md entity 4) is not satisfiable against a run whose `threats.md`/`threats.sarif` do not carry the required `OI-`/CWE-943 shape.
- **US-3 (durable SARIF-regen byte-identity check) is deferred to this Issue** rather than counted as a US-3 failure (FR-018 structural gate: US-3 proceeds only on US-2 regen success, which never became reachable because T013 stopped Phase 4 before T014's regen step).
- **This Issue inherits the US-3 re-run**: once this compilation defect is fixed, re-run the T026 pipeline over `examples/multi-tenant-rag-app/architecture.md`, confirm the Cat 6 gate now passes (`OI-*` prefix + CWE-943 primary), commit the 5-artifact baseline (`threats.md`, `threat-report.md`, `risk-scores.md`, `risk-scores.sarif`, `threats.sarif`), then land the deferred SARIF-regen byte-identity test + workflow per `specs/295-f292-verification-runs/contracts/regen-byte-identity-contract.md`.
- The FR-014 URI-derivation enabler (input-path-derived `artifactLocation.uri` in `scripts/generate-threats-sarif.py`, commit `995359f`) is unaffected by this gate failure and stays landed — it is an enabler, not a verification-tier fix (tasks.md Story Dependency note).

## Evidence path

Full run-provenance, gate-evaluation commands, and disposition narrative: `specs/295-f292-verification-runs/sc-015-verification-record.md` (Feature #295, this feature's own honest-failure record).

items.title: Workflow Pipeline Design and Implementation Architecture
items.body:
# English translation

## Overall idea

The current `pipeline.workflow` is not a traditional pipeline that merely runs several ONNX files in sequence. It is an **executable, strongly typed, declarative inference IR**:

```text
package metadata
  └─ pipeline.workflow
       ├─ public inputs / outputs
       ├─ components
       ├─ typed SSA dataflow
       ├─ loop / branch / emit
       ├─ semantic state
       ├─ effects
       └─ serving contracts
```

The central goal is:

> The package describes what inference must do semantically; the runtime decides how to execute it efficiently on the current machine.

The same IR can therefore describe decoders, VLMs, Whisper, CTC, diffusion, video generation, state-space models, speculative decoding, continuous batching, LoRA, grammar guidance, and streaming audio without runtime branches such as:

```rust
if model_type == "qwen" { ... }
else if model_type == "gemma" { ... }
```

## 1. Four ownership layers

This is the most important boundary in the design.

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Package metadata** | Inference semantics, component ABIs, dataflow, state semantics, tokenizer facts, permitted substitutions, and rollback constraints |
| **Runtime** | EP, device, placement, paging, batch formation, workers, CUDA Graph, allocators, and cache eviction |
| **Caller** | Prompts, images, audio, grammars, adapter selection, and generation overrides |
| **Distribution** | File hashes, signatures, provenance, mirrors, and integrity verification |

For example:

- Whether KV state represents full attention, sliding attention, or recurrent state belongs to metadata.
- Whether KV is paged, its page size, and whether it resides on GPU or host belong to the runtime.
- Which LoRA a request selects belongs to the caller.
- The LoRA file SHA/signature belongs to distribution.

This prevents metadata from becoming a deployment configuration file for one particular runtime.

## 2. The single execution authority: `pipeline.workflow`

Every package, including an ordinary LLM with only one `model.onnx`, describes execution through:

```yaml
pipeline:
  workflow:
```

The former `model.io` surface has been removed because it created two writable graph ABIs:

```text
model.io                   one copy
workflow.components.ports  another copy
```

Two independently writable answers inevitably drift.

The current ownership split is:

- The ONNX graph is the **physical ABI authority**:
  - real port names
  - dtype
  - rank
  - shape
  - opset
- The workflow is the **semantic and composition authority**:
  - which ports mean tokens, logits, positions, or KV
  - how upstream values connect to downstream components
  - who owns state
  - batching axes
  - loops, branches, and emits
  - session lifetime

The flattened ABI required by an optimized decoder path is derived through:

```rust
InferenceMetadata::decoder_io()
```

It is derived from the workflow and is never serialized a second time.

## 3. Workflow object model

A `WorkflowSpec` primarily contains:

```text
manifest
inputs
outputs
components
state
effects
serving
steps
```

### 3.1 Inputs

An input describes:

- its tensor contract
- its source
- its semantic role
- whether it is required and its default
- observable optional presence

```yaml
request.input_ids:
  contract:
    dtype: int64
    rank: 2
    shape: [batch, sequence]
    batch_layout:
      kind: request_aligned
      axis: 0
  role:
    kind: runtime
    version: "1.0"
    role: prompt_tokens
  source:
    kind: request
  required: true
```

Optional media does not use fake tensors or magic sentinels. It uses:

```yaml
required: false
present_as: request.image_present
```

A `branch` then explicitly handles the media-present and media-absent paths.

### 3.2 Outputs

An output declares the public boundary, but only `emit` publishes it:

```yaml
outputs:
  tokens:
    contract: ...
    role: tokens
```

```yaml
- kind: emit
  value: step.token
  output: tokens
  mode: append
```

`emit` supports:

- `replace`: a final value
- `append`: accumulated tokens or chunks
- `event`: streaming events
- `valid_length`: the valid prefix of a fixed-capacity buffer
- `when`: per-row publication control

### 3.3 Components

Three component kinds are executed uniformly through `invoke`.

| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Neural ONNX component** | Decoder, vision encoder, denoiser, VAE, codec |
| **Policy component** | Sampler, termination, CFG, solver, state update, speculative verifier |
| **Runtime/native binding** | Tokenizer/media decode, grammar engine, telemetry, runtime token policy |

```yaml
- kind: invoke
  component: decoder
  inputs:
    input_ids: current.tokens
  outputs:
    logits: step.logits
```

Component names are entirely producer-defined. The runtime does not infer meaning from a component name.

Meaning is declared through port roles:

```yaml
ports:
  roles:
    input_ids: token_ids
    logits: logits
```

or through a versioned contract:

```yaml
contract:
  id: onnx-genai.token-sampler
  version: "2"
  bindings:
    logits: scores
    token: selected_token
```

## 4. Only five structural node kinds

The workflow IR is intentionally small:

| Node | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sequence` | Execute child nodes in order |
| `invoke` | Invoke a component |
| `loop` | Iteration, induction value, and carried state |
| `branch` | Control-flow selection and phi merging |
| `emit` | Publish a package output |

There are no concepts such as `phase`, `strategy`, `run_once`, or `prefill_stage`.

Execution frequency follows structural placement:

- a root invoke executes once per invocation;
- `loop.setup` executes once when entering the loop;
- `loop.steps` execute once per iteration;
- nodes after a loop execute after the loop completes.

Device transfers are not authored in metadata either. After placement is selected, the planner inserts `transfer` nodes into its internal lowered IR.

## 5. SSA, branches, and effects

### SSA values

Ordinary workflow tensors are SSA values:

- a value is produced once;
- it may be read many times;
- it is released according to liveness.

A loop-carried value is an explicit state carry:

```yaml
carried:
  - cell: cache
    initial: cache.initial
    next: decoder.present
```

### Branches

A branch may export only declared phi values:

```text
true branch  ─┐
              ├─ phi result
false branch ─┘
```

Every case must produce every exported phi output, making types, lifetimes, and effect ordering statically verifiable.

### Effects

Ordinary tensor state is not an external effect.

Actual external side effects include:

- grammar-engine mutation
- telemetry
- external session mutation
- stream emission
- stateful native adapters

They are ordered through linear effect tokens.

Each effect domain declares two independent dimensions:

```yaml
retry: idempotent
speculation_safety: rewindable
```

Being safe to retry and being safe to rewind under speculation are different properties.

## 6. The role of policy graphs

Policy graphs are one of the main differences between this design and a traditional GenAI runtime.

Traditional implementations often hard-code the following in host code:

- sampling
- EOS termination
- logits filtering
- cache-length updates
- position updates
- CFG
- diffusion schedulers
- speculative acceptance
- overlap stitching

The current principle is:

> Tensor mathematics that affects observable results should ship with the package as an executable component.

For a decoder:

```text
decoder
  → logits policy
  → sampler
  → termination
  → token/mask/position/state update
  → next iteration
```

For diffusion:

```text
text encoder
  → noise initialization
  → loop:
       denoiser
       CFG
       solver step
       history update
  → VAE decoder
```

Runtime policies such as batch windows, device placement, priorities, and page sizes do not belong in policy graphs.

### ONNX policies and runtime bindings

Both forms are supported:

1. The package provides `token_sampler.onnx` and `termination.onnx`.
2. The package declares an `onnx-genai.token-policy` binding implemented by the runtime.

The first form is more portable and leaves semantics entirely package-owned.

The second permits high-performance runtime features such as:

- fused sampling
- paged KV
- device-side token selection
- optimized continuous batching
- specialized speculative execution

The loop itself still comes from the workflow.

## 7. Runtime implementation architecture

The implementation can be understood in six stages.

### 7.1 Parsing and fail-closed validation

`onnx-genai-metadata`:

1. checks `schema_version`;
2. strictly deserializes the document;
3. rejects unknown core fields;
4. validates SSA references;
5. validates invoke port bindings;
6. validates loop carries, branch phis, and effects;
7. validates state and state-service groups;
8. derives required capabilities;
9. verifies that the manifest declares the capabilities its structure uses;
10. checks the physical ABI against the ONNX artifacts.

Unknown required contracts, capabilities, and adapter ABIs are rejected.

Only profiles explicitly marked `ignorable` may be skipped.

### 7.2 Compiling into `WorkflowPlan`

The loader lowers concise YAML into an internal plan containing:

- lexical SSA names
- loop read/write versions
- branch phis
- effect tokens
- liveness
- resolved port bindings
- state-group references
- component-contract dispatch

The compiled plan is immutable and can be shared between workers through `Arc`.

### 7.3 Structural classification

The runtime does not classify by model family. It performs structural recognition.

For example, a single decoder requires:

- exactly one ONNX graph component;
- port roles identifying that component as a decoder;
- `onnx-genai.autoregressive-decode` when the package wants the fused core.

A VLM remains a composite workflow because it also contains vision and embedding graphs, even if one component is decoder-shaped.

### 7.4 Placement and execution islands

The planner considers:

- component implementation
- device
- effects
- control-flow boundaries
- shape
- substitution
- provider capability

It may link adjacent, pure, same-device ONNX invokes into one execution island:

```text
decoder → logits filter → sampler → termination
```

That island may execute as one ORT session run without returning intermediate tensors to the host.

Component boundaries are semantic boundaries, not mandatory kernel or session boundaries.

### 7.5 CUDA Graph

Capture eligibility is evaluated per island and concrete shape signature:

- stable device addresses
- bounded or stable shapes
- no host control
- no external effects
- explicit seed/counter RNG tensors
- provider kernels that support capture

The first run resolves shapes and prepares stable bindings. A later run captures, and subsequent runs replay.

Capture failure may fall back to ordinary island execution, but may not change workflow semantics.

### 7.6 Interpreter

All execution ultimately enters the unified walker:

```rust
pipeline::workflow::run_workflow_node
```

It manages:

- the SSA value environment
- loop state
- branch results
- effects
- package outputs
- session leases
- runtime state services

Component invocations pass through a unified backend seam whose implementation may be:

- ORT
- native CPU
- native CUDA
- a runtime binding
- a specialized contract executor

## 8. Three generation-iteration algorithms

There are no longer three independent host loops. One interpreter `Loop` invokes different executors according to its authored body.

| Loop body contract | Algorithm |
|---|---|
| `autoregressive-decode` + `token-policy` | Single-token decode |
| `continuous-batch` | Row-major continuous-batch step |
| `speculative-block` | Propose/verify/accept block |

All of the following still come from the package workflow:

- termination
- loop bounds
- carried state
- active/done values
- accepted length
- emits

Only the executor behind a particular `invoke` differs.

If the package provides its own proposer, verifier, and acceptance ONNX graphs, the interpreter executes them directly instead of using the runtime speculative-block executor.

## 9. State design

Metadata describes **semantic state contracts**, not physical storage classes.

### 9.1 State cells

A state cell declares:

- tensor contract
- `scope: invocation | session`
- initializer
- recurrence
- management owner
- release boundary
- service group

Recurrence forms include:

- `invariant`
- `growing`
- `bounded`
- replacement or other update disciplines

### 9.2 State-service groups

A state-service group describes the semantics the runtime must implement:

```yaml
kind: full_attention
sequence_axis: 2
layout: bnsh
logical_lengths: cache_lengths
aliasing: permitted
update: ...
reuse: ...
capabilities:
  rollback_positions: 32
  snapshot: true
  fork: true
```

It does not describe:

- paged versus contiguous storage
- page size
- allocator
- GPU versus CPU placement
- slot tables

Those belong to runtime-private state classes.

This also answers the earlier Transformers Cache-class question: **the runtime may absolutely use a class hierarchy with `update()`, `rewind()`, `fork()`, and `compact()` methods; metadata defines only the portable invariants those implementations must satisfy.**

### 9.3 Supported state semantics

#### Dynamic append KV

The current logical length determines the next append position.

#### Static/fixed-capacity KV

It uses:

```yaml
update:
  kind: indexed_scatter
  write_indices: ...
  capacity: ...
  write_indices_ports: ...
  kv_length_ports: ...
```

The runtime checks indices before execution to prevent negative or out-of-range writes from silently corrupting cache state.

#### Fixed recurrent state

The same representation covers:

- linear-attention accumulators
- SSM state
- causal-convolution history
- recurrent hidden state

Typically:

```yaml
kind: recurrent
update: {kind: replace}
```

There is no need for separate Qwen-, Mamba-, or RWKV-specific schema state kinds.

#### Prefix reuse

Reuse dependencies are not manually enumerated by the producer. They are derived by tracing every input that may affect state:

- model/component identity
- LoRA
- media-encoder results
- preprocessing
- generation-affecting facts
- externally supplied state

The runtime then owns hashes, tenant namespaces, and security isolation.

## 10. Batching and the row model

Metadata never stores request IDs, slot IDs, or epochs.

It describes only how a tensor corresponds to positions in the current batch.

### 10.1 Batch layouts

```yaml
shared
request_aligned
request_expanded
token_packed
runtime_sequence_state
```

#### `shared`

One value is shared by all requests.

#### `request_aligned`

Each row along a declared axis corresponds to one request.

#### `token_packed`

Variable numbers of items are packed along axis 0 and mapped through an ownership chain:

```text
frames → clips → requests
tokens → segments → requests
```

Up to two ownership levels are currently supported:

```yaml
levels:
  - {offsets: frame_offsets, owner: frame_owner}
  - {offsets: clip_offsets, owner: clip_owner}
```

### 10.2 Padding

A dense rectangle uses:

```yaml
padding:
  - dimension: max_tiles
    valid_lengths: tile_lengths
```

`valid_lengths` is the sole contract authority for the valid prefix. It is not inferred from a mask or padding sentinel.

### 10.3 Component grouping permission

Only:

```yaml
batch_capacity:
```

asserts that grouped execution is semantically equivalent to per-item execution under the declared shape, uniformity, and budget constraints.

Without `batch_capacity`, the component must run per item.

Its presence does not require the runtime to batch. Whether to group, how long to wait, and the target batch size remain runtime policy.

### 10.4 Continuous decoder batching

Policy v2 contracts use per-row:

- `active`
- `done`
- `temperature`
- `top_k`
- `top_p`
- `min_p`
- `seed`
- `counter`
- `accepted_len`

Inactive rows:

- consume no RNG;
- do not update semantic state;
- emit no token;
- preserve their previous KV and logical length.

Compaction applies one permutation to every `request_aligned` tensor and every row-scoped component.

A row-scoped native component must implement:

```rust
compact(selection)
release(row)
```

`selection` may repeat an index, which supports beam cloning and speculative forks.

## 11. Expressing different model types

### 11.1 Ordinary decoder-only LLM

#### Logits-only

```text
prompt → decoder → logits → emit logits
```

No sampler, EOS termination, or generation loop is required.

#### Complete generation

```text
prompt
  → loop:
      decoder
      sampler/token-policy
      termination
      emit token
      carry KV/state
```

The sole authority for numeric special-token facts is:

```yaml
package.tokenizer.special_tokens
```

Multiple EOS values are represented as:

```yaml
eos_token_id: [eot, eom]
```

A request EOS set replaces the package defaults; the two sets are not merged.

### 11.2 VLM

A typical structure is:

```text
optional encoded image/video
  → preprocess
  → vision encoder
  → projector/embedding mixer
prompt tokens
  └──────────────────────────→ decoder loop
```

Text-only requests use `present_as + branch` rather than a fake image.

The model supports:

- image/video placeholder IDs
- vision-start tokens
- packed media
- grids and coordinates
- multi-axis position IDs
- mixed image/video/audio inputs
- externally supplied encoder features

### 11.3 Encoder-decoder

For example, Whisper:

```text
audio features → encoder → encoder_hidden_states
decoder tokens ───────────→ decoder/cross-attention → logits
```

Cross-attention state may use a separate state-service group.

Translation, ASR, and speech generation use the same structural form.

### 11.4 Encoder-only

```text
input → encoder → pooling/decoding policy → emit
```

This can represent:

- embedding
- classification
- reranking
- reward models
- protein encoders
- CTC

CTC blank/padding semantics, frame valid lengths, and vocabulary are profile/package facts.

The ORT embedding path is currently relatively complete. General profile executors for classification, reranking, reward, and CTC remain incomplete.

### 11.5 Diffusion and image generation

```text
text encoder
  → latent/noise initialization
  → denoising loop:
      denoiser
      CFG
      solver
      latent/history update
  → VAE decode
  → emit image
```

Euler and DPM++ are not runtime model-family switches. They are different solver policy artifacts.

Image editing, ControlNet-like conditioning, shared prefixes, and inpainting masks are expressed through ordinary inputs, components, and dataflow.

### 11.6 Video diffusion

The diffusion structure can add:

- temporal state
- frame/chunk ownership
- causal temporal emission
- a video decoder
- streaming chunk emits

No `model_type: cogvideox` runtime branch is required.

### 11.7 Streaming/full-duplex audio

For a PersonaPlex- or music-style package:

```text
microphone audio
  → audio encoder
  → dialogue/talker loop
  → nested codec/codebook loop
  → speech decoder
  → streaming audio emit
```

Dialogue state, codec history, and conversation state are separate session-scoped states.

### 11.8 World-model/weather rollout

```text
initial observation/state
  → rollout loop
      dynamics model
      state update
      optional event emit
```

Continuity across observations is represented by session state rather than adding network-aware `receive` or `await` operations to the IR.

### 11.9 MoE

MoE is normally internal structure of a neural component. Metadata records:

- expert count
- legal sharding facts
- weight-quantization facts

The workflow does not orchestrate each expert unless experts are actually split into separate components or pipeline stages.

## 12. Speculative decoding

Metadata declares:

- proposer
- target
- vocabulary compatibility
- shared state and weights
- rollback state
- maximum proposal width
- distribution-preserving semantics

The runtime decides:

- the actual K
- tree shape
- scheduling
- whether speculation is enabled
- kernel implementation

The verifier policy produces:

```text
accepted_tokens
accepted_len
correction token
done
next RNG state
```

`emit.valid_length = accepted_len` publishes only the valid accepted prefix.

### Hybrid speculation

A hybrid-attention target may simultaneously contain:

- full/sliding KV
- a linear-attention accumulator
- causal-convolution history

These remain ordinary state groups connected by `cascade` requirements so they snapshot, fork, and rewind together.

Metadata does not prescribe whether the runtime:
