# Environment

* Working: Cloud Firestore 26.0.0 (BoM 34.1.0)
* Broken: Cloud Firestore 26.0.2 (BoM 34.4.0)
* Platform: Android (tested on physical devices and emulators)
* Client: Flutter 3.32+, Dart 3.11+

# Tooling

This regression was identified and isolated using **Claude Opus 4.6 Thinking** (Anthropic) via the Windsurf Cascade plugin in IntelliJ. 

Claude assisted with:

- Diffing the releases of our production app to identify candidate changes
- Systematically reverting changes one at a time to isolate the root cause
- Tracing the Flutter `cloud_firestore` version bump to the underlying native Android SDK BoM and changelog
- Developing a minimal reproduction app

All testing and verification were performed by the developer on physical hardware.

# Suspected root cause

The thread pool replacement in #7376 is the most likely culprit. The AsyncTask thread pool was well-integrated with Android's threading model. The replacement self-managed thread pool may have different scheduling characteristics that cause thread starvation or priority inversion when:

* Multiple Firestore query listeners compete for the same pool
* Large document deserialization blocks pool threads
* Background CPU work causes OS scheduler contention

items.title: Move live memory to Postgres and keep vector search in ClickHouse
items.body:
### Component

Memory and search

### Use case

Loom needs to support frequent point reads and writes alongside tenant-scoped retrieval and scans over billions of records. These workloads should not all use the same write path.

A memory write needs ordered versions, compare-and-set, locks and pin checks. ClickHouse serves retrieval and analytics, but its part creation and merge costs make individual committed inserts a poor fit for this workload. [#129](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/129) batches several request-path tables; it leaves the main memory tables committed.

The sizing assumptions are 5,000 tenants, 50,000 namespaces, 1,000–50,000 memory writes/sec and up to 10,000 user searches/sec. These are design inputs, not measured capacity or production traffic. If all 50,000 writes need a semantic conflict check, that adds 50,000 retrievals/sec before user search, extra retrieval legs or background work. At a sustained 50,000 writes/sec, the system also produces 4.32 billion write events/day.

Quality is the highest priority: retrieval and admission verdicts must use the right revisions, preserve tenant and access boundaries, and retain the evidence needed for recovery. Scalability and low end-to-end latency are required alongside that quality. Optimize cost and component count only within those guarantees; do not trade away recall, durability or access checks to meet a throughput number.

The goals are point reads without a second database lookup, transactional writes, fresh search results, and bounded ingest and retention costs. Postgres and ClickHouse are the only databases. All stored vectors and vector search stay in ClickHouse. The sizing inputs describe a deployment spread across placement units; they are not a promise that one Postgres primary or one namespace sustains the aggregate peak.

### Describe the solution you'd like

#### Storage ownership

Postgres stores current memory content, not just its latest version and hash.

| Workload | Storage |
| --- | --- |
| Current memory content, metadata, versions, locks, pins and compare-and-set | Postgres |
| Working memory, task state, idempotency and delivery claims | Postgres |
| Identity, grants, revocation and mutable namespace configuration | Postgres |
| Revision journal and enrichment jobs | Postgres, retained until their required deliveries complete |
| Embeddings, lexical and vector retrieval, searchable metadata and derived graph projections | ClickHouse |
| Historical revisions, conversation archives, audit queries, usage and rollups | ClickHouse |
| Large immutable code-index artifacts and compiler graph generations | ClickHouse |

Every live record has one authority. Preserve `(org, namespace, agent, user_id, session_id)`, stable record identity, source revision, actor, source class and attestation through both stores. The server derives provenance from the authenticated writer and operation. Org-wide identifiers must still pass the same scope checks without revealing another tenant's records. A ClickHouse projection cannot grant access to a record Postgres refuses.

The Postgres transaction atomically records current content, the complete immutable revision, required delivery jobs, the idempotency state and a hash-only mutation audit event. Keep mutable delivery progress separate from revision payloads so job updates do not replicate the content again. A search document is a derived serving representation, not the revision journal or the audit record. Required audit events are durable before the audited operation completes; best-effort usage metrics have a separate delivery contract.

Keep the existing ClickHouse-only install path for smaller deployments. This proposal defines the Postgres+ClickHouse path. Record the selected authority and reject replicas configured for a different one; an outage must not silently switch a deployment between them.

#### WalShadow replication and enrichment have different jobs

Use [ClickHouse Managed Postgres](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres) with [WalShadow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/sync-to-clickhouse/walshadow) for selected database mirrors and revision events. WalShadow is the first implementation path. Loom should not build a general WAL transport or run two writers into the same destination projection.

Build and test the replication path with WalShadow. Judge it by source load, replication lag, payload correctness and recovery under Loom workloads. Its private-preview status alone is not a reason to defer implementation or choose ClickPipes. A documented or reproduced limitation that blocks a required guarantee is a release blocker, not an accepted reduction in quality. Replication benchmarks are not a latency guarantee for a Loom operation.

Pin the evaluated WalShadow build and replication configuration. Its documented limits include failure to continue after an unplanned primary promotion and unresolved large-value reconstruction cases. Validate complete revision payloads, including large text and JSON values, against source hashes through initial load, updates, cleanup and restart. A selected value mode that can substitute missing or incorrect bytes does not qualify for archival delivery. Keep WalShadow as the first implementation path, resolve blocking limitations, and reconsider the transport if it cannot satisfy the required guarantees ([limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/limitations.md), [failover protocol](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/failover.md)).

Replicate an explicit allowlist of tables and columns. Destination identities must distinguish source placement units, databases and tenants, including during a tenant move. Mutable configuration mirrors serve analytics, not authorization. Account for WalShadow recovery state and large-value mirrors in capacity, access control, backup and erasure inventories.

Loom still needs enrichment jobs. CDC does not generate embeddings or decide when a revision is searchable. These jobs read committed revisions directly from Postgres and publish search documents into ClickHouse without first waiting for the CDC mirror.

A search document carries its source revision, content hash, embedding-model and preprocessing versions, chunk identity, text and filter metadata. Reuse an embedding only when its input and model contract match. A worker can rebuild the document from a retained revision or its confirmed archive. Vectors never pass through Postgres tables or its revision journal.

Readiness is recorded only after every projection required by that operation is delivered and visible. Optional graph or analytics work does not delay a write unless its contract requires it. Lexical publication can precede embedding completion, but it must not mark semantic search ready or weaken ordinary `memory.set` success semantics.

#### Writes and point reads

For a semantic `memory.set`:

1. Validate the value and access scope. Start embedding work and the required search-freshness check concurrently.
2. Check duplicates, conflicts and protected memories against sufficiently fresh state.
3. In a short Postgres transaction, recheck the key version and relevant guards, update current content, and record the complete revision and required jobs.
4. Publish the required search projection directly into ClickHouse.
5. Return success after the operation's promised visibility is satisfied.

Do not hold a database transaction open during inference or ClickHouse queries. Reuse embeddings computed during admission, and reuse existing embeddings for metadata-only changes.

Postgres handles same-key compare-and-set atomically. For cross-key semantic admission, capture a generation for every scope whose state can change the verdict and wait for its required search projections. Every relevant creation, update, pin, blacklist, access-policy or model-manifest change advances the corresponding generation in the mutation transaction. After inference and retrieval, compare those generations again in the short commit transaction and advance them with the write. Checking only returned candidate versions misses a peer created while the check was running. A Postgres isolation level alone does not track predicates evaluated in ClickHouse. Recheck time-based expiry and lock leases at commit; a generation does not track the passage of time.

Enforce pinned and blacklist protections separately from approximate result ranking. A contract that refuses peers above a similarity threshold needs a complete check over eligible protected peers; an ANN or quantized shortlist alone cannot prove that no protected peer matches. Evaluate the false-accept and false-refusal rates of semantic verdicts as well as retrieval recall.

Use a deterministic lock order across affected scopes, bounded retries and one request deadline. Batch admissions within busy conflict scopes, including interactions between writes in the batch; vector comparisons still execute in ClickHouse. A namespace-wide invariant still needs namespace-wide coordination; do not split that scope or omit checks to claim horizontal scalability. Measure its sustainable rate and reject excess work explicitly before queues grow without bound.

`memory.set` and `bulk_set` keep their inline verdicts, including pinned refusals. Deferred ingestion is a separate contract that reports pending enrichment. Ordinary transactional operations that need no semantic work finish at the Postgres commit.

A crash after that commit leaves a durable revision and a repairable job. Scope idempotency to the authenticated caller and operation, bind it to a request digest, and replay it only after current authorization. Reusing a key with different input is rejected. A projection timeout returns the committed revision, operation identity and pending state; a retry resumes that revision instead of admitting a second mutation. Specify status lookup, cancellation after commit, idempotency retention, expired-key behavior and the HTTP, MCP and SDK responses before changing the write path.

`memory.get` reads current content directly from Postgres. Strict current reads, final authorization and admission guards use the primary; replicas serve other reads only when their replay position meets the request's consistency requirement.

#### Retrieval and visibility

Strict search captures a finite committed barrier for its authorized scopes when admitted, including any caller-supplied write dependencies, then checks that the selected ClickHouse reader can serve the required projections. Later writes do not keep moving that barrier. This promises coverage through the captured barrier, not an atomic snapshot across the two databases. Current access and deletion checks still apply, and concurrent content changes can require bounded refill or an explicit incomplete result. Any weaker consistency mode is an explicit API contract, never an automatic timeout fallback.

Several writes share one visibility wait at a dependent search. Track a completed prefix with gaps or an equivalent durable manifest; event allocation order and the largest observed revision do not prove that earlier work committed or finished. A superseded revision can be resolved only when the protocol proves that its required serving effect is covered. An insertion acknowledgement or a readiness row on one replica is not proof for every reader. Bind the proof to the actual tables, serving generation and reader; re-establish it after rerouting or replica changes ([ClickHouse read consistency](https://clickhouse.com/docs/resources/support-center/knowledge-base/data-management/read-consistency)).

Track committed state and searchable readiness separately. Readiness includes the source revision, model version and reader visibility. A replication cursor or `max(event_id)` is not enough. WalShadow documents that different tables from one Postgres transaction can become visible in ClickHouse at different times ([consistency limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/main/docs/limitations.md#ordering-and-consistency)).

Retrieve lexical, semantic, entity and temporal candidates in ClickHouse. Apply tenant and known eligibility filters inside every retrieval leg, then batch-check candidate revisions, permissions, expiry and deletion state in Postgres before exposing snippets or sending content to an external reranker or answer model. Never attach current content to a score computed from an older revision. Apply the same checks to graph expansion, context assembly, caches, traces, exports and history APIs; an analytical mirror is not an access authority.

Candidate validation cannot recover a relevant revision absent from the search projection. Discard obsolete candidates, deduplicate by source identity and revision, and refill within bounded rounds, rows, bytes and time. Report readiness failures, refill exhaustion and missing required retrieval legs as explicit unavailable or incomplete outcomes. Do not label a truncated pool a complete empty result or let an answer model present it as complete evidence. Define authorization and revision check points for external dispatch and final response, and revalidate when the relevant access generation changes during a long request.

Tenant policy controls external model use and content egress. Partition result and model caches by access scope, source revisions, model and serving generation. Revocation and erasure invalidate affected entries; raw ClickHouse tables and `pg_clickhouse` must not expose an alternative route around these checks.

Keep the existing retrieval path as the baseline. Small eligible sets use tenant-scoped exact scans or an evaluated quantized shortlist with original-vector rescoring. Large tenants get dedicated placement and serving capacity.

[#131](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/131) found that the tested HNSW layout did not serve tenant reads and had recall and stale-version problems. Adding the same index is not the solution. Evaluate immutable indexed generations plus recent changes for large tenants, but require evidence that the index is used and that filtered recall holds before making that layout part of the serving path. [ClickHouse documents](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/annindexes) both filter trade-offs and index-building cost during inserts and merges.

Version the complete retrieval contract: embedding input and dimensions, lexical tokenization and ranking, filters, fusion, candidate budgets, reranking and temporal rules. Evaluate exact identifiers and phrases, semantic paraphrases, multilingual queries, negation, conflicting revisions, expiry and sparse tenants. Model size or exact vector-neighbor recall alone is not evidence of better final relevance or agent outcomes. Compare candidate generators, embedding and reranking choices on the same evaluation set; the existing path is a control, not a quality ceiling. Choose the strongest measured end-to-end quality that meets the declared capacity and latency requirements, then optimize p99 without lowering the quality gates. Keep citations tied to the validated source revision and test abstention when evidence is insufficient.

Build model and index changes as separate ClickHouse serving generations. Backfill, replay intervening changes and erasures, compare quality against the baseline, prove reader visibility, then atomically switch the Postgres serving manifest. A request pins one compatible model and generation until completion or timeout; retire a generation only after its readers drain. Never compare vectors from incompatible models. Retain a verified generation for rollback only within erasure and retention rules. Measure concurrent rebuild load and bound the recent-change set so it cannot become an unbounded exact scan.

Use [`pg_clickhouse`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse/blob/main/doc/pg_clickhouse.md) for unified SQL and analytical queries where the installed version pushes the work down. Keep native ClickHouse queries for the initial serving path. Check `EXPLAIN` before routing a query through Postgres: unsupported filters can prevent limit pushdown, and SQL compatibility alone says nothing about the cost.

#### Tenant placement and database branching

Tenant placement belongs to this architecture; [#157](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/issues/157) consumes its routing and isolation contract. A tenant is the customer organization represented by `org`. A contract requiring a separately isolated workspace can register its owned namespace set as an explicit placement unit. Neither a user nor an agent/session automatically creates a new database.

| Boundary | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Tenant or registered workspace placement | Region, capacity, authority epoch, and shared or dedicated Postgres service |
| Namespace and collection | Project/content scope and sharing within the tenant |
| User and agent | Grants, private content and permitted actions within those scopes |

Use shared Postgres shards for ordinary tenants and a dedicated always-on service when measured load, residency or the isolation contract requires it. Dedicated placement means an independently sized service with the required HA configuration, not merely `CREATE DATABASE` inside the same resource pool. Personal accounts may have one user and one tenant; that does not make database-per-user the organization model. Keep users who collaborate on documents and memory within the same transactional placement unless an explicit isolation contract requires otherwise.

Route ordinary tenant transactions to one Postgres shard and colocate their transactional dependencies. Promote large tenants to dedicated services when measured load requires it. Managed Postgres offers vertical scaling and read replicas; horizontal write sharding remains a Loom placement decision ([scaling](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/scaling)). Keep APIs, authoritative transactions, retrieval and validation in the tenant's home region to avoid inter-region round trips in ordinary requests.

Tenant placement includes a durable authority epoch. A move or shard split copies a consistent state, catches up required deliveries, fences and drains the old writers, verifies the destination and switches the route under a bounded write pause. Stale routers and workers cannot write through the old epoch. Split a large tenant only along independent transaction and admission scopes; cross-scope invariants do not become safe merely because the rows moved to separate shards.

Dedicated Postgres does not replace application isolation. Continue to bind every query and job to the identity tuple, current grants and placement epoch. ClickHouse, object storage and caches keep their own scoped access and placement contracts; a Postgres endpoint does not automatically isolate the rest of the product.

Evaluate Xata for dedicated-service provisioning, migration/CI environments and tenant sandboxes. Xata describes copy-on-write branches with independent compute ([branching](https://xata.io/postgres-branching)). That is a candidate capability, not a decision to replace ClickHouse Managed Postgres or a reason to create an instance for every tenant. Keep the first implementation path above until a provider comparison establishes the required guarantees.

Production services with interactive latency SLOs stay warm. Permit hibernation only for profiles whose declared SLO includes wake-up and cache warming; test reconnection storms and whether replication/background connections prevent idling ([scale-to-zero lifecycle](https://xata.io/scale-to-zero)). Copy-on-write reduces the cost of cloned unchanged blocks, not the compute and distinct data of thousands of independently active tenants.

Create new tenants from a clean schema/template. Never clone a shared multi-tenant production database into a new customer's security boundary. Data-bearing test branches stay within their tenant's authorized boundary, with anonymization or synthetic fixtures where required.

A Postgres branch is not a complete Loom fork. Register an environment/branch identity and pin a consistent baseline of database revisions, ClickHouse serving generations and artifact manifests. Use separate writable projection destinations, job claims and external-effect destinations. Cloned outbox rows, credentials or erasure jobs must not execute against production. An older copy of grants cannot restore revoked production access. Branch promotion uses the same fenced, reconciled cutover as any other authority change; do not assume automatic merging of business-state mutations.

Manage the fleet with bounded active-tenant connection pools, migration orchestration, credential rotation, per-source CDC progress, backups, failover and retirement. Budget source/replication connections, compute including HA, storage divergence and catch-up capacity at the expected number of concurrently active tenants. Database-per-tenant improves isolation and placement options; it does not remove a hot namespace's semantic coordination limit or establish better retrieval relevance.

Before changing the provider or placement default, qualify durability and failure-domain behavior, primary failover/fencing, PITR, regional availability, fleet limits, and the selected CDC path. A PostgreSQL-compatible endpoint does not prove access to the physical WAL and recovery state WalShadow requires. Report warm and wake-up latency, sustained mixed load, noisy-neighbor effects and full operating cost against the shared-shard baseline. Track all retained branches in erasure and backup recovery inventories.

#### Batching, capacity and retention

Use a bounded number of enrichment writers per ClickHouse destination shard and table, shared across API replicas. Batch by rows, bytes and a bounded deadline. Avoid stacking a long application timer on top of a long ClickHouse async-insert timer. Prioritize work that a caller is waiting to search.

Validate vector dimensions and partition counts before sending a block. Isolate bad rows, retry ambiguous inserts with stable identities, and apply backpressure when queues or merges fall behind. Leased job claims carry fencing generations so overlapping workers cannot advance progress for a newer claim. Use stable revision, chunk, model and destination identities for logical deduplication: ClickHouse insert-deduplication windows are finite and are not a permanent exactly-once guarantee. Verify retry behavior after the window, across rebatching and with dependent materialized views ([insert retry limits](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/operations/insert/deduplicating-inserts-on-retries)).

Use separate concurrency limits, connection pools and scheduling shares for interactive admissions, searches, archival delivery, imports and rebuilds. Enforce per-tenant and global bounds on outstanding work and provider calls; reserve capacity for interactive work without starving repair and erasure. Count overload rejections and timeouts in service-level results. Bulk work must not exhaust interactive capacity, and overload must not silently select a weaker model or skip a quality check.

Separate ClickHouse retrieval compute from analytics and heavy index construction. Avoid one partition per namespace in shared tables. Keep historical revisions out of ordinary live retrieval. High-volume best-effort telemetry can be buffered directly into ClickHouse; it should not require a Postgres transaction for each metric.

The revision journal has bounded retention after required delivery, not a time-based permission to drop undelivered data. Confirm archive completeness and payload hashes before removing source payloads. Reconciliation detects missing revisions, not just duplicate rows. Retain enough delivery state to rebuild serving data from the journal or confirmed archive. If archival delivery stalls, apply backpressure before storage or WAL retention is exhausted rather than discard history.

The archive consumes immutable revision events with a key that includes source identity and revision; a current-row mirror cannot preserve every revision. Routine source cleanup is not erasure. Configure and test archival handling of source `DELETE`, partition retirement, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP`: WalShadow tees also receive destructive DDL, so mirroring a journal and truncating it can remove the archive. Keep archive lifetime independent of source cleanup, with explicit erasure through Loom's erasure workflow ([destination behavior](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/destination-tables.md)). Durable memory and retained history expire only under writer-authorized deletion or retention policy.

Size journal, WAL/archive retention, vector writes and ClickHouse merges from sustained rates, payload bytes, chunk fan-out, content-changing fraction, model rebuilds and outage recovery time. Include per-shard validation lookups, all retrieval legs, generation retries and reranker concurrency. Report normal and catch-up capacity with headroom; peak API throughput alone does not establish sustained capacity.

#### Failure, erasure and rollout

- With ClickHouse unavailable, point reads and operations independent of semantic retrieval continue. Semantic admissions and strict search fail explicitly.
- With Postgres unavailable, authoritative mutations and access decisions fail closed. Do not serve a stale ClickHouse copy as current content.
- Worker restarts replay versioned jobs. Late enrichment cannot overwrite a newer revision. Readiness and job completion survive lost acknowledgements and overlapping claims.
- Deletes and access changes take effect through Postgres authority. Erasure first fences the affected generation, then drains all in-flight publishers or rejects their writes at the destination before cleanup and the final residue check. Expiring a worker lease alone does not establish that quiescence. A check immediately before an unfenced insert cannot prevent a worker from writing after erasure completes. Apply the fence to imports, index builds, CDC recovery and restore as well as enrichment.
- The erasure inventory includes Postgres content, revisions, jobs, idempotency payloads, ClickHouse vectors, graph and text projections, archives, replication recovery state and caches. Preserve deletion evidence across the backup recovery window. Restore in quarantine and apply erasures before serving or replaying jobs. State backup expiry or cryptographic-erasure rules and distinguish live-data completion from backup retention obligations.
- Use synchronous Postgres HA across failure domains for acknowledged-write durability. For Managed Postgres, select two HA standbys; its documented one-standby configuration is asynchronous. Verify the actual commit and promotion policy, including fencing the old primary and choosing a standby that preserves acknowledged commits ([HA options](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/high-availability)). Replica count alone is not a durability proof.
- Test automatic source failover with the selected WalShadow build. Its planned switchover procedure does not cover abrupt primary loss. Define a bounded recovery or rebootstrap procedure for replication, while retaining all source revisions not confirmed in the archive; a fresh snapshot of current content cannot reconstruct revisions already removed from the source journal. Quarantine or remove abandoned-timeline output before trusting the recovered archive; a larger replication cursor is not proof of valid history. Production acceptance requires that procedure to meet the history durability and recovery objectives.
- Restore both stores with compatible authority epochs and serving manifests. Reconcile source revisions, erasure state and delivery gaps before advertising readiness. Define separate recovery-point and recovery-time objectives for primary/AZ failure and regional disaster; do not present a regional backup policy as zero-loss synchronous HA.

Moving write authority breaks the existing rolling-upgrade assumption that all shared state is in ClickHouse. Seed Postgres from a consistent snapshot, reconcile changes, verify identities and versions, then switch authority under a controlled write pause. Shadow comparisons must not repeat external side effects. Any duplicate inference needs an explicit benchmark budget. Old and new authorities must not accept writes for the same scope. Deploy and verify fencing-capable APIs and workers before cutover while the old authority is still active. Drain or deny storage writes from any older binary that cannot enforce the fence; a new configuration row cannot stop a binary that never reads it. Enforce the authority epoch at admission and commit on every remaining writer. Once the new authority accepts writes, rollback requires a fenced, reconciled reverse cutover; changing a configuration flag is not a rollback. Update the architecture and rolling-upgrade rules with the implementation.

#### Implementation and acceptance

Split the work into:

1. Postgres current-content storage, provenance, atomic audit, admission generations and revision/job/idempotency contracts.
2. Direct search projection, bounded batching, idempotent recovery, reader-visible barriers and explicit API outcomes.
3. WalShadow qualification, retained history, reconciliation, erasure and failover/restore procedures.
4. Search quality validation, model-generation rollout, SDK behavior and fenced authority cutover.
5. Tenant placement, fair scheduling, capacity qualification and any large-tenant index changes justified by measurements.

These are implementation workstreams, not permission to cut over before history, erasure and recovery pass. Keep the existing serving path until the required gates pass for the intended deployment profile.

Define a deployment profile and numeric acceptance thresholds before capacity qualification: tenant and eligible-set distributions, content sizes, write mix, chunk counts, model versions, candidate limits, concurrency, freshness contract, failure domain, hardware and replicas. Keep the existing operation budgets, including the 200 ms p99 target for `memory.set`, as targets to test; they are not results of this proposal. Establish separate end-to-end SLOs for current point reads, semantic admission, strict search, deferred visibility, failover and archival recovery. Report provider-inclusive latency and service-only time separately without excluding queueing, visibility waits, retries or errors from the relevant SLO.

Release gates:

| Gate | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Isolation and correctness | No observed cross-tenant or unauthorized disclosure, lost acknowledged mutation, mismatched revision score, skipped protection, duplicate logical side effect or erased-content resurrection in the correctness and fault suites. Any occurrence blocks release. |
| Retrieval and answer quality | Paired evaluation against the existing retrieval path and exact eligible-set vector results, plus labeled relevance, citation accuracy, abstention and downstream agent outcomes. Set minimum filtered recall and non-inferiority margins per required query and tenant slice before testing; aggregate averages cannot hide a failing slice. |
| Semantic admission | Concurrent same-key and cross-key writes, new peers, pin/blacklist changes, intra-batch conflicts and model failures produce the promised inline verdicts; record false accepts, false refusals and retry rates. |
| Sustained capacity and latency | Mixed traffic at each advertised rate, including admission retrievals, all query legs, validation and model calls. p95/p99 and error rates meet the declared SLOs while queues, journal/WAL storage, dead tuples and parts remain bounded. Include hot scopes, large tenants and small tenants sharing capacity. |
| Degraded operation | Imports, model/index rebuilds, provider throttling, lost replicas, source failover and archive outages preserve correctness and tenant scheduling. Report degraded capacity, recovery backlog and catch-up time. |
| History and recovery | Every required revision and audit event is reconciled across initial load, cleanup, duplicate delivery, restart, source promotion and restore. Validate payload hashes, source epochs and deletion evidence before readiness. |
| Placement and branches | Shared and dedicated profiles pass the same isolation, durability and semantic tests. Tenant moves, stale routes, forked jobs, branch erasure and provider failover cannot cross tenant/environment boundaries. Qualify fleet-scale provisioning, migration, warm latency and any advertised wake-up profile before changing defaults. |

Run at a fixed offered load long enough to exercise checkpoints, autovacuum, merges, journal cleanup and archival delivery, then inject failures and measure catch-up. Report achieved throughput, rejection/timeout counts, CPU, memory, I/O, lock waits, generation retries, queue age, projection lag and parts/merge load. Use representative content and tenant filters as well as synthetic stress data; record queries, seeds, configuration and execution plans so comparisons can be repeated.

Test delivery on replicated ClickHouse tables and every supported serving engine. Cover ambiguous commit and insert responses, out-of-order completion, gaps in readiness, retry after deduplication expiry, replica rerouting, poison rows, expired leases, interrupted tenant moves, planned and abrupt source promotion, erasure racing a publisher, model-generation cutover and recovery from backup. No enterprise capacity, latency or durability claim is accepted from an untested configuration.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Postgres heads with content in ClickHouse.** This keeps ClickHouse insertion on the write path and adds a second database lookup to each point read. Storing current content in Postgres removes both dependencies for point operations.
- **Waiting for CDC before enrichment starts.** This adds replication lag before embedding and search publication. Enrichment can read the committed revision directly.
- **A custom general replication pipeline.** WalShadow supplies the native replication path. Loom needs domain-specific enrichment and readiness, not another WAL transport.
- **ClickPipes.** Reconsider it if a documented or reproduced WalShadow limitation blocks a required guarantee. Qualify WalShadow first and do not build both replication paths in parallel.
- **Vectors in Postgres or another search database.** Out of scope. Vector storage and execution remain in ClickHouse.
- **One owner API replica per namespace.** This ties availability to process placement. API replicas remain interchangeable; durable coordination belongs in Postgres.

### Where the need comes from

The need is mine, an AI tool helped shape the proposal

### Additional context

This is an architecture proposal. The review checks the contracts against the linked replication, HA and retrieval evidence; it does not establish measured capacity or production readiness. No new load or recall measurements were run for this revision. The sizing inputs remain assumptions. Implementation and release require the quality, isolation, durability, latency, capacity and recovery gates above.

items.title: RFC: richer graph claims for routing, lifecycle and protocols, with TLA+ and Lean verification
items.body:
> **Status (2026-11-06):** the standalone Python approach was withdrawn ([2026-10-16 comment](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/issues/1327#issuecomment-6221155503)), and nine children were closed as not planned. **Shipped** in the compiler's own model:
> - **§1 `cover keys`:** #1496 (spec/verification.md);
> - **§2, configuration half, `no_silent_loss`:** #1492;
> - **§5 `separate_domains`:** #1573 and #1577;
> - **§6 foundation:** `lifecycle_order` is a canonical relation produced by `derive_lifecycle`, plus the lifecycle trace.
>
> **Open:** §2 accepted-message accounting, §3 failure containment, §4 aggregate retained resources, §5 cross-domain delivery budgets, §6 user-facing lifecycle claims, §7 protocols (`transitions` and `runs_under` still reserved), §8 progress and conservation, and a TLA+ or Lean pilot. The checkboxes below predate this note.


---

## Summary

Extend Hale's claim vocabulary across the graph layers consolidated by #1212: exact routing coverage, loss policy, failure containment, retained-resource bounds, placement policy, lifecycle safety, request protocols, conservation, and progress. Evaluate TLA+ for behavioral exploration and Lean for independently checkable certificates and reusable proof rules.

This is an umbrella design proposal building on #1212 (F.40/F.41) and related to the formal-verification roadmap in #18. It develops possible user-facing claims over the lifecycle and evented foundations already discussed in #1212. Individual features and tool integrations should be accepted and scoped separately.

**Source baseline:** Analysis performed September 30, 2026 against PR #1287 head [`85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505`](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/tree/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505), with the [claims guide](https://hale-lang.org/docs/claims/). This issue is being opened October 3, 2026. Implementation-status observations below describe that pinned baseline; reconcile them with current main before splitting implementation work. Proposed claim sentences describe desired semantics and are not accepted Hale syntax.

## Candidate families at a glance

| Family | Example promise | Main prerequisite |
|---|---|---|
| Routing coverage and exclusivity | Every permitted order key selects exactly one intended worker. | Shared key/recipient queries and complete instance populations. |
| No configured silent loss | Critical routes cannot swallow unmatched keys, shed work, or silently discard at a binding. | Explicit delivery-policy contracts, including custom adapters. |
| Failure containment | A tenant's failure cannot restart or quarantine another tenant. | Typed failure propagation and recovery targets joined with ownership. |
| Retained resources | Bound simultaneous queue cells, children, and storage, including restart overlap. | Population, capacity, layout, and lifetime bounds. |
| Placement policy | Selected groups share no execution domain; cross-domain deliveries stay within a bound. | Instance-aware placement and dispatch facts. |
| Lifecycle safety | Reclaim only after relevant work completes; close admission before teardown. | Authoritative action prerequisites, completion, and incarnation semantics. |
| Request protocols | Preparation precedes commit for the same request; terminal outcomes are unique. | States, guards, updates, request identity, and completion obligations. |
| Progress and conservation | Finite work drains; credits and obligations are neither duplicated nor lost. | Transition semantics, invariants, ranking arguments, and explicit assumptions. |

## Proposal

**Yes. Hale's graph architecture could support substantially stronger claims. The most distinctive opportunity is to make ownership, delivery, lifecycle, and protocol behavior jointly checkable.**

Some useful additions need only new queries over existing facts. Others need the compiler to represent execution states, guards, updates, and completion. TLA+ and Lean become useful at different points in that progression.

The graph registry matters because a claim engine and code generation can consume the same meaning of ownership, placement, dispatch, and lifecycle. That reduces opportunities for a verifier to certify one interpretation while emission implements another. It does not itself prove that either the producer or the emitted program is correct. The source explicitly distinguishes semantic facts, claim IR, evidence, lowering plans, and execution evidence. [Model architecture](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/model.md)

The proposed sequence is **routing coverage now; lifecycle safety as the next major capability; a restricted event protocol model after that; independent certificates alongside those steps.**

## What is already there, and what would actually be new

The existing claims cover structural reachability, permitted boundaries, declared endpoint coverage and counts, and quantitative effects. The `avoiding` modifier already expresses structural interposition. `during` chooses a source slice; it does not express an ordering in time. [Claims guide](https://hale-lang.org/docs/claims/)

Several tempting proposals would duplicate existing work:

- Fanout budgets already account for routing scenarios and replica multiplicity.
- Fleet claims already count instance-qualified publisher and subscriber endpoints.
- Resource ceilings and leak analyses already exist for several structural resources.
- Sealing, secret-use effects, and local secret checks already exist. Their documentation distinguishes these from full information-flow guarantees.

The extensions worth pursuing concern **per-key coverage, live configurations, simultaneous resource retention, correlated requests, and changes of state**. [Fanout implementation](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/evidence.rs#L373-L488), [fleet and security contracts](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/verification.md), [resource analysis](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/resource_budget.rs)

There are four identities to keep separate throughout: a source declaration, an arranged replica, a deployed component instance, and a restarted incarnation. A uniqueness theorem about one does not automatically cover the others.

## 1. Every routing key has exactly one intended recipient

**Example:** For every permitted key on `Orders`, exactly one worker instance is selected in this arrangement.

Let `R(k)` be the recipients selected for key `k`. The obligation is `∀ k ∈ permitted_keys, |R(k)| = 1`. This combines two useful checks: no uncovered keys, and no overlapping recipients. A diagnostic can identify an uncovered key or the two conflicting registrations.

Hale already records key domains, subscription predicates, fallback policy, replica identities, and subscription sites. Its fanout analysis computes recipient scenarios. Extracting that computation into a shared query would provide much of the machinery for a coverage judgment. Supporting symbolic intervals or predicate partitions can avoid enumerating every integer. [Key schema](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-model/src/keys.rs), [recipient scenarios](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/evidence.rs#L373-L488)

The claim must say whether it counts every recipient or just recipients in a selected worker group; an audit subscriber should not accidentally invalidate an intended worker-uniqueness rule. Unknown predicates and incomplete populations must prevent certification of exact coverage.

This establishes routing uniqueness for the modeled configuration. Preserving it during replacement, startup, and restart requires a stronger invariant over live registrations and incarnations. Exactly-once processing additionally needs request identity, retry, persistence, and acknowledgement semantics.

**Priority: highest near-term value.** It strengthens a language feature whose necessary facts largely exist already.

## 2. Critical routes have no configured silent discard

**Example:** Every route carrying `Payments` forbids unmatched-key swallowing, queue shedding, explicit discard, and lossy bindings.

The schema already records capacity, shedding, send disposition, and binding loss behavior. Its own documentation identifies future no-loss claims as a reason to preserve these facts. [Delivery and loss distinctions](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-model/src/lib.rs#L66-L96)

Start with a policy claim whose meaning is precise: no modeled boundary is configured to discard silently. A refused send might be acceptable if refusal is observable to its caller. A custom refusal handler that ignores the failure needs its own behavioral account; the mere presence of a handler proves little.

A later obligation could require every accepted message to remain accounted for until processing or explicit cancellation. That introduces transitions and ownership of messages in flight. Neither version should silently promise durability across process failure or eventual service by an unavailable dependency.

**Priority: near term for configuration policy; later for accepted-message accounting.**

## 3. Recovery stays inside a declared failure boundary

**Example:** A failure in tenant A can affect only A's subtree, except for explicitly permitted escalation to a shared supervisor.

This is a valuable join of ownership, error types, supervision, and recovery actions. Initial claims could require supervisor coverage and restrict the operations declared by handlers. The stronger version would compute a failure's possible propagation and recovery targets, then compare that set with a permitted subtree.

The current supervision summary cannot prove that full property. It records deduplicated recovery operations and the last authored retry literal, without the control flow needed to establish actual targets, ordering, resets, or total attempts. Add typed failure transitions and operation targets before certifying behavioral containment. [Handler summary](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/handler_routing.rs#L65-L81), [supervision schema](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-model/src/relation.rs#L330-L384)

“At most three recovery attempts” needs counters and reset rules. “Eventually healthy or quarantined” additionally needs a progress argument and terminating recovery handlers. Shared execution pools and transports may also create interference outside the ownership subtree, so the claim should define which kinds of effect it contains.

**Priority: structural policy soon; behavioral containment after lifecycle extraction.**

## 4. Aggregate retained resources stay within a reservation

**Example:** This service subtree retains at most N queue cells and M live request children, including overlap during restart.

This would go beyond existing per-call budgets and structural resource counts. The new question concerns the maximum resources retained simultaneously across instances and phases.

A useful first version sums queue-slot reservations for a closed, finite arrangement. A byte ceiling then needs proven upper bounds for payload storage, instance population, runtime metadata, temporary work, and overlapping old/new incarnations. A schematic calculation is:

`maximum retained storage ≤ Σ(max live instances × per-instance reservation) + maximum shared/transient storage`

Each term needs a justified bound. An allocation count alone provides none of the missing payload-size or lifetime information. Unbounded dynamic admission must remain visible rather than disappearing from the sum.

The current working-set estimator explicitly uses approximations for alignment, arena overhead, and scratch space. It is useful for locality reporting; it is not evidence for a hard byte ceiling. [Estimator scope](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/working_set.rs#L1-L39)

A related, inexpensive policy would forbid resident request children at selected birth sites. Hale already distinguishes flow children, reclaimed when `run()` completes, from residents. That classification does not establish that `run()` eventually completes. [Flow classification](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-types/src/flows.rs#L1-L18)

**Priority: finite reservation counts first; lifetime-aware byte envelopes later.**

## 5. Placement obeys isolation and communication budgets

**Examples:** `Realtime` and `BulkIO` share no execution domain. A selected request causes at most N cross-domain deliveries.

Ownership and realization identify the relevant instances; placement identifies their domains; routing identifies their communication. The dispatch plan already records whether endpoints share a domain. New claims could quantify over these joined facts, including weighted delivery budgets. [Dispatch plan](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-model/src/dispatch_plan.rs)

The outcome would be a claim about the declared or admitted execution arrangement. A CPU-isolation theorem needs the backend's actual placement contract; the current specification permits approximation on some backends. Dynamic births with unresolved placement must withdraw the corresponding guarantee. [Placement contract](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/registry.md#L1033-L1038)

Neither crossing counts nor a separate pool establish a latency bound. Timing would need additional service-time, scheduling, blocking, and environment assumptions.

**Priority: useful once instance selectors and placement adequacy are explicit.**

## 6. Lifecycle operations obey safety invariants

**Examples:**

- Reclamation occurs only after all work capable of accessing the child has completed or been revoked.
- A released incarnation can never be scheduled again.
- Shutdown closes admission before teardown makes resources unavailable.
- Restart cannot deliver an old incarnation's messages into a new incarnation unless explicitly permitted.

**This is the strongest fit for Hale's particular design.** Ownership, execution domains, failure delivery, and teardown are language/runtime concepts, so the compiler can give the obligations precise subjects and source locations.

The registry already anticipates an explicit lifecycle action plan containing domains, prerequisites, liveness, and completion. At the reviewed head, `lifecycle_order` has no producer and the ordering remains distributed across emission and runtime paths. [Lifecycle inventory](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-graph/src/registry.rs#L1104-L1139)

A lifecycle action graph could make some obligations inexpensive: every reclaim action must require completion of the relevant join, unregister, and in-flight work obligations. But the dependency must be enforced on every applicable execution path. Finding a path from `join` to `reclaim` is insufficient if another path can reclaim early.

Separate unconditional runtime invariants from user policy. Safe reclamation should be an invariant of every legal lowering. A user's choice about cancellation, restart overlap, or admission during draining can be a configurable claim built on that foundation.

**Priority: the next major semantic investment.**

## 7. Requests obey protocols and discharge obligations

**Example:** Each accepted request reaches one terminal outcome: success, rejection, or cancellation. Commit requires successful preparation for that request and incarnation.

This is substantially stronger than checking that a path passes through a named function. The compiler must know what state changes mean and which request they concern. A call to `authorize` whose result is ignored cannot establish authorization of a later commit.

Split the terminal-outcome claim into distinct obligations:

1. **Safety:** a request cannot acquire two terminal outcomes, commit before preparation, or consume a stale incarnation's approval.
2. **Liveness:** every accepted request eventually reaches a terminal outcome under stated scheduling, termination, and environment assumptions.

The first can be checked as an invariant of a transition system. The second constrains entire executions. A publish upper bound of one permits zero publications; it cannot establish eventual completion or correlate an output with an input.

A particularly natural Hale design would create a typed completion obligation on admission. Ownership transfers it through queues and handlers. Success, rejection, or cancellation consumes it. Checking uniqueness and forbidden destruction would establish useful safety properties. An obligation can still be retained forever, so eventual discharge needs a separate progress proof.

This suggests an opt-in evented core with explicit states, guards, updates, request identities, and reset rules. The registry reserves `transitions`, but its producer is absent; input/output event signatures alone do not supply those semantics. [Transition reservation](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-graph/src/registry.rs#L854-L867)

**Priority: highest-value longer-term language feature.** Start with safety and useful counterexample traces, then add liveness.

## 8. Finite work drains, and resources are conserved

**Examples:** After external input stops, the selected event network becomes quiescent. Credits cannot be created or lost while moving between available, reserved, queued, and committed states.

For progress, allow a nonnegative measure that strictly decreases with each relevant transition, with terminating handlers and a scheduler that eventually runs enabled work. A finite acyclic event network is a simpler special case when every handler produces finite work and there are no unmodeled inputs.

The planned restriction of at most one output per delivery does not establish this: a handler can emit one self-event forever. Retries and restarts also need to respect the measure or have a separately bounded budget.

For conservation, restricted guarded updates could support invariants such as `available + reserved + committed = initial + replenished`. Routes represent transfers; queues and in-flight messages must own their share of the accounting. Arithmetic must match Hale's overflow behavior. Aggregate counts alone can hide a duplicated request A and a lost request B, so per-token uniqueness is needed when identity matters.

These properties can be tractable without supporting arbitrary mathematical postconditions on every function. They require a small, precise state language and well-defined transfer primitives.

**Priority: after the evented core; conservation safety may precede full progress proofs.**

## TLA+: explore behavior and find bad interleavings

TLA+ models a system through states and permitted steps. Its tools include the TLC model checker and a separate proof system. TLC can explore finite state spaces and check safety, deadlock, and liveness properties. [Lamport's overview](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/tla/high-level-view.html), [TLC documentation](https://docs.tlapl.us/using:tlc:start), [TLA+ Proof System](https://proofs.tlapl.us/doc/web/content/Home.html)

Hale's best integration would generate a small protocol model from authoritative transition and lifecycle rows. Include the behavior relevant to the claim: queue capacity, refusal/drop policy, scheduling, restart, failure, and incarnation changes. Make guards and state updates explicit. Map a bad trace back to the source events that produced it.

There is an excellent pilot already identified by the repository: the current GenMC mailbox and cooperative-pool models exclude missed-wakeup liveness, and the verification README specifically suggests TLA+ for that handshake. This is a focused system with an existing verification gap and a concrete success criterion. It would also establish a workflow for keeping the model aligned with runtime changes. [Current verification boundary](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/verification/README.md#L160-L189)

Be precise about scope. Exhaustively exploring a finite model can cover its infinite executions through cycles; that is different from checking only traces up to a chosen length. Apalache's bounded mode is explicitly depth-limited, although inductive proof obligations offer another route. Neither a small instance count nor a depth-limited pass automatically generalizes to every deployment. [Apalache modes](https://apalache-mc.org/docs/apalache/running.html)

Bounded queues also do not make a program finite if integer domains, live instances, or other state remain unbounded. A finite abstraction can establish a safety property of a larger program only with a justified relationship between their behaviors. Liveness requires particular care: a scheduler fairness assumption in the model must be supported by the implementation contract.

A counterexample in an abstraction can be spurious. Report it as a model trace and validate its feasibility before presenting it as a concrete Hale execution. A bus cycle alone is neither a deadlock witness nor proof of nontermination.

## Lean: make claims independently checkable

Lean produces explicit proofs checked by a small kernel. That makes it useful for validating the mathematical part of a claim independently of the compiler's search procedure. The first target I would choose is a certificate verifier for existing graph judgments. [Lean's proof architecture](https://lean-lang.org/faq/)

For example, consider a forbidden-reachability claim over a fully specified relevant graph:

- A violation certificate supplies an edge path from a source to a target.
- A holding certificate supplies a set containing all sources, closed under the selected outgoing edges, and disjoint from all targets.
- A small verifier checks those conditions; a Lean theorem proves that an accepted certificate implies the corresponding graph property.

This is a proposal for Hale, not a claim that Lean already understands Hale. Relevant holes and adequacy must be checked too. The theorem initially establishes a fact about the supplied model. The correctness of extraction and its connection to execution remain separate obligations.

Hale has a useful place to carry this evidence: `EvidenceTable` is outside `ApplicationModel` and is associated with model, law, analysis-input, and coverage digests. However, today's `CertificateEvidence` contains an engine result and diagnostics; its name does not make it a kernel-checked proof. [Evidence schema](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-model/src/application.rs#L346-L401)

A future proof bundle should bind the precise proposition, necessary semantic facts, completeness account, assumptions, semantics version, and proof/checker versions. The current topology artifact is a lossy projection; exporters must obtain missing facts from their authoritative producers rather than reconstructing a full model from topology JSON. [Model and artifact boundary](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/model.md)

Later Lean work could prove reusable results: lifecycle plans preserve reclamation invariants; a ranking rule ensures termination; dispatch lowering preserves permitted observable behavior; a component contract composes with a compatible peer. Audit the theorem statement and its assumptions: proving a theorem that assumes extractor correctness does not prove the extractor. The checking path also matters; native computation can extend the trusted implementation. [Lean proof validation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/)

The goal would be for most Hale authors to use ordinary claims and receive checkable evidence. Handwritten Lean should be needed mainly for new proof rules, difficult application invariants, and backend correctness work.

## Two further directions worth reserving room for

**Compositional behavioral contracts.** A component could guarantee terminal outcomes provided its environment respects an input protocol and eventually accepts replies. Fleet composition would verify that the routed peers and transports discharge those assumptions. Typed component identities and routes offer a foundation, but behavioral summaries and sound composition rules are new work. Circular promises require special treatment: A assuming B eventually responds while B assumes A eventually responds is not a progress argument. This is also a route toward proofs that hold for any replica count under suitable independence conditions.

**Semantic information-flow and authority claims.** Once `runs_under` is implemented, principal-sensitive reachability and authority attenuation would be natural extensions. Stronger confidentiality could assert that changing a secret cannot change a defined public observation except through a specified declassification operation. This compares executions and needs data/control dependencies plus a semantic contract for declassification. Passing through an approved function establishes only mediation. State explicitly whether observations include termination, message counts, timing, and scheduling. The current authority relation is reserved, and existing secret checks should be treated as a starting point. [Authority reservation](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/crates/hale-graph/src/registry.rs#L838-L851), [current verification contracts](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/verification.md)

## Soundness and developer experience

Keep the four verdicts, but make evidence scope unavoidable. “Holds for this finite deployment under these assumptions” is a different proposition from a theorem for every permitted population. A timeout, unsupported state semantics, or relevant unknown foreign behavior cannot become an unqualified pass. Expose contradictory assumptions and vacuous checks.

For each new family, define the quantified identity, required relations, exactness requirements, and witness before choosing surface syntax. Prefer the cheapest adequate checker: ordinary graph queries for structural laws, arithmetic or induction for resource invariants, state exploration for finite protocols, theorem proving when reusable lemmas or generality justify it.

The current specification already requires shared queries, declared dependencies, scoped uncertainty, execution-site grain, and aggregation after complete scenarios. Follow those rules for temporal claims too; a TLA+ exporter should not become another independent interpreter of Hale source. [Rules for adding a judgment family](https://github.com/hale-lang/hale/blob/85d11721c5144e64907a3fa74cc4d5f2109b6505/spec/model.md#L698-L742)

Proposed implementation sequence:

1. Add exact key coverage/exclusivity and explicit loss-policy claims using shared queries.
2. Finish the lifecycle action representation; make reclamation and shutdown invariants consume it alongside emission.
3. Model the wake handshake in TLA+ as a focused runtime project.
4. Introduce a restricted evented protocol core; start with request-correlated safety and source-linked counterexamples.
5. Add proof certificates for selected graph laws, then grow reusable Lean lemmas for lifecycle, conservation, and refinement.
6. Add liveness and compositional contracts with visible assumptions and verified connections to implementation.

**The opportunity is a language where a developer can state a systems obligation in ordinary program terms, and the compiler can assemble its proof obligations from facts it already owns.** The deepest work is defining those facts and their relationship to execution. Hale's ongoing graph consolidation makes that work more plausible and more maintainable.

## Design acceptance and follow-up tracking

This checklist concerns agreeing and scoping the design. It does not require every candidate family or both external tools to ship before this umbrella issue can be resolved into follow-up work.

- [ ] Reconcile the pinned analysis with current main and existing work under #1212 and #18.
- [ ] Define each selected family's exact promise, quantified identity, required relations, adequacy requirements, horizon, and diagnostic witness.
- [ ] Scope routing coverage/exclusivity and explicit loss-policy claims as the first implementation candidates, reusing authoritative shared queries.
- [ ] Specify the lifecycle action semantics needed for reclamation, admission closure, restart, and stale-incarnation delivery.
- [ ] Identify missing facts for recovery containment, aggregate retained-resource bounds, and placement/communication policies.
- [ ] Design the restricted protocol representation and completion obligations, separating safety from eventual progress.
- [ ] Evaluate conservation, quiescence, compositional contracts, and authority/information-flow guarantees as later extensions.
- [ ] Define a focused TLA+ wake-handshake pilot with stated bounds, environment/fairness assumptions, and a method for checking correspondence with runtime code.
- [ ] Define a graph-certificate pilot and evaluate Lean for verifier soundness, documenting the remaining extraction, lowering, and runtime obligations.
- [ ] Specify evidence scope, assumptions, versions, relevant holes, vacuity, and counterexample feasibility; distinguish finite-model results, depth-bounded checks, and general proofs.
- [ ] Split accepted work into linked implementation issues with focused acceptance tests and counterexamples.

items.title: [CI] diffusion: perf checks depend on which runner a job lands on, and in-job retries can't fix a slow host
items.body:
[by Claude Code]

## Summary

Whether a diffusion perf check passes depends heavily on which runner the job lands on. A slow host stays slow for the whole job, so the in-job retries (up to 6 of failed items) can't recover. They only add runtime, and a green result ends up depending on where the job ran rather than on the code. @mickqian raised this on #48176. This issue collects two concrete cases, from B200 and 5090.

## Case 1: `b200-cirrascale2`, slow denoise steps

The [`multimodal-gen-test-4-gpu-b200` job](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41728291276/job/126334241079) on #48256 (2026-11-04) ran on `b200-cirrascale2`. That PR adds a cirrascale2 entry to `b200.json` with expected E2E 17346.65 ms, limit 21683 ms. `qwen_image_2512_modelopt_nvfp4_t2i` passed only on the last of 7 attempts:

| Attempt | E2E (ms) | Avg denoise step (ms) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 26883 | n/a |
| 2 | 29418 | n/a |
| 3 | 24770 | 490 |
| 4 | 20065 | 395 |
| 5 | 23379 | 462 |
| 6 | 23680 | 468 |
| 7 (pass) | 19511 | 385 |

Earlier CI runs on the same host are summarized in #48256's `PERFORMANCE.md` section:

| Case | Earlier CI runs on cirrascale2: E2E (ms) | Avg step (ms) | This run: E2E (ms) | Avg step (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `flux1_modelopt_nvfp4_t2i` | 1169–1196 | 80.7–82.9 | 1211 | 84.2 |
| `qwen_image_2512_modelopt_nvfp4_t2i` | 16136–16967 | 317.5–334.0 | 19511–29418 | 385–490 |

`wan22_modelopt_nvfp4_t2v` also failed its first attempt: `Denoise Step 7` took 797 ms against 443 ms expected.

Unlike the 5090 case, the slowdown here is in the denoise steps themselves. Those are GPU compute, and they varied by up to 27% between attempts within one job. Flux, which ran first in the job, was normal. Qwen and Wan2.2, which ran a few minutes later, were slow. That points to something changing on the host during the job (another tenant, clocks, thermals) rather than to a stale baseline. I haven't verified which.

## Case 2: `5090-sm*`, Wan VAE decode spikes (#48196)

Full data is in #48196. In short:
- Since the `1-gpu-5090` job moved to the `5090-sm*` runners on 10-17, `wan2_1_t2v_1.3b` `DecodingStage` goes over its 945 ms limit on **45 / 78** attempts. Before that, on the `a`/`b`/`c` pools, it was 10 / 60.
- `turbo_wan2_1_t2v_1.3b` E2E goes over on **44 / 85**, against 9 / 65 before.
- Every `sm*` host sampled (sm1, sm2, sm4, sm5, sm6, sm8) spikes. Denoise and text encoding don't move; only decode does.
- Retries on the same runner swing between normal and spiked. For example, `5090-sm5-runner-2` gave 2761, 2591, 1961, 3218, 4623, 5752 and 951 ms, and failed after its retries ran out ([job](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41251070653/job/124684593583)).
- A PR run on `5090-sm8-runner-3` failed all 7 attempts with decode at 2297–7278 ms ([job](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/41730713528/job/126247726069)). Main had passed on that same runner the same day.
- Refreshing the baseline doesn't help. Fitting it to the `sm*` normal level only cuts failures from 45/78 to 36/78.
- I checked whether neighboring scheduled jobs on the same host explain it ([comment](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/48196#issuecomment-6611848142)). They don't, as far as main's scheduled jobs show.

## What the two cases have in common

1. The slowdown is per host and can last a whole job, so retries in the job don't help. #48176 only makes `/rerun-test` behave like regular CI here; it doesn't fix this.
2. A baseline can't absorb it without a tolerance so wide the check becomes meaningless.
3. Within one GPU class, the same case runs at very different speeds on different hosts. For example, Wan decode ran at about 320 ms on `5090-c` and about 760 ms on `5090-a`/`b`, and `b200.json` already has per-host `runner_overrides`.

## Options

None of these are tested. They're starting points for discussion:

- **Check the host before trusting the timings.** Run a short fixed GPU microbenchmark before and after the perf cases. If the host is below its normal speed, mark the result inconclusive or rerun elsewhere, instead of failing the PR.
- **Retry on a different runner.** When perf checks fail, rerun the job elsewhere instead of retrying in place. Alternatively, have `/rerun-test` exclude the previous runner.
- **Track speed per host.** Record each host's per-step times from scheduled runs and pull a host out of the pool when it drifts. Here, cirrascale2 would have been flagged by its Qwen step time.
- **Make some checks advisory on noisy pools.** For example, the 5090 `DecodingStage` check could warn instead of failing until #48196 is understood.

cc @mickqian (diffusion CI, raised this on #48176), @em-dreyer (5090 runner hosts), @mmangkad (CI)

## Related

- #48196: 5090 Wan decode spikes
- #48256: B200 `cirrascale2` baseline (its CI produced Case 1)
- #48176: `/rerun-test` retry
- #42752: flaky-test tracker
