items.title: [Audit][Roadmap] Ragbot platform architecture audit and prioritized execution plan
items.body:
## Executive summary

Audit baseline: `main` at the September 2026 architecture after durable worker reliability, staged knowledge generations, parser/chunker ports, Golden Dataset and parser/PDF benchmark work.

Ragbot is already beyond a prototype RAG application. Its strongest current properties are:

- PostgreSQL-backed durable ingestion queue with lease/heartbeat/retry/DLQ/reconciliation
- staged source knowledge generations with PostgreSQL activation authority and durable Qdrant cleanup
- dense Qdrant + PostgreSQL CJK-aware lexical hybrid retrieval + RRF + reranking
- Parser/Chunker ports and promotion benchmarks
- multi-tenant ACL/RBAC enforcement
- SaaS/local/object-source ingestion coverage
- Prometheus/OpenTelemetry plus quality benchmark infrastructure
- OpenAI-shaped compatibility API and a preliminary Node client

The next architecture risk is **integration growth without stable platform contracts**. Current factories and ingestion dispatch still branch on implementation/source names; model routing is not wired as the production composition boundary; embeddings are synchronous; vector index schema has no first-class lifecycle; persistence has a legacy inheritance stack/fat repository; and the SDK/identity/object-storage surfaces are not yet at the same maturity as the ingestion core.

The recommendation is therefore **not** to add dozens of providers/connectors/vector databases immediately. First establish stable extension and index contracts, then expand implementations behind them.

---

## Priority 0 — platform correctness and evolvability

### #50 Platform registry / typed runtime profiles
Make connector/model/embedding/vector/upload implementations resolvable behind one stable registry and shared config/capability schemas.

### #51 LLM provider/router plane
Wire capability-aware model routing into production; remove global environment mutation; add OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/Azure/Bedrock/Ollama adapters behind one contract.

### #52 Embedding plane
Replace synchronous embedding transport with bounded async batching/retry/rate-limit handling and a complete embedding contract identity.

### #53 Vector index lifecycle
Introduce versioned indexes, shadow validation, Qdrant alias activation and rollback for embedding/vector-schema upgrades.

### P0 exit criteria

- adding a provider/connector no longer requires editing core dispatch switches
- model and embedding clients use pooled bounded transports with explicit capabilities
- every indexed chunk can be associated with an immutable embedding/index contract
- incompatible embedding changes build a new index and support atomic cutover/rollback
- current production paths remain regression-compatible

Do not start broad provider/connector expansion before these boundaries are stable.

---

## Priority 1 — production platform surface

### #54 Connector SDK
Standardize snapshot/incremental/checkpoint/deletion/ACL/rate-limit semantics and then validate with SharePoint/OneDrive, Azure/GCS, Slack/Teams or other new connectors.

### #55 Storage architecture
Split the monolithic `Repo`, retire the `postgres_repo -> pg_repo -> managed_pg_repo` inheritance stack and clarify transaction/capability boundaries.

### #56 PostgreSQL performance gates
Keyset pagination, SQL-side filtering, COPY/staging batch paths, queue claim/reconciliation hot-path cleanup, pool/timeouts and query-plan benchmarks.

### #57 Retrieval engine
Move hybrid retrieval to a reusable async/composable pipeline. Keep current hybrid RRF as control, then benchmark Qdrant dense+sparse, alternate fusion, MMR and multi-vector plans.

### #58 Public API / SDK / MCP
Freeze versioned knowledge/search contracts, add maintained Python+Node SDKs, typed retry/error/pagination/stream semantics and a scoped MCP/tool surface.

### #59 Upload object storage
Keep `UploadStore`, add S3/MinIO first and then Azure Blob/GCS, including direct upload and lifecycle/GC semantics.

### #60 Enterprise identity/security
Add OIDC/JWT, service accounts, hashed/rotatable API keys and unified SecretResolver backends while preserving Ragbot RBAC/ACL as authorization truth.

### #61 Durable quality/observability
Tie production requests and evaluation runs to parser/chunker/embedding/index/retrieval/reranker/model contract IDs; use benchmark evidence as promotion gates.

### P1 exit criteria

- platform can horizontally scale API/workers without shared upload PVC
- source catalog/job APIs remain bounded at large cardinality
- retrieval has deadline/cancellation and measurable stage-level latency
- Python and Node consumers have supported, versioned SDKs
- operators can identify exactly which data/model/index contracts produced a response
- identity/secrets no longer depend on one static plaintext API-key mapping pattern

---

## Priority 2 — controlled capability expansion

### #62 Multimodal RAG
Preserve tables/images/layout and visual citations in the normalized document/index contracts, benchmarked against the text-only baseline.

### #63 Release governance
Remove roadmap drift, lock/constraint CI/runtime dependencies, add SBOM/security/compatibility checks and mechanically validate capability/version documentation.

P2 can be partially parallelized, but multimodal indexing should wait for #52/#53 and object artifacts should build on #59.

---

## Dependency graph / recommended order

1. **Foundation:** #50
2. In parallel after the foundation shape is agreed: **#51, #52, #55**
3. Build **#53** on the embedding/index contract from #52
4. Run database operational work **#56** alongside storage consolidation, but do not delay obvious pagination/hot-path regressions
5. Use the registry in **#54 and #59** rather than adding new branches
6. Refactor retrieval in **#57** after the embedding/index interfaces are stable; preserve the current RRF path as the benchmark control
7. Productize **#58** over stable public contracts rather than exposing internal service objects
8. Implement **#61** across all preceding work so promotion decisions become evidence-based
9. Harden enterprise identity with **#60** before positioning Ragbot as a multi-tenant shared service
10. Add **#62** multimodal representations only after index/artifact lifecycle is explicit
11. **#63** begins immediately and stays cross-cutting

---

## Architectural principles to freeze

1. PostgreSQL is the authoritative control-plane/system-of-record store; Qdrant is a derived vector index.
2. Source publication and vector-index publication are different lifecycles; both require atomic activation/rollback semantics.
3. Product semantics/config schemas live in stable handwritten contracts; vendor adapters sit behind them.
4. Connectors emit normalized source changes; parsers emit normalized document blocks; chunkers emit chunks; embedding/index stages do not reach back into vendor connectors.
5. Tenant/ACL filtering happens before evidence is returned, not as a post-generation cleanup.
6. New retrieval/vector techniques are promoted by Golden Dataset + latency/cost evidence, not by feature novelty.
7. Public API/SDK contracts are smaller and more stable than internal service classes.
8. Production network clients use pooled transports, bounded concurrency, explicit deadlines, retries and structured errors.
9. Secrets and identity are references/claims, not arbitrary plaintext configuration fields.
10. Runtime capabilities and release documentation should be machine-verifiable.

---

## Industry baseline used for the audit

- LangChain: common provider/document-loader/vector-store interfaces and separately packaged integrations
- Haystack: composable pipeline components + distinct Document Store abstractions
- Unstructured: source/destination connector architecture, optional connector packages and configurable ingestion stages
- Qdrant: dense+sparse/named vectors, multi-stage Query API and atomic collection aliases for vector-version cutover
- Weaviate / Azure AI Search: explicit hybrid fusion + reranking stages and multi-tenant/filter-aware retrieval
- Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases: decoupled Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate, metadata filtering, reranking, structured/multimodal knowledge paths and retrieval traces
- Vercel AI SDK: provider registries/capability normalization
- OpenAI / Anthropic SDKs: typed streaming/errors, configurable timeout/retry and provider transport concerns kept out of application logic

This audit intentionally treats these products as architectural references, not dependencies to copy wholesale.

---

## Overall target state

Ragbot should converge from a feature-rich RAG service into a **versioned Knowledge Retrieval Platform** with five explicit planes:

1. **Connector/Ingestion plane** — durable source sync, parsing/chunking, generation publication
2. **Index plane** — embedding contracts, vector/sparse indexes, version/cutover/rollback
3. **Retrieval plane** — filters, candidate retrieval, fusion, rerank, evidence/citations
4. **Model/Agent plane** — provider registry, capability routing, bounded tool/model execution
5. **Control/Developer plane** — PostgreSQL metadata/jobs/evals, identity/RBAC, observability, SDK/MCP/admin

The existing code already contains many of these concepts; the next milestone is to make the boundaries explicit enough that new integrations can grow without destabilizing the core.

items.title: Run image embedding on idle CPU via a dedicated queue instead of on the GPU

milestone.title: Sprint 3: Cost and performance
milestone.description: Storage, request volume, cold start and caching work.

items.body:
## Idea

Image embeddings are currently computed on the GPU, inside the same job that runs vision-model inference. The embedding model is small enough to run acceptably on CPU, and the worker instances have substantial idle CPU while the GPU is busy. Moving embedding to those idle cores would free GPU time and decouple two workloads that do not need to share a device.

## Measured, not assumed

CPU utilisation on the worker fleet (4 vCPU instances):

| workload | avg CPU | max CPU | headroom |
|---|---|---|---|
| vision-model inference (real upload burst) | **~27%** | ~33% | **~73%** |
| embedding-only batch run | ~6-18% | ~52% | large |

So the premise holds: roughly three quarters of the CPU sits idle during GPU inference.

## Where the actual saving is

Two distinct paths, with very different payoffs — worth separating before designing:

1. **Inline path (embedding computed during enrichment).** Embedding is a small fraction of a per-image vision-inference job. Moving it off the GPU frees real but modest GPU time. The bigger win here is *pipelining*: computing image N's embedding on CPU while the GPU is already working on image N+1, so the embedding cost disappears from the critical path entirely rather than merely moving.

2. **Bulk re-embedding path.** This is where the money is. A full catalogue re-embed is *entirely* embedding work — it currently spins up the whole GPU fleet to do something with no GPU-specific requirement. Running it on CPU removes the GPU dependency for that path completely. A recent full-catalogue run took ~16 minutes on a fully scaled GPU fleet; the same work on CPU would be slower in wall-clock but would not touch a GPU instance at all, and would not compete with live enrichment for the fleet.

The second is the stronger argument for doing this, and it is also the lower-risk one to build first — it is a standalone batch path with no effect on live enrichment latency.

## Proposed architecture

Decouple embedding from enrichment with its own queue, so the two scale independently:

```
upload → enrichment (GPU) → [embedding queue] → embedding workers (CPU) → record updated
```

Properties worth preserving:
- Enrichment completing should not block on embedding. A record is useful with its analysis and gains search ranking shortly after.
- The embedding stage must be **idempotent and re-runnable** — it already is, which is what makes a separate queue safe.
- A failure to embed must never touch the analysis or the curation verdict. (See #73 — this exact coupling caused data loss.)
- Bulk re-embedding and live embedding should use the same consumer, so there is one code path to trust.

Open design questions to settle before building:
- Do CPU embedding workers live on the existing GPU instances (using idle cores, no new infrastructure) or as their own scalable service (cleaner, independently scalable, more moving parts)?
- What CPU throughput per core does the model actually achieve? This needs measuring on the target instance type before sizing anything.
- Does the queue-depth-driven scaling model transfer, or does a CPU pool want different bands?

## Related: newer model generation

A newer generation of this embedding model family is now published, in both a fixed-resolution variant (backwards compatible with the current one) and a dynamic-resolution variant that preserves native aspect ratio. The latter is relevant for a photography catalogue, where aspect ratio carries real signal and the current model squares every input.

Important constraint: **embedding spaces are not compatible across model generations.** Adopting a new model means re-embedding the entire catalogue — every stored vector becomes meaningless against the new query encoder. That is exactly the bulk path described above, which is a further argument for building it first and making it cheap.

Sequencing suggestion: build the decoupled CPU embedding path, prove it on the current model, then evaluate the newer model as a re-embed through that same path rather than as a coupled change.

items.title: `Saas` Capabilities
items.body:
Here is the complete catalog of **Cloud-Only SaaS Abilities** you can offer to subscribers on **`app.aryorithm.com`**. 

These are features that cannot be run easily on isolated edge appliances alone—they leverage cloud scale, multi-site aggregation, centralized storage, massive GPU compute, and global crowdsourced intelligence.

---

# Master Architecture: Aryorithm Cloud SaaS Capabilities (`app.aryorithm.com`)

```text
========================================================================================================
                               ARYORITHM CLOUD SAAS CAPABILITY MATRIX
========================================================================================================

  1. FLEET ORCHESTRATION           2. CLOUD FORGE & AI HUB          3. GLOBAL THREAT INTELLIGENCE
  • Global Single Pane of Glass    • Cloud GPU Retraining Farm      • Global Collective Immunity Feed
  • 4-Tier Topology & Asset Tree   • Cross-Tenant Federated AI      • Curated SCADA/ICS Zero-Day Feed
  • Central eBPF Rule Dispatch     • 15-Platform Silicon Compiler   • Real-Time JA4 / IP Reputation
  • Configuration Drift Guard      • Automated Canary OTA Manager   • Threat Actor Campaign Tracking
  • Remote Appliance Reboot/Triage • Model Drift & A/B Analytics    • Attacked-Once-Immune-Everywhere

  4. COMPLIANCE & GOVERNANCE       5. FORENSICS & DFIR VAULT        6. SIMULATION & DIGITAL TWINS
  • Continuous NIS2 / DORA Auditor • Tamper-Evident PCAP Vault      • On-Demand Matrix Digital Twins
  • Assessor-Ready CMMC 2.0 Export • AI-Assisted PCAP Deep Carver   • Real Malware Replay Theater
  • Cyber Insurance Risk Verifier  • Cloud CDR Document Sanitizer   • Automated Breach & Attack (BAS)
  • Automated Executive Reports    • Firmware & BIOS CVE Scanner    • Resilience & MTTR Certifier
  • Dynamic SBOM & VEX Tracker     • Cryptographic Chain-of-Custody • Pre-Deployment PLC Validation

  7. BEHAVIORAL & IDENTITY CLOUD   8. ENTERPRISE INTEGRATION & SOC
  • Cloud ITDR (Entra / AD Abuse)  • Universal SIEM / Data Lake Multiplexer (Splunk, Sentinel, Kafka)
  • Kinematic Bot Defense API      • Emergency Pager Hub (SMS, PagerDuty, Slack, Teams)
  • AI TRiSM Prompt Firewall       • Enterprise SSO, SAML & FIDO2 YubiKey Governance
  • Dynamic ZTNA Risk Regressor    • Multi-Tenant MSSP Partner Console (Hierarchical Client Views)
========================================================================================================
```

---

## 1. Global Fleet Observability & Central Management (Nexus Cloud)

* **Global Single Pane of Glass:** Monitor hundreds of physical sites (substations, refineries, hospital networks, naval vessels) across multiple continents on a single interactive map.
* **4-Tier Asset Hierarchy Visualization:** Live topological tree showing `Tenant` $\rightarrow$ `Nexus Hubs` $\rightarrow$ `Edge Appliances` $\rightarrow$ `Individual Sensors / PLCs / Cameras` with real-time health indicators.
* **Fleet-Wide Kernel Rule Dispatch:** Push eBPF drop rules, IP blocklists, or CIDR restrictions across 5,000 edge appliances globally with a single click.
* **Configuration Drift Detection & Auto-Healing:** If an engineer locally modifies a node’s configuration or disables a module, the cloud detects the drift, raises an alarm, and automatically pushes the approved baseline.
* **Remote Appliance Lifecycle & Triage:** Reboot edge daemons, inspect ring-buffer saturation, review interface errors, and restart subsystems remotely without SSH or VPN access.
* **Predictive Hardware Failure Telemetry:** Analyzes CPU temperatures, NPU throttling, and SSD write endurance across edge appliances to warn administrators before physical hardware fails.

---

## 2. Cloud Model Forge & Distributed AI Lifecycle (`xinfer` & `forge`)

* **Cloud GPU Retraining Farm (H100 / L40S Clusters):** Edge nodes lack the compute to train heavy models. Edge appliances upload high-uncertainty latent vectors to the cloud, where massive GPU clusters retrain your Masked Autoencoders (MAE) and InfoNCE neural models in minutes.
* **Cross-Tenant Federated Learning:** Models improve continuously by aggregating encrypted mathematical embeddings from thousands of appliances worldwide, creating hyper-accurate base models without exposing private customer data.
* **Silicon Compilation-as-a-Service (15 Hardware Targets):** A cloud compiler where customers upload an ONNX model, select target hardware (Intel OpenVINO, NVIDIA TensorRT, Rockchip RKNN, Hailo-8, Qualcomm QNN), and download optimized, quantized runtime binaries in seconds.
* **Automated Canary Over-The-Air (OTA) Orchestrator:** Centrally manages the model rollout lifecycle: automatically staging weights in `Shadow Mode`, deploying to a 5% canary cohort, validating metrics, and pushing fleet-wide updates.
* **Model Drift & A/B Shadow Analytics:** Visualizes real-time performance curves comparing candidate models against baseline models (ROC curves, precision-recall, inference latency, false-positive ratios).

---

## 3. Global Threat Intelligence & Collective Defense (CTI SaaS)

* **Global Collective Immunity Network:** The cloud version of "Attacked Once, Immune Everywhere." When a zero-day exploit or brute-force attack hits an appliance in Finland, the anonymized signature is validated in the cloud and fanned out to all subscribers globally within seconds.
* **Curated SCADA/ICS Exploit Early Warning Feed:** Dedicated intelligence stream tracking active, weaponized exploits targeting industrial protocols (Modbus, DNP3, Siemens S7Comm, IEC 60870-5-104, BACnet) before public CVE disclosure.
* **Real-Time JA4 / TLS & Malicious IP Reputation Stream:** Continuously updated database of malicious TLS fingerprints, C2 beacon infrastructure, and bulletproof hosting IPs pushed into edge eBPF maps.
* **Threat Actor Campaign Tracking:** Correlates detections across edge appliances to identify coordinated nation-state campaigns targeting critical infrastructure sectors.

---

## 4. Compliance, RegTech & Continuous Auditing (GRC Vault)

* **Continuous EU NIS2 & DORA Compliance Auditor:** Tracks continuous incident-handling metrics and automatically proves that mitigation executes within mandated timeframes ($< 1\,\mu\text{s}$ SLA).
* **CMMC 2.0 (Level 2) & NIST SP 800-171 Evidence Vault:** Aggregates cryptographic TPM 2.0 hardware quotes and eBPF drop logs, compiling them into audit packages for defense assessors.
* **Cyber Insurance Risk Verifier:** Generates certified, cryptographically signed risk scores based on hardware attestation and mitigation performance, enabling customers to qualify for **20% to 40% discounts on cyber insurance premiums**.
* **Automated Executive & CISO PDF Reports:** Automatically schedules and emails weekly/monthly PDF summaries detailing threats blocked, microsecond SLA performance, and compliance postures for board presentations.
* **Continuous SBOM & VEX Tracking:** Indexes firmware and container binaries, cross-referencing dependencies against the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) to fulfill EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) mandates.

---

## 5. Digital Forensics & Incident Response Vault (DFIR Cloud)

* **Cloud Evidence Vault with Legal Chain-of-Custody:** Secure cloud storage for PCAP evidence carved from edge ring buffers during attacks, signed with SHA-256 manifests for court and insurance admissibility.
* **AI-Assisted PCAP Deep Carver:** Automated cloud dissection of captured PCAP files: reconstructs full TCP streams, visualizes attack steps, and provides plain-language explanations of complex multi-stage exploits.
* **Content Disarm & Reconstruction (CDR) API:** Cloud API where incoming email attachments (PDFs, Office documents) are stripped of active macros, embedded scripts, and zero-day exploits before reaching mailboxes.
* **Firmware Binary Dissector & Backdoor Scanner:** Cloud-based static analysis engine where engineers upload compiled router or PLC firmware to detect hidden backdoors, hardcoded private keys, and vulnerable third-party libraries.

---

## 6. Cyber-Range & Digital Twin as a Service (Matrix Cloud)

* **On-Demand Digital Twin Lab:** Spin up virtual replicas of customer physical network topologies (substations, refineries, hospital networks) in an isolated cloud sandbox with one click.
* **Malware Replay Theater:** Replay authentic historical malware captures (Industroyer, Triton/Trisis, Stuxnet, BlackEnergy) against virtual appliances to test defensive policies before applying them to physical PLCs.
* **Automated Breach & Attack Simulation (BAS):** Scheduled non-destructive simulation runs (using the `matrix-adversary` engine) to continuously probe customer defenses with live `nmap` sweeps and protocol queries.
* **Resilience & Mean-Time-to-Immunity Certification:** Computes empirical resilience scores: measures Mean Time to Fleet Immunity (MTTFI) and validates automated rollback circuits under simulated chaos conditions.

---

## 7. Identity, Behavioral & Application Security SaaS

* **Cloud Identity Threat Detection & Response (ITDR):** Correlates authentication signals across hybrid Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID to catch Kerberoasting, golden tickets, and privilege escalation.
* **Kinematic Bot & Human Behavior API:** A cloud API endpoint for web applications to analyze mouse trajectory acceleration and keystroke jitter, blocking automated bots without CAPTCHAs.
* **AI TRiSM Gateway (LLM Security Proxy):** Cloud firewall that sanitizes prompts and token streams before they reach corporate Large Language Models, blocking prompt injection and data exfiltration.
* **Dynamic Zero Trust (ZTNA) Risk Scorer:** Computes continuous session risk ratings ($0.0 - 1.0$) based on user telemetry and impossible geographic travel velocity, integrating with Okta and Microsoft Intune to adjust access privileges dynamically.

---

## 8. Enterprise Operations, Integration & MSSP Hub

* **Universal SIEM / Data Lake Multiplexer:** Automatically forwards edge telemetry and threat events into customer enterprise data lakes: **Splunk HEC**, **Microsoft Sentinel**, **Datadog**, **Snowflake**, or **Apache Kafka**.
* **Emergency Critical Incident Pager:** Instant alerts via **SMS**, **PagerDuty**, **Opsgenie**, **Slack**, and **Microsoft Teams** when an in-kernel drop or SCADA threshold violation occurs.
* **Enterprise SSO & Hardware Key Governance:** Enforces mandatory SAML single sign-on (Okta, Entra ID) and FIDO2/YubiKey hardware token verification for all administrative actions.
* **Multi-Tenant MSSP Management Portal:** Allows security service providers and industrial integrators to manage multiple isolated client organizations from a single master dashboard.

---

# Commercial Packaging: 3 Subscription Tiers

========================================================================================================

items.body:
CI-shaped workloads need what GHA calls runners: pools of different machines (OS, arch, GPU, network position), steps routed to the right pool, hostile code contained, and the whole thing surviving a machine dying mid-run. Flowstate sits on the one substrate where most of this is already true by construction — the design work is *surfacing* Temporal's primitives without breaking the file-meaning invariant, plus an isolation ladder the field never built properly.

## 1. Task queues are the runner-pool primitive — this is #133's row, elevated

Temporal already routes work by **task queue**: workers subscribe, activities land on whichever subscribed worker is alive. A "runner pool" is a task queue with a name. What's missing is only the spelling:

```yaml
- id: build-arm
  runs_on: linux-arm64        # a pool name the deployment defines
  container.run: { image: "ghcr.io/acme/builder@sha256:…" }
```

**The invariant question, answered up front**: does `runs_on:` make a file's meaning deployment-dependent? No — the same way plugin tasks don't. The file names a *requirement*; a deployment either satisfies it (workers on that queue) or the run **fails loudly** when nothing serves the queue (with a schedule-to-start–shaped diagnostic naming the pool — the run-that-cannot-continue-must-fail invariant, not a silent hang; note today's design deliberately avoids ScheduleToStartTimeout, so "nothing serves this pool" needs its own honest detection). What the step *does* never varies by placement; only *whether this deployment can run it*.

Capabilities beat hostnames: a pool names what a step needs (`linux-arm64`, `gpu`, `in-vpc-prod`), never which machine. Deployment maps names to workers; `flow validate` stays silent about pools (a deployment fact, per the diagnostics rule) while `flow run` fails closed.

## 2. The isolation ladder — each rung explicit, none pretended

| Rung | What | When | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| in-process | built-in tasks (http, log) | trusted, engine-authored | today |
| subprocess | plugins — own process, own deps, bounded transport | trusted-ish code, operator-vetted (#146 pinning) | today |
| container | `container.run` — image **by digest**, bounded output, no ambient anything | arbitrary-but-yours code: builds, tests, tools | design here |
| microVM / VM | Firecracker-class, or a dedicated queue of sacrificial workers | genuinely hostile code — PR builds from forks | design here, later |

The GHA sin to not repeat, precisely: **arbitrary code with ambient credentials on a long-lived shared machine**. The answers are already house rules — secrets reach only declared inputs (the plugin-secrets design generalizes: a container gets exactly the env/files the step declares, nothing ambient); egress from a containerized step goes through netpolicy's posture (network-namespace design needed — the one genuinely new mechanism here); runners for hostile tiers are **ephemeral by policy**, one workload per instance, which is also #145's provenance rule enforced physically.

`container.run` should be a *plugin* (the docker/podman/k8s families differ; #149's factoring applies — `container.*` portable core, `k8s.*` specifics), but the *isolation contract* it must meet is engine-defined, here.

## 3. Disruption: mostly already solved — say so, then close the gaps

What Temporal gives by construction, worth stating in docs because CI people don't believe it: a worker dying mid-step is a **retry on another worker**, not a failed pipeline — history survives, position survives (frames), heartbeats (#143) make the takeover prompt instead of timeout-slow, and a run in flight during a deploy of new workers continues pinned to its version (worker versioning, already enforced). "Self-healing" is not a feature to build; it is the substrate's default that the whole field's CI systems lack.

The honest gaps: (a) a *step* whose side effects are half-done when the worker dies — that's `retry_on_unknown_outcome` semantics, per-task, already the house pattern, and containers must adopt it; (b) local scratch dying with the worker — already the rule (#145: one invocation, content results); (c) "no worker will ever come" detection per §1.

## 4. Spanning machines is the default, not a feature

Steps already run wherever a subscribed worker is; with `runs_on:` it becomes deliberate: build on `linux-amd64`, sign on the HSM-attached pool, deploy from `in-vpc-prod`. Data crosses only as values through history (bounded) or offloaded payloads (#150) — never a shared filesystem, which is what makes the spanning *correct* rather than accidental. A multi-OS matrix is `for_each` over pools once `runs_on:` accepts an expression.

## Sequencing

`runs_on:` (per-step queue) is small and unblocks everything — schema field, options plumbing, the fail-loud detection, docs. The container task rides #149's plugin factoring plus the isolation contract here. MicroVM tier is design-only until someone needs it. The Argo/Tekton findings from the workflow-systems research in flight feed §2 directly.

Related: #133 (task queues row — this is its design), #100/#146/#151 (isolation posture, pinning, remote), #145/#150 (data between machines), #153/#155 (the DX these must not degrade).

items.title: Future capability: Olin Studio — user-generated mini-apps and AI provider gateway
items.body:
## Status

**FUTURE CAPABILITY — NOT APPROVED FOR IMPLEMENTATION**

Preserve this product/architecture idea for later evaluation. It must not interrupt the current Knowledge → Health roadmap.

## Concept

**Olin Studio** (working name): a consumer-facing personal software studio where ordinary users can turn an idea into a small, safe extension of their own Olin / Family OS without needing to program.

The experience should begin from intent, not code:

```
Idea
→ understand the real-world process
→ define data + permissions
→ generate a bounded mini-app / automation / dashboard / workflow
→ test + security checks
→ sandbox preview
→ user approval
→ install into that household's Olin
```

This follows Olin's PROCESS FIRST principle:

```
PROCESS
→ DOMAIN MODEL
→ SERVICES / APIs
→ AGENT TOOLS
→ UI
```

## Target user experience

A normal user could say:

- "Build me a water-consumption tracker."
- "Make a dashboard to compare houses we're considering."
- "Create a baby feeding log for our family."
- "Every Sunday prepare our grocery list for the week."
- "Alert me when home electricity use looks abnormal."

Olin should decide whether the intent is best represented as a:

- mini-app
- dashboard
- tracker/form
- calculator
- checklist
- automation
- monitoring rule
- workflow
- bounded agent capability

The user should not need to understand GitHub, containers, Python, React, MCP, or deployment.

## Initial scope

Start with **Olin-native mini-apps**, not arbitrary SaaS creation.

Good first-class generated artifacts:

- dashboard
- form
- tracker
- calculator
- checklist
- small automation
- custom view

Defer unrestricted "build any software" until the security model is proven.

Possible navigation later:

```
Olin
├── Today
├── Health
├── Nutrition
├── Home
├── Family
├── More
│   └── My Apps
└── Studio
```

## Relationship to the existing AI Dev Factory

Episteck already has an early AI development-factory concept that can move an idea/change request through an idea→product pipeline.

For Olin Studio, that factory may become backend implementation infrastructure, but **must not be exposed directly to consumers**.

Conceptually:

```
Olin Studio
→ AppSpec
→ AI Dev Factory
→ generator/reviewer/test agents
→ sandbox build
→ preview
→ approval
→ Olin App Registry
```

The consumer workflow should be much lighter than the enterprise ERPNext change-request workflow.

## Critical security invariant

**Generated software must never inherit Olin's trusted runtime privileges.**

Generated code must not receive:

- direct production DB credentials
- root/sudo
- Home Control Plane admin credentials
- raw provider secrets
- unrestricted MCP access
- unrestricted family/health/finance access

Instead:

```
Generated Mini-App
→ Capability Gateway
→ least-privilege grant
→ approved Olin/domain APIs
```

Example:

```
app: water-tracker-...
permissions:
  HEALTH:
    CREATE hydration
    VIEW hydration
  subject:
    current authorized Person only
```

A generated app must remain inside the same Person/Circle/Consent and future tenant-security boundaries as the rest of Olin.

## AI Provider & Budget Gateway

A core future Studio capability is **Connect your AI provider**.

Do not assume a consumer chat subscription automatically grants API access. Model/provider integration should be an explicit Olin capability.

Potential provider modes:

### 1. BYOK — Bring Your Own AI

Technical users connect their own supported provider/API account.

Examples later may include:
- OpenAI API
- Anthropic API
- Gemini API
- other approved providers

### 2. Olin-managed AI credits

Episteck manages provider billing and the user receives included/purchased AI usage.

This is likely simpler for mainstream consumers.

### 3. Local / private model

Advanced/privacy-conscious users may point Olin at an approved self-hosted endpoint.

## Secrets isolation

Provider credentials must live in server-side secret storage and must never be exposed to:

- generated source code
- generated mini-app runtime
- browser after setup
- prompts
- Git
- logs
- normal agent/tool outputs

Generated software asks for an AI capability, not a secret.

Conceptually:

```
Generated App
→ Olin AI Gateway
→ policy + budget + model allowlist
→ user's/provider account
→ model provider
```

## Budget / model policy

Studio should eventually support controls such as:

- monthly development budget
- per-build spending limit
- provider allowlist
- model allowlist
- cost/quality profile: cheap / balanced / best
- estimated build cost before execution
- actual usage/cost history

A future UX might say:

> Estimated build cost: €1.20–€3.50  
> Using your connected AI provider.

## Development AI vs runtime AI

Do not treat all AI usage as one pool.

A household may later choose:

```
Development:
high-capability coding model
budget €20/month

Daily Olin:
lower-cost model
budget €5/month

Sensitive Health:
private/local provider only
```

The AI Gateway should support **per-purpose policies**.

A generated app should request a capability such as:

```
ai.generate
purpose = app-development
budget_class = standard
```

The app/model does not select arbitrary credentials or bypass the user's policy.

## Knowledge integration

Authorized Knowledge may later help Studio personalize generated software:

- preferred language
- preferred units
- household conventions
- UX preferences
- family-sharing context

But authorized Knowledge used during generation must not be silently copied into generated source code or permanently embedded in the app.

## Process classification

Studio should determine whether an idea really needs software.

Examples:

- "Track houses we're considering" → mini-app
- "Prepare grocery list every Sunday" → automation
- "Tell me when electricity use is abnormal" → monitoring rule

This keeps implementation proportional to the real process.

## Commercialization relevance

For technical/privacy-conscious customers, Studio can become a differentiator if Olin can truthfully show:

- generated apps are sandboxed
- capabilities are explicit
- household/tenant boundaries remain enforced
- provider credentials are isolated
- users control spend/model policy
- generated apps cannot escalate privileges

## Dependencies / gates before implementation

Do **not** implement Studio before the following are mature enough:

- trusted actor / ConsentGrant foundation
- Knowledge architecture and safe context access
- commercial tenant/security-partition model
- capability/permission model for generated apps
- sandbox/runtime isolation
- secrets-vault strategy
- AI Provider & Budget Gateway design
- generated-code review/test/security pipeline

## Questions for a future Olin Studio Architecture Gate

- What artifact types are supported first?
- What is the AppSpec contract?
- How is a generated app sandboxed?
- What permissions/capabilities can it request?
- How are approvals shown to nontechnical users?
- How are app updates/versioning/rollback handled?
- Who owns generated app data?
- Can generated apps create their own durable schema?
- How are generated apps backed up/exported/deleted?
- How do generated apps interact with Knowledge?
- How are AI provider credentials and budgets managed?
- Which models are allowed for development vs runtime?
- How does a household uninstall an app and remove its data?
- When should Olin create an app vs an automation/workflow/rule?
- Can the existing Episteck AI Dev Factory safely serve as the backend build factory?

## Product principle

> **Olin should let ordinary people safely extend their Personal/Family OS without becoming programmers.**

And the architectural companion:

> **Generated software may use explicitly granted capabilities; it must never inherit Olin's trusted privileges.**

items.title: Visual identify: make 'photo on the wall → book page' actually work (Embassy use case)
items.body:
## Vision

A visitor at the Embassy of the Free Mind (or anyone, anywhere) photographs an engraving on a wall, a page in a physical book, or a print in the wild — and lands on that exact image in Source Library: the gallery entry, the book it comes from, the very page in the reader, with translation. \"Shazam for historical images.\"

## What already exists

- **`/identify`** (live at https://sourcelibrary.org/identify, mobile camera capture enabled) → `POST /api/identify`.
- Pipeline per request: Gemini vision identification (reads inscriptions — invenit/fecit/excudit — very good prompt) ∥ CLIP visual search against `clip_embeddings` (152K rows: artworks, covers, gallery extractions) → then semantic artwork search + Google-grounded verification + Mongo name/title strategies → merged `matches` + a `page` guess.
- CLIP server on Hetzner (`scripts/workers/clip-server.mjs`, Xenova ViT-B/32 quantized, healthy as of 2026-07-18).

## Empirical test (2026-07-18, prod)

Test image: Khunrath *Amphitheatrum* \"Entrance to the Cave of Wisdom\" gallery crop (`gallery-695906c895a91542b28bf73f-0`, book `6952d08677f38f6761bc5477`) — an image that IS in `clip_embeddings`.

**Clean crop (exact copy of an indexed image):**
- Gemini ID: correct title, medium confidence. Correct book found via text strategies; `page` guess = correct book, page 264. ✅
- CLIP: the exact self-match scored only **0.907**, with unrelated Kircher diagrams at 0.892–0.903 — no separation. `matches` array not sorted by score (a 0.892 rendered above a 0.907). ⚠️

**Simulated wall photo (900px, 4° rotation, wall-colored padding, JPEG q65):**
- Gemini ID: **correct, HIGH confidence** — \"Entrance to the Cave of Wisdom (from the Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae)\". ✅
- CLIP matches: pure noise — Piranesi prison, hydraulic diagram, ice-skating emblem, all ~0.845. The indexed image never surfaced. ❌
- `page` guess: **wrong book** (`69487f16b75c15feb90b27ef` p21). ❌

**Diagnosis: identification works; retrieval and ranking are broken.**

## Root causes

1. **Gallery CLIP rows embed the full page scan, not the illustration crop.** `scripts/backfill-clip-embeddings.mjs` Phase 3 embeds `gallery_images.image_url` (= `archived/<book>/<n>.jpg`, the whole page) instead of `extracted_url` (the bbox crop). Example: the Petreius printer's mark row embeds a page that is ~97% Latin text. A photo of the artwork alone mathematically cannot match well.
2. **CLIP ViT-B/32 (quantized) is a semantic model, not an instance matcher.** It clusters \"dense baroque circular diagram\" together; it does not separate *this* plate from *that* plate, especially under perspective/frame/glare.
3. **No query-side cropping.** The visitor photo goes to CLIP with wall, frame, and perspective included.
4. **Fusion/ranking bugs:** matches unsorted; high-confidence Gemini identification does not boost the matching library records to the top; `page` guess can contradict a high-confidence ID.
5. **Rate limit is 10/hour/IP** — a museum's guest wifi NATs all visitors to one IP; the exhibit would break after 10 scans.
6. **Discoverability:** `/identify` is linked from nowhere (no nav, no gallery link).

## Plan

### Phase 1 — fix retrieval with current infra (cheap, high impact)
- [ ] Re-embed `source_type='gallery_image'` rows from `extracted_url` (fix backfill, delete gallery rows, re-run on Hetzner CLIP server — local CPU, $0, idempotent).
- [ ] Query-side crop: add an artwork `bbox` field to the Gemini identify JSON; server-side crop the visitor photo (sharp) and run the CLIP query on the crop. Keep the raw-photo CLIP call as fallback.
- [ ] Fix fusion: sort merged matches; when Gemini confidence is `high`, library records matching the verified title/author rank first; suppress the `page` guess when it contradicts a high-confidence ID; dedupe by book.
- [ ] Re-rank top-K visual candidates with `gallery_images.dhash` (already stored) for near-exact-plate confirmation — free precision boost.
- [ ] Benchmark harness: script that takes N indexed gallery images, generates wall-photo distortions (scale/rotate/pad/compress), and reports top-1/top-5 hit rate. Run before/after every change above.

### Phase 2 — stronger matcher (if Phase 1 benchmark still short)
- [ ] Evaluate an instance-retrieval model (DINOv2-small or SigLIP2, ONNX on Hetzner CPU) beside CLIP; new embedding column; re-embed 152K crops locally ($0). Decide on the benchmark, not vibes.

### Phase 3 — the Embassy experience
- [ ] **Exhibit mode:** curated registry of the works actually on the Embassy walls; match against that shortlist first (near-bulletproof precision), full-corpus fallback. Audit that every wall work exists in `gallery_images` first.
- [ ] QR code at the Embassy → identify page scoped to the tenant (BPH subdomain must respect the tenant-lockdown invariants — results filtered to tenant corpus, no off-subdomain links).
- [ ] Rate limiting compatible with shared museum wifi (per-device token in the QR URL or per-session limits, not per-IP).
- [ ] Result UX: identified card → deep link to `/book/<slug>/page/<pageId>` reader, gallery image page, \"more from this book / this collection\".
- [ ] Link `/identify` from the gallery and site nav so anyone can find it.

## Notes
- Wall-photo test artifacts + JSON responses in scratchpad from the 2026-07-18 session; benchmark harness will reproduce them properly.
- The Gemini identify prompt is genuinely good — don't rewrite it; the wins are all retrieval-side.

items.body:
## Problem

Currently, guidellm generates synthetic datasets **in-memory** at runtime. This creates three significant problems for benchmarking workflows:

### 1. Results are not comparable across runs
Each benchmark run generates a different random dataset, even with identical configuration. When comparing TP=4 vs TP=8, each configuration gets different prompts with different token lengths — the dataset itself becomes an uncontrolled variable.

### 2. Prefix cache benchmarks are unreliable
Prefix cache hit rates depend on exact prompt content. When the dataset changes between runs, the cache behavior changes too, making cache sweep results noisy and unreproducible.

### 3. Large dataset generation is slow and memory-intensive
For large-scale benchmarks (100K+ rows, ISL=15000), generating the dataset in a single process consumes significant memory and time. Multi-turn conversation datasets with 540 turns and 160K first_prompt_tokens can easily exhaust pod memory.

## Proposed Solution

Add support for **persistent, pre-generated datasets** with three key features:

### Feature 1: Deterministic seed-based dataset identity

Generate a deterministic seed from the workload configuration so the same config always produces the same dataset:

```python
import hashlib

seed_input = f"{model_name}:{isl}:{osl}:{hit_pct}:{isl_stdev}:{osl_stdev}:{cache_mode}:{groups}"
seed = int(hashlib.sha256(seed_input.encode()).hexdigest()[:8], 16)
```

The dataset filename includes the seed, enabling automatic reuse:
```
prefix-cache-identical-3510887134.jsonl   # Same config → same seed → reuse
calibration-decode-1-1000-1184319629.jsonl
```

When a benchmark run starts, check if the dataset file already exists before regenerating:
```python
dataset_path = f'/datasets/prefix-cache-{cache_mode}-{seed}.jsonl'
if os.path.exists(dataset_path):
    print(f"Reusing existing dataset: {dataset_path}")
else:
    generate_dataset(config, seed, output=dataset_path)
```

### Feature 2: Multi-worker parallel generation

Split dataset generation across multiple workers using `multiprocessing.Pool`. Each worker generates a chunk with a deterministic seed offset:

```python
import multiprocessing
import random

def _generate_chunk(chunk_args):
    start_idx, count, seed, isl, osl, isl_stdev, osl_stdev, model_name = chunk_args
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    vocab = [t for t in tokenizer.get_vocab().keys()
             if len(t) > 2 and t.isascii() and t.isalpha()]
    
    rows = []
    for i in range(count):
        rng = random.Random(seed + start_idx + i + 1)
        row_isl = isl + int(rng.random() * isl_stdev) if isl_stdev > 0 else isl
        row_osl = osl + int(rng.random() * osl_stdev) if osl_stdev > 0 else osl
        
        # Generate token-accurate prompt using actual model tokenizer
        words = [rng.choice(vocab) for _ in range(row_isl * 2)]
        text = ' '.join(words)
        tokens = tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
        if len(tokens) > row_isl:
            text = tokenizer.decode(tokens[:row_isl], skip_special_tokens=True)
        
        rows.append(json.dumps({'prompt': text, 'output_tokens_count': row_osl}))
    return rows

def generate_parallel(config, seed, output_path):
    num_workers = min(multiprocessing.cpu_count(), 8)
    chunk_size = config.rows // num_workers
    
    chunks = []
    offset = 0
    for w in range(num_workers):
        n = chunk_size + (1 if w < config.rows % num_workers else 0)
        chunks.append((offset, n, seed, config.isl, config.osl, 
                       config.isl_stdev, config.osl_stdev, config.model))
        offset += n
    
    with multiprocessing.Pool(num_workers) as pool:
        results = pool.map(_generate_chunk, chunks)
    
    with open(output_path, 'w') as f:
        for chunk_rows in results:
            for row in chunk_rows:
                f.write(row + '\n')
```

This produces identical results to sequential generation (same seed → same output) but runs N× faster. For 100K rows with ISL=15000, 8 workers complete in ~30 seconds vs ~4 minutes single-threaded.

### Feature 3: Prefix cache simulation modes

Support three cache simulation modes for realistic prefix cache benchmarking:

**Identical mode** — A percentage of rows share the exact same prompt (simulating FAQ bots, fixed system prompts):
```python
def generate_cache_dataset(config, seed, output_path, hit_pct):
    # Generate one shared prompt at max ISL
    shared_rng = random.Random(seed)
    max_isl = config.isl + config.isl_stdev
    shared_prompt = make_prompt(max_isl, shared_rng, tokenizer, vocab)
    
    hit_count = int(config.rows * hit_pct / 100)
    unique_count = config.rows - hit_count
    
    rows = []
    # hit_pct% of rows use the shared prompt (truncated to their ISL)
    for i in range(hit_count):
        rng = random.Random(seed + i)
        row_isl = isl + int(rng.random() * isl_stdev)
        prompt = tokenizer.decode(
            tokenizer.encode(shared_prompt)[:row_isl])
        rows.append({'prompt': prompt, 'output_tokens_count': osl})
    
    # Remaining rows get unique prompts (cache misses)
    for i in range(unique_count):
        rng = random.Random(seed + hit_count + i + 1)
        rows.append(make_unique_row(rng, ...))
    
    random.Random(seed + 999).shuffle(rows)  # Mix hits and misses
    write_jsonl(rows, output_path)
```

**Prefix group mode** — N groups of rows share a common prefix (simulating multi-tenant platforms, multi-repo coding assistants):
```python
def generate_prefix_group_dataset(config, seed, output_path, 
                                   num_groups, prefix_pct):
    # Generate N unique group prefixes
    group_prefixes = []
    for g in range(num_groups):
        grng = random.Random(seed + g * 10000)
        prefix_tokens = int(config.isl * prefix_pct / 100)
        group_prefixes.append(
            make_prompt(prefix_tokens, grng, tokenizer, vocab))
    
    # Each row gets: group_prefix + unique_suffix
    for i in range(config.rows):
        group_idx = i % num_groups
        prefix = group_prefixes[group_idx]
        suffix = make_prompt(isl - len(prefix_tokens), rng, ...)
        prompt = prefix + '\n' + suffix
        rows.append({'prompt': prompt, ...})
```

**Multi-turn conversation persistence** — For multi-turn datasets, use guidellm's existing `SyntheticTextDataset` but persist to disk with parallel workers:
```python
from guidellm.data.deserializers.synthetic import (
    SyntheticTextDataArgs,
    SyntheticTextDataset,
)

def _worker_generate_turns(worker_args):
    worker_id, model_name, config_dict, num_rows, seed = worker_args
    config = SyntheticTextDataArgs(**config_dict)
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    ds = SyntheticTextDataset(
        config=config, processor=tokenizer, random_seed=seed)
    
    results = []
    for i, sample in enumerate(ds):
        results.append(json.dumps(sample))
        if i + 1 >= num_rows:
            break
    return results

# Split across workers with different seed offsets
worker_args = []
for w in range(num_workers):
    worker_seed = seed + w * 10000  # Deterministic per-worker seed
    worker_args.append((w, model, config_dict, chunk_size, worker_seed))

with multiprocessing.Pool(num_workers) as pool:
    chunks = pool.map(_worker_generate_turns, worker_args)
```

## CLI Interface

```bash
# Single-turn with prefix cache simulation
guidellm generate-dataset \
    --model google/gemma-4-26B-A4B \
    --isl 15000 --osl 1000 \
    --isl-stdev 5000 --osl-stdev 500 \
    --mode cache --hit-pct 40 \
    --rows 100000 --seed 3510887134 \
    --output /datasets/benchmark.jsonl

# Multi-turn conversations
guidellm generate-dataset \
    --model RedHatAI/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-FP8-block \
    --isl 1500 --osl 425 \
    --first-prompt-tokens 160000 \
    --prefix-tokens 3000 --prefix-count 1 \
    --turns 540 --rows 100 --seed 42 \
    --output /datasets/agentic.jsonl

# Prefix group mode (multi-tenant simulation)
guidellm generate-dataset \
    --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct \
    --isl 4000 --osl 500 \
    --mode prefix_group --prefix-groups 10 --hit-pct 60 \
    --rows 50000 --seed 12345 \
    --output /datasets/multi-tenant.jsonl
```

## Then use the pre-generated dataset in benchmarks

```bash
# All benchmark runs use the EXACT same dataset
guidellm run \
    --data '{"kind":"json_file","path":"/datasets/benchmark.jsonl"}' \
    --backend "http://localhost:8000/v1" \
    --profile "concurrent:30"
```

## Why This Matters

In our benchmarking platform ([ServeIt Studio](https://github.com/openshift-psap/serveit-studio)), we test 10-30 different deployment configurations per optimization run. Each configuration needs identical input data to produce comparable results. We implemented this externally using the approach above, and it solved:

- **A/B test accuracy**: TP=4 vs TP=8 comparisons now show real performance differences, not dataset noise
- **Cache sweep reliability**: Testing 0%/20%/40%/60%/80% cache hit rates with deterministic prefix sharing produces clean, reproducible curves
- **Generation speed**: 100K rows with ISL=15000 generates in ~30s with 8 workers vs ~4 minutes single-process
- **Memory efficiency**: Workers process chunks independently — no 100K×15K token array in memory at once
- **Reuse**: Same model+workload config auto-detects existing dataset and skips regeneration, saving minutes per run

We're happy to contribute the implementation if there's interest. The code is MIT-licensed at:
- Single-turn generator: [`docker/scripts/generate_dataset.py`](https://github.com/openshift-psap/serveit-studio/blob/main/docker/scripts/generate_dataset.py)
- Multi-turn generator: [`docker/scripts/generate_turn_dataset.py`](https://github.com/openshift-psap/serveit-studio/blob/main/docker/scripts/generate_turn_dataset.py)
