items.title: yet another redesign
items.body:
i'd like to do a complete redesign of this package. we may be able to use or salvage bits and pieces, but the fundamental design needs an overhaul.

i'm seeing three interrelated components. i haven't thought through all of the details, so there are going to be gaps and inconsistencies, and many edge cases i haven't fully thought through.

# component 1: recursive problem breakdown

## basic description

given a task, it should be broken down into a series of concrete steps. this is what a "pipeline" is. ideally a pipeline should small number of steps-- like aiming for on the order of 10 or fewer, but possibly (for very complex tasks) this could be potentially unbounded. pipelines may also have loops, conditionals, and goto statements; the control flow of pipelines must be a complete (albeit simple) "language".

each step in a pipeline takes one of two forms:

1. an atomic step (see component 3) that we already know how to solve. essentially this is either (a) a simple or trivial task or (b) a complex task that we already had to solve and whose solution is stored and searchable/deemed relevant. in either case, the "point" is that the step doesn't require substantial additional work; we can just proceed by running an existing skill or pipeline, and then "smoothing over the outputs" (i.e., parsing, adapting the answer, converting it to the desired format, or other trivial operations that can be deterministic OR that might require a reasonably capable LLM to accomplish).

2. an ambiguous step that we do NOT know how to solve. instead of trying to solve it immediately, we describe (briefly) what *happens* at this step (what are the inputs, what are the outputs/consequences). then it gets fed recursively into the same "break down a problem" system. in other words, the step becomes its *own* pipeline, that can be called and referenced from its parent pipeline when the corresponding step of the parent pipeline is reached. the parent (i.e., process storing the pipeline where the child pipeline is one of the steps) assumes responsibility for calling that child pipeline and smoothing over its outputs/consequences (same process as for atomic steps).

a critical special case, which we need to handle, is that we may not KNOW how to break the step down further. e.g., it may be its own research project. in that case, we invoke a planning tool, which may involve its own (separate) research and experimentation pipeline. it must be allowed to search the web, read existing literature, download data, and run code (simulations, real commands). doing this properly requires careful thought and planning.

## other thoughts

the goal here is to come up with a GENERAL solution for *solving arbitrary problems* by recursively breaking them down into successively smaller and smaller pieces, until the pieces become simple enough that it's obvious how to solve them.

in some cases we might know how to solve the problem from the start-- but in other cases, breaking down a problem into a pipeline may NOT be obvious...or the "obvious" solution may not actually work in practice.

therefore, the system for constructing pipelines needs to incorporate three additional tools that will end up being used repeatedly by many parts of the toolbox:

a) critical review. this entails launching a SEPARATE subagent with access to the solution or plan, AND a high-level description of the problem to be solved. the job of the subagent is to red-team the proposed solution and identify gaps and bugs. the original authoring agent and the red-team agent continue looping until the red-team concerns come back clean. note that concerns MUST be tracked so that the scope doesn't simply drift endlessly with the problem being constantly redefined in each round. fundamental rule: no authoring agent can (ever) self-review its own work. the same *model* may be allowed to self-review another instance of itself, but that instance must be run in a fresh session from the one used to construct the artifact under review.

b) context recursion. when the problem or context grows too large, this needs to be managed via a system analogous to file descriptor tables on storage devices. the original problem/contents is stored in a table that points to either (i) a complete document, if it is sufficiently small to fit in no more than 25% of the model's context, or (ii) a set of summaries of documents, each of which may be prepared by other agents who themselves use file descriptor table like objects to store/summarize anything "below" their scope. the total length of the set of summaries must be small enough to fit in no more than 25% of the model's context. the "recursive" part comes in as follows:

suppose our max available context is 1M tokens. So we can use up to 250k for a document or summary. if the document is more than 250k tokens long, it MUST be broken down (considered in pieces), each no more than 250k tokens long. each piece is then summarized. then the *summaries* are stitched back together. but suppose the stitched-together summaries are *also* longer than 250k tokens. then the *summaries* need their own summaries, and so on. this needs to happen recursively (like for file descriptor indices and inodes, where a file may point to a location on disk where something is stored, OR another inode table) to enable documents or content of ANY arbitrary length to "fit" into no more than 25% of ANY (abritrary) model's context.

note that this entire process must be fully traceable and searchable, in case the "details" need to be retrieved later. on disk the full content must be available, with pieces (at each level of summarization) accessible on demand in a RAG database, keyword search, and similar. (need to think about the right way to do this!)

c.) data-driven design. we can't know how to solve a problem that has never been solved before. but we can say: IF each piece of the problem looks like THIS, and if each step behaves like THAT, does the full proposed solution hold together logically? we can turn the proposed solution into a series of deterministic operations that are applied to a set of concrete objects with the assumed form. for each object, we also need criteria for determining (when we see real data or try the thing out in practice) whether it's going to match our expectations or not- and if not, we may need to re-evaluate our assumptions and possibly re-design a solution! we also need a system for writing down (in advance) expectations about how the solution should behave (e.g., what are its results, what other observable patterns should we see in the behavior). then that simulation should be written and run, and (via the system "a" described above) red-teamed and critically evaluated, in a fully traceable way, by *independent* agents (i.e., agents that didn't produce the original artifacts or predictions). again, this needs super careful planning and designing. essentially we're trying to automated the process of quickly generating "estimated solutions" as runnable code that can be checked deterministically against the assumptions, as a means of evaluating the strengths or weaknesses of the approach.

# component 2: organization tree

each "step" of a pipeline (including the full pipeline itself-- which is a single step: "run pipeline X") is a "node" in a tree that represents the structure of the problem. each node is an agent (LLM instance):

- if the corresponding "step" is atomic (known solution), the node is a "leaf". the agent simply runs its step, red-teams the outputs for quality control, and then passes the results (in the desired format) to its parent node (or the user, if the node is the root of the tree).
- if the corresponding "step" is ambiguous (NO known solution), the node's children are the pipeline steps represented by the broken-down version of that problem. to "run" that node's step, it needs all of its children to run *their* steps, in the proper sequence. the node must take responsibility for steering the process, stitching together results from its children, and then passing the result to its parent node (or the user, if the node is at the root of the tree).

nodes in the org tree must also maintain an ability to send, receive, and route messages:

a. SENDING a message means: compose a *new* message, based on the node's current scope of work, and send it to either that node's parent (including the user, if needed, and if the node is the root of the tree) or an immediate child.
b. RECEIVING a message means: interrupt ongoing operations to process the message content. this may alter how a problem is processed, how the pipeline the node is running is administered, it may be simply ignored, or anything else the node deems necessary or appropriate given its current task.
c. ROUTING a message means: pass along a received message that the node can't handle itself because it is outside of the scope it is immediately handling. there are two ways to route a message: pass it to an immediate parent (if it is HIGHER level than the current node's responsibilities) or pass it to an immediate child (in which case, select the specific child or children who is/are most likely to benefit from or be affected by the message.

# component 3: shared resources and communication

## shared scratchpad of ALL thinking from EVERY agent

ALL agents take notes in the shared scratchpad, whose access is controlled by a semaphore (lock/mutex). before executing a step, wait for the lock to become available. then grab the lock. then read recent messages and consider whether it alters the current plans/action. if YES, make a quick note about what you were planning to do BEFORE and why recent info means you should alter those plans. if you know how to proceed now (in a different way), say that.  if NO, just write down your plans. then release the lock.

the last [5% of the reading model's context length] tokens should be read directly from the scratchpad. use the context recursion strategy above to summarize anything else so that it uses no more than an additional 10% of the reading model's context length. the summarizations should be cached.

an important special case is: my plans might be affected by some other thought that was written down previously, but it's no longer in the latest "direct read" portion of the scratchpad. in this case, since context recursion always must preserve the original text (and/or lower level summaries), the agent is allowed to replace its [15% of its total context length] tokens of "scratchpad context" with a "focused" set of text that is more directly relevant to the agent's current goals. accomplishing this needs careful thought and planning.

## shared insights across agents

whereas the scratchpad provides a largely undiluted "stream of consciousness" view of the team's thinking, a seperate searchable system (RAG database?) should be used to track "insights" from the agents. when any agent gains a special insight into the problem-- something non-obvious, something non-trivial, correcting a critical misunderstanding, etc.--it should go into the insights database. each insight is its own entity. agents should use RAG (or similar) to seed its context with relevant insights (using up to 10% of additional context, and using context recursion to summarize as needed), prior to starting a next chunk of work.

special cases:
 - if an agent wants to contribute a NEW insight, it MUST be red-teamed by an independent agent to verify relevance and accuracy. only after a red-team pass may it be added to the pool
 - if an agent thinks an insight should be REMOVED from the pool, that decision needs to be red-teamed by an independent agent who reviews the insight + reasoning for removal and makes a decision. only after red-teaming may an insight be removed from the pool.

## shared tools and skills

agents must organize themselves using principles of "compound engineering." initially, we seed a common pool of tools and skills with some useful simple operations that cover a variety of common tasks: browsing the web, web search, text extraction, executing code in a sandboxed virtual environment (in a way that properly handles dependencies), reading/writing/downloading files, and so on. (research is needed to come up with this pool.) but as a pipeline proceeds, NEW skills and tools-- either comprised of existing tools/skills, or entirely new tools/skills constructed from scratch, or combinations thereof--get added to the pool. once added (and red-teamed by an independent agent that must USE the tool/skill and evaluate the quality of the output, fix issues, etc.), anything in the pool may be used by any agent from that point onward.

each tool and skill must be attached to a complete history of when and how it was called.

if a tool or skill is discovered to NOT work as expected by a given agent, a request for review must be initated. effectively, this is a bug report. it must be processed by a DIFFERENT agent.

- describe the use case
- describe the expected outcome
- describe the observed outcome
- provide any other relevant context or notes

when the reviewer agent picks up a bug report, it must examine the bug report AND the history of that tool/skill's use. the reviewer must then decide to fix the skill/tool, modify it (e.g., clarify where/when/how it should be used), or remove the skill/tool from the pool (if it is broken). removal should happen only if there is sufficient evidence that it is broken, per the log file.

items.title: [Epic]: End-to-End Async Request Queue & Batch API Benchmarking (inference-perf + llm-d-benchmark)

labels.name: Epic
labels.description: Umbrella issue tracking a multi-PR feature

items.body:
### Goal

Provide a unified, reproducible benchmark suite across asynchronous request queues and Batch API workloads whose primary objective is to answer:

> **"How many successfully completed, on-time requests (or tokens) did we get for every accelerator-hour we were billed for?"**

 alongside end-to-end **batch makespan** (how long a submitted batch takes to finish) while enforcing strict deadline/window attainment SLOs across both fixed-capacity baselines and dynamic `0 <-> N` autoscaling.

---

### Problem Statement

Asynchronous request queues ([`llm-d-async`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-async) + [`llm-d-router`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router) Coordinator `async-broker`) and bulk batch processing ([`llm-d-batch-gateway`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-batch-gateway) OpenAI Batch API) relax immediate interactive token latency (TTFT/TPOT) in exchange for **serving work within a deadline or completion window at high accelerator efficiency**.

Standard synchronous open-loop benchmarks do not capture async and batch serving trade-offs:
1. **Unbounded raw throughput is misleading under deadlines:** A saturated system can report high raw `req/s` or `tok/s` while delivering responses *after* caller deadlines have expired (wasting GPU capacity on late work).
2. **Multiple production ingress paths:** Workloads enter `llm-d-async` either directly via the Redis SortedSet producer contract or via the `llm-d-router` Coordinator `async-broker` HTTP plugin (`wait` and `enqueue` modes).
3. **Autoscaling cold-start vs. idle GPU burn:** Scaling `0 <-> N` or `M <-> N` saves idle GPU-hours between bursts, but incurs pod scheduling, image pull, model weight loading, and KEDA scale-down stabilization costs that must be accounted for in GPU-hour efficiency metrics.
4. **Batch API job makespan:** Bulk file-based jobs (`/v1/files` + `/v1/batches`) require measuring end-to-end **batch makespan** (how long an entire batch takes to be served) alongside item/token throughput and GPU-hour efficiency.

---

### Proposed Solution

Establish end-to-end async request queue and Batch API benchmarking across a clean two-layer architecture:

1. **[`kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf) (Client Load, Wire Protocols & Lifecycle Reporting):**
   Owns arrival generation (`constant`, `poisson`, `concurrent`, `trace`, multi-stage bursts + idle gaps), tokenized prompt synthesis (`random`, `shared_prefix`, `sharegpt`), wire protocols (**native `llm-d-async` Redis SortedSet client**, **Coordinator HTTP `wait` & `202 enqueue + poll`**, and **OpenAI Batch API `/v1/files` + `/v1/batches`**), and client-side deadline/makespan reporting.
2. **[`llm-d/llm-d-benchmark`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-benchmark) & [`llm-d/llm-d-autoscaling`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-autoscaling) (Cluster Orchestration, GPU-Hour Telemetry & Goodput Scoring):**
   Owns Kubernetes deployment (`standup`/`teardown` for fixed-replica control and KEDA autoscaling stacks), pod/GPU lifecycle sampling (`collect_metrics.sh` + `process_metrics.py`), post-stage scale-to-zero & duty-cycle accounting windows, **Allocated GPU-Hour (`H_alloc`)** integration, Benchmark Report v0.2 generation, and Constrained Goodput scoring (`score.py`).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph IP["kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf (Load, Wire Clients & Lifecycle Reporting)"]
    DG["Datagen + HF Tokenizers (random, shared_prefix, sharegpt, trace)"]
    LG["Stage & Arrival Engine (constant, poisson, concurrent)"]
    DG --> LG
    LG --> C1["OpenAI Client: Wait Mode (x-llm-d-async-mode: wait)"]
    LG --> C2["OpenAI Client: Enqueue+Poll (202 + GET /v1/requests/{id})"]
    LG --> C3["llm-d-async Redis Client (server.type: llmd_async_redis)"]
    LG --> C4["OpenAI Batch API Client (api.type: batch -> /v1/files, /v1/batches)"]
    C1 & C2 & C3 & C4 --> RG["reportgen: goodput_metrics + per_request / batch lifecycle JSON"]
  end

  subgraph SUT["Cluster Under Test (Deployed by llm-d-benchmark standup)"]
    C1 & C2 --> Coord["llm-d Coordinator (async-broker)"]
    Coord --> Redis[("Redis SortedSet")]
    C3 --> Redis
    Redis --> AP["llm-d-async Worker Pool"]
    C4 --> BG["llm-d-batch-gateway (/v1/files, /v1/batches)"]
    BG --> Router["llm-d Router + EPP"]
    AP --> Router
    Router --> Pool["vLLM Model Servers (Fixed N Control vs. KEDA 0..N Autoscaled)"]
  end

  subgraph Bench["llm-d-benchmark (Cluster Telemetry, GPU-Hours & Scoring)"]
    Collect["collect_metrics.sh + KEDA Scale-Down / Duty-Cycle Window"]
    Proc["process_metrics.py (H_alloc, pod startup) + metrics_embed.py (BR v0.2)"]
    Score["score.py (Gate on max_failure_ratio / attainment + Goodput / H_alloc)"]
    Collect --> Proc --> Score
  end

  RG --> Proc
  Pool -- "PodScheduled / Ready / GPU requests / /metrics" --> Collect
```

---

#### Core Benchmarking Requirements & Measurement Definitions

##### 1. Control Group — Fixed Accelerators & Deadline Compliance
Evaluates a **fixed number of model-server pods (`M`) and accelerators (`G`)** over a defined time window `T_window = t_1 - t_0` with autoscaling disabled:

- **On-Time ("Good") Request (`N_good`):** Completes successfully (`2xx`, no error) at or before its deadline (`t_done - t_submit <= D_i`).
- **On-Time Request & Output Token Throughput (Control Base Rates):**

$$
\text{RequestGoodput} = \frac{N_{\text{good}}}{T_{\text{window}}} \quad (\text{req/s}), \qquad
\text{OutputTokenGoodput} = \frac{T_{\text{out,good}}}{T_{\text{window}}} \quad (\text{tok/s})
$$

- **Normalized Base Goodput (`req/GPU-hr`, `tok/GPU-hr`):** Dividing by fixed accelerator-hours `H_alloc = G * (T_window / 3600)` expresses the Control Group in the exact same units used for Autoscaling treatments.
- **Deadline Miss Penalty (Aligned With `inference-perf` & `llm-d-benchmark` `score_slo_goodput`):**
  1. *Zero-Credit Numerator:* Requests exceeding their deadline (`504 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, client timeout, late `2xx`, or error) contribute `0` to `N_good` and `T_out,good`, while any wall-clock time and GPU capacity they consume remain in `T_window` and `H_alloc`.
  2. *Hard Miss-Ratio Gate:* Consistent with `score_slo_goodput()`, runs whose deadline miss ratio `(N_submitted - N_good) / N_submitted` exceeds `max_failure_ratio` (e.g., `0.01` for `99%` attainment) receive `verdict = "fail"` and are disqualified from passing Goodput comparisons.

##### 2. Dual Async Queue Ingress Paths
Both async queue ingress mechanisms are benchmarked through `inference-perf` using identical arrival schedules, token distributions, and scoring:
1. **`llm-d-async` Redis SortedSet Client (`server.type: llmd_async_redis` in `inference-perf`):** Enqueues OpenAI payloads directly into Redis using `llm-d-async`'s atomic SortedSet Lua contract (`request-seq:*`, `request-active:*` TTL, EDF priority score `deadline_unix + seq / 2^21`) and consumes completion envelopes asynchronously from the Redis result list (`BRPOP`).
2. **`llm-d-router` Coordinator `async-broker` Plugin (`openai_client` in `inference-perf`):** Benchmarks standard OpenAI HTTP requests through Gateway + Coordinator with `x-llm-d-tenant` and per-request relative deadlines via `x-llm-d-request-timeout-seconds`:
   - **`x-llm-d-async-mode: wait`:** Held HTTP connection woken via Redis keyspace notification (`200 OK` or `504 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`).
   - **`x-llm-d-async-mode: enqueue`:** Immediate `202 Accepted` (`{"id": "..."}`) followed by asynchronous `GET /v1/requests/{id}` polling with matching `x-llm-d-tenant` header until terminal delivery or `504`.

##### 3. Autoscaling Treatments — Cold-Start & GPU-Hour Goodput
Evaluates dynamic replica scaling (`0 <-> N` and `M_min <-> M_max` across KEDA Cron, Backlog, and Deadline-Proximity strategies) under the **same workload and duty-cycle window `[t_0, t_1]`** as the Control Group:

$$
H_{\text{alloc}} = \frac{1}{3600}\int_{t_0}^{t_1} G_{\text{alloc}}(t)\,dt, \qquad
\text{ReqGoodput}_{\text{GPU-hr}} = \frac{N_{\text{good}}}{H_{\text{alloc}}}, \qquad
\text{OutputTokGoodput}_{\text{GPU-hr}} = \frac{T_{\text{out,good}}}{H_{\text{alloc}}}
$$

- **Cold-Start Penalty in `H_alloc`:** Once a scaled-up serving pod is bound to a node (`spec.nodeName != ""`), its GPUs count toward `G_alloc(t)` during image pull, weight loading, and warmup (`Ready=False`) while serving `0` requests.
- **Scale-Down Cooldown Accounting:** Post-stage accounting waits for KEDA cooldown/stabilization to settle replicas back to target (e.g., `0`) and holds duty-cycle windows so Always-On idle burn and Scale-to-Zero cooldown burn are measured over identical horizons.
- **Efficiency Gain:** Using fewer accelerators for less time shrinks `H_alloc` and increases Goodput, provided cold-start latency is absorbed within request deadlines (`A >= 1 - max_failure_ratio`). Also reports pod cold-start latency (`C_mean`, `C_p90`) and `overhead_gpu_fraction = (H_alloc - H_ready) / H_alloc`.

##### 4. Batch API Benchmarking — Batch Makespan & Efficiency (`llm-d-batch-gateway`)
Evaluates file-based OpenAI Batch API jobs (`POST /v1/files` -> `POST /v1/batches` -> `GET /v1/batches/{id}` -> `GET /v1/files/{output_file_id}/content`):
- **Batch Job Makespan (`T_batch_job`):** `t_completed - t_batch_created` — wall-clock time required to serve an entire batch job to terminal `completed` status.
- **End-to-End Batch Turnaround (`T_batch_e2e`):** `t_output_downloaded - t_file_upload_start` — includes input JSONL upload and output JSONL download.
- **Phase Breakdown:** Upload duration, queue/validation wait (`t_in_progress - t_batch_created`), active execution (`t_finalizing - t_in_progress`), and finalization/download.
- **Batch SLO Window & Ordering:** Completion within requested `completion_window` (`30m`, `2h`, `24h`), item success ratio (`completed / total`), priority ordering across concurrent batches, effective item/token drain rate (`N_items_ok / T_batch_job`), and Batch GPU-Hour Goodput (`N_items_ok / H_alloc`) across Fixed vs. Autoscaled pools.

---

#### Workstream & Task Breakdown

##### Workstream 1: `kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf` Async & Redis Capabilities
*Goal: Enable `inference-perf` to drive scale-to-zero endpoints, evaluate per-request deadline Goodput across all submitted requests, and support both Coordinator `async-broker` (`wait` + `enqueue`) and native `llm-d-async` Redis SortedSet transport.*
*Dependencies: None (can start immediately; Tasks `1.1`–`1.4` are independent of each other and can land as separate PRs).*

- [ ] **Task 1.1 — Scale-to-Zero Readiness Bypass (`openai_client.py`):** Add `server.skip_readiness_check: bool = False` so `openAIModelServerClient` does not block on `GET /v1/models` when KEDA has scaled model servers to `0` replicas prior to traffic arrival.
- [ ] **Task 1.2 — Deadline Goodput & Total-Submitted Attainment (`reportgen/base.py`):** Add per-request deadline header extraction (`api.slo_request_latency_header`, e.g., `x-llm-d-request-timeout-seconds` with configurable unit `s`/`ms`) and extend `goodput_metrics` with `good_output_tokens`, `output_token_goodput`, and total-submitted attainment (`good_requests / (len(successes) + len(failures))`) so `504 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` responses are reflected in attainment percentages.
- [ ] **Task 1.3 — Coordinator HTTP `202 Enqueue + Poll` Mode (`openai_client.py`):** Add optional `api.async_polling` (`poll_url_template: "/v1/requests/{id}"`, `id_json_field: "id"`, `poll_interval_sec`, forwarded tenant/auth headers) so `202 Accepted` responses are polled asynchronously until `200 OK` or `4xx/5xx`/timeout.
- [ ] **Task 1.4 — Native `llm-d-async` Redis SortedSet Client (`llmd_async_redis_client.py`):** Add `ModelServerType.LLMD_ASYNC_REDIS` (`server.type: llmd_async_redis`) implementing `ModelServerClient` (`redis_url`, `request_queue_name`, `result_queue_name`, `default_deadline_seconds`) using atomic EDF Lua `ZADD` submission and async `BRPOP` result collection compatible with multiprocess `forkserver` workers.

##### Workstream 2: `kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf` OpenAI Batch API Support
*Goal: Enable `inference-perf` to benchmark OpenAI-compatible Batch APIs (`/v1/files` + `/v1/batches`) and measure end-to-end batch makespan.*
*Dependencies: None (independent of Workstream 1; can start immediately in parallel, with Task `2.2` building on Task `2.1`).*

- [ ] **Task 2.1 — `APIType.Batch` & JSONL Materialization:** Add `api.type: batch` (`endpoint`, `completion_window`, `batch_size`, `poll_interval_sec`), serializing prompts from any `inference-perf` `DataGenerator` (`random`, `shared_prefix`, `sharegpt`) into OpenAI Batch JSONL files.
- [ ] **Task 2.2 — Batch Lifecycle Execution & Makespan Reporting:** Implement async `/v1/files` upload -> `/v1/batches` creation -> `/v1/batches/{id}` status transition & progress polling -> `/v1/files/{output_file_id}/content` & error JSONL download, emitting batch makespan (`T_batch_job`, `T_batch_e2e`, stage durations, `completion_window` attainment, item success/error counts, and token totals) alongside per-item lifecycle metrics.

##### Workstream 3: `llm-d-benchmark` Stack Deployment, GPU-Hour Telemetry & Goodput Scoring
*Goal: Deploy async queue and Batch Gateway stacks, measure scheduled GPU-hours across cold-start and scale-down lifecycles, and produce Benchmark Report v0.2 + Goodput scores.*
*Dependencies: Tasks `3.1`–`3.3` have no external dependencies and can run in parallel with Workstreams 1 & 2; Task `3.4` depends on Task `3.3` plus Workstream 1 (for async deadline report fields / `Dockerfile` pin) and Workstream 2 (for Batch API makespan report fields / `Dockerfile` pin).*

- [ ] **Task 3.1 — Async Queue & Coordinator `async-broker` Deployment:** Support deploying `llm-d-async` + Redis (`notify-keyspace-events Kl`, `maxmemory-policy noeviction`, `result_ttl_seconds`), `llm-d-coordinator` (`async-broker` pipeline step + `/v1/requests/*` `HTTPRoute`), KEDA `ScaledObject` triggers (`cron`, `prometheus`, `fallback`), and `0`-replica standup/smoketest readiness handling.
- [ ] **Task 3.2 — `llm-d-batch-gateway` Deployment:** Add optional `batchGateway` standup/teardown templates deploying `apiserver`, `batch-processor`, and `batch-gc` (with PostgreSQL/Redis metadata and PVC/S3 file storage) for both sync AIMD Router dispatch and `llm-d-async` queue dispatch.
- [ ] **Task 3.3 — Pod-Level `H_alloc` Telemetry & Post-Stage Accounting Windows:** Extend `collect_metrics.sh` and `process_metrics.py` to scrape `llm-d-async` / `batch-gateway` pods, sample pod-level `scheduled_gpus` (`spec.nodeName != ""`) vs. `ready_gpus`, hold post-stage scale-to-zero settlement / duty-cycle windows in `inference-perf-llm-d-benchmark.sh`, and compute `allocated_gpu_hours`, `ready_gpu_hours`, and `overhead_gpu_fraction`.
- [ ] **Task 3.4 — Benchmark Report v0.2 & Constrained Goodput Scoring:** Embed `H_alloc` and cold-start metrics into `inference-perf` Benchmark Report v0.2 outputs (`metrics_embed.py` / `native_to_br0_2.py`), extend `score.py` to evaluate Deadline/Batch Goodput (`N_good / H_alloc`, `T_out,good / H_alloc`, `T_batch_job`) gated on `max_failure_ratio` and `scale_down_settled`, and pin the updated `inference-perf` commit/release in `build/Dockerfile`.

##### Workstream 4: Control & Autoscaling Benchmark Suite (`llm-d-autoscaling` + `llm-d-benchmark`)
*Goal: Provide reproducible scenario & workload matrices comparing Fixed-Replica Control against Autoscaling treatments.*
*Dependencies: Task `4.1` depends on Workstream 1 + Workstream 3 (`3.1`, `3.3`, `3.4`), except Fixed-Replica Control + Coordinator `wait` (`3.1` + `3.3` only) and M3 Deadline-Proximity (also requires upstream `llm-d/llm-d-async#526` release). Task `4.2` depends on Workstream 2 + Workstream 3 (`3.2`, `3.3`, `3.4`) and is independent of Task `4.1`.*

- [ ] **Task 4.1 — Async Queue Workload Profiles & Scenarios:** Define `inference-perf` profiles (single burst, multi-wave duty cycle with idle gaps, sustained Poisson load, and two-cohort urgent+bulk deadlines) for both `llmd_async_redis` and Coordinator `async-broker` (`wait` & `enqueue`) across **Control (Fixed `N`)**, **M0 (`1 <-> N`)**, **M1 (Cron `0 <-> N`)**, **M2 (4-Layer Backlog `0 <-> N`)**, and **M3 (Deadline-Proximity `0 <-> N`)**.
- [ ] **Task 4.2 — Batch API Makespan & Autoscaling Scenarios:** Define single-batch makespan profiles (`100` / `1,000` / `10,000` items with `shared_prefix` prompts) and concurrent multi-batch SLO priority profiles (`30m` vs. `2h` vs. `24h` `completion_window`) across Fixed Control and KEDA Autoscaling pools.

---

### Alternatives Considered

- **Custom standalone async/batch harnesses inside `llm-d-benchmark`:** Duplicates arrival scheduling (`poisson`/`constant`/trace), HuggingFace tokenization, shared-prefix prompt synthesis, and lifecycle report schemas already maintained in `kubernetes-sigs/inference-perf`. Extending `inference-perf` directly keeps load generation unified across online, async queue, and Batch API benchmarks while keeping `llm-d-benchmark` focused on cluster orchestration, KEDA scale-to-zero windowing, and GPU-hour accounting.
- **Subtractive miss-penalty weights (`N_good - lambda * N_missed`):** Diverges from existing `inference-perf` Goodput (`good_requests / benchmark_time`) and `llm-d-benchmark` `score_slo_goodput` (`max_failure_ratio` disqualification gate). Using zero-credit numerators paired with a hard `max_failure_ratio` / attainment gate keeps async and batch Goodput consistent with online SLO Goodput.

---

### Willingness to Contribute

Yes, I can submit a PR

---

### Additional Context

- Related async/batch autoscaling proposal & KEDA blueprints: `llm-d/llm-d-autoscaling#1572`, `llm-d/llm-d-autoscaling#1573`, `llm-d/llm-d-autoscaling#1604`
- Related deadline-proximity metric producer: `llm-d/llm-d-async#526`
- Coordinator `async-broker` specification: [`llm-d/llm-d-router/docs/coordinator_async_broker.md`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/blob/main/docs/coordinator_async_broker.md)
- Batch Gateway architecture: [`llm-d/llm-d/docs/architecture/batch/batch-gateway.md`](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/main/docs/architecture/batch/batch-gateway.md)

items.title: Prometheus/LLM as judge?!
items.body:
# Integrating Local LLM-as-Judge ## TL;DR The Mozilla AI blog describes a stack for **offline, local LLM-as-Judge evaluation** — using [Prometheus](https://prometheus-eval.github.io/prometheus/) (an open-source judge model), [llamafile](https://github.com/Mozilla-Ocho/llamafile) (single-binary portable LLM runtime), and [lm-buddy](https://github.com/mozilla-ai/lm-buddy/) (evaluation job orchestration). Candela already has all the right primitives to integrate this: | Blog Concept | Candela Equivalent | |---|---| | **Prometheus judge model** served via OpenAI-compatible API | `candela-local` already manages Ollama/vLLM runtimes + unified `/v1/` API | | **llamafile** as a portable, GPU-free LLM runtime | Could become a new runtime backend alongside Ollama/vLLM/LM Studio | | **lm-buddy** evaluation orchestration + W&B tracking | Candela's span processor pipeline + CQRS storage already does artifact tracking | | **Custom scoring rubrics** submitted to judge | New proto types: `EvalRubric`, `EvalResult`, `EvalDataset` | | **Prometheus prompt template** (instruction + response + reference + rubric) | Template construction in a new `pkg/eval/` package | --- ## What the Blog Post Describes **Core idea:** Use a quantized, locally-running open-source LLM (Prometheus 13B) to evaluate other LLMs' outputs — without needing GPUs or paid API access. **Key takeaways:** 1. **Prometheus** is a fine-tuned Llama-2-Chat-13B that scores LLM outputs on customizable rubrics (1-5 scale) with 0.897 Pearson correlation to human evaluators 2. **Quantized versions** (GGUF via llamafile) work surprisingly well — Q5 has 0.68 PCC with original while needing only 12GB RAM; Q8 gets 0.76 PCC at 16GB 3. **Cost is dramatic**: $2.95 for 960 evaluations on A100 vs. free on a MacBook Pro M3 (at ~20 tok/s, 2h45m) 4. **OpenAI-compatible API** is the glue — llamafile serves Prometheus via the same API that vLLM uses, making it a drop-in replacement 5. **lm-buddy** orchestrates evaluation jobs via YAML configs and tracks results in W&B --- ## Why This is a Natural Fit for Candela Candela already captures **every LLM interaction** with full input/output content. The blog's approach essentially says: "take those captured prompts and responses, and feed them to a local judge model." Candela is sitting on all the data needed. ### Candela's existing assets that align: 1. **`candela-local` runtime management** — already manages Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio with health monitoring, model pull/delete, and auto-detection. Adding llamafile (or just using Ollama to serve Prometheus-GGUF) is straightforward. 2. **Span data with full content** — `GenAIAttributes` already stores `input_content` and `output_content` (lines 50-53 of trace.proto). This is exactly what Prometheus needs: the instruction + the response. 3. **Proxy with OpenAI-compatible routing** — The proxy already fans requests to multiple providers. The judge model is just another OpenAI-compatible endpoint. 4. **Span processor pipeline** — The batch processor already enriches spans with cost data in the flush loop. Adding a quality score enrichment step is architecturally identical. 5. **CQRS fan-out** — Evaluation results can be written as a new sink or as enrichments on existing span data, fanning out to DuckDB/BigQuery/Pub/Sub. --- ## Proposed Integration Architecture ### Tier 1: Inline Judge Scoring (Lowest Effort, Highest Impact) Add evaluation scoring as an **enrichment step** in the span processor, analogous to how cost calculation works today. ```mermaid graph LR subgraph "Span Processor (existing)" A[Span Ingested] --> B[Cost Enrichment] B --> C["🆕 Judge Enrichment"] C --> D[Fan-out to Writers] end C -->|OpenAI API| J["Local Judge Model
(Prometheus via Ollama/llamafile)"] J -->|Score + Feedback| C ``` **How it works:** - When a span arrives with `gen_ai.output_content` populated, optionally send it to a locally-running judge model - Use a configured rubric (or a default quality rubric) - Store the score + feedback on the span itself (new fields on `GenAIAttributes`) **Proto changes:** ```protobuf message GenAIAttributes { // ... existing fields ... // Evaluation (populated by LLM-as-Judge enrichment) EvalResult eval = 50; } message EvalResult { double score = 1; // 1-5 scale from judge string feedback = 2; // Natural language feedback from judge string rubric_id = 3; // Which rubric was used string judge_model = 4; // e.g. "prometheus-13b-v1.0.Q5_K_M" google.protobuf.Timestamp evaluated_at = 5; } ``` **Config:** ```yaml evaluation: enabled: true mode: "async" # async (background) or sync (inline) judge: endpoint: "http://localhost:11434" # Ollama with Prometheus model: "prometheus:13b-v1.0-q5" rubric: default: "quality" # Built-in rubric # custom_path: "rubrics/my-rubric.yaml" sampling: rate: 0.1 # Evaluate 10% of spans (cost control) min_output_tokens: 50 # Skip trivially short responses ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **Latency consideration**: Evaluation should be **async** — don't block the span pipeline. The processor can submit evaluation jobs to a separate goroutine pool. Scores arrive eventually and get written as updates. --- ### Tier 2: Dedicated EvalService (Medium Effort) A new ConnectRPC service for managing evaluations as a first-class concept. ```protobuf // proto/candela/v1/eval_service.proto service EvalService { // Run evaluation on a set of traces/spans rpc EvaluateTraces(EvaluateTracesRequest) returns (EvaluateTracesResponse); // Manage rubrics rpc CreateRubric(CreateRubricRequest) returns (Rubric); rpc ListRubrics(ListRubricsRequest) returns (ListRubricsResponse); // Get evaluation results rpc GetEvalResults(GetEvalResultsRequest) returns (GetEvalResultsResponse); // Compare models (aggregate scores across traces) rpc CompareModels(CompareModelsRequest) returns (CompareModelsResponse); } message Rubric { string id = 1; string name = 2; string description = 3; // The scoring criteria text (maps to Prometheus rubric format) map score_descriptions = 4; // 1→"poor", 5→"excellent" string reference_answer = 5; // Optional ideal reference } ``` This enables: - **Batch evaluation**: "Evaluate all traces from last week using my custom rubric" - **A/B model comparison**: "Compare GPT-4o vs Gemini 2.5 Pro quality on my RAG pipeline" - **Regression detection**: "Alert me if average quality score drops below 3.5" --- ### Tier 3: UI Integration New pages in the Next.js UI: 1. **Evaluation Dashboard** — aggregate quality scores over time, by model, by project 2. **Rubric Manager** — CRUD for custom scoring rubrics 3. **Trace Detail Enhancement** — show eval score + feedback inline on trace detail page 4. **Model Comparison View** — side-by-side quality/cost/latency comparisons --- ## Key Design Decisions ### 1. Where does the judge model run? | Option | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **A. candela-local manages it** (new runtime: llamafile or Ollama-served Prometheus) | Fully local, zero cost, fits existing runtime management UI | 12-16GB RAM for the judge model; slow on CPU | | **B. Sidecar container** (Docker Compose) | Clean separation, works in cloud deployments | Extra container to manage | | **C. External endpoint** (any OpenAI-compatible) | Flexible — could use cloud judge model for higher quality | Loses the "local, free" advantage | > [!TIP] > **Recommendation**: Start with **Option A** — Ollama can already serve GGUF models, including Prometheus quantized versions. This means zero new infrastructure. `candela-local` already has model pull + management UI. Users just `ollama pull` a Prometheus GGUF. ### 2. Synchronous vs Asynchronous evaluation **Async is the clear winner.** The blog shows even on an M3 MacBook, evaluation takes ~10 seconds per prompt at 20 tok/s. Making this synchronous would be unacceptable for the span pipeline. Architecture: ``` SpanProcessor → Cost Enrichment → Write to storage ↘ Submit to EvalQueue (async) ↓ EvalWorker pool ↓ Judge model (local) ↓ Update span with score (storage.UpdateSpan) ``` ### 3. Sampling strategy Not every span needs evaluation. Options: - **Rate-based**: Evaluate N% of spans - **Rule-based**: Only evaluate spans matching certain criteria (model, cost threshold, etc.) - **On-demand**: User clicks "Evaluate" on a trace in the UI - **Batch**: Scheduled evaluation of recent traces (daily cron) ### 4. Prometheus 2 vs Prometheus 1 The blog references Prometheus 1 (13B). [Prometheus 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01535) has since been released with significant improvements. The integration should be model-agnostic — any OpenAI-compatible judge model works. --- ## What's Different from the Blog's Approach | Blog (lm-buddy) | Candela Integration | |---|---| | Standalone evaluation pipeline | Integrated into observability platform | | Reads prepared datasets from files | Evaluates live production traces | | Results tracked in W&B | Results stored in DuckDB/BigQuery alongside traces | | One-off batch jobs | Continuous, async evaluation with sampling | | Separate infrastructure | Reuses candela-local's runtime management | The key differentiator: **Candela already has the data.** The blog requires you to prepare datasets of instruction/response pairs. Candela captures these in real-time from production traffic. The evaluation becomes a natural extension of the observability pipeline rather than a separate workflow. --- ## Suggested Implementation Phases ### Phase 1: Foundation - [ ] Add `EvalResult` proto fields to `GenAIAttributes` - [ ] Add `pkg/eval/` package with Prometheus prompt template builder - [ ] Add evaluation config to `config.yaml` - [ ] Wire async eval queue into span processor ### Phase 2: Judge Integration - [ ] OpenAI-compatible client for calling judge model - [ ] Default quality rubric - [ ] Sampling logic (rate-based + rule-based) - [ ] Storage: update spans with eval results ### Phase 3: EvalService + API - [ ] `eval_service.proto` with rubric CRUD + batch evaluation - [ ] ConnectRPC handlers in `pkg/connecthandlers/` - [ ] Rubric storage in Firestore (or embedded in config) ### Phase 4: UI - [ ] Evaluation score on trace detail page - [ ] Quality dashboard with time-series charts - [ ] Rubric management UI - [ ] Model comparison view --- ## Open Questions > [!IMPORTANT] > 1. **Which judge model to default to?** Prometheus 1 Q5 (proven in blog), Prometheus 2, or make it fully configurable from the start? > 2. **Should eval results live on the span proto or in a separate `eval_results` table?** Keeping it on the span is simpler but makes the span larger. Separate table is cleaner for querying aggregate stats. > 3. **Is candela-local the right home for the judge runtime, or should the server also support it for Team Mode?** > 4. **Rubric management**: Config file (simple) vs Firestore (dynamic, multi-tenant) vs both? > 5. **Do we want to support the blog's "compare quantization levels" workflow**, where users can run the same eval with different judge model variants?

items.title: Workflow definition contract: step types, agent registry, and correct pipeline semantics
items.body:
### Parent

#548

### Problem

`WorkflowStep` (`backend/src/agents/workflows/definition.py`) is a stub of the contract that #545's
Design Direction section specified. Four separate defects follow from that:

**1. Two declared fields are inert.**

- `tool_names` is declared but ignored — `engine.py:236` carries `# TODO: resolve step-specific tools
  from tool_names in future`. Only a single global `extra_tools` list reaches every step.
- `input` is declared (with a docstring describing input-source semantics) but has **zero**
  references anywhere in `engine.py`.

Both are placeholders someone added with intent and never wired. Callers can set them and nothing
happens, with no error — the worst failure mode.

**2. Pipeline semantics are wrong.**

`AgentExecutor` is constructed as `AgentExecutor(agent=agent, id=step.id)` (`engine.py:251`) with no
`context_mode`. MAF's default is `"full"`, which hands each downstream agent the **upstream agent's
full conversation — its input messages *and* its response messages**.

Consequence: in `web_research_report`, step 2 ("Report Writer") receives the user's original request
*as well as* step 1's research, then writes its own prompt saying "Synthesize the research findings
provided below." That is not progressive refinement; it is a two-node conversation that re-supplies
the original request. The intended behaviour is `context_mode="last_agent"` — "each agent consumes
only the upstream agent's response messages" — which MAF exposes as
`SequentialBuilder(chain_only_agent_responses=True)`.

**3. Named-agent references cannot be expressed, and there is no registry to point at.**

There is no agent-reference field in `WorkflowStep`, and no registered-agent primitive anywhere in
the codebase. `registry.py` registers *skills* and *workflows* by `MAF_KEY`; `agent_name` appears
only in A2A code as a remote server's name (`services/a2a_service.py:331`), which is unrelated. So
the composition layer cannot reference the primitives layer at all — not because a UI is missing, but
because neither the field nor the target exists.

**4. References do not distinguish roles from tenant resources.**

There is no way to express "any model suitable for reasoning" as opposed to "this specific tenant's
model row". Without that distinction, a developer-authored definition must hardcode a tenant resource
— which is why `web_research_report` hardcodes `model_ref: "gpt-4o"` and breaks in a clean
deployment.

### Goal

Make `WorkflowDefinition` / `WorkflowStep` the real, validated contract that the rest of the roadmap
builds on: restore correct sequential semantics, introduce the agent primitive that admin composition
will later select from, and give references an unambiguous role-vs-resource syntax.

### Reference vocabulary: roles vs. tenant resources

A definition must not hardcode tenant configuration. A developer cannot write
`model_ref: "gpt-4o"`, because models are tenant-configured rows — a clean deployment may not have
that model, and two tenants will configure different ones. This is already a live bug:
`web_research_report` hardcodes `model_ref: "gpt-4o"`, which no migration seeds.

Two reference kinds, distinguished by an explicit prefix:

| Syntax | Meaning | Resolved against |
|---|---|---|
| `@reasoning` | A logical role | The tenant's role binding |
| `deepseek-reasoner` | A concrete tenant model | The tenant's `Model` rows |

- **Developers** reference `@roles`. Roles are a **closed vocabulary declared centrally in code** —
  not free-form strings — so validation can reject unknown roles and the UI can present exactly the
  roles an admin must bind.
- **Admins** bind each role to one or more of their tenant's models. A binding is a set of `Model`
  ids, mirroring the existing skill↔tool join pattern; the model's `enabled` and
  `auto_route_eligible` flags (`db/orm/models.py:31-38`) already express pool membership.
- **Admins** may also use a concrete tenant model id where they explicitly want a specific model.
- A single-model-per-role binding is the recommended starting point; whether a role may hold several
  models (making it a pool a step can choose from) is an open decision that must be settled in #550
  and reflected in #555.

The same problem applies to tools and agents — a developer declaring `TOOL_REFS = ["web_search"]`
assumes that tool exists in every tenant. Apply the identical `@`-prefixed convention to tool and
agent references.

**This issue defines the syntax and validation of these references; #550 implements resolution.**

### Step contract

Replace `WorkflowStep` with a discriminated model. Three concepts are currently conflated by similar
names and must be separated explicitly:

| Concept | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Step identity | `id` | Executor ID. Stable across rebuilds; anchors checkpoint resume and `WorkflowInvocationKwargs.executor_kwargs` |
| Step display | `name` | Label only — used for the MAF agent name and stream events |
| Agent reference | `agent_ref` | Role or registered-agent key; only when `type == "agent"` |

```python
class WorkflowStep(BaseModel):
    id: str
    name: str
    type: Literal["inline", "agent"]
    agent_ref: str | None = None        # required iff type == "agent"; "@role" or a registered key
    instructions: str | None = None     # used iff type == "inline"
    model_ref: str | None = None        # "@role" or a concrete tenant model id
    reasoning_effort: str | None = None
    temperature: float = 0.7
    tool_refs: list[str] = []           # "@role" or concrete tenant tool refs
    input: str = ""                     # "user_message" | "output_of:<step_id>" | literal
    context_mode: Literal["full", "last_agent"] = "last_agent"
    on_error: Literal["stop", "continue"] = "stop"
```

Notes on specific decisions:

- **Use `agent_ref`, not `agent_name`.** #545 sketched `agent_name`, but it collides with the step's
  display name and reads as "name this step" when it means "refer to that agent". Same reasoning for
  `tool_refs` over `tool_ids`/`tool_names`.
- **`@` prefix is the discriminator.** A role reference is `@`-prefixed and resolved through tenant
  bindings; an unprefixed value is a concrete tenant resource. This avoids the collision case where a
  tenant happens to name a model `reasoning` while a role named `reasoning` also exists.
- **`context_mode` defaults to `last_agent`.** Sequential is the meaning of the existing feature; the
  current `"full"` default is the defect. `"full"` remains available for conversational pipelines.
- **`context_mode="custom"` is deliberately not supported.** MAF requires a `context_filter` callable,
  which is code and cannot come from an admin-authored definition. Two values only.
- **`on_error` keeps its existing `"stop" | "continue"`.** Note #545's sketch said `"fail"`; the
  shipped validator uses `"stop"` and there is no reason to churn it.

### Agent registry

Add the missing primitive. Reuse the existing scan-and-register pattern in
`backend/src/agents/registry.py` — a module exports `MAF_KEY` plus agent defaults, and is registered
under that key. `agent_ref` resolves against it at build time.

```python
MAF_KEY = "web_researcher"
NAME = "Web Researcher"
INSTRUCTIONS = "..."
MODEL_ROLE = "@reasoning"      # a role, not a tenant model id
TOOL_REFS = ["@web_search"]    # roles, not tenant tool ids
```

Exact shape and location are open — the requirement is only that a named agent is (a) developer-defined,
(b) discoverable by key, (c) resolvable at build time, and (d) free of tenant-specific resources.
Do **not** build a UI picker here.

### `input` semantics

Wire it, since a declared-but-inert field is the defect being fixed:

- `"user_message"` — the original user message
- `"output_of:<step_id>"` — the named step's output; `<step_id>` must exist in the definition
- anything else — literal text passed as the step's input
- empty — inherit current behaviour

This is distinct from `context_mode`: `input` selects what the step is *asked*, `context_mode`
controls what conversation the agent *sees*.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorkflowStep` is the contract above, with a `type` discriminator that makes inline vs. agent
      steps explicit rather than inferred from which fields happen to be populated
- [ ] Validation rejects a step with `type == "agent"` and no `agent_ref`, and one with
      `type == "inline"` and no `instructions`
- [ ] `model_ref`, `tool_refs` and `agent_ref` validate the `@`-prefix convention: an `@`-prefixed
      value is checked against the declared role vocabulary and rejected if unknown; an unprefixed
      value is treated as a tenant resource reference
- [ ] A step declaring a role that the authoring tenant has not bound fails validation with an error
      naming the unbound role — **not** a silent fallback
- [ ] `agent_ref` is validated to exist in the registry on save and on execute; a missing reference
      produces a clear error naming the key
- [ ] An agent can be registered and referenced from a workflow step end-to-end
- [ ] `context_mode` is applied to every `AgentExecutor`; a two-step workflow with
      `context_mode="last_agent"` gives step 2 only step 1's response messages, and `"full"` gives
      step 1's input as well
- [ ] A regression test asserts the `context_mode="last_agent"` message list explicitly, so the
      default cannot silently regress
- [ ] `input` is honoured for all four forms, with `output_of:<step_id>` validated against the
      definition's step IDs
- [ ] `tool_refs` is either wired or **removed** — not left declared and ignored. If wiring is
      deferred, it does not appear in the model
- [ ] `engine.py:236`'s TODO is deleted or replaced with a real implementation
- [ ] `web_research_report` is migrated to the new contract — including replacing its hardcoded
      `model_ref: "gpt-4o"` with a role reference — and still covered by tests

### Verification note

The `context_mode` defect is currently a documentation-plus-code-reading inference: MAF documents
`"full"` as the default, `AgentExecutor.__init__` defaults `context_mode` to `None`, and nothing in
`backend/src` ever sets it. **Confirm it empirically before implementing** — build the two-step
workflow and assert what step 2 actually receives. If step 2 already gets response-only context, this
issue is a schema change only and the `context_mode` field is additive rather than a fix; if it gets
the original input too, the fix is a behaviour change users will notice.

### Out of scope

- Per-step tool and model *resolution* mechanics and the tenant role-binding storage/API (#550) —
  this issue declares the reference syntax and validates it
- Tenant scoping of `resolve_model`
- Checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, branching, visualization, admin UI
- A UI for selecting agents or binding roles

items.title: Qwen3 is rebuilding the cache on every request
items.body:
<!-- worklog:id=LP-0MQS214BF004Q055 -->

# Intake Brief: Qwen3 is rebuilding the cache on every request (LP-0MQS214BF004Q055)

## Headline

Investigate and fix the regression where Qwen3 rebuilds the KV cache on every request within a session, restoring the previously working slot save/restore behavior lost after recent changes.

---

## Problem Statement

Qwen3 has started rebuilding the KV cache from scratch on every exchange in a session. This was resolved previously (commit `e9c94d8`, LP-0MPPGCH9K003JEL7) by setting `force_full_prompt: true` and `session_slot_pool_size: 1` along with slot save/restore infrastructure. A recent change has caused the problem to return — every request triggers a full prompt reprocess, negating the KV cache savings from slot save/restore and delta routing.

The slot thrashing investigation (LP-0MQR75QYM001HAUB) confirmed that with `pool_size=1` and ≥2 concurrent sessions, the slot steal rate is 95–98%, meaning nearly every turn transition results in a different session acquiring the slot and overwriting the previous session's KV cache.

---

## Users

- **AI agents** (1–8 concurrent, sharing 1 GPU) making multi-turn requests through the proxy. User story: "As an AI agent, I want my session's KV cache to be preserved between turns so my response latency stays low and I don't pay the full prompt processing cost on every turn."
- **Operators/developers** deploying the proxy. User story: "As an operator, I want cache behavior to be stable and predictable so I can plan capacity and diagnose performance regressions."
- **Developer implementing the fix**. User story: "As a developer, I want to understand why the original fix stopped working so I can restore cache reuse and add regression protection."

---

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **Regression cause identified**: The specific change that caused the cache rebuild regression is identified and documented (commit, file, and mechanism).

2. **Cache reuse restored**: Within a single session with no intervening requests from other sessions, KV cache is reused between turns (confirmed via `slot_restore success` log messages and reduced prompt tokens on follow-up requests).

3. **Slot thrashing mitigation**: The 95–98% slot steal rate is reduced to ≤10% for typical workloads (1–8 concurrent agents, pool_size=1 or higher), measured by slot persistence between session turns.

4. **No mid-job preemption**: While a session has an active job (multi-turn conversation), its slot is not preempted by other sessions' requests.

5. **Regression tests pass**: Proxy integration tests covering the cache path (slot save/restore, delta routing, session continuity) pass reliably.

6. **Full project test suite must pass** with the new changes.

7. **All related documentation is updated** to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.

---

## Constraints

- **Single GPU**: Only 1 physical GPU is available, limiting concurrent inference to one at a time. The solution must work within this constraint.
- **No llama-server changes**: The fix must operate at the proxy level; we cannot modify llama-server's slot management or KV cache internals.
- **Existing session machinery intact**: Single-flight coordination, delta ingestion, slot save/restore, and session header resolution must continue to function.
- **Backward compatibility**: Existing client agents that retry on 503 must not break.
- **Pipeline pressure**: Work items for slot management redesign (LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6), prompt-cache tests (LP-0MQMC4MKY006J08E), and slot-cache cleanup (LP-0MQMC4MNU002QJK4) are in flight — this fix must coordinate with or work alongside those efforts.

---

## Existing State

### Architecture Overview (current)

1. **Config**: `force_full_prompt: true` for Qwen3, `session_slot_pool_size: 1`, `session_slot_timeout_seconds: 3.0`
2. **Slot save/restore**: Proxy saves KV cache snapshots to disk (`slot-cache/` directory) after responses and restores them before the next request in the same session.
3. **SlotLockCoordinator**: An `asyncio.Lock` per slot-id serializes access, but provides no session affinity — the lock is released immediately after response completion.
4. **Session single-flight**: Only one request per session can be inflight at a time.
5. **Delta routing**: `_classify_delta_routing()` in `server.py` decides whether to forward incremental messages or the full prompt. With `force_full_prompt: true`, delta routing is disabled for Qwen3.

### What was the original fix?

Commit `e9c94d8` (LP-0MPPGCH9K003JEL7) added:
- `force_full_prompt: true` for Qwen3 in config.yaml
- `session_slot_pool_size: 1` 
- `_should_force_full_prompt()` helper in server.py
- Slot save/restore infrastructure

### What changed?

Recent commits on the `dev` branch that could have affected cache behavior:
- `80985e1` — **Release session/slot when upstream returns error** (modifies router.py to decrement active queries on error paths). This changes slot lifecycle but only for error responses (≥400).
- `95239da` — **Remove anthropic/openai providers from config.yaml** — config restructured to `providers[]` format. Qwen3 config was converted but `force_full_prompt: true` was preserved.
- `00eab82` — **Extract session coordination from server.py to session.py** — Pure refactor; extracted slot helpers, observability, and coordination classes into session.py.
- `80185aa` — **Extract core proxy routing to router.py** — Proxy-to-local routing moved to router.py with reconstructed slot save/restore calls.
- Various config changes on dev: `session_guardrail_invalidate_on_cutoff: true` → `false`, `session_guardrail_max_runtime_seconds: 120` → `1800`, `backend_retry_attempts: 3` → `8`, `llama_start_script` changed to `podman_start_llama.sh`.

### Slot thrashing evidence (from LP-0MQR75QYM001HAUB)

- `pool_size=1`: 95–98% steal rate
- `pool_size=4`: 40% steal rate
- 1 session (control): 0% steals
- Gap windows avg ~0.03ms (asyncio cooperative scheduling)
- Save+restore overhead adds ~10ms per turn per session

### Design recommendation (from LP-0MQR7AYRA006IU0P)

The slot management design doc recommends **Approach D (Hybrid reservation + queue, 27–42h)** over simpler approaches, with Phase 1 (Core Reservation, 17–26h) as the MVP.

---

## Desired Change

This work item will:
1. **Identify the specific regression** — determine which commit/config change caused cache rebuilds to resume.
2. **Fix or revert the regression** — if the cause is a simple regression, apply a targeted fix.
3. **Implement slot-affinity improvement** — if the root cause is the slot thrashing (95–98% steal rate), implement at minimum the Phase 1 recommendation from the slot management design doc (session-level slot reservation with idle timeout).
4. **Add regression protection** — tests or instrumentation to detect future cache-rebuild regressions.

The work item should coordinate with the ongoing slot management redesign (LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6) — either by implementing a subset of the recommended approach or by fixing the regression independently if it's a simpler cause.

---

## Related Work

|------|-------|--------|-------------|
| LP-0MPPGCH9K003JEL7 | Disable delta routing for models that reprocess full prompt | Completed | **Original fix** — added `force_full_prompt: true` for Qwen3; this work item's fix regressed |
| LP-0MPNVX2HT00774XC | Proxy RCA and full stabilization for cache path | Completed | Parent epic that delivered the original cache stability package |
| LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6 | Improve slot management | In review | Slot management redesign; design recommends hybrid approach; this item should coordinate |
| LP-0MQR75QYM001HAUB | Slot thrashing reproduction & evidence | In review | Confirmed 95-98% slot steal rate; key evidence for this issue |
| LP-0MQR7AYRA006IU0P | Slot management design proposal | In review | Design doc recommending Approach D (hybrid); Phase 1 (reservation) is the MVP |
| LP-0MQPUCOFJ000QIRF | Release session/slot when upstream returns error | On dev | **Potential regression cause** — modified router.py slot lifecycle for error paths |
| LP-0MPN83BD4004TMAG | Fix session-based cache restore not functioning | Completed | Earlier fix for session_id-based cache restore signal detection |
| LP-0MQMC4MKY006J08E | Prompt-cache / session reuse tests & small fixes | Open | Related — session prompt cache preservation tests |
| LP-0MQMC4MNU002QJK4 | Cleanup: slot-cache retention & cleanup script | Open | Related — slot cache file lifecycle management |

### Key Files

- `proxy/config.yaml` — Qwen3 model config (`force_full_prompt: true`, `session_slot_pool_size: 1`)
- `proxy/proxy/router.py` — Slot save/restore calls, recently modified for error path handling
- `proxy/proxy/session.py` — `SlotLockCoordinator`, slot persistence helpers, session coordination
- `proxy/proxy/server.py` — `_classify_delta_routing`, `_should_force_full_prompt`
- `docs/dev/slot-management-design.md` — Full design proposal for slot management improvement
- `docs/dev/slot-thrashing-investigation/findings.md` — Confirmed thrashing evidence

---

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Risk: Scope creep into full slot management redesign.** The slot management redesign (LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6) proposes a 49–78h effort. This work item could naturally expand into implementing that full design. **Mitigation:** Focus on identifying the regression first. Only implement slot-affinity improvements if the regression is directly caused by thrashing, and scope to Phase 1 (reservation) of the design doc. Record additional features as follow-up work items.

- **Risk: Regression cause may be difficult to pinpoint.** Multiple commits affect the slot/cache path — extraction refactors, config changes, router.py modifications. The cause could be subtle (e.g., an import order issue, a config default change). **Mitigation:** Use `git bisect` between the last-known-good and first-known-bad commits. Add targeted logging if needed.

- **Risk: Fix may conflict with ongoing slot management redesign.** The slot management design work is in review and may recommend changes that conflict with a targeted regression fix. **Mitigation:** Coordinate with LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6. If the regression fix is simple (e.g., config default), apply it independently. If the fix requires slot-affinity changes, align with the design doc's Phase 1.

- **Risk: The thrashing problem may mask the regression.** The 95–98% slot steal rate means that even without a regression, cache would be rebuilt frequently. The "every request" behavior might be the thrashing, not a regression. **Mitigation:** Test with a single session to isolate whether cache is preserved without contention. Compare behavior before and after the suspected regression commits.

- **Assumption:** The regression is caused by a specific recent commit, not a pre-existing condition that was previously undetected.
- **Assumption:** A single-session test (no contention) can distinguish between a cache regression and the known thrashing problem.
- **Assumption:** The original fix (commit `e9c94d8`) was working correctly before the regression.
- **Risk: Overlap with Improve slot management (LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6).** This work item's fix may duplicate or conflict with the slot management redesign, which is already in review. **Mitigation:** Identify the regression cause first. If the fix is a simple regression (config, import, or missing call), apply it independently. If the fix requires slot-affinity changes, align with LP-0MQR0780Z006TLX6's Phase 1 scope and document the boundary explicitly.
- **Assumption:** Config defaults on the `dev` branch are correct and `force_full_prompt: true` is still being applied for Qwen3.

---

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

- **Q1:** "Is the cache rebuild happening on every request even with a single session (no slot contention), or only under multi-session load?"
  - **Status:** OPEN QUESTION — This distinction determines whether the issue is a regression in cache mechanics vs. the known slot thrashing problem.
  - **Importance:** Critical for scoping. If single-session cache is broken, the fix is in a different code path than if only multi-session thrashing is the problem.

- **Q2:** "Which specific deployment/environment is showing the symptom? (dev branch or main branch?)"
  - **Status:** OPEN QUESTION — The dev branch has significant changes (config restructure, extraction refactors, error-path modifications) not yet on main. The regression may only affect the dev branch.
  - **Importance:** Determines whether the fix targets dev-branch changes or main-branch behavior.

- **Q3:** "Has the symptom been observed on a branch where `force_full_prompt: true` is confirmed active for Qwen3?"
  - **Status:** OPEN QUESTION — If the config restructuring (commit `95239da`) inadvertently dropped or altered the `force_full_prompt` flag, the proxy would try delta routing, which is known to fail for Qwen3.
  - **Importance:** Quick check — verify that the running config still has `force_full_prompt: true` for the Qwen3 model entry.

- **Q4:** "Is the cache rebuild confirmed via proxy logs (e.g., absence of `slot_restore success` messages) or via llama-server logs (e.g., 'forcing full prompt re-processing')?"
  - **Status:** OPEN QUESTION — Different log evidence points to different root causes. Missing proxy-side restore indicates slot lifecycle issues; llama-server forcing reprocess indicates model compatibility issues.
  - **Importance:** Diagnostic — guides the investigation toward the right code path.

## Child Work Items

This work item has been decomposed into 12 implementation work items by the `intakeall` process, organized into 4 phases following the Job-Level Slot Ownership design (see `docs/dev/slot-management-design.md`):

**Phase 1 — Core Scheduler (P1–P3):**

**Phase 4 — Testing and Config (P10–P12):**

items.title: P0: Hyperion Linux clean-rebuild proof and mandatory host change documentation
items.body:
## Why
The owner needs Hyperion-96 to be **reconstructible from zero** without remembering historical terminal sessions. Today the configuration is spread across an older local inference repository, a staged-only greenfield repo, machine receipts, private Control Tower execution-source PRs, and cloud/Mac workstation infrastructure. The existence of receipts is **not** a complete rebuild or a clean-restored machine proof.

This is a **Linux host reproducibility and agent documentation acceptance child** of Workstation Bootstrap #18 and Control Tower #349, not a second bootstrap or general-purpose secret exporter.

## Existing evidence and proposed source

- Private, draft Control Tower [PR #1046](https://github.com/pinklon/shareplane-control-tower/pull/1046) is the host-specific reconstruction and recovery baseline, includes a sanitized host metadata collector and a **candidate** cross-agent change receipt contract. It is not yet merged/admitted.
- Existing workstation-manager release/doctor implementation is primarily Mac-oriented. Do not equate Mac conformance with a qualified Hyperion Linux installation.
- Existing Skills owner: `pinklon/skills#323`. Host source and installed profile must reconcile as desired -> selected -> materialized -> invoked -> consumed independently.
- Existing owner compute source: Control Tower #349 and draft PR #1045 (owner-only synthetic job); no external user access admitted.
- Historical local inference state and credentials require separate audited extraction. Never upload raw `~/llmstack` Git history, .env files, credential backups or a raw home-directory archive.

## Acceptance tasks and explicit owners

**Workstation Bootstrap source/maintainer:**
1. Define an owner-approved Linux capability profile for Hyperion under the existing managed Workstation Bootstrap source. Host-specific configurable release inputs, identity, packages, kernels/drivers, distro repos, mounts and runtime versions require exact source identity.
2. Implement dry-run, install, doctor, activation receipt, compatibility and rollback for a **clean Ubuntu host**; preserve current Mac behavior. Do not mutate an active owner machine merely to satisfy CI.
3. Add a host configuration documentation gate: a declared Linux host-affecting change must include an exact signed/owner-admitted change receipt (or explicit disposition), source+actual version+verification, secret-handling classification, rollback and updated rebuild guide. Reuse existing receipt contracts, don't invent another authority.
4. Test a clean VM installation twice and ensure results are deterministic or differences explicitly documented.

**Hyperion host administrator (privilege/maintenance approval required):**
5. Inventory disk UUID and firmware/boot dependencies privately, verify and **restore from an independently off-host encrypted backup**, including WebUI assets, model weights, historical artifacts, and key re-enrollment path. Store no keys in public source.
6. Qualify remote-access reconnect from at least two independent Macs, NoMachine or VNC current surface, clipboard, audio and file transfer, and reboot persistence with out-of-band recovery.
7. Reconcile GPU driver 595 to separately planned qualified Blackwell stack, host firewall/SSH/Tailscale/desktop ingress and safe rollback without exposing tenant access.

**Skills/Control Tower conformance owners:**
8. Compare canonical Skills exact SHA/digest to scoped installed and actual runtime consumption; keep Production and external compute gates separate.
9. Enforce or check sanitized documentation receipts across active Hyperion writer lanes and issue claim closeout. Merely documenting policy does not establish agent-wide compliance.
10. Have an independent witness perform cold restore into a clean host/VM and score every service outcome PASS/FAIL/UNOBSERVED.

## Terminal criteria

Only close when a third party can rebuild without chat archaeology using:
- versioned source + immutable artifact lock manifest,
- explicit non-secret dependency/credential enrollment instructions,
- retained off-host backup and verified restore,
- transactional installer plus rollback,
- exact acceptance tests and reboot-persistence results,
- desired-versus-actual-versus-consumed capability proof,
- source/host/agent receipt reconciliation,
- no private value leaked to the repository or logs.

**Current disposition: OPEN. No claim of reproducible rebuild, global agent compliance, or tenant-ready compute.**
