items.title: Spec: future-state DocuFlow backend architecture and nine-phase migration

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent

items.body:
## Problem Statement

TECHMA operates DocuFlow today as a single-company installation: one Express process serving one React SPA and one REST API, one PostgreSQL database with no tenant boundary, background work running as in-process intervals, hosting coupled to Replit sidecar credentials, and an admin-impersonation API key in the authentication path. The product vision — an all-in-one operations platform sold to service businesses and individuals — cannot be hosted on this backend: there is no Workspace boundary, no Membership or role model, no Subscription or billing machinery, no public API or webhooks, no audit or GDPR posture, and no safe way to run replicas or recover from failure. Meanwhile the existing installation carries real operational history — projects, documents, files, time entries, activity evidence, enrolled desktop devices — that must survive any change with its identity and behavior intact.

## Solution

Evolve the production backend in place into the decided target architecture: a modular monolith in one repository with separate HTTP and durable-worker runtimes, ten domain modules behind strict interfaces, shared-schema Workspace tenancy with row-level security in depth, Clerk-backed authentication with DocuFlow-owned authorization, Stripe-backed billing behind an adapter with DocuFlow-owned entitlements, three contract surfaces (web BFF, versioned desktop sync protocol, additive public `/api/v1` with signed webhooks), an S3-shaped object-storage port, a Postgres-backed jobs port with transactional-outbox events, an Intelligence module serving retrieval and gated AI, platform audit/privacy/compliance ports, and Render + Neon + Cloudflare R2 hosting in Frankfurt with an independent immutable evidence account.

The path there is the nine-phase, in-place migration recorded in ADR-0017: stabilize and de-Replit, lift hosting, stand up durable jobs, establish the Workspace seam, migrate identity, carve out modules with the data splits, expose the new contract surfaces, take billing live, and retire legacy surfaces — every phase made of expand/contract deploys with verifiers, temporary flags, and rollback paths, preserving every legacy ID, contract, and running Timer.

## User Stories

1. As a prospective customer, I want to start a trial workspace without a card and receive the complete product, so that I can evaluate DocuFlow before paying.
2. As a workspace owner, I want my Workspace to be the sole boundary for data, members, policy, and subscription, so that my records never mix with another tenant's.
3. As an individual user, I want a one-member Workspace with the same product, so that I can add members later without migrating to a different product type.
4. As a workspace owner, I want ownership transfer required before my membership can lose access, so that a workspace always has an ultimate authority.
5. As a workspace administrator, I want to invite, add, edit, archive, restore, and remove members, so that access always matches current responsibility.
6. As a workspace administrator, I want roles built from named capabilities — Owner, Administrator, Member plus custom roles — so that permission is explicit rather than implied by flags.
7. As a user, I want memberships in several workspaces under one login with an Active Workspace switcher, so that I can work for multiple organizations without separate accounts.
8. As a user, I want to authenticate through a managed identity provider with MFA and session rotation, so that my credentials are protected by a specialist.
9. As a member, I want my Timer to be a single globally active tracker scoped to one workspace and one project, so that my recorded time is always unambiguous.
10. As a member, I want timer starts, pauses, resumes, and stops applied as idempotent commands at their claimed effective time, so that duplicates and retries never distort my hours.
11. As a desktop member, I want offline timer commands and activity evidence queued locally and synchronized later, so that connectivity problems never cost me recorded work.
12. As a member, I want late or clock-skewed submissions flagged for review rather than rejected, so that my time is never silently lost.
13. As a member, I want to inspect the Tracking Policy currently applied to me and all of my own Activity Evidence, so that monitoring is transparent to its subject.
14. As a workspace administrator, I want versioned Tracking Policy where stale-policy capture fails closed while the Timer stays open, so that policy is enforced without punishing the member.
15. As a timesheet approver, I want Timesheets to move through Open, Submitted, Approved, and Rejected with approval locking entries until an audited reopening, so that reported time is trustworthy.
16. As a member, I want one Daily Update per Workday grouped by project, so that my reporting matches my working schedule and time zone.
17. As a workspace administrator, I want Opportunities separated from Projects with Won and Lost as fixed terminal outcomes, so that sales conversion and delivery status have unambiguous meanings.
18. As a member, I want the Project Dossier connecting tasks, time, activity, updates, Documents, and Files, so that everything about one engagement lives in one place.
19. As a member, I want Project Assignments to grant project responsibility and visibility without workspace authority, so that being on a project never leaks admin power.
20. As a member, I want Workspace Documents with folder-inherited Document Access enforced identically in browsing, search, and AI citations, so that visibility rules cannot be bypassed by asking differently.
21. As a member, I want Files uploaded directly to object storage through signed slots with versions, previews, and derived artifacts, so that large uploads are fast and never overwrite history.
22. As a member, I want user uploads to pass a fail-closed scan before becoming available, so that malware never spreads through shared files.
23. As a member, I want deleted Documents and Files held in Trash with a restore window before an irreversible purge, so that mistakes are recoverable but deletion is real.
24. As a member, I want automatic transcription of audio and video Files in French and English producing immutable, citable Transcripts, so that recorded knowledge becomes searchable.
25. As a member, I want source-cited AI Answers over the knowledge corpus, kept in my per-workspace history under configurable retention, so that I can trust and revisit what the AI told me.
26. As a workspace owner, I want Workspace AI Policy controlling purposes, providers, regions, and retention with contractual no-training guarantees, so that my content never trains a model.
27. As a member, I want lexical search guaranteed even when AI is disabled or a provider is down, and semantic features failing explicitly rather than returning silently empty results, so that degradation is honest.
28. As a workspace owner, I want AI usage entitlement-gated and metered per purpose, so that spend is bounded and predictable.
29. As a member, I want notifications from all my workspaces in one cross-workspace inbox with origin visible, so that I never miss work from a workspace I'm not currently viewing.
30. As a member, I want per-workspace, per-category Delivery Preferences with mandatory security, billing, and membership notices always delivered, so that I control noise without missing what matters.
31. As a workspace owner, I want seat-based billing where only accepted active memberships consume purchased seats, so that invitations and archived members never cost money.
32. As a workspace owner, I want plan and seat changes inside DocuFlow with immediate prorated increases and period-end decreases floored at consumption, so that billing follows my team's reality.
33. As a workspace owner, I want an expired trial, cancellation, or failed dunning to end in a Read-only Workspace — viewing, export, and recovery preserved — so that my data is never held hostage.
34. As a workspace owner, I want entitlements derived from a versioned Plan Registry with version pinning, so that plan changes never silently alter what I bought.
35. As an external integrator, I want an additive public `/api/v1` authenticated by Service Account API keys with rate limits, idempotency keys, cursor pagination, and RFC 9457 errors, so that my integration stays stable for years.
36. As an external integrator, I want thin, HMAC-signed webhooks with retries, replay, and auto-disable, so that I learn about changes without polling and re-fetch state with my own credentials.
37. As a workspace administrator, I want Service Accounts as non-member principals with explicitly granted capabilities and no seat consumption, so that integrations act with least privilege.
38. As a desktop member, I want the sync protocol versioned with a drain window in which an outdated agent can still upload queued offline work, so that version hygiene never destroys recorded evidence.
39. As a workspace administrator, I want Device Enrollments revocable per workspace without touching the user's other enrollments, so that offboarding one engagement is surgical.
40. As a customer data controller, I want DocuFlow to operate as GDPR processor for workspace content with a published Subprocessor Registry and signed DPAs, so that my own compliance story holds.
41. As a user, I want account deletion with guided workspace transfer, a cancelable grace window, controller-side erasure, and pseudonymized memberships, so that I can leave without breaking the workspaces I contributed to.
42. As a workspace owner, I want a self-serve account-level export, so that leaving or auditing DocuFlow never requires support tickets.
43. As a workspace administrator, I want security-relevant actions recorded in an append-only audit trail with immutable exports, so that investigations have evidence.
44. As a workspace owner, I want platform staff to reach my content only through time-boxed, workspace-visible Support Access Grants or loudly audited break-glass, so that operator access is consented and visible.
45. As a platform staff member, I want a separate audited operator surface with dedicated principals and no standing content access, so that support work is safe by construction.
46. As a DocuFlow operator, I want RPO ≤ 5 minutes and RTO ≤ 4 hours with quarterly timed restore drills and Erasure Journal replay, so that recovery is proven rather than assumed.
47. As a DocuFlow operator, I want one OpenTelemetry pipeline into managed EU sinks with hard-failure-only paging and a public status page, so that incidents surface without alert fatigue.
48. As a DocuFlow operator, I want per-provider spend alerts at 80% of the €300–500/month ceiling, so that cost surprises cannot accumulate silently.
49. As a DocuFlow developer, I want expand/contract deploys with rollback by image redeploy and never a down-migration, so that every release is reversible.
50. As a DocuFlow developer, I want every deferred effect running as a durable idempotent job with declared retries, dead-letter capture, and audited replay, so that background work is observable and recoverable.
51. As a DocuFlow developer, I want domain events on a transactional outbox with at-least-once delivery and per-aggregate ordering, so that consequences never depend on a dual-write.
52. As a DocuFlow developer, I want strict module interfaces with service extraction only on measured evidence, so that the monolith stays modular without premature distribution.
53. As a DocuFlow developer, I want billing, email, storage, AI, and identity providers behind replaceable adapters, so that no vendor decision is irreversible.
54. As a TECHMA legacy user, I want every existing project, client, document, file, time entry, screenshot, device, and URL to keep its identity through migration, so that history and bookmarks survive.
55. As a TECHMA legacy user, I want my password login to keep working across the identity cutover without a forced reset, so that migration is invisible to me.
56. As a TECHMA legacy user, I want my enrolled desktop agent to keep syncing through every migration phase without re-login, so that evidence capture never stops.
57. As a workspace owner of the migrated workspace, I want a pinned legacy plan with no billing surprises, so that becoming tenant number one costs nothing.
58. As a DocuFlow developer, I want temporary DB-backed feature flags with named owners and removal gates, so that migration switches cannot become permanent architecture.
59. As a DocuFlow developer, I want every backfill to ship a verifier whose output lands in an in-repo evidence trail, so that "did we lose anything?" is answerable from the repository.

## Implementation Decisions

The authoritative record is ADR-0001 through ADR-0017 in the repository's ADR directory plus the two research artifacts linked from the wayfinder map ([map issue #1](https://github.com/Lamakira/docuflow/issues/1)). Summary of the decided architecture:

**Topology and modules** (ADR-0005, 0008, 0014)
- Modular monolith, one repository, one authoritative PostgreSQL database, two runtimes from one Docker image: HTTP and durable worker.
- Ten domain modules: Identity & Access, Workspace, Clients & Sales, Projects, Time, Activity, Knowledge, Billing, Notifications, Intelligence. Modules own implementation and persistence behind explicit interfaces.
- Immediate invariants use synchronous calls; deferred consequences use transactional-outbox events. Workspace provisioning is the single sanctioned synchronous cross-module command chain, with compensation.
- Policy lives with its enforcing module: Tracking Policy in Activity, Work Schedule in Time, Workspace AI Policy in Intelligence.
- Read models start as composed queries; materialization per module only on measured need. Service extraction only after interface and data ownership stabilize plus a measured need.

**Tenancy** (ADR-0004, 0006)
- One Workspace model for individuals and organizations. Shared-schema pooled tables; immutable `workspace_id` on every workspace-owned row, propagated through requests, workers, caches, queues, objects, search records, analytics, and audit records.
- Application scoping + composite relational constraints + PostgreSQL row-level security as defense in depth. Small global allowlist for identity and system control data. Privileged cross-workspace operations only through a separate audited interface. Single-home-region placement seam for later relocation.

**Identity and authorization** (ADR-0007)
- Clerk as managed identity provider behind an `IdentityProvider` seam: credentials, authentication flows, MFA, session rotation. DocuFlow owns Users, Workspaces, Memberships, Workspace Roles, Capabilities, Service Accounts, Devices, Device Enrollments, and every authorization decision, evaluated centrally against a PrincipalContext carrying explicit workspace scope.
- Reassessment triggers: EU identity-residency customer or enterprise-procurement requirement.

**Time and activity** (ADR-0009)
- Server-authoritative Timer state machine; at most one active Timer per User enforced by partial unique index. All surfaces submit idempotent Timer Commands (origin, per-origin sequence, claimed effective time, explicit workspace scope) applied in effective-time order, materializing Time Entries that split on pause and overlap; late arrivals trigger bounded re-materialization; append-only command log is provenance.
- Claimed device times pair with server receive times under monotonic-clock anchoring, clamped to the present, flagged not rejected. Activity Evidence enters via two-phase uploads and idempotent batch commits; derived processing rides outbox workers. Capture obeys immutable versioned Tracking Policy; stale cache fails capture closed with the Timer open.

**Billing** (ADR-0010)
- Stripe Billing behind a replaceable BillingProvider adapter; DocuFlow as merchant; Stripe Tax from launch. Subscription = Plan + purchased seat capacity; increases immediate with proration, decreases at period end floored at active Billable Seat consumption.
- DocuFlow-owned versioned Plan Registry; effective entitlements are a pure function of billing state, plan, and registry version; audited overrides; grandfathering by version pinning. DocuFlow-owned billing state machine (Trialing, Active, PastDue, ReadOnly, cancel-at-period-end); no-card trials with no Stripe objects; full access during dunning; ReadOnly enforced centrally by capability write-classification.
- Webhooks land in a signature-verified deduplicating inbox; workers re-fetch the authoritative object into a provider-neutral projection, recompute entitlements, bump the authorization version, emit outbox consequences; daily drift-alerting reconciliation. Checkout and payment methods on hosted Stripe surfaces; plan/seat changes only in DocuFlow.

**Contract surfaces** (ADR-0011)
- Three surfaces on one HTTP runtime, all calling the same module interfaces: private web BFF in lockstep with the web client; separately versioned desktop sync API; public `/api/v1` with URL major versions and additive-only evolution.
- Public auth: per-Service-Account static API keys → PrincipalContext; token-bucket rate limits per Service Account plus per-workspace aggregate from the Plan Registry; optional Idempotency-Key replay. Errors RFC 9457, cursor pagination only, opaque IDs, RFC 3339 UTC timestamps.
- Webhooks: workspace-owned endpoints, explicit public event allowlist from the outbox, HMAC-signed, at-least-once unordered, ~72h backoff, auto-disable, replay; thin payloads (event type + resource IDs).
- Desktop protocol: agent-initiated HTTPS; handshake carries clock anchor, Tracking Policy version, minimum protocol version, directives; 12-month/two-version support plus 6-month drain window for uploading queued offline work. Public majors live ≥ 12 months with Deprecation/Sunset signaling.

**Documents, files, storage** (ADR-0012)
- Native Document content in PostgreSQL; Files and derived artifacts in an S3-shaped object store behind one shared port. Immutable, ID-only, workspace-prefixed object keys; names and scope only in database metadata.
- Direct signed-PUT two-phase uploads with finalize verification; short-lived audit-logged signed GETs after backend authorization; proxy streaming for sensitive classes. App-owned versioning on both planes. Eager derived artifacts via outbox workers. Fail-closed scan state machine for user uploads; agent screenshots exempt.
- Two-phase deletion everywhere: 30-day Trash then idempotent purge cascade across rows, objects, derived artifacts, indexes; workspace deletion freezes 30 days then sweeps the prefix. Erasure primitives and purge-blocking hold flag in the port. Legacy objects keep existing keys; database row is key authority.

**Jobs, events, email, notifications** (ADR-0013)
- All deferred effects in the worker runtime through a DocuFlow-owned jobs port on a PostgreSQL queue in the authoritative database; enqueue commits transactionally with domain writes; HTTP runtime does no background work.
- Outbox event log (UUIDv7, versioned type, workspace + principal provenance, thin PII-minimized payload); dispatcher claims with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, fans out one job per registered consumer: at-least-once, per-aggregate ordering, per-consumer retry isolation, bounded replay window. Job types declare attempts, backoff, timeout, concurrency class; dead-letter table with audited replay. Lease-elected scheduler tick; module-owned schedules expanding into idempotent occurrence-keyed jobs.
- Resend behind a narrow email port (SES named successor); DocuFlow-owned templates, delivery projections, suppression; thin emails. Notification fan-out materializes per-recipient rows with snapshot resolution and read-time membership gating; Delivery Preferences per user/workspace/category/channel; in-app always on; security, billing, membership mandatory.

**Intelligence** (ADR-0014)
- Intelligence module owns index artifacts, ingestion, retrieval, AI gateway and adapters, AI Purpose taxonomy, Workspace AI Policy, content-minimized AI audit. Retrieval covers the knowledge corpus only (Documents, File extracted text, Transcripts).
- First-wave engine: PostgreSQL FTS + pgvector, outbox-fed, full provenance on index rows; side-by-side index generations with per-workspace atomic cutover for model/chunker migrations; managed-service extraction only on measured thresholds.
- No ACL duplication in indexes: retrieval joins canonical Document Access and Project Assignment at query time; deletions ride the purge cascade plus nightly reconciliation; citations re-check access at read.
- Gateway exposes `generate`, `embed`, `transcribe`; authorizes capability and Document Access, evaluates policy and purpose, minimizes payloads, allowlists provider/region/retention, enforces budgets/rate limits/circuit breakers, audits every call. Providers: OpenAI direct (embeddings, generation); Azure Speech provisional STT (French + English), gated on a consented benchmark. Transcripts immutable, copy-out only; Loom scraping retired. AI on by default under a non-negotiable floor (no-training, payload minimization, no raw prompt logging) with per-purpose opt-out; entitlement-gated, metered in units; lexical search is the no-external-call floor; generation hard-stops at budget exhaustion; no automatic PII redaction in v1.

**Security, audit, privacy, compliance** (ADR-0015)
- Append-only audit port in PostgreSQL, one log with workspace and platform scopes, mutation grants revoked, closed segments exported to immutable object storage. Audited actions: authentication, membership/role lifecycle, policy changes, billing changes, sensitive exports/downloads, deletions/restores, credential and Service Account lifecycle, device enrollment, privileged access, AI gateway calls.
- GDPR: processor for workspace content, controller for account/billing/telemetry. Account deletion: guided transfer/delete of owned workspaces, cancelable grace window, controller-side erasure, in-place Membership pseudonymization, workspace notification. Six fixed Data Classes drive the control matrix; retention lives with owning modules as idempotent scheduled jobs; bounded backup window with ID-only Erasure Journal replayed after restores.
- Encryption: provider-managed at rest + TLS; KMS envelope encryption for Secret-class fields; credentials as one-time-shown hashes. Host-managed secret store, versioned signing keys; legacy ephemeral JWT secret and `MCP_API_KEY` retired. Platform Staff from a dedicated identity pool on a separate audited surface; Support Access Grants time-boxed and workspace-visible; audited break-glass. 72-hour breach runbook; Legal Hold as purge-blocking primitive; Subprocessor Registry gated on DPAs, regions, no-training; in-repo compliance control matrix; quarterly access reviews.

**Hosting, deployment, observability, recovery** (ADR-0016)
- Render (two-instance HTTP + worker, one image) + Neon PostgreSQL (plain SQL, no vendor-specific features) + Cloudflare R2 `eu` jurisdiction, all Frankfurt; standalone AWS account with Object-Locked S3 for nightly encrypted exports and audit segments. Cloudflare DNS/CDN/WAF/edge rate limits.
- OpenTelemetry through a collector into Better Stack (EU) + Sentry (Germany); telemetry carries IDs only. GitHub Actions trunk-based: auto-deploy staging (synthetic data), manual promotion, migrations as a gated pre-deploy step under expand/contract, rollback by image redeploy.
- Targets: 99.9% monthly internal HTTP SLO; worker lag SLO 95% under 60s; RPO ≤ 5 min (PITR), RTO ≤ 4 h; daily independent logical exports; quarterly timed restore drill with Erasure Journal replay recorded in-repo; annual restore-from-export drill. Hard-failure-only paging; 80% spend alerts against €300–500/month; sized ≤ 25 workspaces at launch with ~10× headroom.

**Migration** (ADR-0017)
- Nine dependency-ordered overlapping phases, each of small expand/contract deploys with verifier, temporary flag, rollback path: (1) stabilize — de-Replit, containerize, CI/CD + synthetic staging, one plain-SQL migration journal applied as gated pre-deploy, delete boot-time DDL/data mutation, characterization + contract tests on legacy web API and desktop v1 protocol, OTel baseline, persistent versioned desktop signing key; (2) hosting lift with GCS still serving; (3) worker runtime + jobs port + outbox; (4) Workspace seam — seed one Workspace and Memberships (main admin → Owner, admin → Administrator, user → Member, special flags → capabilities, archived users → Archived Memberships, global settings → Workspace policy rows), per-table lineage backfill nullable → resumable job → zero-orphan verifier → NOT NULL, core composite uniques, RLS table-by-table after verified scoping, Teams dropped after evidence snapshot; (5) Clerk migration — bcrypt import, dual-auth drain, OIDC-only invites, then Replit OIDC and `MCP_API_KEY` removed; enrolled devices untouched; (6) module carve-outs carrying the data splits — Opportunity/Project by stage rule with legacy IDs staying on Projects, Document/File split preserving object keys with access defaulting to everyone-in-workspace, embeddings dropped and rebuilt, GCS → R2 bulk-copy/dual-write/read-flip, legacy Time Entries kept with legacy provenance and no synthesized commands; (7) new contract surfaces; (8) billing go-live with the legacy workspace pinned; (9) retirement.
- Cross-cutting: DocuFlow-owned DB-backed feature flags (global/workspace/user) behind a cached port, each flag temporary with owner and removal gate; flags are not entitlements and not policy. Bounded announced maintenance windows allowed for hosting and identity cutovers while single-tenant; all else zero-downtime. Destructive drops gated on ≥ 14 days zero-reference telemetry plus two backup cycles. Desktop v1 endpoints removed after two weeks of zero v1 traffic from the force-updated internal fleet. Legacy web API retires only after v2 UI cutover; backend and UI never block each other. Per-phase evidence (verifier outputs, snapshots, cutover timestamps) recorded in an in-repo migration evidence directory.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test asserts external behavior at a contract, never implementation details. Renaming internals, moving code between modules, or swapping a provider adapter must not break tests.
- **Primary seam: HTTP contract surfaces against a real PostgreSQL.** Phase 1 captures characterization/contract tests on the legacy web API and desktop v1 protocol before anything moves; those suites run continuously against the compatibility adapters through every later phase. Each new surface — web BFF, desktop sync v2, public `/api/v1`, webhook delivery — gains contract tests as it lands. Real PostgreSQL in tests so tenancy scoping, RLS, composite constraints, and outbox writes are exercised, not mocked.
- **Test doubles only at the architecture's own ports:** storage port (S3-shaped in-memory or MinIO), jobs port (inline synchronous test driver), email port, BillingProvider (fake Stripe), IdentityProvider (fake Clerk token verifier), AI gateway (canned responses). No seams invented for testing.
- **Direct module-interface tests only where HTTP cannot reach the logic:** Timer command application and re-materialization edge cases, entitlement derivation from the Plan Registry, outbox dispatcher delivery semantics, backfill verifiers.
- Migration backfills are tested by their verifiers: every backfill ships an invariant/orphan/count check whose output is preserved as migration evidence.
- Prior art: none — the current repository exposes no automated test suite, so the Phase 1 harness is net-new and becomes the repository standard.

## Out of Scope

- Web-app, desktop-app, and marketing-site interface design (the v2 web UI proceeds in parallel under its own effort; the backend only preserves legacy contracts until its cutover).
- Exact pricing, commercial plan values, and trial duration.
- Marketing-site architecture.
- Customer-managed, self-hosted, and on-premise deployments.
- Active-active multi-region operation and per-customer regional deployment.
- Completing formal SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification (readiness only).

## Further Notes

- Decision authority: ADR-0001–0017 in the repository plus the wayfinder map ([issue #1](https://github.com/Lamakira/docuflow/issues/1)) with its closed decision tickets and two research artifacts (provider candidates; current-backend inventory and migration constraints). Where this spec and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins.
- Vocabulary: `CONTEXT.md` is the glossary; every term capitalized here (Workspace, Membership, Timer Command, Plan Registry, …) is defined there and must be used verbatim in code-facing naming.
- Deliberately deferred to implementation, per the map: exact public API resource catalogue and webhook event list; exact audit event catalogue, control-matrix values, retention schedule values, DPA text, incident severity ladder, vendor-onboarding checklist, access-review cadence; exact per-table lineage/backfill matrix, verifier queries, flag inventory, and phase calendar. Resolve each inside its owning phase/module, recording catalogue-level choices in the migration evidence trail or new ADRs as warranted.
- Implementation should proceed phase by phase in ADR-0017 order; phases overlap but never reorder their dependencies (jobs before backfills, Workspace seam before Clerk, carve-outs after the seam lands per area).
- Reassessment triggers recorded across ADRs: EU identity-residency or enterprise-procurement customer (Clerk), hosting-on-AWS or EU-residency customer (SES), measured retrieval thresholds (managed search), enterprise BYOK demand (KMS scope).

items.title: [RFC] OpenSearch Memory API: events and memories for AI agents
items.body:
## What are you proposing?

Agent memory has evolved rapidly across the industry. Agents used to keep a chat history. More and more, they keep facts, summaries, and preferences that a large language model (LLM) extracts from conversations, carry them across sessions and agents, and act on them. As memory moves from a log of messages to knowledge an agent relies on, applications need three things that today's memory APIs do not give together:

- **Lineage.** Knowing which conversation each memory came from, so it can be checked, corrected, or deleted with its source.
- **Configurability.** Choosing, for each application, what gets extracted, with which prompt and model, how long raw records and memories are kept, and who can read and change them.
- **The raw record.** Keeping the original conversation searchable, because extraction leaves details out.

This RFC proposes a new memory API for OpenSearch, under `/_plugins/_memory`, built around those needs. It stores two kinds of records in a **Space**, which holds an application's extraction strategies, models, expiry settings, and access:

- **Events.** What an agent or application writes: conversation turns, agent state, tool results, or any JSON document. Events are kept as written and never change.
- **Memories.** What an LLM extracts from events in the background: facts, session summaries, user preferences, or whatever a custom prompt asks for. Each memory records the events it came from. An application can also write memories it extracts itself.

The API is **experimental**: it is off unless a cluster turns it on with a static setting, and it can change between releases until the community agrees it is stable. This RFC does not decide where the code lives. It could be part of the ML Commons plugin, or a dedicated plugin that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search plugin does; the API design does not depend on the answer.

## What problems are you trying to solve?

An agent's memory holds two kinds of records: what happened, such as conversation turns, tool results, and agent state, and what an LLM inferred from it, such as facts, summaries, and preferences. The two need different rules. Raw records should never change, while inferred ones are updated as new turns refine them. They need their own lifetimes and their own permissions. Each inference also needs a link back to the records it came from, so a detail it left out can still be found, and so it can be deleted with its conversation. Agentic memory does not keep the two apart, as the next section shows. This RFC makes them two resources, events and memories, linked by lineage.

## Why events and memories are separate resources

An event is something that happened. A memory is something an LLM inferred from what happened. The two differ in who writes them, whether they can change, how long they are kept, and how they are found:

|  | Event | Memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A raw record: a conversation turn, agent state, a tool result, or a JSON document | An inference: a fact, a summary, a preference, or the output of a custom prompt |
| Who writes it | The agent or application | The extraction pipeline, or the application with CreateMemory |
| How it is made | Stored exactly as sent | An LLM call, which is not deterministic |
| Can it change? | No | Yes. Consolidation updates it when new events refine it, and the application can update or delete it |
| How long it is kept | Usually short: days to months (`event_expiry_days`) | Usually long: months to years, or forever (`memory_expiry_days`) |
| Typical size | A whole turn or document | A sentence or a paragraph |
| How it is found | By session and time, by ID, or by keyword and vector search over its chunks | By keyword and vector search, filtered by actor and strategy |

The relationship between them is many to many:

- One event can produce several memories of different types, for example a fact, an updated session summary, and a user preference.
- One event can produce no new memory, when consolidation finds that existing memories already cover it.
- One memory can come from several events, when consolidation merges what they said.

**Lineage.** Every memory records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`. That link supports a two-step retrieval pattern. An agent searches memories first, which returns a few short records instead of whole conversations. If a memory lacks the detail the agent needs, such as the exact error message or the full list a user gave, the agent follows `source_event_ids` to the original events. The link also works the other way: a memory search can filter by `source_event_ids`, so an application can find every memory that came from given events and delete them. Events are usually kept for less time than the memories made from them; once an event is deleted, BatchGetEvent reports its ID as not found.

**How agentic memory models this.** Agentic memory in ML Commons keeps both under one memory container API, with the raw records as one memory type (working memory) and the extracted records as another (long-term memory), next to sessions and history. The same paths and fields then serve records with different lifetimes and rules: working memory can be edited after it is written, and a long-term memory does not reference the messages it came from.

Agent memory systems commonly call these two kinds of records short-term memory and long-term memory. In this API, short-term memory is events, and long-term memory is memories.

## Why a new API, and how it relates to agentic memory

The ML Commons plugin has two memory APIs today: conversation memory and agentic memory. Given that conversation memory is on the deprecation path ([maintainer comment on ml-commons#4552](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4552#issuecomment-3844465824)), this RFC mainly compares the new memory API with agentic memory. The section "Long-term direction: one memory API" describes the proposal to converge on one.

Agentic memory (experimental in 3.2, generally available in 3.3, `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`) stores messages in memory containers and extracts long-term memories from them. ML Commons agents use it, and other applications can call it directly.

Another API has a real cost: more code to maintain, and more for users to choose between. We propose it because the event and memory model changes the data model of agentic memory, not just its features:

- **Two record types instead of four.** Agentic memory has sessions, working memory, long-term memory, and history, each under the same generic paths. Splitting them into events and memories changes its paths.
- **Raw records that never change.** Agentic memory's working memory can be updated. Making it immutable breaks callers that update it.
- **Fixed actor and session fields on every record.** Agentic memory scopes records with namespace keys that each strategy chooses, such as `user_id`. A strategy whose key is missing from a write is skipped. Replacing namespaces with two fixed fields changes every request and response.
- **A link from every memory to its events.** This part is additive, and agentic memory could add it on its own.

Changing agentic memory this way would break its current users, including ML Commons agents. A new, experimental API leaves both existing APIs as they are, and lets the new model prove itself before anything is deprecated.

The table compares the three:

| Area | Memory API (proposed) | Agentic memory | Conversation memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Containers and records | A Space holds events and memories | A memory container holds four memory types: sessions, working, long-term, and history | A memory holds one conversation's messages, each an input and a response, with optional traces |
| User and session | Every event and memory has an `actor_id` and an optional `session_id` | Each strategy names the namespace keys it needs, for example `user_id`, or `agent_id` and `session_id` | One memory per conversation, owned by the OpenSearch user who created it |
| Long-term memories | Extracted by an LLM, or written by the client | Extracted by an LLM | None |
| Source of a memory | Each memory records `source_event_ids`, and memory search can filter by them | Not recorded | Not applicable |
| Updating a raw record | No. Events cannot be changed | Yes, working memory can be updated | Yes, messages can be updated |
| Consolidation | Yes | Yes. For each new fact, the LLM decides to add, update, or delete against similar stored memories (`max_infer_size`, 5 by default, at most 10), and a history index records each change | Not applicable |
| Search over raw records | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword only. Working memory is not embedded | Keyword only |
| Search over memories | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid. Semantic queries since 3.3; dedicated semantic and hybrid APIs since 3.6 | Not applicable |
| Expiry | Per Space, for events and for memories. An expired memory is left out of reads before it is deleted | Since 3.8, with age and count limits and pinning. On-demand runs and a dry run since 3.9. An expired record is returned until the retention job deletes it | None |
| Strategies | SEMANTIC, SUMMARY, and CUSTOM | SEMANTIC, USER_PREFERENCE, and SUMMARY, each with an optional custom prompt | None |

The new API starts with a focused feature set. Features that agentic memory has, such as a change history, delete by query, per-request hybrid weights, count limits and pinning in retention, a built-in user-preference strategy, and checkpoint fields, can be added based on community interest.

**What changes in existing components:**

| Component | Change |
| --- | --- |
| ML Commons plugin | Either it hosts the new API, or it is called through its client for model predictions, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins call it. Its two memory APIs do not change. With a dedicated plugin, it adds a memory type extension point for agents (see "Long-term direction") |
| Security plugin | None required. When it is installed, Spaces can be registered with its resource sharing framework |
| k-NN and Neural Search plugins | None. The k-NN plugin provides vector fields, and the Neural Search plugin provides the `text_chunking` processor and `neural` and `hybrid` queries |
| Job Scheduler plugin | None. The implementation registers its own jobs for the extraction backlog and for expiry |
| OpenSearch core | None |

## What is the developer experience going to be?

### Use cases

Some common use cases for the API:

- When an agent needs a detail from earlier turns, such as an error code, a file name, or a value a user gave, the agent developer wants to search the raw turns by keyword and by meaning, so the agent finds the exact detail even when no extracted memory kept it.
- When memories go stale or a retention rule applies, the developer wants events and memories to expire after a set time, so old memories stop shaping answers and data is not kept longer than allowed.
- When an agent resumes a session or restarts, the agent developer wants to reload the session's recent turns, so the conversation continues where it left off.
- When a user returns to an agent in a new session, the agent developer wants the agent to recall facts and preferences from earlier sessions, so the user does not repeat them.
- When a conversation runs long, the developer wants a running summary of the whole session, so the agent can keep context without sending every turn to the model.
- When an application serves more than one end user, the developer wants each end user's memories stored under that user's ID and searchable by user and session, so the application shows each user only their own memories.
- When an agent needs a detail a memory left out, or an application must show where a memory came from or delete what a conversation produced, the developer wants each memory linked to the events it came from, so the agent can read the original turns and the application can check or delete memories by their source.

### Experimental status

The API is off by default. A cluster turns it on with a static setting in `opensearch.yml`, for example `plugins.memory.experimental.enabled: true`. The final name follows from where the code lives. With the setting off, the memory paths do not exist.

While the API is experimental:

- It can change in breaking ways between releases. The release notes list every change, and any step needed for data written by an earlier release.
- The documentation marks it with one notice: "Experimental: this API can change between releases until it is marked stable."
- It does not replace or change the ML Commons memory APIs.

### Resources

- **Space.** A container for one application's memory. It holds the memory strategies, the ML Commons model used for extraction (`extraction_model_id`), the ML Commons model used for vectors (`embedding_model_id`), and how long to keep events (`event_expiry_days`, default 90) and memories (`memory_expiry_days`, default 365, where 0 means never). Without an extraction model, a Space stores events and extracts nothing. Without an embedding model, search is by keyword only. The embedding model cannot be changed after the Space is created, because stored vectors would no longer match. A Space with an embedding model also gives `embedding_dimension`, the size of the model's vectors.
- **Event.** One conversation turn, a group of turns, or a JSON document. An event has an actor ID (for example, the end user), an optional session ID, a timestamp, the payload, and string key-value pairs of metadata.
- **Memory.** A record extracted from events by a strategy, or written directly with CreateMemory. Each memory belongs to one strategy, one actor, and optionally one session, and records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`.

### Strategies

A strategy tells the extraction pipeline what to extract. Two types ship with built-in prompts, and `CUSTOM` brings its own:

| Type | What it extracts |
| --- | --- |
| `SEMANTIC` | Facts stated in the conversation, as short standalone statements |
| `SUMMARY` | One running summary per session, updated with each event |
| `CUSTOM` | Whatever the strategy's `extraction_prompt` asks for, for example user preferences |

On any strategy, `configuration.consolidation_enabled` turns consolidation with stored memories on or off. Strategies read a JSON event as JSON text.

### Operations

All paths are under `/_plugins/_memory`, whichever plugin serves them.

| Operation | Method and path |
| --- | --- |
| CreateSpace | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| GetSpace | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| UpdateSpace | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| DeleteSpace | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| ListSpaces | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| CreateEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events` |
| GetEvent | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| BatchGetEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_mget` |
| ListEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_list` |
| SearchEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_search` |
| DeleteEvent | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| CreateMemory | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories` |
| GetMemory | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| UpdateMemory | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| DeleteMemory | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| ListMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_list` |
| SearchMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search` |
| Node statistics | `GET /_plugins/_memory/stats` |

Reads are scoped by actor and session:

- ListEvents requires one `actor_id` and one `session_id`.
- SearchEvents and SearchMemories require one `actor_id`, and accept an optional list of `session_ids`.
- ListMemories accepts optional lists of `actor_ids` and `session_ids`.
- GetEvent, BatchGetEvent, and the memory get, update, and delete operations accept the actor, and the session for events, as optional scope checks. A record outside the scope answers as not found.

Request options:

- CreateSpace, CreateEvent, and CreateMemory accept a `client_token`, so a retried write is stored once and the retry returns the stored record.
- CreateEvent accepts `infer: false` to store an event without extracting memories from it.
- List and search operations take `max_results` for the page size, and return a `next_token` for the next page.
- ListEvents and ListMemories take their filters in a request body, sent with `POST` to `_list`.
- CreateEvent and UpdateMemory accept `refresh` (`wait_for` by default, `true`, or `false`). Other writes, except CreateMemory, always wait for the refresh.

### Example

Create a Space with three strategies:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces
{
  "name": "support-assistant",
  "memory_strategies": [
    { "type": "SEMANTIC", "name": "facts" },
    { "type": "SUMMARY", "name": "session_summary" },
    {
      "type": "CUSTOM",
      "name": "preferences",
      "configuration": {
        "extraction_prompt": "List the user's stated preferences, one per line.",
        "consolidation_enabled": true
      }
    }
  ],
  "extraction_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_dimension": 1024,
  "event_expiry_days": 90,
  "memory_expiry_days": 365
}
```

Write a conversation turn:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "session_id": "session-1",
  "payload": {
    "conversational": {
      "unified": {
        "source": {
          "object": {
            "messages": [
              { "role": "USER", "content": { "text": "I always want a window seat." } },
              { "role": "ASSISTANT", "content": { "text": "Got it. I'll book window seats from now on." } }
            ]
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "metadata": { "channel": "web" }
}
```

The event is stored, the call answers `201 Created`, and memories are extracted in the background. Later, in a new session:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "query": { "match": { "memory_text": "seat" } },
  "max_results": 5
}
```

Each result carries `source_event_ids`, so the agent can read the original turns with BatchGetEvent when it needs more detail.

The `conversational.unified.source.object` levels leave room for other payload kinds and sources. Search takes `query` at the top level of the body, as `_search` does. The Space, actor, and session filters are separate fields, so a query cannot widen them.

## Long-term direction: one memory API

We propose that OpenSearch converge on one memory API. This RFC asks only for agreement on the event and memory model as an experimental API. How and when the two APIs converge is decided with the ML Commons maintainers once the new API is stable. Before agentic memory is deprecated, the new API needs to support existing memory workloads, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable through the new API or a way to move that data into Spaces.

ML Commons agents can use a Space through a memory type. In ML Commons, this is a new memory type next to `AGENTIC_MEMORY`. In a dedicated plugin, ML Commons will add a memory type extension point, which we would contribute; ML Commons still runs without the plugin. Saving to a Space calls no model in the agent's request; extraction runs later in the memory API's own thread pool.

Agent runtimes outside ML Commons can use the new API from the experimental release:

- The [OpenSearch Agent Server](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-agent-server), for its threads, runs, messages, and events.
- Framework integrations, such as the Strands session manager requested in [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) and the Strands store in [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919).
- The memory tools in [opensearch-mcp-server-py](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py).
- Checkpoint stores for agent frameworks, such as [LangGraph checkpointers](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/).

## How it works

This section outlines one implementation. It holds whether the code lives in the ML Commons plugin or in a dedicated plugin.

Diagram 1 shows how an event is stored, how its text is chunked and embedded, how memories are extracted and consolidated, how searches are served, and how records expire. Numbered arrows are the write path, blue arrows are searches, and dashed boxes and arrows run in the background.

<img width="3820" height="2200" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/254636cf-59ec-4b8f-a0e0-3da958810e35" />

*Diagram 1. How the Memory API works on a cluster.*

- **Storage.** Spaces, events, event chunks, and memories live in four system indexes: `.plugins-memory-spaces`, `.plugins-memory-events`, `.plugins-memory-event-chunks`, and `.plugins-memory-memories`. The Job Scheduler jobs live in `.plugins-memory-jobs`. Each event is one document: the full payload, kept as written but not indexed, and a text field with its messages. Each chunk of an event's text is its own document in the chunks index, with the event's ID, Space, actor, session, timestamp, and metadata. Deleting or expiring an event deletes its chunks. Every document stores its Space ID, and its tenant ID when multi-tenancy is on. A get, update, or delete by ID compares the document's Space with the Space in the request and answers 404 on a mismatch, and every search and list filters on the Space. IDs that come from a caller or a model, such as `source_event_ids` or the memories consolidation changes, are checked the same way. Spaces whose embedding models need different vector settings, such as the vector size, use separate chunk and memory indexes. Each index mapping carries a schema version, and older indexes are upgraded in place when a new release adds fields. Application metadata is stored in a `flat_object` field, so the keys an application chooses do not add fields to the shared index mappings.
- **Chunking and embedding.** CreateEvent splits the event's text into chunks by running the Neural Search plugin's `text_chunking` processor through the ingest simulate API, which needs no code dependency on Neural Search, then writes the event and one document per chunk in a single bulk request, so keyword search finds the event at once. Chunk IDs are derived from the event ID, so a retry with the same `client_token` rewrites the same chunks. When a Space names an embedding model, the background work calls it through ML Commons predict and adds a vector to each chunk, so a slow or unavailable model never delays or fails the write. If embedding fails, the Space's backlog job retries it. Event search runs on the chunks index, so each result is one matching chunk with the ID of its event. Extraction embeds each memory before storing it, so consolidation can compare it with stored memories at once. Memories written with CreateMemory get their vector in the background, like chunks. UpdateMemory re-embeds changed content before it returns.
- **Extraction.** Extraction runs on the cluster, in its own bounded thread pool, so there is no second process to deploy. Models are called through ML Commons predict as the implementation's own identity, and only with the model IDs stored on the Space. Whoever sets a Space's models must be allowed to use them. SUMMARY updates one summary per session from the stored summary and the new event, so the summary covers the whole session. Each memory records every event it came from in `source_event_ids`. Consolidation compares a new memory only with memories of the same Space, actor, and strategy, and the model can update or delete only those memories.
- **Extraction under load.** The node that receives an event runs its extraction in the bounded thread pool. Every event stays marked pending until its extraction finishes, so the backlog job retries work lost when a node stops, up to a set number of tries. Each Space has a Job Scheduler job that picks up the Space's pending events on a configurable interval, one minute by default. Job Scheduler runs each job on one of the data nodes that hold a copy of the job's shard, under a lock, so only one node works on a Space's backlog at a time, and the cluster manager node does no extraction. Index State Management, Anomaly Detection, Alerting, and agentic memory's retention job use the same pattern.
- **Search.** Event search and memory search accept only query types whose cost is bounded and that never read other documents: `match`, `match_phrase`, `match_all`, `term`, `terms` (values only), `ids`, `exists`, `bool`, `constant_score`, `boosting`, `range` and `function_score` decay on the time fields, and, when the Space has an embedding model, `neural` and `hybrid`. The implementation checks every clause against that list before the query runs, and rejects anything else with 400. It adds the Space, actor, and session filters itself, inside each `neural` and `hybrid` clause as well as around the query, so a query cannot widen its scope, and a semantic search still finds the closest matches within it. `neural` always uses the Space's embedding model, and `hybrid` scores are combined by a normalization search pipeline that the implementation creates. Both searches can filter by the application's metadata under `metadata.<key>`, and memory search can also filter by `source_event_ids`.
- **Read-after-write.** By default, CreateEvent and UpdateMemory return after the next refresh (`refresh=wait_for`), so a get, list, or keyword search that follows sees the write. CreateMemory answers 202 with the new memory's ID and stores the memory in the background; GetMemory finds it once it is indexed. Semantic search sees a new event once its vectors are added.
- **Expiry.** A Job Scheduler job deletes events older than `event_expiry_days`, with their chunks, and memories older than `memory_expiry_days`. A memory's age counts from when the implementation last wrote it; UpdateMemory does not reset it. An expired memory reads as not found, even before the job deletes it.
- **Running next to the ML Commons memory APIs.** The new API shares no path, index, setting, or permission with the ML Commons memory APIs, so they can run on the same cluster at the same time, and an application can move from one to another at its own pace.

## What is the user experience going to be?

- A cluster administrator turns on the experimental setting, and connects a model through ML Commons.
- A developer creates a Space and starts writing events. Memories are extracted and appear without further calls.
- Optionally, the application writes memories it extracts itself with CreateMemory, using any model or framework it already has, and a single event can skip extraction with `infer: false`.

## Are there any security considerations?

The API relies on the Security plugin for access control. Cluster admins, and the front end that sets the tenant ID, are trusted. OpenSearch users, usually applications, are kept apart per Space. End users do not call the API; their text is untrusted input to the models, and it leaves the cluster for the configured model providers.

- **Permissions.** Each operation is its own transport action, so Security plugin roles can grant operations one by one. Changing a Space's models or prompts, and searching SUMMARY or CUSTOM memories, can reveal event text, so those permissions count as read access to events.
- **Space access.** A Space is private to its owner and to admins (`all_access`) by default. The owner shares it through a `backend_roles` field: a user who holds one of those backend roles can use the Space. Only the owner or an admin can change `backend_roles`, the models, the strategies and prompts, and the expiry settings, and a user who is not an admin can add only backend roles they hold.
- **Records inside a Space.** Access is checked per Space, not per record. A user who can use a Space can read all of its events and memories. Agentic memory, by contrast, limits users who are not admins to the records they wrote. The `actor_id` and `session_id` on a request narrow what it returns, but the application supplies them, so they are not an access check.
- **Tenant isolation.** With multi-tenancy on, the REST layer reads the tenant ID from the `x-tenant-id` header, as ML Commons does, and every Space lookup checks it. The header is trusted as sent, so a deployment must set it from the caller's authenticated identity in a front end, and drop any value the client sends.
- **System indexes.** The memory indexes are system indexes. With the Security plugin, they are closed to users only when `plugins.security.system_indices.enabled` is true, which is off by default, so the implementation warns at startup when it is off. Even then, the super-admin certificate, roles granted `system:admin/system_index`, and snapshot restores can read every Space. Without the Security plugin, there is no access control.
- **Models.** ML Commons connectors hold the model credentials; the memory indexes store none. Event text goes to whatever endpoint a Space's models call, which is why only the owner or an admin can change the models, and the ML Commons setting `plugins.ml_commons.trusted_connector_endpoints_regex` limits where connectors can send it.
- **Model input.** Event text goes into the extraction prompt, and memories are later returned to agents, so text in an event can steer what is stored. Applications need to treat memories as user input. Each event write causes model calls, so a busy writer raises model cost for the whole cluster. ML Commons model rate limits, when set, cap it.

We also propose registering Spaces with the Security plugin's [resource sharing framework](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/security/access-control/resources/), so an owner can share one Space with specific users, roles, or backend roles. When the framework is on for Spaces, it alone decides who can use a Space; otherwise the backend-role rule above does. The two are never combined.

## Are there any breaking changes to the API and User Experience?

No. The API adds new paths under `/_plugins/_memory`, which exist only when the experimental setting is on. The ML Commons memory APIs, `/_plugins/_ml/memory` and `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`, do not change.

## Why should it be built? Any reason not to?

**Why build it:**

- **One memory API for every agent runtime.** Agent state is kept in several places today: agentic memory, the OpenSearch Agent Server's own SQLite store of threads, runs, messages, and events, and each framework adapter. One API lets a memory written by one runtime be read by another.
- **Search over the raw conversation.** Events are indexed for keyword search, and for semantic and hybrid search when a Space names an embedding model, so an agent can find a detail that extraction did not keep.
- **Memories that trace back to their source.** Every memory records the events it came from, whether it was extracted or written with CreateMemory. The link is used to fetch a memory's source events, audit where it came from, and delete what a conversation produced.
- **Safe retries.** A retried write with the same `client_token` is stored once.

**Alternatives we considered:**

- **Change agentic memory to the event and memory model.** Rejected because it breaks agentic memory users, as the section "Why a new API" describes.
- **A client library on top of agentic memory**, as [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919) and [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) propose for Strands. Rejected because the differences are on the server: the source links, the immutable events, and the actor and session fields. A client library cannot add them.

**Reasons not to:**

- **"I don't think we want to implement memory management twice"** ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150)). This is the main cost. OpenSearch would have two memory APIs that extract long-term memories until they converge. The long-term direction proposes converging them on one API, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable or a way to move it into Spaces.
- **More memory APIs confuse users.** The experimental setting means nobody adopts the new API by accident, and the documentation will say which API fits which need until agentic memory is deprecated.
- **Agentic memory has more features today.** The new API starts with a focused set, and features can be added based on community interest.

## What will it take to execute?

- **Dependencies.** The ML Commons plugin for model calls, the Job Scheduler plugin for the extraction backlog and expiry, the Neural Search plugin for chunking and for `neural` and `hybrid` queries, the k-NN plugin for vector fields, and optionally the Security plugin.
- **Versions.** The API runs its background work under its own plugin identity, which needs the Security plugin fix that lets a plugin identity use its own system indexes ([security#5858](https://github.com/opensearch-project/security/pull/5858), in 3.5). If the code lives in ML Commons, ML Commons first adopts plugin identity.
- **Clients.** The API is added to opensearch-api-specification after it is implemented, so clients can be generated from it.
- **Cost.** Each event leads to model calls for each strategy: one to extract, one to consolidate when consolidation is on, and embedding calls when the Space has an embedding model. The implementation can batch these calls, such as several turns of a session in one extraction call, without changing the API.
- **Process.** This RFC, open for community review. If the community chooses a dedicated plugin, a repository request and the project's security review for a new repository follow.

## Any remaining open questions?

We would like the community's view on these questions:

1. **Where should the code live?** The API design is the same either way.

   - *In the ML Commons plugin*, next to the existing memory APIs. No new repository, release pipeline, or set of maintainers. Changes are reviewed in the existing ML Commons community and its weekly meeting, where backward compatibility is already checked. Other plugins already call ML Commons through a small client layer.
   - *In a dedicated plugin* that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins do. Memory gets its own owners and an optional install, and ML Commons stays focused on models and inference, a split proposed for memory in 2023 ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150#issuecomment-1666021113)) and for agents in [.github#398](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/398). The cost is another repository to build, release, and secure.
   - *Paths.* We propose `/_plugins/_memory` in both cases, so the answer does not change the API. If the community prefers ML Commons' own prefix when the code lives there, the same operations would sit under it, for example `/_plugins/_ml/spaces/{space_id}/events`. `/_plugins/_ml/memory` is taken by conversation memory.
2. **Agentic memory.** What should the path to one API look like, and would ML Commons add the memory type extension point described in "Long-term direction"? The existing `REMOTE_AGENTIC_MEMORY` memory type calls fixed agentic memory paths ([ml-commons#4572](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4572)), so it cannot reach a Space as it stands.
3. **Leaving experimental status.** What should the API show before it becomes stable: a number of releases without breaking changes, use by ML Commons agents, or a benchmark of extraction quality?

Out of scope for this RFC: OpenSearch Dashboards support and framework adapters (LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Strands). With a dedicated plugin, the memory type extension point would be its own ML Commons change.

items.title: RFC: knowledge — retrieval seams, a CJK-aware keyword index, hybrid search and source sync
items.body:
## Summary

June agents have channels, connections, durable turns and a data layer, but nothing for **retrieval**: no embedding seam, no vector resource, no keyword index that works on CJK text, no fusion, no way to keep an index in step with its source. Every app that answers from its own knowledge writes all of it itself.

This RFC proposes a `knowledge` layer for June: a few small seams, each with a local default that runs offline and a deploy adapter, following the binding model in [`docs/data-layer-boundary.md`](https://github.com/junebuild/june/blob/main/docs/data-layer-boundary.md). An app declares a knowledge index, syncs sources into it, and gets a retriever and a tool. What it keeps is its own content and domain.

## Motivation: two apps already wrote it twice

- **A production support agent on June** (Crisp + Slack channels, durable runtime on Cloudflare) reads each customer message, retrieves precedent from past conversations and help-center articles, and records a draft judgment for a person to review. About half of its non-generated code is retrieval it had to build:
  - `Embedder`, `VectorStore` and `Retriever` interfaces, each with two backings: local (SQLite, a brute-force vector scan, an on-device bge-m3) and Cloudflare (D1, Vectorize, Workers AI bge-m3);
  - FTS5 with a CJK bigram tokenizer, because FTS5's `unicode61` reads a whole CJK sentence as one token and Chinese search silently returns nothing;
  - reciprocal rank fusion of keyword and vector results, plus a bounded boost for documents attributed to the asker's own tenant;
  - incremental document sync: a source-scoped doc id, a content hash so unchanged documents skip re-embedding, deletion when a document leaves the source, and a pipeline version;
  - a recall@k harness over held-out real questions, used to gate changes to the corpus (for example, PII scrubbing) and to the ranking.
- **[Lorehouse](https://github.com/solcreek/lorehouse)** (on June) indexes Slack threads into SQLite FTS and wrote its **own** CJK bigram index (`src/knowledge.ts`, `INDEX_VERSION = "cjk-bigram-1"`). It has no vector search yet, and its ADR 0005 plans knowledge-source connectors with per-document visibility.

The two CJK tokenizers differ in detail. Their index texts are not interchangeable, and each fixes the same bugs on its own.

## Proposal

### 1. Seams

```ts
interface Embedder {
  readonly model: string;        // e.g. "bge-m3"
  readonly dimensions: number;   // e.g. 1024
  embed(texts: string[]): Promise<Float32Array[]>;   // L2-normalized, order-preserving
}

interface VectorStore {
  upsert(records: { id: string; vector: Float32Array }[]): Promise<void>;
  query(vector: Float32Array, topK: number, filter?: Filter): Promise<{ id: string; score: number }[]>;
  delete(ids: string[]): Promise<void>;
}

interface KeywordIndex {           // FTS5 on the app's `db` resource (SQLite / D1)
  upsert(docs: { id: string; text: string }[]): Promise<void>;
  query(text: string, topK: number, filter?: Filter): Promise<{ id: string; rank: number }[]>;
  delete(ids: string[]): Promise<void>;
}

interface Retriever {
  retrieve(query: string, k: number, opts?: { filter?: Filter; boost?: Boost }): Promise<Hit[]>;
}
```

### 2. Resources, local first

| Resource | Local default (`june dev`) | Deploy adapters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vectors` | brute-force scan persisted in the `db` SQLite file (about 11 ms for 10k × 1024 dims in plain JS in the support agent; exact recall, nothing to tune) | **Vectorize**; others later |
| `embedder` | an on-device model, as an **optional peer** | **Workers AI**; a provider's embeddings API |

**The embedder is pinned to the index.** The index records the model, dimensions, pooling and normalization it was built with, and a query embedder that doesn't match fails loudly instead of returning nonsense. Local and deploy then share one index only when they really run the same model. The support agent relies on this: it builds the index offline with bge-m3 on CPU and serves queries with Workers AI bge-m3.

**The local embedder must stay optional.** Today the on-device path, Transformers.js, pulls in `onnxruntime-node` (208 MB on disk: native binaries for six platforms in one package, so `supportedArchitectures` cannot trim it) and `onnxruntime-web` (86 MB of `dist`). Every install of an app that declares it pays that cost, including CI and teammates who never run ingest. So it must be a separate package or an optional peer, never a dependency of `@junejs/core`. That also keeps a `bun build --compile` binary free of the native addon.

### 3. CJK-aware keyword index

- Ship one tokenizer: CJK runs become overlapping character bigrams, Latin and digit runs become lowercased words, and documents and queries go through the same function.
- The index text format is versioned (`indexVersion`), so a tokenizer change is a detected rebuild rather than silent drift.
- Supported on SQLite and D1, through the same FTS5 queries.

### 4. Hybrid retrieval

- Reciprocal rank fusion (`k = 60`) of the keyword and vector lists, with a deterministic tie-break (score descending, then id ascending).
- An optional `boost` hook adds a bounded bonus to the ids a caller marks (for example, documents from the asker's own organization). It is expressed on the RRF scale so its overtake capacity can be tested.
- **Without a boost, the output is byte-identical to the unboosted path.** This is pinned by a test.
- **`filter` runs before anything reaches the model.** It is the hook a visibility or audience rule plugs into (Lorehouse ADR 0005 §6). June provides the hook; the rule belongs to the app.

### 5. Source sync

`defineKnowledgeSource({ id, list, read })` provides the sync loop:

- doc ids are `<source>:<source-scoped id>`;
- a content hash per document: unchanged means skip, changed means re-chunk and re-embed the whole document, gone from the source means delete its chunks, vectors and hash row;
- every change is scoped by `(source, docId)`, so one source's sync never touches another's chunks;
- a `pipelineVersion` (chunker, embedder, index text), whose change re-embeds everything.

Chunking is the app's. June ships a markdown-section chunker as a helper, not a requirement.

### 6. A tool

`knowledgeTool(retriever, { name, description })` returns a tool that retrieves, and returns hits with ids the model can cite.

### 7. Retrieval evals belong to #342

A known-item recall@k probe needs no human labels: take real questions, use the documents that contain their answers as ground truth, and compare recall between two index builds. This should be a case type in `june eval` (#342), not a separate harness.

## Non-goals

- A hosted vector database, ANN index tuning, or rerankers. Brute force covers tens of thousands of vectors; past about 50k, a binary prefilter plus rerank is the next step, and it can come later behind the same seam.
- Visibility and access policy. June supplies `filter`; the app decides what may be seen.
- Chunking strategy beyond the markdown helper.

## Open questions

1. Is this `@junejs/knowledge`, or new resource kinds (`vectors`, `embedder`) in the `resources` config next to `db`, `blob` and `kv`?
2. Should the index's embedder pin be strict (refuse to query) or a startup check with an explicit override?
3. Which on-device embedder? Transformers.js (heavy, as above), or a smaller ONNX runtime path that `bun build --compile` can embed?
4. The CJK tokenizer: is a JS pre-tokenizer (as both apps do today) enough, or is a custom FTS5 tokenizer worth it where the driver allows one?

## Slices

1. Seams plus the local defaults: `Embedder`, the SQLite-persisted `VectorStore`, the CJK `KeywordIndex`, RRF and `Retriever`.
2. Cloudflare adapters: Vectorize, the Workers AI embedder, FTS5 on D1.
3. The embedder pin and index metadata.
4. `defineKnowledgeSource` and the sync loop.
5. `knowledgeTool`.
6. A retrieval case type in `june eval` (after #342).

## Acceptance

- The support agent replaces its `rag/` seams, stores and fusion with the package, and its recall@k on the same query set and corpus is unchanged.
- Lorehouse's knowledge index can move onto the shared tokenizer, with a rebuild detected through `indexVersion`.
- An app that declares no local embedder installs no onnxruntime.
