items.title: Phase 5: shared-pool pressure response (reconciliation-triggered eviction scoped to the co-location group)
items.body:
Part of **Phase 5 — kvcached oversubscription & co-location policy** (spec: `docs/project/overall-plan.md:385-398`; plan: `.omp/plans/phase5-plan.md`, review-clean after two adversarial rounds).

## Summary
When a device's kvcached pool is under pressure (used ≈ pool total), the control plane's reconciliation tick reclaims capacity through the eviction engine, scoped to the pressure device's co-location group — the first memory-pressure eviction trigger in the system (eviction is demand-only today).

## Ground truth (verified against code)
- No memory-pressure/idle/background eviction trigger exists (`grep idle|autoSleep|sleepAfter|inactivity control-plane/src`: nothing); the two existing triggers are deploy-fail (`models.ts:472-514`) and wake-shortfall (`models.ts:1814-1878`).
- Hook point: `ReconciliationService.tick` → `safeStep('refreshMemoryBudgets')` (`reconciliation.ts:164`); `DeviceBudget.kvCache` is validated + attached every tick (`memory-budget.ts:83-113, :269-270`).
- Victim selection: `EvictionEngine.selectVictims` (`eviction.ts:62-117`), LRU by per-model `lastInferenceAt`, candidates ACTIVE|SLEEPING unpinned, sized by configured `requiredMemory`; `EvictionStrategy` is the pluggable seam (`eviction.ts:16-18`). `EvictionCandidate` has no `deviceIndex` — device scoping must not re-derive the co-location group (#276 owns the helper).
- vLLM sleep = weights→host RAM (L1); a slept co-tenant's kvcached pool segment persists (`kvcached_pools.py`), so pool stats keep flowing after sleep — pressure logic must check lifecycle state.
- Drain semantics per ADR-028 (two-valued signal, unknown ≠ drained, fail-open, 409-in-window deliberate).

Labels: component/control-plane, area/orchestration, enhancement, priority/P2-medium

items.title: [RFC]: Disaggregated Speculative Decoding with Standalone Parallel Draft Model
items.body:
### Motivation. Speculative decoding in vLLM today co-locates the draft model with the target: the draft runs on the target's TP group, competes for the same SMs / HBM bandwidth, and is driven by the target's scheduler. This is efficient for small draft models (EAGLE, MTP), but has two structural limits: 1. **Draft compute steals from target compute.** On a TP=2 Llama-3-70B target at high concurrency, a 1B–8B draft can add 10–30% to per-step latency on the target GPUs even when the draft itself is idle-compute-bound, because it shares the forward-pass critical path. 2. **Cache-build parallelism is capped by the target's schedule.** Any "predict what the target will verify next round" caching scheme has to complete between target steps — the draft cannot run ahead. Disaggregated speculative decoding (**Disagg-SD**) moves the draft model to a dedicated GPU (or pool of GPUs) reached over a fast interconnect (ZMQ + shared host for same-node, RDMA for cross-node). The target sends a *verification outcome* after each step; the draft server returns *K draft tokens per request* from a **speculation cache** that was pre-built while the target was verifying the previous round. This gives: - **Fully overlapped draft/target compute.** The target's latency is independent of draft work. - **Pre-computed fan-outs.** The draft predicts the most likely verification outcomes `(k_accepted, bonus_token)` for the next round and has the K draft tokens ready before the target asks. - **N:M scaling.** N verify servers can share M draft servers; each draft can run a larger model than the target's per-step budget allows. We have an internal POC of Disagg-SD on vLLM (integrated via ZMQ, standalone `draft_server` process, `SpeculationCache` with geometric fan-out, per-VS dedicated KV blocks). It is functional end-to-end at N:M=3:2 on Llama-3.1-70B (verify) + Llama-3.2-1B (draft), and we have latency/throughput benchmarks showing ~1.4× TPOT improvement vs co-located spec decode at the same total GPU budget. The **bottleneck in the POC** is cache build: at K=6, N=56 branches, it's launch-bound (6 small kernels per round). We are working on a **standalone parallel draft model** (mask-token MTP-style) which can compute all fan-out branches in a single forward pass. Combined with Disagg-SD, this would push draft-side latency from `K × small_forward` to `1 × medium_forward`, unlocking higher N:M ratios and larger draft models without hurting target latency. ### Co-located vs disaggregated timeline illustration ```mermaid gantt title Three consecutive decode rounds (time units, illustrative) dateFormat X axisFormat %s section Co-located (today) Target verify round N :t1, 0, 10 Draft speculate (K steps) :d1, after t1, 14 Target verify round N+1 :t2, after d1, 10 Draft speculate (K steps) :d2, after t2, 14 Target verify round N+2 :t3, after d2, 10 section Disagg-SD — target Target verify round N :u1, 0, 10 Target verify round N+1 :u2, after u1, 10 Target verify round N+2 :u3, after u2, 10 section Disagg-SD — draft Cache build for round N+1 :e1, 0, 14 Cache build for round N+2 :e2, after e1, 14 ``` Let `v` be a target verify step and `d` be a draft K-step forward. In the co-located path target and draft serialize on the same GPU: each round adds `v + d` to the critical path, so `R` rounds take `R·v + (R−1)·d`. Wall time per round asymptotically approaches `v + d`. In Disagg-SD the draft runs on its own GPU. **Cache build for one round is typically longer than a single target verify (`d > v`)**, but it overlaps across multiple target rounds. Target verifies run back-to-back unblocked (`R·v` for `R` rounds); each `SPECULATE` response is served from the cache (a tensor lookup, negligible vs `v`). Wall time per round approaches `v`. The asymptotic target-throughput speedup is `(v + d) / v = 1 + d/v`. Disagg-SD stops winning if cache build exceeds the time between consecutive `SPECULATE` calls (i.e. `d > v`, *and* no amount of pipelining can hide it — cache hits start missing and fall back to JIT). This sets the upper bound on draft model size / fan-out budget for a given target throughput. Another approach we are considering is parallel-draft cache build (fewer kernel launches → shorter `d` → higher ceiling on draft size). ### Proposed Change. The change is in three parts: (1) a standalone draft server process, (2) verify-side integration as a drop-in speculator, (3) a speculation cache with geometric fan-out for hiding draft latency across rounds. ### N:M topology ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Verify side V1[Verify Server 1
Llama-3-70B TP=2] V2[Verify Server 2
Llama-3-70B TP=2] V3[Verify Server 3
Llama-3-70B TP=2] end R{{DraftRouter
round_robin / affinity}} subgraph Draft side D1[Draft Server 1
Llama-3.2-1B + SpecCache] D2[Draft Server 2
Llama-3.2-1B + SpecCache] end V1 -- ZMQ DEALER --> R V2 -- ZMQ DEALER --> R V3 -- ZMQ DEALER --> R R -- ZMQ ROUTER --> D1 R -- ZMQ ROUTER --> D2 ``` Each `DisaggSpeculatorProxy` lives on TP rank 0 of its verify server and holds a `DraftRouter` with one `ZmqDraftConnector` per draft server. Each draft server partitions its `SpeculationCache` and dedicated KV blocks per verify-server ID so tenants do not thrash each other. ### 1. Standalone `DraftServer` process A new process (`python -m vllm.v1.spec_decode.draft_server`) hosts a dedicated draft model on a GPU separate from the target's TP group. It: - Binds a ZMQ `ROUTER` socket at a configurable address (default `tcp://*:50051`). - Loads the draft model with its own `ModelRunner` (does not participate in the target's TP or scheduler). - Handles three commands over ZMQ: - `PREFILL(seq_id, prompt_tokens)`: run prefill for a new request. - `SPECULATE(seq_id, k_accepted, bonus_token, temperatures)`: return K draft tokens using the speculation cache, falling back to JIT speculation on cache miss. - `FREE_SEQ(seq_id)`: release KV blocks when a request finishes. - Maintains a `SpeculationCache` (tokens + logits + dedicated KV blocks) keyed by `(seq_id, k_accepted, bonus_token)`. - Supports timeout-based eviction of dead verify-server sessions. State is partitioned per verify server to prevent cross-tenant cache thrashing (internal seq IDs are remapped, dedicated KV blocks are reserved per-VS). #### Per-round lifecycle ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant T as Target (verify) participant P as DisaggSpeculatorProxy participant D as DraftServer Note over T,D: New request T->>P: propose(new_req, prompt) P->>D: PREFILL(seq_id, prompt_tokens) D-->>P: ack loop each decode round T->>T: target forward + sampling T->>P: propose(k_accepted, bonus_token, temps) P->>D: SPECULATE(...) D-->>P: cache lookup → K draft tokens (or JIT) Note over D: background: cache build for next round end T->>P: request finished P->>D: FREE_SEQ(seq_id) ``` The response to `SPECULATE` is returned immediately from the cache (or JIT on miss); cache building for the *next* round happens after the response is sent, overlapping with the target's next verify step. ### 2. Verify-side integration: `DisaggSpeculatorProxy` A proxy speculator on the verify side (replaces the in-process speculator when `disagg_draft_addresses` is set): - Lives on TP rank 0 of the target's model runner. Other ranks short-circuit `propose()` and receive draft tokens via TP broadcast. - Holds a `DraftRouter` with one `ZmqDraftConnector` per draft server. Routing policies: `round_robin` (default) and `affinity` (stable mapping by `hash(verify_server_id) mod num_drafts`). - After each target step, sends `(seq_ids, k_accepted, bonus_tokens)` via ZMQ and blocks on the response with a configurable timeout (default 5s). - Implements graceful degradation: marks unresponsive servers unavailable, returns zero-token drafts until reconnect succeeds, with periodic reconnect attempts. New `SpeculativeConfig` fields: ```python disagg_draft_addresses: list[str] | None = None disagg_fan_out: int = 1 # per acceptance position (geometric allocation) disagg_saguaro_c: float | None = None disagg_jit_fallback: bool = True disagg_draft_routing_policy: Literal["round_robin", "affinity"] = "round_robin" disagg_draft_timeout_ms: int = 5000 disagg_draft_latency_warn_ms: float = 500.0 ``` A single new predicate `use_disagg()` gates all Disagg-SD code paths. When unset, behavior is identical to mainline. ### 3. Speculation cache with geometric fan-out For each in-flight request, the draft pre-builds `F_k` K-token branches per acceptance position `k ∈ [0, K]`. Each branch is rooted at a different `(k_accepted, bonus_candidate)` — the top-`F_k` bonus candidates from the previous round's draft logits. Budget is allocated geometrically per SSD Theorem 12 (acceptance probability decreases with k, so lower k gets more budget). ```mermaid flowchart LR P[prefix KV] P --> A0((k=0)) A0 --> a["a — [L draft tokens]"] A0 --> b["b — [L draft tokens]"] P --> S1[s₁] S1 --> A1((k=1)) A1 --> c["c — [L draft tokens]"] A1 --> d["d — [L draft tokens]"] S1 --> S2[s₂] S2 --> A2((k=2)) A2 --> e["e — [L draft tokens]"] ``` *Fan-out example, L=2, F=[2, 2, 1], B=5 branches.* Cache build runs **tree decode** — K forward passes, each a varlen-batched step over all B branches in parallel, with per-branch block tables to keep KV writes isolated. On cache hit the branch's dedicated blocks are swapped into the main sequence so subsequent decode/JIT attends to valid KV. On cache miss the server falls back to **JIT speculation** (K sequential decode steps for the main sequence only) so latency stays bounded. ### Summary of new/changed files New: - `vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_server.py` — ZMQ `ROUTER` draft server with speculation cache, JIT fallback, timeout eviction. - `vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_connector.py`, `draft_router.py` — verify-side ZMQ `DEALER` connector + multi-draft router. - `vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_data_models.py` — wire protocol (msgpack-encoded commands + tensor frames). - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/disagg_draft/` — `DisaggSpeculatorProxy`, `DraftModelRunner` (with `DraftKVCacheMixin`), `SpeculationCache`, `OutcomePredictor` (geometric fan-out), `SaguaroSampler`. - `vllm/entrypoints/draft_server.py` — CLI launcher. Changed: - `vllm/config/speculative.py` — new disagg fields. - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` — lazy `DisaggSpeculatorProxy` init on first `propose()`; TP broadcast of draft tokens. ### Backward compatibility All changes are gated on `disagg_draft_addresses` being set. When unset, the code paths are inert. No change to the in-process spec decode path. ### Feedback Period. Four weeks from posting. We have an internal implementation for Disagg-SD framework described above, and are actively working on parallel draft model. ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: Investigate FL jobs staying queued while exact-profile availability reports ready
items.body:
Parent: #20. Related availability contract: #99; original execution lifecycle: #16.

## Observed production problem
A single creator-authorized first/last-frame probe passed preflight and was accepted, but remained `queued` / `phase=queued` for at least 177 seconds while fresh observations for the exact deployment profile continuously reported `ready`, `available=true`, `reason_code=matching_worker_ready`. There was no error, output, queue position or actionable wait reason. This is a reproducible admission/dispatch or status-diagnostics investigation, not a proven GPU failure or an SLA claim.

## Reproduction and evidence (2026-10-10 UTC)
- Use the published HTTPS Skill and SHA-verified public helper, owner-scoped creator-full connection saved with Windows user DPAPI. Connection and authenticated API reads succeeded. No operator calls.
- Upload two existing local static JPEG frames, each 864x480; both returned ready. Create one explicit FL card preserving session settings: 480P, requested 5 seconds, 20 Euler steps, seed decimal string 424242, generated audio, one copy.
- Exact deployment profile: `h3-pruned-rank8-int8-quanto-int8-vae-int8-sdpa-p4-lowram-v1`; recipe `h3-base-fl2va-v1`.
- Preflight `preflight-fb097a81e7724a388e9dddfb53754dd7` was ready with no blockers or warnings. Effective request retained both first/last input roles. Output specification 832x480,124 frames at24fps (5.1667s). Reservation USD0.80; actual charge unknown.
- Accepted original job: `d12e78c9-5fec-4c69-b044-97e7fcb4e03a`, created epoch1791625138.577905 (09:38:58 UTC). Original submission `submission-8baa218e6eb84c6b85ed9b32eb14fdc4`; revision `revision-0660b2d0166e4491b8de5eeb14dc4327`.
- At epoch1791625316 (09:41:56 UTC), job remained queued; updated_at stayed1791625138.6789522; error_code=null; artifacts empty. Submission had one execution only. Fresh availability at epoch1791625230.8592598 and the final observation remained ready for this exact FL profile.
- Authenticated Chrome showed the saved card and correct first/last filenames, card header execution active, item waiting for execution, and FL2VA available / matching machine ready. No inference progress was observed.

## Expected / investigation
- Eligible matching ready capacity should dispatch the accepted original job, or explain the actual scheduling/ownership/configuration/lease condition preventing dispatch.
- Compare availability/admission eligibility with worker claim eligibility, owner/tenant scope, immutable execution configuration, draining/quarantine state and scheduler liveness. These are hypotheses, not established causes.
- Preserve the original job, submission, inputs, key/body, reservation and history. Reconcile that original record; do not create a replacement test or reset a ledger.
- Verify eventual original video/audio and hashes if execution advances. No visual first/last adherence claim is possible yet.

## Boundary and handoff
Only public creator APIs and authenticated browser reads were used. No source, deployments, infrastructure or budget configuration changed; no retry, cancellation or replacement was submitted. Existing unrelated historical jobs remain untouched. Safe business receipts are retained locally; no credentials, signed URLs, private prompts or media are attached here. Live media-quality acceptance is blocked on original execution. Source/release owner is unclaimed.

items.title: [P0/C03] Establish observability and reproducible single-group performance baselines
items.body:
<!-- kv9-roadmap-20260908:C03 -->
Parent: [Roadmap tracker](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/issues/9)

**Stage:** P0 - Verified foundation
**Depends on:** [#10](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/issues/10)
**Code entry points:** server metrics; raft/driver; engine persistence and remote I/O; new benchmark scripts

## Problem and outcome

Per-record fsync, full checkpoints and O(tail) reclamation currently have no reproducible cost baseline.

## Implementation sequence

1. Instrument proposal/commit/apply/read-barrier latency, fsync, queue bytes, apply lag, upload/flush backlog, memory, logs, objects and recovery time. Separate metadata from user traffic and bound metric cardinality.
2. Build a persistent-connection client with explicit open/closed-loop semantics, client queue time, service time, timeouts and refusals. Detect client saturation and coordinated omission.
3. Record commit, build profile, hardware, disk/network/MinIO topology, key/value sizes, access distribution, read/write mix and concurrency; publish workload setup and raw results.
4. Measure local WAL versus MinIO, steady state versus flush, cold versus warm cache, and uniform versus hot keys. Keep durability and consistency enabled and add C02 correctness sampling.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Repeatable reports include throughput, p50/p95/p99, error rate, CPU/RSS, I/O amplification, recovery time and run-to-run variation.
- [ ] Metrics export overhead and labels stay bounded; clients and per-request CLI startup are not hidden bottlenecks.
- [ ] The repository contains runnable benchmarks and a report format. Subsequent budgets come from measured results, not invented QPS targets.

## Scope boundary

Establish measurement before optimization; weakening fsync or consistency is not an acceptable performance improvement.

## Mandatory correctness and availability gates

The [shared correctness contract](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/master/docs/CORRECTNESS-GATES.md) supplements this issue's original scope.

- [ ] Core protocol changes have rigorous proofs, checked lemmas and an explicit implementation refinement record; unresolved assumptions remain visible. Infrastructure-only changes identify the proof obligations they preserve.
- [ ] Applicable E2E scenarios run under actual Chaos Mesh with observed fault effects, correct operation histories and retained success/failure evidence. Record any uncovered fault family explicitly.
- [ ] The component's authority, recovery and client path require no indispensable database node or singleton service. State the quorum/failure-domain assumptions and provide every-voter or role-takeover evidence as applicable; the object store is the sole allowed dependency exception.

## Completion evidence

Link the implementation commits or PRs and actual check runs. Record selected tests, failure cuts, and known coverage limits. Performance claims require the configuration and raw results from C03.

Implementation reference: [ec50678](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/commit/ec506780f273663da9b1d37fe9357495d549bf7c). See the published [audit](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/ec506780f273663da9b1d37fe9357495d549bf7c/docs/TAKEOVER-AUDIT.md) and [validation record](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/ec506780f273663da9b1d37fe9357495d549bf7c/docs/TAKEOVER-VALIDATION.md).

## Current direction (2026-09-16)

**Horizontal scaling is the active mainline.** The user explicitly ended the current performance iteration at the validated CRC/rpds baseline. Redis parity and completion of experimental radix work are no longer prerequisites. Preserve every existing storage/recovery, rigorous proof, actual Chaos Mesh and no-singleton acceptance gate. See the [implementation and benchmark contract](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/3dc6a131c825ba7a97d233d3bc1138630ea1b9be/docs/HORIZONTAL-SCALING-PLAN.md).

Effective scale-out must be demonstrated in benchmarks: independent 3/6/9-node topologies with three replicas per data group, fixed semantics/durability and dataset controls; both sustainable throughput under a fixed p99 budget and latency at equal offered load. Separate group parallelism from added hardware, and report uniform, multi-hotspot, single-hot-key and online-expansion behavior. The predeclared primary target is 1.6x throughput at 6 nodes and 2.4x at 9 nodes, with raw repetitions, uncertainty, per-node resource costs and independent correctness evidence. These are targets, not measured results; same-host processes do not prove horizontal scaling.


## Multi-group throughput baseline (2026-09-16)

Commit `2aefab0` ([measured scaling and bottleneck ledger](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/2aefab048fc8ca6e6330b9a806922e3db45b387e/docs/MULTI-GROUP-THROUGHPUT.md), [portable validation](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/blob/2aefab048fc8ca6e6330b9a806922e3db45b387e/docs/multi-group-baseline-v1/README.md)):

- A predeclared single-host sweep harness binds G data groups to G fresh Raw keyspaces and drives G concurrent qualified `kv9-workload` processes, reporting measurement-window overlap, merged integer histograms and per-thread server CPU; 599 qualified run reports across four rounds are retained, including every failed cell with failure-moment forensics.
- Equal per-group load (32 workers/group, admission 1024/node, tmpfs, 30 s cells, two reps): put 126.1k -> 203.6k (S=1.61) -> 270.4k (S=2.14) -> **292.2k ops/s at eight groups (S(8)=2.32)**; p99 0.5-1 ms rising to 2-4 ms. Fixed-aggregate panels for put/get/mixed peak at four groups. The single-group baseline is consistent with the retained 137.9k/s tmpfs measurement.
- The shared data-group driver pool is now configurable (`data_workers`, default 2, 1..=32, CLI `--data-workers`). The default is kept by evidence: two workers beat 1/4/8 at every measured point, under and at saturation (88% utilization at four groups).
- Evidence-backed bounds: the default `KV9_PUBLIC_MAX_REQUESTS=64`/node admission budget binds first (0.55 M refusals in one 30 s cell); per-group pipeline depth governs batching at fixed aggregate load; sixteen full-rate groups exceed this fixture's 2 s read-barrier startup envelope, shown insensitive to worker count, admission and launch stagger, with stable-term/healthy-probe forensics retained; the RAID5-HDD per-append-fsync panel (0.86k/0.73k ops/s) stays separate from tmpfs.
- 914 serial workspace tests pass with strict Clippy; six Lean models and the retention TLA/TLAPS model are rechecked after the pool plumbing.

This is a development diagnostic on one host: same-CPU processes are not added nodes, and no 3/6/9-host scaling, online expansion, split/placement, sustained p99-budget acceptance or durability-panel change is claimed. Proposal batching/group commit remains [#20](https://github.com/c4pt0r/kv9/issues/20); the independent 3/6/9-host benchmark contract remains the only acceptance path for effective horizontal scaling.

items.body:
## Problem
Enforce tenant isolation in the database: enable row-level security on every tenant table, add the `withWorkspace(tx, workspaceId)` helper that sets `app.workspace_id` with `SET LOCAL` at the start of each transaction, make the application role non-owner so RLS applies, and build the CI-blocking cross-tenant test suite covering SQL, server actions, API, storage presign, vector search and a user who belongs to two workspaces.

Why: PRD PL-1, spike §4.1 and architecture §6.3 make RLS the backstop of isolation. A leak across workspaces is a professional-privilege and DPDP incident. This issue must make it hard to forget RLS (lint plus a schema test) and impossible to merge a regression (CI-blocking suite).

## Root Cause (if known)
Greenfield: no existing implementation. Specified by the technical spike (#1) §4.1 (Tenancy and RLS) and §10 (cross-tenant suite green).

## Affected Files
1. `packages/db/src/rls.ts` (`withWorkspace(db, {workspaceId, userId?}, fn)`: `db.transaction(async tx => { await tx.execute(sql`select set_config('app.workspace_id', ${id}, true), set_config('app.user_id', ${uid}, true)`); return fn(tx) })`; validates uuid; throws if nested with a different workspace; exports `withoutWorkspace` for global tables only, flagged `@internal`)
2. `packages/db/src/rls-policies.ts` (helper `tenantPolicy(table)` generating `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, `CREATE POLICY ws_isolation USING (workspace_id = nullif(current_setting('app.workspace_id', true), '')::uuid) WITH CHECK (same)` for all commands)
3. `packages/db/migrations/0005_rls_baseline.sql` (applies policies to `workspace`-scoped tables that exist at this point (`member`, `invitation`, `workspace_settings`, `job_effect`); `workspace` row policy allows rows where `id = current workspace` or the caller is a member via `app.user_id`; creates SQL function `app_current_workspace()`; revokes default public privileges; grants DML to `causedeck_app`)
4. `packages/db/scripts/check-rls.ts` (introspects `pg_class`/`pg_policies`: every table with a `workspace_id` column must have RLS enabled AND forced and a policy referencing `app.workspace_id`; allow-list `GLOBAL_TABLES` documented; run as `pnpm db:check-rls`)
5. `packages/db/src/schema-helpers/tenant-table.ts` (`tenantTable(name, cols, extras)` wrapper that adds `workspace_id`, the index and registers the table for policy generation so later issues cannot forget; unit-tested)
6. `packages/db/src/testing/two-tenants.ts` (fixtures: workspaces A and B, users `ua` (A), `ub` (B), `uboth` (member of both) with seed rows in every tenant table)
7. `packages/db/src/__tests__/rls/{sql.test.ts,no-guc.test.ts,with-check.test.ts,pooling.test.ts}` (as app role: SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT across tenants; missing GUC returns zero rows and inserts fail; `WITH CHECK` blocks writing a foreign `workspace_id`; GUC does not leak between pooled connections since `SET LOCAL` is transaction scoped)
8. `packages/core/src/__tests__/cross-tenant/{services.test.ts,two-workspace-user.test.ts}` (every service exported from `packages/core` is called by user B against A's ids and must return not-found or forbidden)
9. `apps/api/src/__tests__/cross-tenant.test.ts` and `apps/web/__tests__/cross-tenant-actions.test.ts` (API routes and server actions)
10. `packages/storage/src/__tests__/cross-tenant-presign.test.ts` (placeholder enabled when #21 lands; the suite registry makes missing coverage fail: see below)
11. `packages/db/src/__tests__/rls/vector.test.ts` (pgvector similarity query as workspace A never returns B's rows; uses a `memory_embedding`-shaped fixture table until the real one exists)
12. `packages/db/src/testing/cross-tenant-registry.ts` (every tenant table and every exported core service must be registered with a cross-tenant test; `pnpm test:tenancy` fails if one is unregistered)
13. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (add required job `tenancy` running `pnpm test:tenancy` and `pnpm db:check-rls`)
14. `apps/web/lib/with-workspace-action.ts` and `apps/api/src/middleware/workspace.ts` updates (use `withWorkspace` for every request that carries workspace context)
15. `docs/engineering/tenancy.md` (how to add a tenant table, GUC semantics, role model, why FORCE RLS, what is global)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every table with a `workspace_id` column has `ENABLE` and `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and a `ws_isolation` policy; `pnpm db:check-rls` fails on a fixture table that lacks either [type:unit]
- [ ] As `causedeck_app`, inside `withWorkspace(A)`, `select * from member` returns only A's rows; inside `withWorkspace(B)` only B's; with no GUC set it returns zero rows [type:unit]
- [ ] `INSERT`/`UPDATE` that sets `workspace_id` to another workspace fails the `WITH CHECK`; `UPDATE ... SET workspace_id` to move a row between workspaces is rejected [type:unit]
- [ ] The app role is not the table owner and cannot `ALTER`, `DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` or `SET ROLE` to the owner; a test attempts each and expects permission errors [type:unit]
- [ ] `withWorkspace` uses `SET LOCAL` semantics (`set_config(..., true)`), so a pooled connection reused for a later transaction without the helper sees no workspace (pooling test with `max: 1`) [type:unit]
- [ ] `withWorkspace` validates the uuid, rejects empty/invalid ids, and nested calls with a different workspace throw `TENANCY_VIOLATION` [type:unit]
- [ ] A user belonging to workspaces A and B can act in each but a single transaction never mixes both; switching requires a new `withWorkspace` call; tested with `uboth` [type:unit]
- [ ] Cross-tenant suite covers: SQL (all tenant tables), every `packages/core` service, server actions, REST API routes, storage presign (once #21 exists; the registry fails CI if a storage presign test is missing then), and vector search [type:api]
- [ ] The cross-tenant registry fails the build when a new tenant table or exported core service is added without a registered cross-tenant test [type:unit]
- [ ] The suite runs as a required CI job named `tenancy` in under 4 minutes and blocks merge on failure [type:manual]
- [ ] No foreign key may reference a tenant table without including `workspace_id` in a composite key (checker extended from #6) so cross-workspace FKs are impossible [type:unit]
- [ ] Admin/global code paths use `withoutWorkspace` only for allow-listed global tables; a lint rule bans importing it outside `packages/db`, `apps/admin` and migrations [type:unit]
- [ ] Migration order is safe: policies are applied in the same migration that creates a tenant table (helper `tenantTable`), verified by a test that creates a table through the helper and checks policies exist [type:unit]

## Context
**Parent**: #1
- Spec: spike §4.1, §10; architecture §6.3 (Isolation assurance: automated cross-tenant tests in CI: SQL, REST, sync, storage, vector search); PRD PL-1.
- Policy template (Postgres): `ALTER TABLE x ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE x FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY ws_isolation ON x USING (workspace_id = nullif(current_setting('app.workspace_id', true),'')::uuid) WITH CHECK (workspace_id = nullif(current_setting('app.workspace_id', true),'')::uuid);`
- `workspace` and `member` need bootstrap rules: listing the caller's workspaces uses `app.user_id` with a dedicated policy `member_self` (`user_id = app.user_id`) for `member` so the switcher can work before a workspace is selected; document it carefully and test it.
- Column-scoped views for the clerk role (strategy notes and memory) are implemented in #20/later milestones; this issue provides the mechanism and registry.
- Security: any failure of this suite is a release blocker; record in `docs/engineering/tenancy.md` the incident procedure link (DPDP breach runbook, Production Infra).
- Credentials: none.
- Out of scope: permission policy `can()` (#20), storage presign implementation (#21), audit writer (#26), per-domain table creation (later milestones, each using `tenantTable`).

- **Out of scope**: `can()` policy (#20), storage implementation (#21), audit (#26), domain tables.

## Dependencies
Depends on #6 — Drizzle conventions, role model and Testcontainers harness
Depends on #18 — workspace, member and invitation tables that the first policies and fixtures apply to

items.title: bug(db): a transaction is held open across model calls while the budget guard opens a second connection; with the default pool (5+10) concurrent turns starve each other

labels.name: type:bug
labels.description: Something doesn't work the way it should

items.body:
## Summary
get_engine() uses create_engine(url, pool_pre_ping=True): QueuePool size 5, overflow 10, pool_timeout 30 s. Agent.handle holds one pooled connection for the whole turn (the with session_scope() block spans every LLM call), and every LLM call goes through BudgetGuard.reserve/settle/fail, each opening a new session_scope, i.e. a second connection. Job handlers (learn, triage, digest) do the same. ADR text for ingest says 'no transaction stays open during the call', but the chat path does the opposite.

## Area
backend: API, pipeline, database, migrations

## Severity
Medium

## How it was found
Code review (read-only, no browser run). Found by reading the code; **not reproduced**, so treat as likely.  
Version: `bd4bdb3` (main)

## Where
- `backend/src/superaide/db/session.py:20`
- `backend/src/superaide/pipeline.py:110`
- `backend/src/superaide/brain/budget.py:243-247`
- `backend/src/superaide/jobs/queue.py:117-122`

## Scenario
15 simultaneous turns (webhook BackgroundTasks run on a 40-thread pool, plus chat requests and jobs) each hold a connection and each wait for a 16th for reserve(). All block until pool_timeout (30 s) and then raise QueuePool TimeoutError; combined with BE-02 the messages are silently lost.

## Evidence
```
return create_engine(url or get_settings().database_url, pool_pre_ping=True)   vs   with use_instance(self.scope), session_scope(self.db_url) as s:  (reserve)
```

## Suggested fix
Do not hold the handle() session across llm.step: commit/close before the model phase (as ingest does), or size the pool and cap concurrent turns with a semaphore smaller than pool_size; set an explicit pool_size/max_overflow/pool_timeout from settings.

## Failing test
None yet. Per `CLAUDE.md`, add a failing test first (`test.fail(true, 'BUG: …')` or `xfail(strict=True)`), then the fix, and commit both together.

## Privacy
No owner data in this report.

_Found by a read-only code review (October 2026); checked against `docs/test-findings.md` and issues #12 to #68._

items.title: Proposal: redesign the Client implementation for composability
items.body:
​#Transport & Extensibility Rewrite — Design Principles

> **Status:** Draft. Principles are proposed, not committed. The one settled
> decision is recorded in [Deferred — the redirect model](#deferred--the-redirect-model).
> **Owners:** @akashsinghal
> **Scope:** `OrasProject.Oras.Registry.Remote` and `.Auth` — the HTTP transport
> and extensibility layer.

## What this document is and is not

**This is not an authentication redesign.** The auth *protocol* behaviour —
challenge discovery, basic/bearer/OAuth2 flows, realm validation, scope
semantics — is carried forward unchanged. We are moving it, not rewriting it.

This document is about the **plumbing**: how the SDK is composed, what a
consumer has to construct, and what a consumer can extend without forking us.

| Aspect | In scope | Out of scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auth protocol (challenge, bearer, OAuth2, realm rules) | — | ✅ unchanged |
| How the SDK is composed (handlers, `HttpClient`, DI) | ✅ | — |
| Who owns auth *state* (scopes, token cache, partitioning) | ✅ | — |
| Where credentials come from (provider → keychain) | ✅ *plumbing only* | ✅ the keychain itself |

The last row matters most. We are **not** building a keychain now. We are making
sure that when we do ([P5](#p5--credential-resolution-is-keychain-ready)), it is
a drop-in against a stable seam rather than another change to a 1,340-line class.

---

## Table of contents

- [Part 1 — How it works today](#part-1--how-it-works-today)
- [Part 2 — Why it fails, from the consumer's side](#part-2--why-it-fails-from-the-consumers-side)
- [Part 3 — The composition rule](#part-3--the-composition-rule)
- [Part 4 — Principles](#part-4--principles)
- [Part 5 — Target shape](#part-5--target-shape)
- [Migration requirements](#migration-requirements)
- [What we explicitly keep](#what-we-explicitly-keep)
- [Deferred — the redirect model](#deferred--the-redirect-model)
- [Non-goals](#non-goals)
- [Open questions](#open-questions)
- [Evidence appendix](#evidence-appendix)

---

# Part 1 — How it works today

## 1.1 The object model

```text
  Repository / Registry  ──►  BlobStore, ManifestStore
                                      │
                                      ▼
        IClient.SendAsync(request, partitionId, allowAutoRedirect, ct)
                                      │
                  ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐
                  ▼                                       ▼
        Auth.Client (1,340 lines)                PlainClient (no auth)
          ICredentialProvider · IAccessTokenProvider
          ICache · IRealmValidator · ScopeManager
                  │                                       │
                  └───────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                      ▼
           HttpClient (follows redirects) · HttpClient (no redirects)
```

The load-bearing type is `IClient`, a single-method interface:

```csharp
Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(
    HttpRequestMessage originalRequest,
    string? partitionId = null,
    bool allowAutoRedirect = true,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
```

That signature is the source of much of [Part 2](#part-2--why-it-fails-from-the-consumers-side):
two transport concerns are positional parameters, so they propagate to every
caller.

## 1.2 What `Auth.Client` does

One class, **1,340 lines**: challenge discovery · scheme caching · basic auth ·
bearer auth · OAuth2 exchange · scope accumulation · token caching · user-agent
injection · redirect selection · request body buffering.

Environment-specific behaviour is injected as strategy interfaces —
`ICredentialProvider`, `IAccessTokenProvider`, `ICache`, `IRealmValidator` —
plus a `ScopeManager` property. **Those interfaces are good and survive the
rewrite.** The problem is the container they live in.

## 1.3 What a request actually does

One `GET` of a manifest, cold cache:

1. `ManifestStore` builds the request and calls `IClient.SendAsync(...)`.
2. `Auth.Client` looks up the cached scheme, keyed `{partitionId}|{registry}`.
3. It asks `ScopeManager` for scopes for that same `(partitionId, registry)`.
4. Miss → send unauthenticated → `401` → parse `WWW-Authenticate` → validate the
   realm.
5. Resolve a credential, exchange it at the token endpoint, cache the token.
6. Replay the original request — having buffered the body up to **4 MiB** so
   replay is possible.

Steps 2 and 3 are the detail that matters: **the token cache and the scope
manager are separate structures that independently compute the same composite
key**, coupled only by a comment saying one "mirrors" the other.

## 1.4 What a consumer writes today

The shipped ACR example, copying between two registries:

```csharp
using var httpClient = new HttpClient();

var srcRepository = new Repository(new RepositoryOptions
{
    Reference = Reference.Parse("mysourceregistry.azurecr.io/myimage"),
    Client = new Client(httpClient,
        credentialProvider: new AzureCredentialProvider("mysourceregistry.azurecr.io")),
});

var dstRepository = new Repository(new RepositoryOptions
{
    Reference = Reference.Parse("mydestinationregistry.azurecr.io/myimage"),
    Client = new Client(httpClient,
        credentialProvider: new AzureCredentialProvider("mydestinationregistry.azurecr.io")),
});

await srcRepository.CopyAsync("v1.1.0", dstRepository, "v1", cancellationToken);
```

The consumer is required to know that credential providers are effectively
per-registry, that each registry therefore needs its own `Client`, and —
implicitly — that each `Client` carries its own token cache and scope state.

---

# Part 2 — Why it fails, from the consumer's side

Each failure is stated as something a consumer wants to do. That is the bar: not
"the class is large", but "the SDK cannot be extended without forking".

## Scenario A — "Registry throttling is flaky; I want retries on 429/503"

Not possible through the SDK. There is **no retry logic anywhere in `src/`**,
and no seam to add it. The options are: wrap every ORAS call site in your own
loop (but `CopyAsync` is multi-request, so you retry the whole graph copy
instead of the one failed blob); or pass an `HttpClient` with your own handler
(but `Auth.Client` holds *two* clients, and its own 401 retry sits above yours,
so attempts multiply unbounded); or fork.

## Scenario B — "I need to log/trace every registry request for support tickets"

Not possible. There is **no `ILogger`, `ActivitySource`, or `EventSource`
anywhere in `src/`**. You can attach a handler to the `HttpClient` you pass in,
but you will not see auth decisions — cache hit/miss, challenge parsed, refresh
triggered — because those never cross a public boundary. When auth fails in
production, the diagnostic path is reading a 1,340-line method by eye.

## Scenario C — "I use DI and `IHttpClientFactory` like every other .NET service"

Partially defeated. `IHttpClientFactory` appears in this codebase **only inside
XML doc comments**. `Auth.Client` takes `HttpClient` instances directly and
holds a static lazy singleton pair as the default. Getting consistent
timeouts/proxy/TLS means constructing and passing two clients with matching
configuration but different redirect settings — a requirement the docs explain
and the type system does not enforce.

## Scenario D — "I'm copying between two registries"

Two `ICredentialProvider`s, two `Client`s, two token caches, two scope managers,
as [§1.4](#14-what-a-consumer-writes-today) shows. Nothing is shared, and
nothing tells you it isn't. `SingleRegistryCredentialProvider`, the only
built-in provider, is single-registry and static by construction.

This is the shape a **keychain** exists to fix: one credential source resolving
*any* registry, so one client can serve the whole operation.

## Scenario E — "I'm multi-tenant; each customer has different upstream creds"

You thread a `partitionId` string through the SDK by hand:

```csharp
var repo = new Repository(new RepositoryOptions
{
    Reference = reference, Client = client,
    PartitionId = customerId,          // (1) here
});

ScopeManager.SetActionsForRepository(
    client, reference, customerId,     // (2) and here — must match (1)
    Scope.Action.Pull);
```

Two independent places, no enforcement that they agree. Get it wrong and there
is no error — you get **silent cross-tenant cache behaviour, or a mysteriously
under-scoped token**. Internally the same `partitionId` is threaded through
**16+ call sites** in `BlobStore`, `ManifestStore`, and `Repository`.

The consumer is being made responsible for keeping two *internal* data
structures consistent. That is the SDK's job.

## Scenario F — "I want to pre-register scopes so I get one token, not a 401 per repo"

The entry point is a **static method that silently does nothing** if handed the
wrong client:

```csharp
public static void SetActionsForRepository(
    IClient client, Reference reference, string? partitionId, params Scope.Action[] actions)
{
    if (client is Client authClient)   // <-- PlainClient? decorator? test double? ignored
    {
        authClient.ScopeManager.SetActionsForRepository(reference, partitionId, actions);
    }
}
```

The signature promises something the implementation may decline to do, with no
diagnostic.

## Scenario G — "I want to plug in a docker-config / chained credential source"

`ICredentialProvider` is *shaped* correctly (`hostname → Credential`), but there
is no chaining primitive, no default keychain, and — critically — credential
resolution is **fused with token exchange** inside `FetchBearerAuthAsync`.
Introducing a keychain means editing the god class and its five constructor
overloads rather than substituting one component.

## Scenario H — "I just want to call `GetBlobLocationAsync` with my own `HttpClient`"

You must supply **two** `HttpClient`s — one following redirects, one not — with
otherwise identical configuration, because `AllowAutoRedirect` is a property of
the *primary handler*, not of a request. That means a second connection pool.

The trap is that it *appears* to work: the shipped example passes a single
client and succeeds, because the unsupplied no-redirect client silently falls
back to an internal singleton — **discarding that consumer's proxy and TLS
settings for this one API**. The failure surfaces only when you supply your own
no-redirect client, as a runtime `ArgumentException` inferred from a URI
comparison, telling you to go reconfigure transport plumbing.

The constraint has leaked into the public interface contract:

```csharp
/// <exception cref="ArgumentException">
/// Thrown when the provided HttpClient has AllowAutoRedirect enabled</exception>
Task<Uri?> GetBlobLocationAsync(Descriptor target, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
```

`IBlobLocationProvider` is an abstraction over *blob location retrieval*. It
should not know that `HttpClient` exists, let alone how one must be configured.

The redirect model has since been decided; see
[Deferred — the redirect model](#deferred--the-redirect-model).

## Three root causes

- **Scenarios A–C — no middleware seam.** Nothing can be added without forking.
- **Scenarios D–G — auth state and credential resolution have no coherent
  owner**, so the consumer is handed the coordination problem.
- **Scenario H — transport configuration leaked into the public API contract**,
  because the SDK had no way to express a per-request transport policy.

---

# Part 3 — The composition rule

This rule decides the shape of the rewrite.

> **Two concerns belong in one handler if and only if one needs to know what the
> other did on a previous attempt. Otherwise they are separate handlers.**

## The test

1. Can each concern decide what to do from the current request/response plus its
   own configuration?
2. Does either need to know what the other *did on a previous attempt* — that
   is, do they share mutable per-attempt state?

(1) yes and (2) no → **separate handlers.** (2) yes → **one handler.**

**Ordering constraints are not part of the test.** Separate handlers routinely
have required positions: logging must be innermost to see every physical attempt
([P9](#p9--observability-is-a-layer-and-every-physical-attempt-is-visible)), and
transport retry must sit outside auth
([P10](#p10--retry-responsibility-is-layered-and-non-multiplying)). A fixed
order is normal. Hidden shared state is the problem.

## Applying it

| Concern | Shares per-attempt state? | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retry on 429/5xx | No — reads the response status | Own handler |
| User-agent | No — stamps a header | Own handler |
| Logging | No — observes | Own handler |
| Attach credential | **Yes**, with 401 recovery | \} one handler |
| Recover from 401 | **Yes** — needs to know *which* credential the last attempt used and where it came from | \} one handler |

"Attach a credential" and "recover from a 401" are a single feedback loop: the
recovery decision depends on what the attach step did (cached token? fresh one?
none?), and the attach step's next action depends on what recovery decided.

## Why this matters

We prototyped the alternative — attach and recover as two handlers — and it
required an `AsyncLocal` ambient context to reconnect them, because the retry
sends a *cloned* request that discards anything written on the original.

That ambient channel costs real safety:

- The credential handler throws `InvalidOperationException` if used in any other
  pipeline — a dependency appearing in **no constructor and no signature**.
- Under `ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow()` the state silently vanishes and the
  pipeline fails deep in the stack.

And it buys nothing: the two stages can never be used independently, which is
the only thing separate handlers are *for*.

> **The tell:** if two handlers need to share mutable per-attempt state, they are
> one handler. Decompose into collaborating **objects** inside it — you keep the
> testability, and the dependency stays visible in a constructor.

For fairness, one common objection to `AsyncLocal` does **not** apply: its
isolation across concurrent operations is sound. The objection is invisible
coupling, not concurrency.

---

# Part 4 — Principles

Format: **Principle** / **Problem today** / **What changes** / **Done when** (an
observable check). "Problem today" links to the scenario rather than restating it.

### Group A — Composition

#### P0 — ORAS is additive: we never override consumer configuration

**Principle.** Everything ORAS contributes to the HTTP stack is **additive**. We
add handlers; we do not mutate, replace, or reconfigure anything the consumer
built. If a capability can only be delivered by overriding a consumer's setting,
it must be redesigned — or not shipped. **This governs every other principle
here.**

**Why it is load-bearing.** Consumer-supplied transport is opaque by
construction: `HttpClient` exposes no public accessor for its primary handler,
`DelegatingHandler`s never observe a `3xx` when `AllowAutoRedirect = true`, and
the property throws if mutated after first use. An "override" would therefore
have to be reflection, or a DI-time `IHttpMessageHandlerBuilderFilter` silently
reversing an explicit consumer choice. Both are action-at-a-distance; both are
rejected.

**Done when.** No ORAS code path reads, writes, or reflects over a
consumer-supplied handler's configuration.

#### P1 — Cross-cutting HTTP concerns use the framework's middleware primitive

**Principle.** Retry, logging, user-agent, and auth are cross-cutting HTTP
concerns. .NET has one idiomatic primitive: `DelegatingHandler` composed into an
`HttpClient`, ideally via `IHttpClientFactory`. We use it rather than inventing
our own.

**Problem today.** `IClient.SendAsync` re-invents `HttpMessageHandler.SendAsync`
with a bespoke signature, and no `DelegatingHandler` exists in `src/`. With no
composition point, Scenarios A–C are unsolvable without forking.

**What changes.** `IClient` and `PlainClient` are deleted. Stores talk to
`HttpClient` directly, with ORAS's handlers composed onto whatever the consumer
supplied. "No auth" stops being a separate class and becomes "the pipeline
without the auth handler".

**Done when.** A consumer adds retry and logging through standard .NET
registration, with zero SDK changes.

#### P2 — Every component is independently constructible

**Principle.** A component's dependencies appear in its constructor.
Constructing it correctly is sufficient to use it. No component may require
another to have run earlier in the same async flow.

**Problem today.** The monolith avoids this by being monolithic; the risk is
introduced by the rewrite. See [Part 3](#part-3--the-composition-rule) for the
failure modes an ambient context produces.

**What changes.** No ambient context. Where per-attempt state must cross a
boundary, it is an explicit object in `HttpRequestMessage.Options`
([P3](#p3--per-request-policy-travels-with-the-request)).

**Done when.** Every handler is unit-testable standalone with a stub inner
handler and no setup ritual.

### Group B — Consumer surface

#### P3 — Per-request policy travels with the request

**Principle.** Per-request policy belongs in `HttpRequestMessage.Options`, not
in bespoke method signatures and not in ambient state.

**Problem today.** Scenario E. `partitionId` is a positional parameter on
`IClient.SendAsync`, threaded through **16+ call sites** in storage classes that
should know nothing about token caching.

**What changes.** `HttpRequestOptionsKey<T>` entries replace the bespoke
parameters. A mutable reference-type object placed in `Options` survives
request-clone-on-retry — every clone references the same object — provided the
cloner preserves `Options`, which
[P8](#p8--request-replay-is-one-audited-utility-with-an-explicit-contract) makes
a contract.

`allowAutoRedirect` is **not** included: it selects a client, not a request
policy — see [Deferred — the redirect model](#deferred--the-redirect-model).

**Done when.** No auth or caching concept appears in any `BlobStore` /
`ManifestStore` / `Repository` method signature.

#### P4 — Scope state and the token cache are one unit with one owner

**Principle.** Scopes and cached tokens are two projections of one thing: *the
authorization state for an identity at a registry*. They must be modelled,
configured, and handed to the SDK as a **single unit**. A consumer should never
be responsible for keeping them consistent.

**Problem today.** Scenarios E and F. They are two independent structures that
each recompute the same composite key:

- `Cache.GetCacheKey(registry, partitionId)` → `{partitionId}|{registry}`
- `ScopeManager.GetScopeKey(registry, partitionId)` → `{partitionId}|{registry}`

**What changes.** One owning abstraction — working name **`AuthSession`** —
encapsulating scope state, token cache, and the partition dimension behind a
single key computed **once, internally**. `partitionId` becomes an internal
dimension, not a threaded parameter. Scope registration becomes an instance
method on it, not a static that may decline to act.

**Done when.** `partitionId` appears in no public method signature outside
constructing the session, and it is impossible to register a scope against a
different partition than the token will be cached under.

> This is the one place the rewrite deliberately changes an auth-adjacent public
> surface. It is in scope because it is a state-ownership and ergonomics
> problem, not an auth-protocol change.

#### P5 — Credential resolution is keychain-ready

**Principle.** The credential-resolution seam must be swappable **without
touching the pipeline**. When we later adopt a keychain (as in crane's
`authn.Keychain`), it must be a new implementation behind an existing seam.

**Problem today.** Scenarios D and G. `ICredentialProvider` is already
keychain-*shaped*, but the only built-in implementation is single-registry and
static, there is no chaining primitive or default source, and resolution is
fused with token exchange inside `FetchBearerAuthAsync`.

**What changes** — plumbing only; we are not building the keychain now:

1. The auth handler resolves credentials **per request, from the target host**,
   never from a client-wide assumption of one registry.
2. Credential *resolution* is separated from token *exchange*.
3. The [P4](#p4--scope-state-and-the-token-cache-are-one-unit-with-one-owner)
   session is keyed so one pipeline can serve many registries and identities
   concurrently.
4. No API is added now that would have to be broken to introduce a chained or
   resource-scoped resolver later.

**Done when.** One pipeline performs a cross-registry copy with one credential
source, and a prototype keychain can be added as one class and one registration
change, touching no handler.

> P4 and P5 are the same design pressure from two sides. One client serving many
> registries and identities is only coherent if auth state has a single owner
> with an internal key. Solve them together or neither works.

### Group C — Correctness and operability

#### P6 — Authenticate before the body

**Principle.** Credentials are resolved **before** a request body is streamed.
Recovering from a `401` must never require replaying a large body, and we never
buffer unbounded content to make a retry possible.

**Problem today.** More careful than it first appears:
`BufferNonSeekableContentAsync` caps buffering at **4 MiB**, skips buffering
over that, and relies on seek-rewind. The code states the residual gap itself —
*"the first send proceeds but a 401 retry would fail because the body cannot be
replayed."* So a token expiring mid-push of a non-seekable, >4 MiB layer is
unrecoverable. The design treats `401`-after-body as normal when it should be
exceptional.

**What changes.** Challenge/scheme discovery becomes an explicit, host-level,
cached step so body-bearing requests go out already credentialed;
`Expect: 100-continue` on large uploads; bounded buffering retained, failing
explicitly rather than confusingly.

**Done when.** A non-seekable stream larger than the buffer cap survives a
registry that `401`s once.

#### P7 — Token acquisition is single-flight

**Principle.** Concurrent requests needing the same token trigger **one** fetch,
coalesced on the session key.

**Problem today.** `ICache` exposes `TryGetToken` / `SetCache` — check-then-act
with no atomic get-or-add. A concurrent `CopyGraph` over N blobs on a cold cache
issues N identical token requests.

**What changes.** The interface gains an async get-or-add-with-factory shape.
**Breaking change to `ICache`, and it interacts with
[P4](#p4--scope-state-and-the-token-cache-are-one-unit-with-one-owner) — decide
both early.**

**Done when.** 50 concurrent requests on a cold cache call the token endpoint
exactly once.

#### P8 — Request replay is one audited utility with an explicit contract

**Principle.** Cloning/rewinding a request for replay is implemented **once**.
Contract: preserve method, URI, request headers, **content headers**, and
**`Options`**; rewind rather than re-buffer.

**Problem today.** No shared utility, because only one place needs replay. The
rewrite adds a second (retry), so settle it first. Hand-rolled cloning is
error-prone: our prototype's clone silently dropped `Accept` and `Content-Type`,
which breaks manifest content negotiation and every manifest `PUT`.

**Done when.** A test asserts a replayed request is header-for-header identical
to the original, including content headers and `Options`.

#### P9 — Observability is a layer, and every physical attempt is visible

**Principle.** Every request actually put on the wire — including auth and
transport retries — is observable, with credentials redacted. The logging
handler sits **innermost**, adjacent to the wire, so it records each physical
attempt rather than one merged logical operation. The auth handler additionally
emits structured events for its internal decisions.

**Problem today.** Scenario B.

**Done when.** A failed push produces a trace showing every attempt, its status,
and the auth decision behind it, with no token material.

#### P10 — Retry responsibility is layered and non-multiplying

**Principle.** Auth owns `401`. Transport retry owns `429`/`5xx`/network faults
and must never retry `401`. Auth recovery is bounded and sits strictly inside
transport retry.

**Problem today.** Scenario A — no transport retry exists, so there is no
layering to get wrong, and no resilience. The moment retry is added above an
auth handler that retries internally, attempts multiply (N × M) unless the
contract is explicit.

**Done when.** A test asserts the exact request count for a `401`-then-`503`
sequence.

---

# Part 5 — Target shape

Working sketch — subject to revision as principles are debated. Applies to each
client the consumer supplies; the redirect / no-redirect pair is retained per
[Deferred — the redirect model](#deferred--the-redirect-model).

```text
HttpClient  (consumer's, or IHttpClientFactory)                         [P0]
  └─ RetryHandler              429/5xx/network only — never 401         [P10]
      └─ UserAgentHandler
          └─ AuthenticationHandler                                   [Part 3]
          │     ONE handler: attach + recover share a feedback loop
          │     collaborators (objects, NOT handlers):
          │       ChallengeResolver   host-level ping + scheme cache     [P6]
          │       AuthSession         scope + token cache + partition,
          │                           one internal key                  [P4]
          │       TokenSource         single-flight on the session key   [P7]
          │       ICredentialProvider resolved per-request by host       [P5]
          │       IAccessTokenProvider / IRealmValidator
              └─ LoggingHandler       innermost: every physical attempt  [P9]
                  └─ (consumer's primary handler — untouched)            [P0]

shared utility:  RequestReplay — rewind + full clone incl. headers,
                 content headers, and Options                            [P8]
```

Every handler is **added** to what the consumer already has. ORAS never replaces
or reconfigures the primary handler.

---

## Migration requirements

Not an architecture principle, but a hard delivery requirement: every removed or
changed public API ships with a documented equivalent and a working example. A
consumer must be able to find "what I wrote before → what I write now" without
reading a diff.

The affected surface is real and in use: `IClient`, `PlainClient`, `Client`'s
five constructor overloads, `ScopeManager` statics, `RepositoryOptions.PartitionId`
— including by the shipped `examples/`.

1. A **before/after equivalency table** covering every removed or changed member.
2. The existing examples (`.Azure`, `.ExternalTokenBroker`, `.RealmValidation`)
   are migrated and **kept compiling** — executable proof the off-ramp works.
3. Each scenario in [Part 2](#part-2--why-it-fails-from-the-consumers-side) gets
   a short "how you do this now" entry.
4. A decision on whether a thin `IClient` shim ships for one release
   ([Open questions](#open-questions) #1).

**Done when.** Every example in `examples/` compiles against the new API and the
equivalency table has no "TBD" rows.

---

## What we explicitly keep

The rewrite targets the *container*, not these:

| Asset | Why it survives |
| --- | --- |
| `ICredentialProvider`, `IAccessTokenProvider`, `ICache`, `IRealmValidator` | The correct seams for what varies by environment. `IAccessTokenProvider` (external token service, no raw credentials in-process) has no go-containerregistry equivalent. |
| `ScopeManager`'s internals | Already thread-safe: `ConcurrentDictionary` + copy-on-write with cloned sets. [P4](#p4--scope-state-and-the-token-cache-are-one-unit-with-one-owner) changes its *ownership and entry points*, not its concurrency design. Do not "fix" it. |
| Spec-correct challenge/scope parsing | `TryReadNextScope` is correct today and must not regress to naive parsing. Pin with tests: `scope="repo:app:pull,push"` must not truncate to `pull`; multiple challenges (`Basic` **and** `Bearer`) must all be considered; a challenge with no `scope` is legal (`GET /v2/`), not malformed. |
| Lazy, per-request auth with a shared host+scope cache | Better than go-containerregistry's per-repo transport with no shared cache, for a long-lived multi-registry client. |
| Partition-aware caching | A real multi-tenant requirement. Only its plumbing changes ([P4](#p4--scope-state-and-the-token-cache-are-one-unit-with-one-owner)). |
| Realm validation as an injectable policy | SSRF protection that go-containerregistry hardcodes; ours is pluggable. |
| Bounded (never unbounded) body buffering | The 4 MiB cap and seek-rewind are the right instincts. |
| Idempotency gating on replay | Never speculatively replay a mutating request. |

---

## Deferred — the redirect model

**Decision (2026-07-28): the existing two-client model is retained.** Consumers
continue to supply a redirect-following client and a no-redirect client. No
redirect work is in scope for this rewrite.

**Why it cannot be solved cheaply.** `AllowAutoRedirect` lives on the **primary
handler** — the one layer that can neither vary per request nor be shared
between two differing pipelines. A redirect / no-redirect split therefore
*necessarily* costs a second connection pool. That is the price of this model,
not an implementation defect.

**Alternatives considered and rejected:**

| Alternative | Why rejected |
| --- | --- |
| Override the consumer's redirect setting (directly or via `IHttpMessageHandlerBuilderFilter`) | Violates [P0](#p0--oras-is-additive-we-never-override-consumer-configuration). Also impossible to do safely: the primary handler is not reachable from an `HttpClient`, and the property throws once used. |
| Reconfigure redirect behaviour per operation | Corrupts concurrent operations sharing the client, and throws after the first request. |
| Derive the location from the response instead of suppressing the redirect | Works, but when redirects are followed it costs an extra request to storage and prevents connection reuse. Also fails outright for callers whose host cannot reach storage. |
| ORAS ships its own redirect handler and requires `AllowAutoRedirect = false` | Viable, but means re-implementing hop bounds, relative `Location`, `303`/`301`/`302` method rewriting, and `307`/`308` body preservation — behaviour the framework already gets right. |

**Mitigations available without changing the model:**

- Create the no-redirect client **lazily** on first `GetBlobLocationAsync`, so
  applications that never call it never pay for a second pool.
- Stop silently substituting an internal singleton when the consumer supplied
  only one client — today that discards their proxy and TLS settings for this
  one API (Scenario H).

---

## Non-goals

- **Not an auth protocol redesign.** Challenge, bearer, OAuth2, and realm
  semantics carry over unchanged.
- **Not building the keychain.** [P5](#p5--credential-resolution-is-keychain-ready)
  only guarantees it will be a drop-in later.
- **Not a redirect redesign.** See [Deferred](#deferred--the-redirect-model).
- No changes to OCI content, graph, copy, or referrers semantics.
- No new external dependencies beyond a resilience library for
  [P10](#p10--retry-responsibility-is-layered-and-non-multiplying), and only if
  justified.
- Not a mechanical port of go-containerregistry. We borrow its composition model
  and keychain direction, not its per-repo transport or its lack of a shared
  token cache.

---

## Open questions

1. **Public API break.** Deleting `IClient` / `PlainClient` is breaking. Major
   version, or a thin adapter for one release?
2. **`AuthSession` shape.** What exactly does the consumer construct in
   [P4](#p4--scope-state-and-the-token-cache-are-one-unit-with-one-owner)? Does
   it subsume `ICache`, or own one?
3. **`ICache` shape.** [P7](#p7--token-acquisition-is-single-flight) needs an
   atomic async get-or-add. New interface, or v2 of `ICache`? Interacts with (2).
4. **Keychain interface preview.** Sketch the target keychain API now to
   validate [P5](#p5--credential-resolution-is-keychain-ready)'s seam, even
   though we won't implement it?
5. **Ping cost.** [P6](#p6--authenticate-before-the-body) adds one round trip per
   registry per process. Acceptable? Skippable on a warm challenge cache?
6. **Resilience library.** Polly, or hand-rolled? Polly is a new dependency
   against our "avoid new dependencies" policy.
7. **Migration order.** Can handlers land incrementally behind the existing
   `IClient` facade, or does this need one atomic change?
8. **`Expect: 100-continue` compatibility.** Interacts badly with some proxies.
   Opt-in per registry, or always on for large uploads?

---

## Evidence appendix

Claims verified rather than assumed. Source-code rows cite the repository.
Rows marked *(harness)* were measured in a scratch console app against a live
local server; those harnesses were not preserved and should be re-created if a
claim needs re-checking.

| Claim | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| `Auth.Client` is 1,340 lines | `src/.../Auth/Client.cs` |
| No `DelegatingHandler` in `src/`; `IHttpClientFactory` only in doc comments | Repo-wide grep — matches only `Client.cs:99`, `PlainClient.cs:55` |
| No transport retry exists | Repo-wide grep `retry\|backoff\|transient` — only 401-path comments |
| No `ILogger` / `ActivitySource` / `EventSource` in `src/` | Repo-wide grep — zero matches |
| `partitionId` threaded through storage classes | 16+ call sites in `BlobStore.cs`, `ManifestStore.cs`, `Repository.cs` |
| Token cache and scope manager compute the same composite key separately | `Cache.cs:70-73`, `ScopeManager.cs:42-43` |
| `SetActionsForRepository` silently no-ops on a non-`Auth.Client` | `ScopeManager.cs:92-100` |
| Consumers build one client per registry | `examples/.../AzureContainerRegistryAuthentication.cs` |
| Only built-in provider is single-registry and static | `SingleRegistryCredentialProvider.cs` |
| Body buffering capped at 4 MiB with a documented replay gap | `Client.cs:258`, `Client.cs:1284-1340` |
| `ScopeManager` is thread-safe via copy-on-write | `ScopeManager.cs:30, 169-179` |
| Two singleton `HttpClient`s for redirect control | `DefaultHttpClient.cs:26-41` |
| A single supplied `HttpClient` is silently bypassed for `GetBlobLocationAsync` | `Client.cs:158-159` — `noRedirectHttpClient ?? DefaultHttpClient.NoRedirectInstance` |
| `GetBlobLocationAsync` infers redirect-following by URI comparison and throws | `BlobStore.cs:305-315`; constraint leaked into `IBlobLocationProvider` |
| A consumer's redirect policy cannot be read, observed, or overridden | *(harness)* no public member exposes the primary handler; a `DelegatingHandler` never sees the `302` when `AllowAutoRedirect = true`; mutation after first use throws `InvalidOperationException` |
| Reconfiguring redirect behaviour per operation corrupts concurrent operations | *(harness)* one mutation broke 100/100 in-flight location calls |
| Deriving location from the response works but is not free | *(harness)* correct across `302`/`200` × redirect on/off; on a 64 MiB blob the follow path cost 1 storage request, ~192 KiB, 105 ms vs 0 / 0 KiB / 3 ms |
| .NET strips `Authorization` on all auto-redirects | `SocketsHttpHandler.AllowAutoRedirect` documentation |
| `Options` survive request clones when the cloner preserves them | *(harness)* inner-handler mutation read back by the outer handler after a clone |
| `AsyncLocal` breaks under `SuppressFlow`, but its concurrency isolation is sound | *(harness)* inner observes `null` under `SuppressFlow`; 50 concurrent ops with 0 cross-contamination |
| Naive challenge parsing truncates `pull,push` and drops headers on clone | *(harness)* `Split(',')` on `scope="repo:app:pull,push"`; hand-rolled clone lost `Accept` and `Content-Type` |

items.title: Hypothesis 1: experience cards as evidence, not rules
items.body:
## What this is

A product hypothesis we can implement as a small, isolated script pack and then measure.

It does **not** touch Architecture v2, Google Memory Bank, the DSPy compiler, OpenSpec components, or the M1–M3 lab pipeline. Those keep running. This is a standalone slice: chat in → card out → later agent sees a recommendation.

Spec (arriving in a follow-up PR): `standalone/h1-experience-cards/`.

---

## The business picture

A shop runs several customer-facing agents. Customers are mostly anonymous. What one agent learns dies when the chat closes. The next agent, on another channel, solves the same jam from scratch.

Hypothesis 1: after each closed chat we extract a short **experience card** and, if it earns the right, show it to the next agent as **evidence** (“this has worked when the request looked like this”), never as a **rule** (“always do this”).

### Walkthrough

Customer to Agent A: *ordered size 42, got 41, want an exchange, tag already cut off.*

Policy blocks exchanges without a tag. Agent A finds a workaround: photo of the defect + order id → warehouse accepts it as a defect, not a change-of-mind. Chat ends.

We do **not** keep the transcript as memory. We keep a card:

- **problem_shape** — exchange, wrong size, tag missing
- **constraint** — no-tag exchange is closed by policy
- **unlock** — reclassify as defect when photo + order id exist
- **what_worked** — the steps that actually ran
- **receipt** — source chat, agent/tenant, time, allowed scope (this shop / this vertical)

No customer identity on the card.

Next day a different customer asks Agent B the same shape of question. Agent B does not get an order. It gets a packet:

> Similar cases in this shop: exchange without a tag is blocked. One workaround that worked: reclassify as defect with photo + order id. This is not policy. Check the current warehouse rule first.

Money movement, account changes, and PII actions never ride on the card alone.

---

## Why this is worth trying

1. The second agent does not re-discover the same dead end.
2. The knowledge survives a model swap, a prompt rewrite, and an agent leaving.
3. Anonymous traffic stops being a knowledge leak: we remember what was learned, not who asked.

This is not a universal brain. It is a shift-handover note inside one line of support.

---

## What we already know vs what this pack must measure

Already measured on ABCD (see #6 / BON-41), used here as a constraint, not as a dependency:

- Matching on customer wording, inside one vertical, can hit the frozen false-friend bar without embeddings.
- A five-field card compresses a chat ~4× with the current schema, not 10×.
- A clean win/loss label is missing on most real chats, so promotion cannot wait on “outcome”.

Still unproven — this pack exists so we can get numbers:

- Does the card keep enough of the chat to be useful?
- Does showing the packet change what the next agent does?
- Does a naïve “seen twice → publish” rule promote junk?

---

## Scope of Hypothesis 1

In:

- extract a card from a finished dialogue (LLM prompt, frozen schema)
- store it `private` by default
- match later dialogues with a cheap lexical key, same scope only
- promote to `shared` after K independent confirmations (default K=2)
- serve as evidence, with a frozen serve prompt
- expire on “wrong / stale” feedback or a hard age cap

Out:

- cross-vertical sharing
- source-reputation scores
- using the card as an instruction
- any existing repo service (Memory Bank, compiler, ranker, graph)

---

## Implementation contract

The spec lists the scripts. Code comes next, in the same isolated folder. Then we (or the lab) drop a pile of dialogues on it and report:

- cards extracted / rejected
- private vs shared split
- match precision on a held-out slice
- how often a served packet would have named the unlock that actually happened

That last number is the usefulness figure this hypothesis owes us.

## Definition of done for this issue

- [ ] Spec merged under `standalone/h1-experience-cards/`
- [ ] Scripts implemented against that spec (follow-up PR)
- [ ] A first fixture set of dialogues run through the pack
- [ ] A short numbers note: extract yield, promote yield, packet usefulness
